The inner subscripts match and "cancel," like conversion factors. Also $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$: if you see a car approaching you at 20 m/s, its driver sees you approaching at 20 m/s in the opposite direction. This is **[[relative velocity]]**, and it is just vector addition.

The rule works because positions add: if A is at $\vec r_{AB}$ relative to B and B at $\vec r_{BC}$ relative to C, then $\vec r_{AC} = \vec r_{AB} + \vec r_{BC}$. Over a time interval the changes in position add the same way, and dividing each change by $\Delta t$ shows that the velocities add too. (Einstein showed this fails at speeds near light; see the relativity lesson.)

### Example 2: crossing a river

A river 80 m wide flows east at 1.2 m/s. A swimmer can swim at 2.0 m/s relative to the water. (a) If she heads straight across (north), how long does it take and how far downstream does she land? (b) Which way must she head to land directly opposite her start, and how long does that take?

Let S = swimmer, W = water, G = ground. $\vec v_{SG} = \vec v_{SW} + \vec v_{WG}$.

(a) $\vec v_{SW} = (0, 2.0)$, $\vec v_{WG} = (1.2, 0)$, so $\vec v_{SG} = (1.2, 2.0)$ m/s. Crossing time comes from the northward component alone: $t = 80/2.0 = 40$ s. Downstream drift: $1.2 \times 40 = 48$ m.

![A river 80 m wide flowing to the right at 1.2 m/s. From the start on the near bank, an arrow points straight across (swimmer relative to water, 2.0 m/s). From its tip, an arrow points downstream along the far bank (water relative to ground, 1.2 m/s). The diagonal from start to the landing point is the swimmer relative to ground, 2.3 m/s. A dimension above the far bank marks the drift of 48 m between the point directly opposite and the landing point.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Drawn to scale, each arrow is the velocity times the 40 s crossing time, so the velocity triangle and the map of the crossing are the same triangle.

(b) To land opposite, $\vec v_{SG}$ must point due north, so the east component of $\vec v_{SW}$ must cancel the current: $2.0\sin\alpha = 1.2$, giving $\alpha = 36.9^\circ$ west of north (upstream). Her northward speed is then $2.0\cos 36.9^\circ = 1.6$ m/s, and the crossing takes $80/1.6 = 50$ s.

```shape
{"x": [-2.7, 2.0], "y": [-0.2, 1.95], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [-1.2, 1.6], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-1.2, 1.6], "to": [0, 1.6], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [0, 1.6], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [-1.55, 0.7], "text": "swimmer/water 2.0 m/s"}, {"at": [-0.6, 1.75], "text": "water/ground 1.2 m/s"}, {"at": [1.08, 0.8], "text": "swimmer/ground 1.6 m/s"}], "caption": "Heading upstream so the resultant points straight across"}
```

Every relative-velocity problem follows the same steps:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Solving a relative-velocity problem
  accDescr: Name the objects and frames with letters, such as swimmer, water and ground. Write the velocity you want as a sum whose inner subscripts match, for example v of swimmer relative to ground equals v of swimmer relative to water plus v of water relative to ground. Sketch the vector triangle. Write the condition the problem gives, such as the resultant pointing straight across. Solve with components or right-triangle trigonometry. Finally use only the component along the direction of travel to find times.
  N["Name objects and frames: S, W, G"] --> E["Write v(S rel G) = v(S rel W) + v(W rel G)"]
  E --> D["Sketch the vector triangle"]
  D --> C["Apply the condition, e.g. resultant points straight across"]
  C --> S["Solve with components or right-triangle trig"]
  S --> T["Time = distance ÷ the velocity component along that distance"]
```

Heading straight across is the fastest way over; heading upstream is the way to land opposite. These are different goals with different answers, and the swimmer can land opposite only if her speed relative to the water exceeds the current's.

### Example 3: airplane in a crosswind

A plane flies with airspeed 220 km/h and must travel due north. A wind blows from west to east at 50 km/h. Find the heading and the ground speed.

$\vec v_{PG} = \vec v_{PA} + \vec v_{AG}$, with $\vec v_{AG} = (50, 0)$. For $\vec v_{PG}$ to point north, $220\sin\alpha = 50$, so $\alpha = 13.1^\circ$ west of north. Ground speed: $220\cos 13.1^\circ = \sqrt{220^2 - 50^2} = 214$ km/h.

## Moving frames agree on acceleration

Suppose frame B moves at constant velocity relative to frame C. Then $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$ at every moment, with $\vec v_{BC}$ never changing. Over any time interval, the change in $\vec v_{AC}$ therefore equals the change in $\vec v_{AB}$: the constant term contributes nothing to $\Delta\vec v$. Dividing by $\Delta t$, both observers measure the same acceleration. Observers moving uniformly relative to each other disagree about velocities but agree about accelerations, and so about forces; that is why Newton's laws hold equally in all such **[[inertial frames]]**.

### Example 4

A train moves east at a steady 20 m/s. A passenger tosses a ball straight up at 4.9 m/s relative to the train and catches it at the same height. Describe the ball's motion as seen by the passenger and by someone on the ground. ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)

Passenger's frame: the ball goes straight up and down. Its time in the air is $2(4.9)/9.8 = 1.0$ s, and it lands back in her hand.

Ground frame: the ball starts with velocity $\vec v_{\text{ball,G}} = \vec v_{\text{ball,T}} + \vec v_{\text{T,G}} = (20, 4.9)$ m/s. It is a projectile: it moves $20 \times 1.0 = 20$ m east during the flight, along a parabola. The hand also moves 20 m east in that second, so the catch works in this frame too.

Both observers measure the same acceleration, 9.8 m/s² downward, and the same flight time. Only the velocities and the shape of the path differ.

![Two panels. Left, the passenger's frame: a ball goes straight up from a hand and straight back down into it. Right, the ground frame: the ball follows a parabola from the hand's starting position to the hand's position 20 m farther along, with a starting velocity of (20, 4.9) m/s. The height of the path is exaggerated: the real ball rises only about 1.2 m.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- Thinking constant speed means zero acceleration (direction changes count).
- Adding relative velocities as magnitudes instead of vectors.
- Getting the subscript order wrong ($\vec v_{AB}$ vs $\vec v_{BA}$ differ by a sign).
- Using the swimmer's speed relative to water for the crossing time when she heads upstream; only the component across the river counts.

## Key points

- $\vec v_{\text{avg}} = \Delta\vec r/\Delta t$, $\vec a_{\text{avg}} = \Delta\vec v/\Delta t$, computed by components.
- Acceleration includes changes of direction; tangential changes speed, radial changes direction.
- Relative velocity: $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$ and $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$.
- Observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other measure different velocities but the same acceleration.

lessons.title: Two moving objects: chases, meetings and stopping distances
lessons.body:
## One clock, two objects

The constant-acceleration lesson followed one object at a time. Many real questions involve two: a police car chasing a speeder, a car closing on a slower truck, two trains on the same track. The physics is no harder (each object still obeys $x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$), but the bookkeeping is, and most mistakes in these problems are bookkeeping mistakes. This lesson gives a method that works every time, a second method borrowed from the relative-motion lesson that is often faster, and then applies both to a question every driver faces: how much room do you need to stop?

## Writing both motions on one set of axes

The rule is simple: *one origin, one positive direction, one clock*, shared by both objects. Write each object's position as a function of that common time $t$. Two objects are side by side when their positions are equal, so a **[[meeting time]]** is a solution of

$$x_A(t) = x_B(t).$$

Head starts go into $x_0$; a late start goes into the time (an object that starts moving at $t = 2$ s has positions in terms of $t - 2$, or you can restart the clock at that moment and give the other object its head start). Because the positions are usually quadratic in $t$, the meeting condition is usually a quadratic equation, and its two roots need interpreting: a root that falls before an object started, or after an assumption stopped holding, is not a real meeting.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Solving a chase or meeting problem
  accDescr: Choose one origin, one positive direction and one clock for both objects. Write each object's position as a function of time, with any head start or delayed start built in. Set the two positions equal and solve for t, which is often a quadratic. Keep only a root that falls in the time when both equations are valid. Then check the assumptions, such as a top speed or a phase change, and if one fails, split the motion into phases and repeat.
  O["One origin, one + direction, one clock"] --> W["Write each object's position as a function of t, with head starts and delays"]
  W --> S["Set the two positions equal and solve for t"]
  S --> R["Keep the root where both equations are valid"]
  R --> C{"Assumptions hold? (top speed, phases)"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["Find the meeting place and speeds"]
  C -- "no" --> P["Split into phases and repeat"]
  P --> W
```

### Example 1

A car speeding at a steady 25 m/s passes a parked police car. At that instant the police car starts from rest with a constant acceleration of 2.5 m/s². When and where does it catch the speeder, and how fast is it going then?

Origin at the police car, $+x$ along the road, $t = 0$ as the speeder passes:

$$x_S = 25t, \qquad x_P = \tfrac12(2.5)t^2 = 1.25t^2.$$

Setting them equal: $1.25t^2 = 25t$, so $t(1.25t - 25) = 0$. The root $t = 0$ is the passing moment itself; the catch is at $t = 25/1.25 = 20$ s. Position: $x = 25(20) = 500$ m. The police car's speed: $v = 2.5(20) = 50$ m/s.

That 50 m/s is exactly twice the speeder's speed, and it is no accident. Both cars covered the same distance in the same time, so their *average* velocities were equal. The police car's average velocity, for constant acceleration from rest, is half its final velocity, so its final velocity must be $2 \times 25$ m/s. The $v$–$t$ graph shows the same thing: the areas under the two lines are equal at the catch.

```plot
{"x": [0, 24], "y": [0, 700], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "x (m)", "functions": [{"f": "25*x", "from": 0, "to": 24}, {"f": "1.25*x^2", "from": 0, "to": 22.5, "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [20, 500]}], "labels": [{"at": [7, 560], "text": "catch (dot): 20 s, 500 m"}, {"at": [12.5, 390], "text": "speeder"}, {"at": [18.5, 190], "text": "police (dashed)"}], "caption": "Positions of the two cars: they meet where the line and the parabola cross"}
```

```plot
{"x": [0, 24], "y": [0, 60], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "v (m/s)", "functions": [{"f": "25", "from": 0, "to": 23, "label": "speeder"}, {"f": "2.5*x", "from": 0, "to": 22, "label": "police", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [10, 25]}], "labels": [{"at": [6.5, 35], "text": "dot: equal speeds, largest gap"}], "caption": "Velocities: at 20 s the triangle under the police line has the same area as the rectangle under the speeder's"}
```

The second graph also answers a question students often get wrong: when is the speeder farthest ahead? Not at the start, and not at the catch, but at $t = 10$ s, when the two speeds are equal. Before that the speeder is faster and the gap grows; after it the police car is faster and the gap shrinks. (Gap at 10 s: $250 - 125 = 125$ m.)

### Example 2

Now make it more realistic. The police car starts 2.0 s after the speeder passes, accelerates at 2.5 m/s², but only until it reaches its pursuit speed of 35 m/s, which it then holds. When and where does it catch the 25 m/s speeder?

Restart the clock when the police car starts. The speeder then has a head start of $25 \times 2.0 = 50$ m.

First test the simple model. With no speed limit, $1.25t^2 = 50 + 25t$ gives $t = 21.8$ s, at which moment the police car would be doing $2.5 \times 21.8 = 54.6$ m/s. That breaks the 35 m/s assumption, so this root is not the answer, and the motion must be split into phases.

Phase 1 (accelerating): it reaches 35 m/s at $t_1 = 35/2.5 = 14.0$ s, having gone $\tfrac12(2.5)(14.0)^2 = 245$ m. The speeder is then at $50 + 25(14.0) = 400$ m, still 155 m ahead, so there was no catch during phase 1.

Phase 2 (both at constant speed): the gap of 155 m closes at $35 - 25 = 10$ m/s, taking 15.5 s. The catch is at $t = 14.0 + 15.5 = 29.5$ s after the police car starts, at $245 + 35(15.5) = 787.5 \approx 788$ m from the start. Check with the speeder: $50 + 25(29.5) = 787.5$ m. They agree.

## The relative-frame shortcut

When one object moves at constant velocity, ride along with it. In its frame, the other object's velocity is the difference of the two velocities, and (because frames moving at constant velocity agree on acceleration) its acceleration is unchanged. A two-object problem becomes a one-object problem.

### Example 3

A car traveling at 30 m/s comes up behind a truck doing a steady 12 m/s in the same lane. When the gap is 40 m, the driver brakes at 5.0 m/s². (a) Does the car hit the truck? (b) Repeat if the driver needs a **[[reaction time]]** of 0.50 s before braking begins.

In the truck's frame, the truck is parked and the car approaches at $30 - 12 = 18$ m/s, slowing at 5.0 m/s². The car avoids a collision if it stops (relative to the truck) within the gap. Its relative stopping distance is

$$\frac{18^2}{2(5.0)} = 32.4 \text{ m}.$$

(a) $32.4 < 40$ m: no collision. The closest approach is $40 - 32.4 = 7.6$ m, reached when the car's speed has dropped to the truck's 12 m/s. (In the ground frame the car travels much farther than 32.4 m; the truck keeps moving away the whole time.)

(b) During the reaction time the car closes the gap at 18 m/s without braking: $18 \times 0.50 = 9.0$ m. Only 31.0 m remain, less than the 32.4 m needed, so the car hits the truck. Solving $31.0 = 18t - 2.5t^2$ gives $t = 2.85$ s after braking starts, when the relative speed is still $18 - 5.0(2.85) = 3.7$ m/s (about 13 km/h). To avoid it the driver would need $a = 18^2/(2 \times 31.0) = 5.2$ m/s².

Half a second of inattention turned a 7.6 m margin into a collision. That is the arithmetic behind "don't tailgate".

## Stopping distance

A driver who sees a hazard does nothing useful for the reaction time $t_r$ (seeing, deciding, moving a foot to the brake), so the car keeps going at its original speed. Then it brakes. The **[[stopping distance]]** is the sum of the two parts:

$$d = \underbrace{v t_r}_{\text{reaction distance}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2a}}_{\text{braking distance}}.$$

The **[[reaction distance]]** grows in proportion to speed; the **[[braking distance]]** grows with the square of speed. At low speed reaction dominates; at highway speed braking does. The table uses $t_r = 1.5$ s and $a = 7.0$ m/s², a typical value for a hard stop on dry pavement (both numbers vary a lot between drivers, cars, tires and roads; they are illustrative, not standards).

| Speed (km/h) | Speed (m/s) | Reaction distance (m) | Braking distance (m) | Stopping distance (m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 8.3 | 12.5 | 5.0 | 17.5 |
| 50 | 13.9 | 20.8 | 13.8 | 34.6 |
| 70 | 19.4 | 29.2 | 27.0 | 56.2 |
| 90 | 25.0 | 37.5 | 44.6 | 82.1 |
| 110 | 30.6 | 45.8 | 66.7 | 112.5 |

```plot
{"x": [0, 120], "y": [0, 130], "xLabel": "speed (km/h)", "yLabel": "distance (m)", "functions": [{"f": "(x/3.6)*1.5", "from": 0, "to": 115, "label": "reaction", "dashed": true}, {"f": "(x/3.6)*1.5 + (x/3.6)^2/14", "from": 0, "to": 115, "label": "stopping"}], "caption": "Stopping distance (solid) and its reaction part (dashed) for a 1.5 s reaction time and 7.0 m/s² braking; the gap between them is the braking distance"}
```

Going from 50 to 70 km/h, 40% faster, raises the stopping distance by about 62%. US highway designers, wanting a margin for nearly every driver, assume a generous 2.5 s reaction time and a gentle 3.4 m/s² deceleration when they work out how far ahead a driver must be able to see.

## The yellow-light dilemma

A light turns yellow as you approach. You can stop if your stopping distance fits before the stop line. In the simple model used here, you can go if, at constant speed, you clear the far side of the intersection before the light turns red. There may be a stretch of road where you can do neither: the **[[dilemma zone]]**, analyzed by Gazis, Herman and Maradudin in 1960.

### Example 4

A car approaches at 15 m/s (54 km/h). The driver's reaction time is 1.0 s and the car brakes at 5.0 m/s². The yellow lasts 3.0 s and the intersection is 15 m wide. Ignore the car's length.

Stopping needs $15(1.0) + \dfrac{15^2}{2(5.0)} = 15 + 22.5 = 37.5$ m, so the driver can stop only if the light changes at least 37.5 m before the line.

Going: in 3.0 s the car covers $15 \times 3.0 = 45$ m, which must include the 15 m of intersection, so the car clears only if the light changes within $45 - 15 = 30$ m of the line.

Between 30 m and 37.5 m from the line, the driver can do neither: that 7.5 m stretch is the dilemma zone.

![A road leading to a stop line and an intersection 15 m wide, for a car at 15 m/s and a 3.0 s yellow. Far from the line, a shaded stretch is labeled can stop, can't clear. Between 37.5 m and 30 m from the line is a short stretch labeled dilemma zone. From 30 m up to the line, a stretch is labeled can clear, can't stop. Dimensions below the road show the stopping distance of 37.5 m and the farthest point that clears, 30 m.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The zone disappears if the yellow is long enough that $v t_y - W \ge v t_r + v^2/(2a)$; here that needs $t_y \ge 3.5$ s. Real signal timing uses the same physics, split in two: a yellow long enough to stop comfortably or reach the line (engineers use about 1 s of reaction and a comfortable 3 m/s², not an emergency stop), then a short all-red interval during which cars already in the intersection clear it. Rules about entering on yellow differ between places, so treat this example as a model of the physics, not of any traffic law.

## Common mistakes

- Using a different origin or clock for each object, so the "meeting" equation compares positions measured from different places.
- Forgetting the head start (or the delay) when one object starts later.
- Accepting a root without checking it: a negative time, or a time when an assumption such as a top speed has already failed.
- Thinking the gap is largest at the start; it is largest when the speeds are equal.
- In the moving frame, using the absolute speed instead of the difference of speeds.
- Leaving out the reaction distance, which is the larger part of stopping distance at town speeds.

## Key points

- Give both objects one origin, one positive direction and one clock; they meet where $x_A(t) = x_B(t)$.
- Check each root against the assumptions; if one fails, split the motion into phases.
- A chaser starting from rest at constant acceleration catches a constant-speed object when its speed is twice that object's speed.
- If one object moves at constant velocity, its frame turns the chase into a one-object problem with the relative velocity and the same acceleration.
- Stopping distance $= vt_r + v^2/(2a)$: reaction distance grows with $v$, braking distance with $v^2$.
- A dilemma zone exists when the yellow is too short for the distance a car can neither stop in nor clear.

lessons.title: Aiming a projectile: targets, slopes and the best angle
lessons.body:
## Turning the question around

The projectile lesson asked: given the launch, where does it land? Archers, basketball players, firefighters and artillery crews face the reverse question: given a target, how should I launch? With the launch speed fixed (a hose, a cannon, a strong but limited arm), the only choice is the angle, and that turns out to be a quadratic problem with zero, one or two answers. The same algebra shows how far *any* shot can possibly reach, why a shot from a height should go out lower than $45^\circ$, and how to handle a launch up or down a hill. As in the core lesson, air resistance is ignored throughout, $g = 9.8$ m/s², and $y$ is measured up from the launch point.

## The angle to hit a target

Eliminating $t$ from $x = v_0\cos\theta\,t$ and $y = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12gt^2$ gave the path

$$y = x\tan\theta - \frac{g x^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}.$$

The trick is the identity $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} = 1 + \tan^2\theta$, which leaves only one trig function. Write $u = \tan\theta$ and $A = \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$ (a positive number once the target is known):

$$y = xu - A(1 + u^2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A u^2 - x u + (y + A) = 0.$$

This is a quadratic in $u$. Its discriminant $x^2 - 4A(y + A)$ decides everything:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Can a target be hit at a given launch speed?
  accDescr: Write the trajectory with u equal to tan theta, which gives a quadratic A u squared minus x u plus y plus A equals zero, where A equals g x squared over 2 v0 squared. Compute the discriminant. If it is positive, two launch angles hit the target, a low direct shot and a high lob. If it is zero, the target lies on the safety parabola and exactly one angle reaches it. If it is negative, the target is out of reach at this speed.
  T["Put u = tan θ: A u² − x u + (y + A) = 0, with A = g x² / (2 v0²)"] --> D{"Discriminant x² − 4A(y + A)"}
  D -- "positive" --> TWO["Two angles: a low direct shot and a high lob"]
  D -- "zero" --> ONE["One angle: target on the safety parabola"]
  D -- "negative" --> NONE["Out of reach at this speed"]
```

The two-angle case is familiar from level ground, where complementary angles give the same range. The low shot arrives sooner and flatter; the **[[lob]]** stays up longer and comes down steeply, which is why a basketball shot or a mortar uses the high one.

### Example 1

A ball can be thrown at 20 m/s. At what angles must it be thrown to land on a ledge 30 m away and 5.0 m above the launch point?

$A = \dfrac{9.8(30)^2}{2(20)^2} = \dfrac{8820}{800} = 11.025$ m. The quadratic is

$$11.025u^2 - 30u + 16.025 = 0.$$

Discriminant: $30^2 - 4(11.025)(16.025) = 900 - 706.7 = 193.3 > 0$, so two angles work:

$$u = \frac{30 \pm \sqrt{193.3}}{2(11.025)} = \frac{30 \pm 13.90}{22.05}, \qquad u = 0.730 \text{ or } 1.991.$$

So $\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.730) = 36.1^\circ$ or $\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.991) = 63.3^\circ$. The flight times, $t = x/(v_0\cos\theta)$, are 1.86 s and 3.34 s. Check the low shot: $30(0.730) - 11.025(1 + 0.730^2) = 21.90 - 16.90 = 5.0$ m. It works.

## The safety parabola: everything within reach

Which targets can be hit at all? Those where the discriminant is not negative: $x^2 \ge 4A(y + A)$. Dividing by $4A$ and putting $A$ back in,

$$y \le \frac{v_0^2}{2g} - \frac{g x^2}{2v_0^2}.$$

The boundary curve is itself a downward parabola, called the **[[safety parabola]]** (or envelope): every trajectory at speed $v_0$ touches it at exactly one point and never crosses it. Points under it can be hit at two angles, points on it at one, points above it not at all. Two checks: at $x = 0$ it gives the height of a straight-up throw, $v_0^2/(2g)$; at $y = 0$ it gives $x = v_0^2/g$, the level-ground range at $45^\circ$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 44], "y": [0, 23], "equal": true, "xLabel": "x (m)", "yLabel": "y (m)", "functions": [{"f": "20.408 - 0.01225*x^2", "from": 0, "to": 40.82, "dashed": true}, {"f": "x*tand(30) - 9.8*x^2/(800*cosd(30)^2)", "from": 0, "to": 35.35}, {"f": "x - 9.8*x^2/400", "from": 0, "to": 40.82}, {"f": "x*tand(60) - 9.8*x^2/(800*cosd(60)^2)", "from": 0, "to": 35.35}, {"f": "x*tand(75) - 9.8*x^2/(800*cosd(75)^2)", "from": 0, "to": 20.41}], "points": [{"at": [30, 5]}], "labels": [{"at": [34, 17], "text": "safety parabola (dashed)"}, {"at": [25.6, 5.6], "text": "target →"}], "caption": "Paths at 20 m/s for 30°, 45°, 60° and 75°: each touches the dashed safety parabola once; the ledge target of Example 1 lies inside it"}
```

On a double root the quadratic gives $u = \dfrac{x}{2A} = \dfrac{v_0^2}{gx}$, so the one angle that reaches a boundary point has $\tan\theta = v_0^2/(gx)$.

### Example 2

From the top of a cliff 20 m high, a stone is thrown at 20 m/s. What is the farthest it can land from the base, and at what angle should it be thrown? Compare with a $45^\circ$ throw.

The landing point is at $y = -20$ m. The farthest landing point is on the safety parabola:

$$-20 = \frac{20^2}{2(9.8)} - \frac{9.8x^2}{2(20)^2} \;\Rightarrow\; 0.01225x^2 = 20.41 + 20 = 40.41 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 57.4 \text{ m}.$$

The angle: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v_0^2}{gx} = \dfrac{400}{9.8(57.4)} = 0.711$, so $\theta = 35.4^\circ$.

At $45^\circ$: $v_{0x} = v_{0y} = 14.14$ m/s, and $-20 = 14.14t - 4.9t^2$ gives $t = 3.93$ s, so $x = 55.5$ m, about 2 m shorter. In general the best angle from a height $h$ satisfies $\tan\theta = v_0/\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$, always below $45^\circ$: the stone has extra time to fall, so it pays to trade height for horizontal speed. This is one reason shot-putters, who release about 2 m up, throw well below $45^\circ$ (another is that people can throw faster at lower angles).

## Launching on a slope

Suppose the ground itself slopes up at angle $\alpha$, so it is the line $y = x\tan\alpha$, and the projectile is launched from a point on it at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal.

![A slope rising at angle alpha from the launch point. A launch velocity arrow v0 makes angle theta with the horizontal dashed line, so it makes angle theta minus alpha with the slope. A dashed parabola lands farther up the slope. A dimension parallel to the slope, labeled d (along the slope), runs from launch to landing, and a horizontal dimension below, labeled x (horizontal), runs to directly below the landing point.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Landing means the path meets the slope: $x\tan\alpha = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}$. Dividing by $x$ (the root $x = 0$ is the launch):

$$x = \frac{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta\,(\tan\theta - \tan\alpha)}{g}, \qquad d = \frac{x}{\cos\alpha}.$$

With the sum and product formulas from trigonometry this simplifies to $d = \dfrac{v_0^2\,[\sin(2\theta - \alpha) - \sin\alpha]}{g\cos^2\alpha}$. Only $\sin(2\theta - \alpha)$ depends on the launch angle, and it is largest when $2\theta - \alpha = 90^\circ$:

$$\theta_{\text{best}} = 45^\circ + \frac{\alpha}{2}, \qquad d_{\max} = \frac{v_0^2}{g(1 + \sin\alpha)}.$$

The best direction bisects the angle between the slope and the vertical. For a level slope ($\alpha = 0$) everything reduces to the familiar $45^\circ$ and $v_0^2/g$. For a downhill slope put in a negative $\alpha$: the best angle drops below $45^\circ$ and the reach grows.

### Example 3

A ball is thrown at 15 m/s, $50^\circ$ above the horizontal, up a hill that slopes at $20^\circ$. How far up the slope does it land, and how far could it go at the best angle?

$x = \dfrac{2(15)^2\cos^2 50^\circ(\tan 50^\circ - \tan 20^\circ)}{9.8} = \dfrac{450(0.4132)(1.1918 - 0.3640)}{9.8} = 15.7$ m, so $d = 15.7/\cos 20^\circ = 16.7$ m along the slope. Check: the flight time is $15.7/(15\cos 50^\circ) = 1.63$ s, and the height then is $11.49(1.63) - 4.9(1.63)^2 = 5.72$ m, which equals $15.7\tan 20^\circ = 5.72$ m. It is on the slope.

Best angle: $45^\circ + 10^\circ = 55^\circ$, giving $d_{\max} = \dfrac{225}{9.8(1 + \sin 20^\circ)} = \dfrac{225}{13.15} = 17.1$ m. The $50^\circ$ throw was close to the best.

## Aim straight at a falling target

A classic demonstration, often called the monkey and the hunter: a launcher is aimed straight at a target hanging some distance away, and the target is released at the instant of firing. Without gravity the projectile would fly along the line of sight and hit the target where it hung. With gravity, both the projectile and the target fall $\tfrac12gt^2$ below where they would otherwise be, at every instant. So when the projectile reaches the target's horizontal position, both have dropped the same distance: it hits, whatever the launch speed, as long as it gets there before the target reaches the ground.

### Example 4

A dart is aimed straight at a target 20 m away horizontally and 10 m up, and fired at 25 m/s as the target is dropped. Where do they meet?

The aim angle has $\tan\theta = 10/20$, so $\theta = 26.6^\circ$ and $v_{0x} = 25\cos 26.6^\circ = 22.4$ m/s. The dart reaches $x = 20$ m at $t = 20/22.4 = 0.894$ s. Both have fallen $\tfrac12(9.8)(0.894)^2 = 3.92$ m, so they meet $10 - 3.92 = 6.08$ m above the ground. (A launch slower than about 15.7 m/s would fail: the target would hit the ground first.)

![A launcher on the ground aimed along a dashed line of sight at a target M 20 m away and 10 m up. The dart's curved path falls below the line of sight. The target, released at the instant of firing, falls straight down; a dimension shows both fall one half g t squared, 3.9 m, and they meet below the target's starting point.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- Solving for $\theta$ with only $\sin\theta$ or only $\cos\theta$ and getting stuck; use $1/\cos^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ to get a quadratic in $\tan\theta$.
- Keeping one root of the quadratic and forgetting the lob, or reporting two angles when the discriminant is negative.
- Using $45^\circ$ for the best angle from a cliff or on a slope; it is best only when launch and landing heights match.
- On a slope, measuring the launch angle from the slope in one formula and from the horizontal in another.
- Thinking that aiming at a falling target needs a correction for gravity; the projectile and the target fall together.

## Key points

- To hit $(x, y)$ at speed $v_0$: $A\tan^2\theta - x\tan\theta + (y + A) = 0$ with $A = gx^2/(2v_0^2)$; two, one or no angles.
- Reachable points lie under the safety parabola $y = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2g} - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$.
- From a height, the best angle is below $45^\circ$: $\tan\theta = v_0/\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$.
- On a slope of angle $\alpha$: best launch $45^\circ + \alpha/2$ from the horizontal, $d_{\max} = v_0^2/[g(1 + \sin\alpha)]$.
- A projectile aimed straight at a target released at the instant of firing hits it, if it arrives before the target lands.

lessons.title: How we know: Galileo, falling bodies and measuring g
lessons.body:
## A claim worth checking

The constant-acceleration lesson stated, as a fact, that every object falling freely near Earth speeds up at the same steady 9.8 m/s², whatever its mass. That fact is neither obvious nor old. For about two thousand years the standard teaching was different, and the evidence that overturned it had to be built with clever experiments, because a dropped stone hits the ground in well under a second and nobody had a clock that could time it. This lesson follows that evidence, and shows how you can test the same law today with a ruler, a stopwatch app and a graph.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How the law of falling bodies was established
  accDescr: About 350 BC, Aristotle taught that heavier bodies fall faster. In 1586 Simon Stevin and Jan de Groot dropped two lead balls, one about ten times heavier than the other, about 30 feet in Delft and heard them land together. In 1638 Galileo published Two New Sciences, with the times-squared law and the odd-number rule from inclined-plane experiments. In 1687 Newton's Principia explained the constant acceleration with his laws of motion and gravitation. In 1971 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon during Apollo 15, and they landed together.
  A["About 350 BC: Aristotle teaches that heavier bodies fall faster"] --> B["1586: Stevin and de Groot drop two lead balls in Delft; they land together"]
  B --> C["1638: Galileo's Two New Sciences: distance grows as time squared"]
  C --> D["1687: Newton's Principia explains why the acceleration is constant"]
  D --> E["1971: Apollo 15 hammer and feather fall together on the Moon"]
```

## The old view and the first doubts

Aristotle taught, roughly, that a heavy body falls faster than a light one, in proportion to its weight, and that a falling body moves at a speed set by its weight and the medium it falls through. (This is a simplified summary of a subtle philosophy, but it is the part later scientists argued with.) Everyday experience seems to agree: a stone does beat a leaf.

Galileo attacked the idea with a thought experiment. Tie a heavy stone to a light one. If light things fall slower, the light stone should hold the heavy one back, so the pair falls slower than the heavy stone alone. But the pair is heavier than the heavy stone, so it should fall faster. Both conclusions can't be right, so the premise is wrong. The leaf loses to the stone because of air, not weight.

Experiments agreed. In 1586 the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin reported that he and Jan Cornets de Groot dropped two lead balls, one about ten times heavier than the other, about 30 feet from a church tower in Delft, and heard them hit a board below at the same moment. The more famous story of Galileo dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa comes from his student and biographer Vincenzo Viviani, written long afterward; historians doubt it happened as told. In 1971, on the airless Moon, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together on live television, and they landed together.

## Slowing gravity down: the inclined plane

Showing that objects fall *together* is easier than showing *how* they fall. Galileo's answer, described in his *Two New Sciences* (1638), was to "dilute" gravity: let a ball roll down a long, gently sloping, smooth groove. The motion is the same kind as free fall, only slower, so it can be timed. He timed it with a water clock, weighing the water that flowed out of a container while the ball rolled.

His result: starting from rest, the distance covered is proportional to the *square* of the time. In 2 time units the ball goes 4 times as far as in 1, in 3 units 9 times as far. Equivalently, the distances covered in successive equal intervals go as the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, …, a pattern called the **[[odd-number rule]]**.

![A ball released from rest at the top of an incline, shown at equal time intervals tau. The total distances from the start grow as 1, 4, 9 and 16 units, so the distances covered in the four successive intervals are 1, 3, 5 and 7 units.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Why constant acceleration gives the odd-number rule

From rest with constant acceleration $a$, the distance after time $t$ is $\tfrac12at^2$. Take equal intervals of length $\tau$. The distance covered during the $n$th interval is

$$d_n = \tfrac12a(n\tau)^2 - \tfrac12a\big((n - 1)\tau\big)^2 = \tfrac12a\tau^2\,(2n - 1).$$

So $d_1 : d_2 : d_3 : \dots = 1 : 3 : 5 : \dots$. The argument also runs backward: if the interval distances follow the odd numbers, the speed is gaining the same amount in every interval, which is what constant acceleration means. Checking the odd-number rule is therefore a test of constant acceleration that needs only equal time intervals and a ruler, with no need to know the size of the time unit.

### Example 1

A ball falls freely from rest. How far does it fall in each of the first four 0.10 s intervals? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)

$\tfrac12g\tau^2 = \tfrac12(9.8)(0.10)^2 = 0.049$ m $= 4.9$ cm. The intervals cover $4.9 \times 1, 3, 5, 7$: that is 4.9 cm, 14.7 cm, 24.5 cm and 34.3 cm, for a total of 78.4 cm $= 4.9 \times 16$ cm after 0.40 s.

### Example 2

In a Galileo-style experiment a ball rolls 0.30 m down a ramp in the first second after release. Predict the distance it covers in the second second, its total distance after 3.0 s, and its acceleration.

By the odd-number rule the second second covers $3 \times 0.30 = 0.90$ m. After 3 s the total is $3^2 \times 0.30 = 2.7$ m (check: $0.30 + 0.90 + 1.50 = 2.70$). From $0.30 = \tfrac12a(1.0)^2$, $a = 0.60$ m/s², far smaller than $g$, which is exactly why the ramp made timing possible.

Why is the acceleration on a ramp constant and smaller than $g$? The forces lesson (next module) shows that an object sliding without friction down an incline of angle $\theta$ has $a = g\sin\theta$. A rolling ball accelerates less again, because some of the effect of gravity goes into making it spin (for a solid ball, $a = \tfrac57 g\sin\theta$, as the rolling lesson shows), but the acceleration is still constant, so the times-squared law still holds. A ramp angle of a few degrees is enough to slow things down by a factor of ten or more.

## Measuring g today: make the graph a straight line

Modern labs drop an object through light gates (a **[[photogate]]** is a beam of light and a detector that records the instant something blocks the beam) or track it with a motion sensor or video. A good way to analyze the data is to arrange it so the theory predicts a straight line, a technique called linearizing.

The model $h = \tfrac12gt^2$ is not a line in $h$ against $t$. But plotted against $t^2$ it is: $h = \left(\tfrac12g\right)(t^2)$ has the form $y = mx$ with slope $m = \tfrac12g$. A straight line through the origin confirms the model, and the slope measures $g = 2m$. A best-fit line uses every data point, so random timing errors partly cancel.

### Example 3

A student drops a ball from rest through a photogate placed at five heights below the release point and records the fall times:

| $h$ (m) | 0.20 | 0.40 | 0.60 | 0.80 | 1.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $t$ (s) | 0.203 | 0.286 | 0.350 | 0.404 | 0.452 |
| $t^2$ (s²) | 0.0412 | 0.0818 | 0.1225 | 0.1632 | 0.2043 |

Find $g$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 0.23], "y": [0, 1.15], "xLabel": "t² (s²)", "yLabel": "h (m)", "functions": [{"f": "4.907*x - 0.0016", "from": 0, "to": 0.22, "label": "best fit"}], "points": [{"at": [0.0412, 0.2]}, {"at": [0.0818, 0.4]}, {"at": [0.1225, 0.6]}, {"at": [0.1632, 0.8]}, {"at": [0.2043, 1.0]}], "caption": "Height against time squared: a straight line through (nearly) the origin, slope 4.91 m/s²"}
```

The points lie on a straight line through (nearly) the origin, confirming $h \propto t^2$. Slope from the first and last points: $\dfrac{1.00 - 0.20}{0.2043 - 0.0412} = \dfrac{0.80}{0.1631} = 4.90$ m/s². A least-squares fit (calculator or spreadsheet) gives slope 4.91 m/s² and intercept $-0.002$ m, close to zero as the model predicts. So $g = 2 \times 4.91 = 9.81$ m/s². A clearly nonzero intercept would point to a systematic error, such as a gate that starts the timer a little late.

Note what the straight line tells you that a single drop cannot: one drop gives a value of $g$ by assuming the model, while five drops on a line *test* the model.

### Example 4: measuring your own reaction time

A friend holds a ruler vertically with its zero mark between your open fingers, then lets go without warning. You catch it after it has fallen 18 cm. What is your reaction time?

The ruler falls freely from rest, so $d = \tfrac12gt^2$ and $t = \sqrt{2d/g} = \sqrt{2(0.18)/9.8} = 0.19$ s. This simple test measures only the reaction to an expected event with your hand already in place; reaction times in traffic, where a driver must notice, decide and move a foot, are several times longer, which is why stopping-distance calculations use 1 s or more.

## How constant is g?

"Constant" means constant during a fall of a few meters. Over Earth's surface, the measured free-fall acceleration varies from about 9.78 m/s² at the equator to about 9.83 m/s² at the poles (because of Earth's spin and its slightly flattened shape), and it decreases slowly with altitude. For calculations and for defining units, scientists use a fixed **[[standard gravity]]**, $g_n = 9.80665$ m/s² exactly. The course's 9.8 m/s² is that value to two significant figures.

## Common mistakes

- Expecting equal distances in equal times; for constant acceleration from rest they grow as 1, 3, 5, 7.
- Applying the odd-number rule when the object does not start from rest at the first mark.
- Plotting $h$ against $t$ and trying to read $g$ from a curve; plot against $t^2$ and use the slope.
- Forgetting the factor of 2: the slope of $h$ against $t^2$ is $g/2$, not $g$.
- Thinking a ramp changes the kind of motion; it lowers the acceleration but keeps it constant.

## Key points

- Without air resistance, all bodies fall with the same constant acceleration; air explains why a leaf loses to a stone.
- Galileo slowed free fall on an inclined plane and found distance $\propto t^2$.
- From rest at constant acceleration, distances in successive equal intervals go as $1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : \dots$ (the odd-number rule), because $d_n = \tfrac12a\tau^2(2n - 1)$.
- Linearize to test a model: $h$ against $t^2$ is a straight line of slope $g/2$.
- A dropped ruler measures reaction time: $t = \sqrt{2d/g}$.
- $g$ ranges from about 9.78 to 9.83 m/s² over Earth's surface; standard gravity is 9.80665 m/s².

lessons.title: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams
lessons.body:
## From describing motion to explaining it

Kinematics told us how to describe motion. Dynamics asks why objects move the way they do, and Newton's three laws answer that for everything from falling apples to orbiting satellites. The central quantity is **[[force]]**: a push or pull exerted by one object on another, measured in newtons (N). Forces are vectors, so all the component methods from the vectors lesson come straight back.

## Newton's first law

An object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net force acts on it. This is **[[Newton's first law]]**, the law of **[[inertia]]**: the tendency of matter to keep its current velocity. A hockey puck sliding on ice slows only because of small friction forces; with none, it would glide forever.

The first law corrects an intuition many people hold: that motion needs a force to sustain it. It doesn't. A force is needed to *change* motion. The law also defines the frames we work in: it holds in inertial frames (non-accelerating ones). In an accelerating car, a coffee cup slides backward with no force pushing it; that's the car accelerating out from under it.

## Newton's second law

The **[[net force]]** $\vec F_{\text{net}} = \sum\vec F$ is the vector sum of all forces on an object. **[[Newton's second law]]** says

$$\sum \vec F = m\vec a.$$

The acceleration points the same way as the net force, and the **[[mass]]** $m$ measures how strongly the object resists acceleration. The same push gives a shopping cart a large acceleration and a car a tiny one. This is also where the newton comes from: 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

Because it is a vector equation, it is really one equation per axis:

$$\sum F_x = ma_x, \qquad \sum F_y = ma_y.$$

If the net force is zero, $\vec a = 0$, and the object is in **[[equilibrium]]** (at rest, or moving at constant velocity; both count).

## Weight and the normal force

The **[[weight]]** of an object is the gravitational force Earth exerts on it, $\vec W = m\vec g$, magnitude $mg$, pointing down. Mass is in kilograms and is the same everywhere; weight is a force in newtons and depends on the local $g$. A 70 kg astronaut weighs 686 N on Earth and about 113 N on the Moon, where $g = 1.62$ m/s², but her mass is 70 kg in both places.

When an object presses on a surface, the surface pushes back perpendicular to itself. This is the **[[normal force]]** $\vec n$ ("normal" means perpendicular). It is whatever size is needed to stop the object sinking into the surface, so don't assume $n = mg$; find it from Newton's second law in the perpendicular direction. A book on a flat table has $n = mg$, but push down on the book and $n$ grows; tilt the table and $n$ shrinks.

## Newton's third law

Forces come in pairs. If object A exerts a force on B, then B exerts a force on A of equal magnitude and opposite direction:

$$\vec F_{\text{A on B}} = -\vec F_{\text{B on A}}.$$

This is **[[Newton's third law]]**. The two forces of a pair act on *different* objects, so they never cancel each other in a single object's free-body diagram. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you equally. When Earth pulls a falling apple down with force $mg$, the apple pulls Earth up with force $mg$; Earth's enormous mass makes its acceleration immeasurably small.

The picture below pulls the objects apart so you can see each pair. Each arrow belongs to the object it starts on: two forces act on the book, and their partners act on the table and on Earth.

![An exploded view of a book above a table above Earth. On the book: an arrow down labeled Earth pulls book, and an arrow up labeled table pushes book up. On the table: an arrow down labeled book pushes table. On Earth: an arrow up labeled book pulls Earth.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A classic confusion: the weight of a book on a table and the normal force on the book are equal and opposite, but they are not a third-law pair. They act on the same object (the book), and they are different kinds of force. The third-law partner of the book's weight is the book's pull on Earth; the partner of the normal force is the book pushing down on the table.

## Free-body diagrams

A **[[free-body diagram]]** (FBD) isolates one object and shows every force acting *on* it, as arrows starting from the object. It is the single most important step in a dynamics problem. A reliable method:

1. Choose the object (or system) and draw it as a dot or simple box.
2. Draw its weight, $mg$ downward.
3. Go around the object's boundary: everything touching it can exert a force (normal force, friction, tension in an attached rope, an applied push).
4. Add any non-contact forces (electric, magnetic) if relevant.
5. Choose axes, ideally with one along the acceleration.
6. Write $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$, and solve.

Never put "$ma$" on the diagram as a force; it's the result of the forces, not one of them.

The whole method, from choosing the object to the answer, as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Solving a Newton's second law problem
  accDescr: Choose the object or system. Draw its free-body diagram with every force acting on it. Choose axes, one along the acceleration if it is known. Write the sum of forces equals m a separately for each axis. Solve the equations for the unknowns. Finally check the units and limiting cases.
  A["Choose the object or system"] --> B["Draw its free-body diagram"]
  B --> C["Choose axes, one along the acceleration"]
  C --> D["Write sum of F = ma for each axis"]
  D --> E["Solve for the unknowns"]
  E --> F["Check units and limiting cases"]
```

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[-0.5, -0.5], [0.5, -0.5], [0.5, 0.5], [-0.5, 0.5]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0.5], "to": [0, 2.2], "arrow": true, "label": "n"}, {"from": [0, -0.5], "to": [0, -2.2], "arrow": true, "label": "mg"}, {"from": [0.5, 0], "to": [2.4, 0], "arrow": true, "label": "F (applied)"}, {"from": [-0.5, 0], "to": [-1.4, 0], "arrow": true, "label": "f (friction)"}], "caption": "Free-body diagram of a box pushed across a floor"}
```

### Example 1

A 12 kg crate on a frictionless floor is pulled by a rope with tension 60 N directed $30^\circ$ above horizontal. Find the acceleration and the normal force.

Forces on the crate: weight $mg = 117.6$ N down, normal force $n$ up, tension 60 N at $30^\circ$.

$x$: $60\cos 30^\circ = 12a$, so $a = \dfrac{51.96}{12} = 4.33$ m/s².

$y$: the crate doesn't leave the floor, so $a_y = 0$: $n + 60\sin 30^\circ - 117.6 = 0$, giving $n = 117.6 - 30 = 87.6$ N. The upward pull of the rope reduces the normal force.

### Example 2: apparent weight in an elevator

A 60 kg person stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator. What does the scale read when the elevator (a) accelerates upward at 2.0 m/s², (b) moves up at constant speed, (c) accelerates downward at 2.0 m/s²?

The scale reads the normal force $n$ it exerts. Take up as positive: $n - mg = ma$, so $n = m(g + a)$.

(a) $n = 60(9.8 + 2.0) = 708$ N, heavier than her true weight of 588 N.

(b) $a = 0$, so $n = 588$ N. Constant velocity is equilibrium.

(c) $a = -2.0$: $n = 60(7.8) = 468$ N. If the cable snapped ($a = -g$), the scale would read zero: she would feel weightless, though gravity still acts on her fully. This **[[apparent weight]]** is what your body senses.

## Reasoning with proportions

Many questions about the second law need no numbers at all. Since $a = F_{\text{net}}/m$, acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass. Double the net force on the same object and the acceleration doubles; put the same net force on twice the mass and the acceleration halves.

### Example 3

A net force gives a cart an acceleration of 2.0 m/s². The net force is tripled and the cart is loaded so that its mass doubles. What is the new acceleration?

$a_{\text{new}} = \dfrac{3F}{2m} = \tfrac32\cdot\dfrac{F}{m} = 1.5 \times 2.0 = 3.0$ m/s². No individual values of $F$ or $m$ were needed, only the ratios.

## Systems of objects

When objects move together, you can apply the second law to the whole group or to any one member. For the whole group, forces the members exert on each other come in third-law pairs inside the system and cancel, so only outside forces count.

### Example 4

Boxes A (4.0 kg) and B (2.0 kg) sit side by side on a frictionless floor. A 30 N horizontal push on A moves both. Find their acceleration and the force A exerts on B.

Whole system (6.0 kg): the only horizontal outside force is the 30 N push, so $a = 30/6.0 = 5.0$ m/s².

Box B alone: the only horizontal force on it is the push from A, so $F_{\text{A on B}} = m_B a = 2.0(5.0) = 10$ N. By the third law B pushes back on A with 10 N, so the net force on A is $30 - 10 = 20$ N $= 4.0(5.0)$ ✓. The push from A on B is not 30 N: part of the 30 N goes into accelerating A itself.

Newton himself stated the second law in terms of momentum, $\vec F_{\text{net}} = \Delta\vec p/\Delta t$ with $\vec p = m\vec v$; for constant mass this is the same as $m\vec a$. You'll use that form in the momentum lesson.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking a moving object must have a net force in its direction of motion.
- Assuming $n = mg$ in every problem.
- Treating weight and normal force as a third-law pair.
- Drawing forces that the object exerts on others in its own free-body diagram.
- Including "$ma$" or "the force of motion" as a force.

## Key points

- First law: no net force, no change in velocity. Second law: $\sum\vec F = m\vec a$, one equation per axis. Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs on different objects.
- Weight $= mg$ downward; the normal force is perpendicular to the surface and found from the equations.
- Always draw a free-body diagram before writing equations.
- $a \propto F_{\text{net}}$ and $a \propto 1/m$: use ratios for "what if" questions.
- For objects moving together, internal forces cancel: $a = F_{\text{ext}}/m_{\text{total}}$.

lessons.title: Friction and inclined planes
lessons.body:
## Why things stop

Push a book across a table and it slows to a stop. The first law says something must be acting on it, and that something is **[[friction]]**: a force that surfaces in contact exert parallel to their surfaces, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide). This lesson adds friction to Newton's second law and then puts it to work on the inclined plane, the standard testing ground for free-body diagrams.

## Kinetic and static friction

Microscopically, even polished surfaces are rough, and contact points form temporary bonds. Two empirical rules describe the result well enough for most purposes.

**[[Kinetic friction]]** acts when surfaces slide over each other. Its magnitude is

$$f_k = \mu_k n,$$

where $n$ is the normal force and $\mu_k$ is the **[[coefficient of kinetic friction]]**, a dimensionless number depending on the pair of surfaces (rubber on dry concrete is about 0.7, steel on ice about 0.03). It points opposite to the sliding velocity, and to a good approximation it doesn't depend on speed or contact area.

**[[Static friction]]** acts when surfaces are not sliding but something is trying to make them. It adjusts to whatever value keeps the surfaces stuck, up to a maximum:

$$f_s \le \mu_s n.$$

The **[[coefficient of static friction]]** $\mu_s$ is usually larger than $\mu_k$, which is why it takes more force to start a heavy box moving than to keep it moving. The key subtlety: $f_s = \mu_s n$ only at the verge of slipping. A box that you're pushing with 20 N without moving it has 20 N of static friction, no matter how large $\mu_s n$ is.

A graph shows how the two kinds fit together. Push a resting box with a slowly growing force: static friction grows with your push, matching it exactly, until it reaches $\mu_s n$. Then the box breaks free and friction drops to the smaller, roughly constant $\mu_k n$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 100], "y": [0, 70], "xLabel": "applied force (N)", "yLabel": "friction force (N)", "functions": [{"f": "x", "from": 0, "to": 50, "label": "static: f = F"}, {"f": "35", "from": 50, "to": 100, "label": "kinetic: μk n"}], "segments": [{"from": [50, 50], "to": [50, 35], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [50, 50], "label": "μs n"}], "caption": "Friction on a box pushed with a growing force (here μs n = 50 N and μk n = 35 N): static friction matches the push up to μs n, then the box slides and friction drops to μk n"}
```

To decide which rule to use in a problem, follow this chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Static or kinetic friction
  accDescr: First ask whether the surfaces are sliding over each other. If yes, friction is kinetic, equal to mu k times n, opposite to the sliding. If not, find the friction force needed to keep them from sliding. If that needed force is no more than mu s times n, static friction equals the needed force. If it is more, the object starts to slide and friction becomes kinetic.
  A{"Are the surfaces sliding?"} -- yes --> K["Kinetic: f = μk·n, opposite the sliding"]
  A -- no --> B["Find the friction needed to prevent sliding"]
  B --> C{"Needed friction at most μs·n?"}
  C -- yes --> S["Static: f = the needed value"]
  C -- no --> K
```

Friction depends on $n$, not on the weight. Pull up on a sled rope and $n$ drops, and so does the friction.

### Example 1

A 25 kg box rests on a floor with $\mu_s = 0.50$ and $\mu_k = 0.35$. (a) What horizontal force is needed to start it moving? (b) If you keep pushing with that force once it slides, what is its acceleration?

Normal force: $n = mg = 25(9.8) = 245$ N (no vertical forces besides $n$ and $mg$).

(a) Maximum static friction: $\mu_s n = 0.50(245) = 122.5$ N. You need just over 122.5 N.

(b) Once sliding, friction drops to $f_k = 0.35(245) = 85.75$ N. Net force: $122.5 - 85.75 = 36.75$ N, so $a = 36.75/25 = 1.47$ m/s².

## The inclined plane

An object on a ramp tilted at angle $\theta$ is the classic problem where good axes matter. Tilt the axes: $x$ along the slope (down the slope positive is often convenient), $y$ perpendicular to it. Then the normal force and friction lie along the axes, and only the weight needs splitting.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [6, 0], [6, 3.464]]}, {"points": [[3.118, 1.8], [3.81, 2.2], [3.41, 2.893], [2.718, 2.493]]}], "segments": [{"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [3.264, 0.346], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [2.398, 3.846], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [4.303, 2.946], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [2.398, 1.846], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [4.13, 0.846], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [3.6, 0.6], "text": "mg"}, {"at": [2.2, 3.95], "text": "n"}, {"at": [4.55, 3.1], "text": "f"}, {"at": [1.65, 1.75], "text": "mg sin θ"}, {"at": [4.85, 0.75], "text": "mg cos θ"}, {"at": [1.2, 0.25], "text": "θ = 30°"}], "caption": "Block on a 30° incline: weight mg splits into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope (dashed); n balances mg cos θ and friction f points up the slope"}
```

The weight makes angle $\theta$ with the $-y$ axis (the same angle as the incline, because both pairs of lines are mutually perpendicular). The picture marks both angles: the vertical weight is turned from the into-the-slope direction by exactly the tilt of the ramp.

![A block on a ramp tilted at angle theta. From the block, the weight mg points straight down; dashed arrows show its components, mg sin theta down the slope and mg cos theta into the slope, and the angle between mg and the into-slope component is marked theta. The normal force n points out of the slope and friction f points up the slope.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

So:

- component down the slope: $mg\sin\theta$;
- component into the slope: $mg\cos\theta$.

Check the limits: at $\theta = 0$ (flat) the down-slope part vanishes; at $\theta = 90^\circ$ (vertical) it's all of $mg$. If you get them backwards, these limits will catch it.

Perpendicular to the slope there's no acceleration, so $n = mg\cos\theta$ (with no other perpendicular forces).

*Frictionless incline.* Along the slope: $mg\sin\theta = ma$, so $a = g\sin\theta$, independent of mass.

*With kinetic friction*, sliding down: $mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta = ma$, so

$$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta).$$

Sliding up (after a push), friction also points down the slope: $a = -g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$, a larger deceleration.

*On the verge of slipping* with static friction, $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so

$$\tan\theta_{\max} = \mu_s.$$

That gives a simple way to measure $\mu_s$: tilt a board until the object just starts to slide and take the tangent of the angle.

### Example 2

A 4.0 kg block slides down a $35^\circ$ ramp with $\mu_k = 0.25$. Find its acceleration and the friction force.

$n = mg\cos 35^\circ = 4.0(9.8)(0.8192) = 32.1$ N, so $f_k = 0.25(32.1) = 8.03$ N up the slope.

$a = g(\sin 35^\circ - 0.25\cos 35^\circ) = 9.8(0.5736 - 0.2048) = 3.61$ m/s² down the slope.

Check using forces: $mg\sin 35^\circ = 22.5$ N down the slope, minus 8.03 N friction, leaves 14.45 N; divided by 4.0 kg gives 3.61 m/s².

### Example 3

A skier on a $20^\circ$ slope with $\mu_s = 0.10$: will she slide from rest?

$\tan 20^\circ = 0.364 > 0.10$, so static friction can't hold her and she starts sliding. A slope gentle enough to stand still on would need $\theta \le \tan^{-1}(0.10) = 5.7^\circ$.

## Air resistance and terminal velocity

Friction between solid surfaces is roughly constant, but fluid resistance (drag) grows with speed. Follow a skydiver who steps out of a plane:

1. At first her speed is zero, so drag is zero: the net force is $mg$ and she accelerates at $g$.
2. As she speeds up, drag grows, the net force $mg - F_D$ shrinks, and her acceleration drops below $g$. She is still speeding up, just more slowly.
3. Eventually drag equals her weight. The net force is zero, so her acceleration is zero and her speed stays constant: this is the terminal velocity.

```plot
{"x": [0, 25], "y": [0, 60], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "v (m/s)", "functions": [{"f": "50*(1 - exp(-9.8*x/50))", "from": 0, "to": 25, "label": "v(t)"}, {"f": "50", "from": 0, "to": 25, "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [15, 54], "text": "terminal velocity"}], "caption": "Falling with air resistance: the v–t graph starts with slope g and levels off at the terminal velocity"}
```

On the $v$–$t$ graph the slope (acceleration) starts at $g$ and decreases to zero as the curve levels off. Setting drag equal to weight gives the terminal speed. For slow motion through a thick fluid, drag is roughly proportional to speed, $F_D = bv$, so $bv_T = mg$ and $v_T = mg/b$. For fast objects in air, drag is closer to $F_D = \tfrac12 C\rho Av^2$ ($C$ a shape factor near 1, $\rho$ the air density, $A$ the cross-sectional area), so

$$v_T = \sqrt{\frac{2mg}{C\rho A}}.$$

A heavier object with the same shape needs more drag to balance its weight, so it falls faster: this is why, in air, a bowling ball beats a beach ball of the same size.

### Example 4

An 80 kg skydiver falls belly-down with $C = 1.0$ and cross-sectional area $A = 0.70$ m², in air of density 1.2 kg/m³. (a) Find her terminal speed. (b) What is her acceleration when she is moving at half that speed?

(a) $v_T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(80)(9.8)}{(1.0)(1.2)(0.70)}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1568}{0.84}} = \sqrt{1867} = 43$ m/s.

(b) Drag grows as $v^2$, so at half the terminal speed it is $\left(\tfrac12\right)^2 = \tfrac14$ of its terminal value, which is her weight. Net force: $mg - \tfrac14mg = \tfrac34mg$, so $a = \tfrac34(9.8) = 7.4$ m/s² downward.

## Common mistakes

- Using $f_s = \mu_s n$ when the object isn't on the verge of slipping.
- Using $n = mg$ on an incline or when a force pulls at an angle.
- Swapping $\sin$ and $\cos$ in the weight components (check $\theta = 0$ and $90^\circ$).
- Pointing kinetic friction along the motion instead of against it.
- Thinking friction depends on contact area or speed (in this model it doesn't).

## Key points

- Kinetic: $f_k = \mu_k n$, opposite the sliding. Static: $f_s \le \mu_s n$, just enough to prevent sliding.
- On an incline: $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope, $mg\cos\theta$ into it; $n = mg\cos\theta$.
- Frictionless: $a = g\sin\theta$. Sliding down with friction: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.
- Verge of slipping: $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.
- Terminal velocity: drag equals weight, so the net force and acceleration are zero ($v_T = mg/b$ for drag $bv$).

lessons.title: Tension, pulleys, and connected objects
lessons.body:
## Objects that pull on each other

Real problems rarely involve one object. Trains pull carriages, cranes lift loads, elevators hang from cables. This lesson extends free-body diagrams to systems of connected objects, linked by ropes and pulleys, and introduces the force that travels along a rope.

## Tension

A rope or cable pulled taut exerts a pull, the **[[tension]]** $T$, on whatever is attached to each end. It always pulls (a rope can't push) and acts along the rope. In this course ropes are usually idealized:

- A **[[massless rope]]** has the same tension throughout. (Apply $F = ma$ to a small piece: with $m = 0$, the forces on its two ends must balance.)
- An **[[ideal pulley]]** (massless, frictionless) changes the direction of a rope without changing its tension.
- An inextensible rope makes the connected objects move together with the same speed and the same magnitude of acceleration.

Tension is not automatically equal to the weight hanging from the rope. It equals $mg$ only if the hanging object is in equilibrium.

### Example 1: a hanging sign

A 20 kg sign hangs from two cables, each making $40^\circ$ with the horizontal. Find the tension in each.

By symmetry both tensions are equal, $T$. Horizontal components cancel. Vertical: $2T\sin 40^\circ = mg = 196$ N, so $T = \dfrac{196}{2(0.6428)} = 152$ N.

Notice each cable carries more than half the weight. As the cables flatten toward horizontal, $\sin\theta \to 0$ and the tension grows without bound, which is why a clothesline can never be pulled perfectly straight with laundry on it.

## Strategy for connected objects

1. Draw a separate free-body diagram for each object.
2. Choose a positive direction for each object consistent with the motion of the system (if block A moves right when block B moves down, call right positive for A and down positive for B). Then all accelerations have the same sign and magnitude $a$.
3. Write $\sum F = ma$ along the motion for each object.
4. Solve the equations together for $a$ and the tensions.

A shortcut for finding $a$ alone: treat the whole chain as one system of total mass $M$. Tensions inside the system are internal forces that cancel in pairs, so only external forces drive it: $a = F_{\text{net, ext}}/M$.

## The Atwood machine

Two masses $m_1 > m_2$ hang on either side of an ideal pulley. Taking the direction in which $m_1$ falls as positive:

- $m_1$: $m_1 g - T = m_1 a$
- $m_2$: $T - m_2 g = m_2 a$

Adding eliminates $T$: $(m_1 - m_2)g = (m_1 + m_2)a$, so

$$a = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g, \qquad T = \frac{2m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g.$$

The tension lies between the two weights: smaller than $m_1g$ (so $m_1$ accelerates down) and larger than $m_2 g$ (so $m_2$ accelerates up). Checks: if $m_1 = m_2$, $a = 0$ and $T = mg$; if $m_2 = 0$, $a = g$ (free fall) and $T = 0$.

```shape
{"circles": [{"center": [0, 4], "r": 0.6}], "segments": [{"from": [-0.6, 4], "to": [-0.6, 1.5]}, {"from": [0.6, 4], "to": [0.6, 2.5]}, {"from": [-1.4, 1.4], "to": [-1.4, 0.4], "arrow": true, "label": "a"}, {"from": [1.4, 1.9], "to": [1.4, 2.9], "arrow": true, "label": "a"}], "polygons": [{"points": [[-1, 0.5], [-0.2, 0.5], [-0.2, 1.5], [-1, 1.5]]}, {"points": [[0.2, 1.8], [1, 1.8], [1, 2.5], [0.2, 2.5]]}], "labels": [{"at": [-0.6, 0.2], "text": "m₁"}, {"at": [0.6, 1.5], "text": "m₂"}], "caption": "Atwood machine: the heavier mass m₁ accelerates down, m₂ up, with the same magnitude a"}
```

### Example 2

In an Atwood machine, $m_1 = 5.0$ kg and $m_2 = 3.0$ kg. Find the acceleration and tension.

$a = \dfrac{5.0 - 3.0}{8.0}(9.8) = 2.45$ m/s². $T = \dfrac{2(5.0)(3.0)}{8.0}(9.8) = 36.75$ N.

Check with $m_2$: $T - m_2g = 36.75 - 29.4 = 7.35$ N $= 3.0(2.45)$ ✓.

## A block on a table pulled by a hanging mass

Block $m_1$ sits on a horizontal table with kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k$; a rope over a pulley at the table's edge connects it to hanging mass $m_2$. Positive direction: $m_1$ moves toward the pulley, $m_2$ moves down.

- $m_1$ (horizontal): $T - \mu_k m_1 g = m_1 a$
- $m_2$ (vertical): $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$

Adding: $a = \dfrac{m_2 - \mu_k m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\,g$. If $m_2 g$ can't overcome static friction ($m_2 < \mu_s m_1$), nothing moves.

The picture shows every force on each block. The rope pulls each block toward the pulley with the same tension $T$; friction acts only on the block that slides on the table.

![A block m1 on a table is tied by a rope over a pulley at the table's edge to a hanging block m2. On m1: tension T toward the pulley, kinetic friction f k away from it, the normal force n up and the weight m1 g down. On m2: tension T up and the weight m2 g down.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 3

$m_1 = 6.0$ kg on the table with $\mu_k = 0.20$; $m_2 = 2.0$ kg hanging. Find $a$ and $T$.

$a = \dfrac{2.0 - 0.20(6.0)}{8.0}(9.8) = \dfrac{0.8}{8.0}(9.8) = 0.98$ m/s².

From $m_2$: $T = m_2(g - a) = 2.0(9.8 - 0.98) = 17.64$ N. Check with $m_1$: $17.64 - 0.20(6.0)(9.8) = 17.64 - 11.76 = 5.88 = 6.0(0.98)$ ✓.

## Mechanical advantage

A movable pulley supported by two rope segments lets you lift a load with half the force: if the load $W$ hangs from a pulley held up by two strands of the same rope, $2T = W$ in equilibrium, so $T = W/2$. The price is distance: to raise the load 1 m, you pull 2 m of rope. Block-and-tackle systems multiply this further. (In energy terms, the work you do is the same; you'll see why in the work lesson.)

![A load hangs from a movable pulley. The rope is tied to the ceiling, runs down under the pulley and back up to the person pulling. Each of the two strands pulls up on the pulley with tension T and the load's weight W pulls down, so 2T = W; pulling 2 m of rope shortens each strand by 1 m and raises the load 1 m.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Why connected objects share an acceleration

The "same acceleration" rule comes from the rope's fixed length. If block A moves 1 cm toward the pulley, exactly 1 cm of rope passes over it, so block B moves 1 cm too. Equal distances in every time interval mean equal speeds at every moment, and equal changes in speed mean equal accelerations (in magnitude, each along its own direction of motion).

The same counting handles a movable pulley. When the load hangs from two strands and you pull the free end 2 cm, each strand shortens by only 1 cm, so the load rises 1 cm. The load moves half as far as the rope end in every interval, so its speed and acceleration are half the rope end's. Counting rope this way is the safe method for any pulley system.

## Ropes with mass

A real rope has weight, and then its tension is not the same everywhere. Any point of a hanging rope holds up everything below it: the rope beneath that point plus whatever hangs from the end. So a hanging rope's tension is largest at the top. For a uniform rope of mass $M$ and length $L$, the rope below a point a distance $y$ above the bottom end has mass $\tfrac{M}{L}y$.

### Example 4

A 2.0 kg rope 4.0 m long hangs from a ceiling and holds a 10 kg bucket at rest at its lower end. Find the tension at the bottom, at the midpoint and at the top of the rope.

Bottom: only the bucket hangs below, so $T = 10(9.8) = 98$ N.

Midpoint: the bucket plus the lower half of the rope (1.0 kg) hang below, so $T = 11(9.8) = 107.8$ N.

Top: the bucket plus the whole rope, $T = 12(9.8) = 117.6$ N, which is also the force the ceiling must supply. If the rope's mass is small compared with the load, these values are nearly equal, which is why the massless-rope idealization usually works.

## Common mistakes

- Setting tension equal to the hanging weight when the system accelerates.
- Using inconsistent sign conventions for the two objects, which makes the accelerations seem to differ.
- Including tension when treating the whole system as one object (it's internal).
- Forgetting friction on the table block, or using $\mu_s$ when it's sliding.

## Key points

- Tension pulls along a rope; ideal ropes and pulleys keep it the same throughout.
- Draw a separate FBD for each object; use one consistent positive direction around the system.
- Atwood: $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$, $T = \dfrac{2m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$.
- Table and hanging mass: $a = \dfrac{m_2 - \mu_k m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g$.
- Whole-system shortcut: $a = F_{\text{ext}}/M_{\text{total}}$.

lessons.title: Uniform circular motion
lessons.body:
## Turning requires a force

A car rounding a bend, a satellite in orbit, a ball whirled on a string: each moves in a circle, and each is accelerating even if its speed never changes, because its velocity keeps changing direction. By Newton's second law, something must supply a net force. This lesson finds how large that acceleration is, where it points, and which real forces provide it.

## Describing circular motion

An object moving in a circle of radius $r$ at constant speed $v$ is in **[[uniform circular motion]]**. The time for one revolution is the **[[period]]** $T$, and the number of revolutions per second is the **[[frequency]]** $f = 1/T$ (unit hertz, Hz $=$ s$^{-1}$). Since one lap is a distance $2\pi r$,

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = 2\pi r f.$$

## Centripetal acceleration

The velocity is always tangent to the circle, and the acceleration points toward the center. It's called **[[centripetal acceleration]]** ("center-seeking"), with magnitude

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}.$$

*Why $v^2/r$?* In a short time $\Delta t$, the object moves through a small angle $\Delta\theta = v\Delta t/r$. Its velocity vector, of fixed length $v$, rotates through the same angle, so the change in velocity has magnitude $|\Delta\vec v| \approx v\,\Delta\theta = v^2\Delta t/r$. Dividing by $\Delta t$ gives $a = v^2/r$. And as $\Delta\theta \to 0$, $\Delta\vec v$ is perpendicular to $\vec v$, pointing inward.

```shape
{"x": [-1.6, 1.6], "y": [-1.25, 1.6], "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "segments": [{"from": [0.707, 0.707], "to": [0.0, 1.414], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0.707, 0.707], "to": [0.283, 0.283], "arrow": true}], "points": [[0, 0], [0.707, 0.707]], "labels": [{"at": [0.47, 1.2], "text": "v"}, {"at": [0.32, 0.6], "text": "a"}, {"at": [0, -0.2], "text": "center"}], "caption": "In uniform circular motion (here counterclockwise), velocity v is tangent and acceleration a points to the center"}
```

## Centripetal force is a role, not a new force

Newton's second law toward the center reads

$$\sum F_{\text{toward center}} = \frac{mv^2}{r}.$$

The left side is the net inward force from real, identifiable forces: tension, gravity, friction, the normal force, or a combination. "Centripetal force" is a job description for whatever force(s) do the turning; it never belongs on a free-body diagram as an extra arrow. When the inward force disappears (a string snaps), the object continues in a straight line along the tangent. It doesn't fly outward; "centrifugal force" is what you feel in the car's non-inertial frame, not a real force in an inertial one.

In every problem, ask which real forces point toward the center. Common cases:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What supplies the centripetal force
  accDescr: The net inward force m v squared over r is always supplied by real forces. Tension supplies it for a ball whirled on a string or a conical pendulum. Static friction supplies it for a car on a flat curve. Gravity supplies it for a satellite or the Moon in orbit. The normal force supplies it on a banked curve, through its horizontal component, and at the top and bottom of a loop together with gravity.
  A["Net inward force = mv²/r"] --> B["Tension"]
  A --> C["Static friction"]
  A --> D["Gravity"]
  A --> E["Normal force"]
  B --> B1["Ball on a string, conical pendulum"]
  C --> C1["Car on a flat curve"]
  D --> D1["Satellite or Moon in orbit"]
  E --> E1["Banked curve, loop-the-loop with gravity"]
```

### Example 1: car on a flat curve

What is the maximum speed at which a car can round a flat curve of radius 50 m if $\mu_s = 0.80$ between tires and road?

The tires don't slide sideways, so static friction provides the inward force. Vertically, $n = mg$. At the limit, $f_s = \mu_s mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so

$$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{0.80(9.8)(50)} = 19.8\text{ m/s} \approx 71\text{ km/h}.$$

The mass cancels: a truck and a motorcycle have the same limit (with the same tires). On ice, with $\mu_s \approx 0.1$, the limit drops to 7 m/s.

## Banked curves

Highway engineers tilt curves so the normal force helps. On a frictionless curve banked at angle $\theta$, the normal force tilts toward the center. Vertically, $n\cos\theta = mg$; horizontally (toward the center), $n\sin\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing,

$$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}.$$

![A car on a road banked at angle theta, seen from behind, with the center of the curve to the left. The normal force n is perpendicular to the road, tilted from vertical by theta toward the center. Dashed components show n cos theta straight up and n sin theta horizontal, toward the center. The weight mg points straight down.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At this design speed no friction is needed at all. Faster than this, friction must act down the slope; slower, up the slope.

## Vertical circles

A roller coaster loop or a bucket swung overhead moves in a vertical circle, usually not at constant speed, but the inward equation still holds at each point.

At the *top*, both gravity and the normal force (or tension) point down, toward the center: $n + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The minimum speed to stay on the track is when $n = 0$:

$$v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}.$$

At the *bottom*, the normal force points up (toward the center) and gravity down: $n - mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $n = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, which is why riders feel pressed into their seats at the bottom.

![A vertical circular loop with its center marked. At the top, a car inside the track has two forces pointing down toward the center, the normal force n and the weight mg, so n + mg = m v squared over r. At the bottom, the normal force n points up toward the center and mg points down, away from it, so n − mg = m v squared over r.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2

A 0.50 kg bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.90 m. (a) What is the minimum speed at the top for the water to stay in? (b) If the speed at the bottom is 5.0 m/s, what tension does the arm supply there?

(a) $v_{\min} = \sqrt{9.8(0.90)} = 2.97$ m/s. At that speed gravity alone provides exactly the needed inward force, and the water is in free fall along the circle with the bucket.

(b) At the bottom: $T = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = 0.50(9.8) + \dfrac{0.50(25)}{0.90} = 4.9 + 13.9 = 18.8$ N.

### Example 3: conical pendulum

A 0.20 kg ball on a 1.0 m string swings in a horizontal circle with the string at $30^\circ$ from vertical. Find its speed and period.

Radius: $r = L\sin 30^\circ = 0.50$ m. Vertical: $T\cos 30^\circ = mg$. Inward: $T\sin 30^\circ = mv^2/r$. Dividing, $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v = \sqrt{rg\tan 30^\circ} = \sqrt{0.50(9.8)(0.577)} = 1.68$ m/s. Period: $T_{\text{period}} = 2\pi r/v = 1.87$ s.

## Angular speed and rpm

Rotating machines are rated by how fast they turn, not by the speed of a point on them. The angular speed $\omega$ is the angle swept per second, in radians per second: one revolution is $2\pi$ rad, so $\omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f$. A point at radius $r$ covers $2\pi r$ per revolution, so $v = r\omega$, and the centripetal acceleration becomes

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{(r\omega)^2}{r} = \omega^2 r.$$

Motors and wheels are often rated in revolutions per minute (rpm). To convert, divide by 60 to get revolutions per second ($f$), then use $v = 2\pi r f$.

### Example 4

A washing machine drum of radius 0.25 m spins at 1200 rpm. Find the speed of the drum wall and the centripetal acceleration, as a multiple of $g$.

$f = 1200/60 = 20$ rev/s, so $v = 2\pi(0.25)(20) = 31.4$ m/s. Then $a_c = v^2/r = 31.4^2/0.25 = 3950$ m/s², about $400g$. Water in the clothes can't get that much inward force from the fabric, so it escapes through the holes in the drum along tangent lines.

When the speed is also changing (a car speeding up around a curve), the acceleration has a tangential part, $a_t = \Delta v/\Delta t$, along the velocity, as well as the centripetal part $v^2/r$ toward the center. They are perpendicular, so the total is $a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + (v^2/r)^2}$.

## Common mistakes

- Drawing a separate "centripetal force" arrow in a free-body diagram.
- Saying an object released from circular motion flies outward (it flies off along the tangent).
- Using $n = mg$ at the top or bottom of a vertical circle.
- Mixing up period and frequency, or forgetting to convert rpm to revolutions per second.

## Key points

- $v = 2\pi r/T$; $a_c = v^2/r$ toward the center.
- Real forces supply the inward net force: $\sum F_{\text{in}} = mv^2/r$.
- Flat curve: $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. Banked, frictionless: $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$.
- Top of a vertical loop: $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$. Bottom: $n = mg + mv^2/r$.
- Angular speed $\omega = 2\pi/T$ (rad/s), $v = r\omega$, $a_c = \omega^2 r$; rpm ÷ 60 gives revolutions per second.

lessons.title: Friction in systems of objects
lessons.body:
## When friction has to be figured out

In the friction lesson the direction of friction was usually obvious: a box slides right, so kinetic friction points left. In the tension lesson, ropes connected objects whose direction of motion was given. Harder problems combine the two, and then the obvious answers stop working. Which way does friction push on a book resting on an accelerating cart? Will a block on a ramp, tied to a hanging weight, slide up, slide down or stay put? How fast can a car take a banked curve before it skids? This honors lesson gives one method that answers all three, and shows that friction can just as easily speed an object up as slow it down.

## Static friction is an unknown, not a formula

The single most useful idea is this: static friction is whatever force is needed to keep two surfaces from sliding over each other, up to a limit.
