### Example 2: a small bridge truss

The truss below is built from equilateral triangles with 4.0 m sides. It rests on a pin at A and a roller at E (the roller pushes only vertically). A 30 kN load hangs from joint C. Find the forces in members AB, AC, BC and BD.

![A bridge truss of three equilateral triangles: bottom joints A, C and E, top joints B and D. Members AB, BC, CD and DE form the slanted sides, AC and CE the bottom chord, and BD the top chord. A pin support is under A, a roller under E, and a 30 kN load hangs from C.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Supports.* Symmetry (or torques about A) gives 15 kN upward at A and at E. The pin at A has no horizontal force, since no load has a horizontal part.

*Joint A* has two unknowns, AB (at $60^\circ$) and AC (horizontal). Assume both in tension, pulling A toward B and toward C. Vertical: $15 + F_{AB}\sin 60^\circ = 0$, so $F_{AB} = -17.3$ kN, **[[compression]]**. Horizontal: $F_{AC} + F_{AB}\cos 60^\circ = 0$, so $F_{AC} = +8.66$ kN, tension.

*Joint B* now has two unknowns, BC and BD. AB, in compression, pushes B away from A: up $17.3\sin 60^\circ = 15$ kN and right $17.3\cos 60^\circ = 8.66$ kN. BC (tension assumed) pulls B down and right toward C. Vertical: $15 - F_{BC}\sin 60^\circ = 0$, so $F_{BC} = 17.3$ kN, tension. Horizontal: $8.66 + 17.3\cos 60^\circ + F_{BD} = 0$, so $F_{BD} = -17.3$ kN, compression.

By symmetry DE and CD mirror AB and BC. *Check at C*: the two slanted members each pull up $17.3\sin 60^\circ = 15$ kN, holding the 30 kN load ✓, and AC and CE pull equally in opposite directions ✓.

The pattern is the same as in a bent beam: the top chord (BD) is squeezed and the bottom chord (AC, CE) is stretched. That's why steel bridges often use slim rods or plates for tension members but thicker, braced sections for compression members, which can buckle.

## Ladders that slip

The core lesson described the ladder qualitatively. Now the numbers. A uniform ladder of length $L$ and weight $W$ leans against a smooth (frictionless) wall at angle $\theta$ above the floor. The floor supplies a normal force $n = W$ and static friction $f$ toward the wall; the wall supplies a horizontal normal force $N_w$.

Torques about the foot (eliminating $n$ and $f$): the wall force acts at height $L\sin\theta$, the weight at horizontal distance $\tfrac L2\cos\theta$:

$$N_wL\sin\theta = W\tfrac L2\cos\theta \quad\Rightarrow\quad N_w = \frac{W}{2\tan\theta}.$$

Horizontal balance: $f = N_w$. The ladder stays put only if $f \le \mu_sn = \mu_sW$, which gives

$$\tan\theta \ge \frac{1}{2\mu_s}.$$

The smallest safe angle depends only on the friction coefficient, not on the ladder's length or weight. (This treats the wall as frictionless, which is the cautious assumption: real wall friction helps.)

### Example 3: how high can the painter climb?

A uniform 5.0 m ladder of mass 15 kg leans at $60^\circ$ against a smooth wall; $\mu_s = 0.40$ at the floor. (a) What is the smallest angle at which the empty ladder can stand? (b) A 75 kg painter climbs it. How far along the ladder can she go before it slips?

(a) $\tan\theta \ge \dfrac{1}{0.80} = 1.25$, so $\theta \ge 51.3^\circ$.

(b) The floor's normal force is now $(15 + 75)(9.8) = 882$ N, so friction can be at most $0.40(882) = 353$ N, and at the slipping point $N_w = f = 353$ N. Torques about the foot, with the painter a distance $x$ along the ladder:

$$353(5.0\sin 60^\circ) = 147(2.5\cos 60^\circ) + 735\,x\cos 60^\circ.$$

$1528 = 184 + 367.5x$, so $x = 3.66$ m. She can climb about three quarters of the way; higher, her weight's lever arm about the foot is too large. Climbing raises the friction needed even though the angle hasn't changed, which is why the top rungs are the dangerous ones.

## Tip or slide?

Push sideways on a tall box, or tilt the surface it rests on, and one of two things happens first: it slides, or it tips over its bottom edge. Each has its own condition, and whichever threshold is lower wins.

*On a tilting ramp.* A uniform box of width $w$ (along the slope) and height $h$ sits on a ramp of angle $\theta$. It slides when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$ (the incline lesson). It tips when the vertical line through its center of gravity passes outside the downhill edge of its base. Measured in the box's own frame, the center is $\tfrac h2$ above the base and $\tfrac w2$ from the edge, and the vertical through it reaches the edge when $\tan\theta = \dfrac{w/2}{h/2} = \dfrac wh$. So:

- it slides first if $\mu_s < w/h$;
- it tips first if $w/h < \mu_s$.

A crate 0.60 m wide and 1.5 m tall ($w/h = 0.40$) on a surface with $\mu_s = 0.50$ tips at $21.8^\circ$, before it could slide at $26.6^\circ$.

*Pushed on level ground.* Push horizontally with force $F$ at height $H$ on a box of mass $m$ and depth $w$ (in the direction of the push). Sliding starts when $F = \mu_smg$. Tipping starts about the bottom edge on the far side from you (the edge the box would tip over), when the push's torque beats the weight's: $FH = mg\tfrac w2$, so $F = \dfrac{mgw}{2H}$. It tips first if $\dfrac{w}{2H} < \mu_s$, that is, if you push above the height $H = \dfrac{w}{2\mu_s}$.

### Example 4: moving a refrigerator

A 90 kg refrigerator is 0.70 m deep, front to back; $\mu_s = 0.45$ with the floor. You push on its front face at a height of 1.2 m. Does it slide or tip? Where should you push instead?

Sliding needs $0.45(90)(9.8) = 397$ N. Tipping needs $\dfrac{90(9.8)(0.70)}{2(1.2)} = 257$ N. Tipping wins: it starts to topple at 257 N before it ever slides. To slide it, push below $H = \dfrac{0.70}{2(0.45)} = 0.78$ m. (This assumes the center of gravity is halfway between the front and back. For a horizontal push, what matters is how far the center of gravity is, horizontally, from the edge the fridge tips over; its height doesn't enter $FH = mg\tfrac w2$. Height does matter on a tilted surface, as in the ramp case above.)

## Common mistakes

- Drawing a truss member's force at an angle to the member. In a pin-jointed truss loaded at the joints, every member force lies along the member.
- Mixing up which way a compression force acts on a joint: a compressed member *pushes* on the joint, away from the member's other end.
- Starting the method of joints at a joint with three unknowns: two equations can't solve it. Find the supports first, then start where only two are unknown.
- Using the ladder's own weight alone for the floor's normal force after someone climbs on.
- Assuming a box always slides before it tips: compare $\mu_s$ with $w/h$ (ramp) or with $w/(2H)$ (push).

## Key points

- In a pin-jointed truss loaded at its joints, each member is a two-force member: pure tension or compression along its length.
- Method of joints: supports first, then $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$ at joints with at most two unknowns; negative means compression.
- Shallow members carry large forces: an A-frame's rafter force is $P/(2\sin\theta)$.
- Ladder on a smooth wall: stands if $\tan\theta \ge 1/(2\mu_s)$; a climber raises the friction needed.
- Box on a ramp tips first if $w/h < \mu_s$; pushed at height $H$, it tips first if $w/(2H) < \mu_s$.

lessons.title: Honors: Elliptical orbits, transfers and weighing the heavens
lessons.body:
## From circles to ellipses

The gravitation lesson worked out circular orbits in detail and stated Kepler's laws for elliptical ones. Most real orbits are ellipses: comets, transfer orbits to the Moon and planets, many satellites. This lesson combines the two conservation laws you already have, energy and angular momentum, to get the speed anywhere on an ellipse. Then it uses that to plan the cheapest move from one orbit to another, and finally turns Kepler's third law around to measure the masses of planets, stars and a black hole.

Throughout, a small body of mass $m$ orbits a much heavier body of mass $M$, which we treat as fixed. (For two stars of similar mass that isn't true; we fix it in the last section.)

## Describing an ellipse

An ellipse has a long axis and two special points on it, the foci; the central body sits at one focus. Three lengths describe an orbit:

- the **[[periapsis]]** distance $r_p$, the closest approach to the central body (called perigee for orbits around Earth and perihelion around the Sun);
- the **[[apoapsis]]** distance $r_a$, the farthest point (apogee, aphelion);
- the **[[semimajor axis]]** $a$, half the long axis. Since the long axis runs from periapsis through the focus to apoapsis, $2a = r_p + r_a$, so $a = \tfrac12(r_p + r_a)$.

A circle is the special case $r_p = r_a = a$. All distances are measured from the *center* of the central body, not its surface.

## Speed at the two ends: two conservation laws

Gravity points at the central body, so it exerts no torque about it, and angular momentum is conserved (Kepler's second law). At periapsis and apoapsis the velocity is perpendicular to the line from the focus, so $r_\perp = r$ and $L = mvr$ there:

$$r_pv_p = r_av_a.$$

Gravity is also conservative, so the energy $\tfrac12mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{r}$ is the same at both ends:

$$\tfrac12v_p^2 - \frac{GM}{r_p} = \tfrac12v_a^2 - \frac{GM}{r_a}.$$

Substitute $v_a = v_pr_p/r_a$ and solve. After some algebra (multiply out and use $r_a^2 - r_p^2 = (r_a - r_p)(r_a + r_p)$):

$$v_p^2 = \frac{2GM\,r_a}{r_p(r_p + r_a)}.$$

Now find the total energy at periapsis:

$$E = \tfrac12mv_p^2 - \frac{GMm}{r_p} = \frac{GMm}{r_p}\left(\frac{r_a}{r_p + r_a} - 1\right) = -\frac{GMm}{r_p + r_a} = -\frac{GMm}{2a}.$$

This is a remarkable result: the **[[orbital energy]]** depends only on the semimajor axis, not on the shape. A circle of radius $a$ and a long thin ellipse with the same $a$ have the same energy (and, by Kepler's third law, the same period). For a circle it reduces to the core lesson's $-GMm/(2r)$.

## The vis-viva equation

Since the energy at any point is $-GMm/(2a)$, write energy conservation at an arbitrary distance $r$:

$$\tfrac12mv^2 - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2a} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v^2 = GM\left(\frac2r - \frac1a\right).$$

This is the **[[vis-viva equation]]** (Latin for "living force," an old name for $mv^2$, twice what we now call kinetic energy). It gives the speed anywhere on an orbit from just the distance and the semimajor axis. Check the special cases: for a circle ($r = a$) it gives $v^2 = GM/r$; for escape ($a \to \infty$, a parabola) it gives $v^2 = 2GM/r$. Both match the core lesson.

### Example 1: a satellite on an ellipse

A satellite orbits Earth with perigee 7.0 × 10⁶ m and apogee 1.40 × 10⁷ m from Earth's center. Find its speeds at perigee and apogee and its period. ($GM_E = 3.98\times10^{14}$ m³/s².)

$a = \tfrac12(7.0\times10^6 + 1.40\times10^7) = 1.05\times10^7$ m.

Perigee: $v_p^2 = 3.98\times10^{14}\left(\dfrac{2}{7.0\times10^6} - \dfrac{1}{1.05\times10^7}\right) = 7.58\times10^7$, so $v_p = 8.71$ km/s.

Apogee, from angular momentum: $v_a = v_p\dfrac{r_p}{r_a} = 8.71 \times \dfrac{7.0}{14.0} = 4.35$ km/s.

Period, from Kepler's third law with $a$: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{a^3}{GM}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(1.05\times10^7)^3}{3.98\times10^{14}}} = 1.07\times10^4$ s $= 2.98$ h.

Compare a circular orbit at the perigee distance: $\sqrt{GM/r_p} = 7.54$ km/s. At perigee the satellite moves faster than circular speed, which is exactly why it swings out to a larger distance.

## Changing orbits: the Hohmann transfer

A spacecraft changes its orbit by firing its engine briefly, changing its velocity by an amount called **[[delta-v]]** ($\Delta v$). Fuel use grows with the total $\Delta v$ (exponentially, by the rocket equation from the rockets honors lesson of the momentum module), so mission planners hunt for the smallest one.

To go from a low circular orbit of radius $r_1$ to a higher circular orbit of radius $r_2$ in the same plane, the classic answer (usually the cheapest when $r_2$ is less than about 12 times $r_1$) is the **[[Hohmann transfer]]**, worked out by Walter Hohmann in 1925:

![Two circular orbits around Earth, a small inner one and a large outer one, joined by a half ellipse. The ellipse touches the inner orbit on one side, where the first burn happens, and the outer orbit on the opposite side, where the second burn happens.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. *First burn*, at the inner orbit: speed up along the direction of motion. The craft is now at the periapsis of a **[[transfer orbit]]**, an ellipse with $r_p = r_1$ and $r_a = r_2$, so $a_t = \tfrac12(r_1 + r_2)$.
2. *Coast* half an ellipse to apoapsis, a time of half the transfer orbit's period.
3. *Second burn*, at the outer orbit: speed up again, to the circular speed there. Without it, the craft would fall back along the ellipse.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Steps of a Hohmann transfer to a higher orbit
  accDescr: The craft starts in the inner circular orbit. A first burn speeds it up to the transfer ellipse's periapsis speed. It coasts half an ellipse, which takes half the transfer orbit's period, arriving at apoapsis on the outer orbit's radius moving slower than circular speed there. A second burn speeds it up to the outer orbit's circular speed, and it stays in the outer circular orbit.
  A["Inner circular orbit, speed square root of GM over r1"] --> B["Burn 1: speed up to the transfer periapsis speed"]
  B --> C["Coast half an ellipse, half the transfer period"]
  C --> D["Arrive at apoapsis, slower than circular speed there"]
  D --> E["Burn 2: speed up to square root of GM over r2"]
  E --> F["Outer circular orbit"]
```

Odd but true: the craft speeds up twice, yet it ends up moving *slower* than it started, because the outer orbit's circular speed is lower. The burns add energy; the climb converts kinetic energy into potential energy.

### Example 2: from low orbit to geostationary

Plan a Hohmann transfer from a circular orbit of radius $r_1 = 6.67\times10^6$ m (300 km up) to geostationary radius $r_2 = 4.22\times10^7$ m. Find both burns and the trip time.

With $GM_E = 3.98\times10^{14}$ m³/s² as before, the circular speeds are $v_1 = \sqrt{GM/r_1} = 7.72$ km/s and $v_2 = \sqrt{GM/r_2} = 3.07$ km/s.

Transfer orbit: $a_t = \tfrac12(6.67\times10^6 + 4.22\times10^7) = 2.44\times10^7$ m. Vis-viva at its two ends:

$$v_{tp} = \sqrt{GM\left(\frac2{r_1} - \frac1{a_t}\right)} = 10.15\text{ km/s}, \qquad v_{ta} = \sqrt{GM\left(\frac2{r_2} - \frac1{a_t}\right)} = 1.60\text{ km/s}.$$

Burns: $\Delta v_1 = 10.15 - 7.72 = 2.43$ km/s, $\Delta v_2 = 3.07 - 1.60 = 1.47$ km/s, total 3.89 km/s.

Trip time: half the transfer period, $\pi\sqrt{a_t^3/GM} = 1.90\times10^4$ s $= 5.3$ h.

(Real launches from Florida must also tilt the orbit into the equatorial plane, which adds to the second burn. We've kept the orbits in one plane.)

The same idea, with the Sun as the central body, plans trips between planets. A Hohmann transfer from Earth's orbit (1.00 AU) to Mars's (1.52 AU) has $a_t = 1.26$ AU; by Kepler's third law in years and AU, its full period is $1.26^{3/2} = 1.41$ yr, so the trip takes half that, about 0.71 yr or 8.5 months. That's why the launch windows to Mars, when the planets are lined up for this path, come only about every 26 months. Missions to the outer planets also borrow speed from planets they pass, using the gravity assists described in the restitution honors lesson of the momentum module.

## Weighing the heavens

Kepler's third law in Newton's form, $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$, can be turned around:

$$M = \frac{4\pi^2a^3}{GT^2}.$$

Measure the size and period of any orbit, and you have the mass of the body being orbited. The orbiting body's own mass doesn't appear, as long as it is small. This is how astronomers know the masses of the Sun, the planets with moons, and much more.

### Example 3: the mass of Jupiter

Jupiter's moon Io orbits at $a = 4.22\times10^8$ m with a period of 1.769 days. Find Jupiter's mass.

$T = 1.769(86\,400) = 1.528\times10^5$ s.

$$M_J = \frac{4\pi^2(4.22\times10^8)^3}{(6.67\times10^{-11})(1.528\times10^5)^2} = 1.90\times10^{27}\text{ kg},$$

about 318 times Earth's mass.

*Binary stars.* When two bodies of similar mass orbit each other, both move around their common center of mass, and the heavier one is not fixed. Newton's analysis then gives the same law with the total mass, and with $a$ now the semimajor axis of their *separation*:

$$M_1 + M_2 = \frac{4\pi^2a^3}{GT^2}.$$

In convenient units (a in AU, T in years, masses in Sun masses) the constants cancel for the Earth–Sun case, so $M_1 + M_2 = a^3/T^2$.

### Example 4: Sirius and the black hole at the galaxy's center

Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, has a faint white-dwarf companion. Their separation has a semimajor axis of about 19.8 AU and the period is about 50.1 yr. Total mass: $19.8^3/50.1^2 = 3.1$ solar masses. Separate measurements of how each star wobbles about the center of mass split this into about 2.1 and 1.0 solar masses.

The same method weighs the black hole at the center of the Milky Way. The star S2 orbits it with a semimajor axis of roughly 1000 AU and a period of about 16 years: $1000^3/16^2 \approx 4\times10^6$ solar masses, packed into a region far smaller than the solar system. (Careful fits to decades of S2 data give about $4.3\times10^6$; this measurement was part of the work honored by the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.)

## Common mistakes

- Using altitude above the surface as $r$ or $a$; orbits are measured from the center of the central body.
- Taking $a$ to be $r_a$, or $r_p + r_a$; it is *half* the sum.
- Assuming the speed on an ellipse is $\sqrt{GM/r}$. That's only for circles; use vis-viva.
- Thinking a craft that ends in a higher orbit must be moving faster: it is moving slower, with more total (less negative) energy.
- Forgetting the companion's mass in a binary: the formula gives the *total* mass.

## Key points

- Ellipse: $a = \tfrac12(r_p + r_a)$; $r_pv_p = r_av_a$ (angular momentum).
- Orbital energy $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$, set by the semimajor axis alone.
- Vis-viva: $v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac2r - \dfrac1a\right)$.
- Hohmann transfer: two forward burns joined by half an ellipse with $a_t = \tfrac12(r_1 + r_2)$; trip time is half its period.
- Mass from an orbit: $M = \dfrac{4\pi^2a^3}{GT^2}$; for a binary this is the total mass; in AU, years and solar masses, $M = a^3/T^2$.

lessons.title: Simple harmonic motion
lessons.body:
## Motion that repeats

A mass bouncing on a spring, a swinging pendulum, a vibrating guitar string, atoms jiggling in a crystal, the alternating current in your walls: nature is full of oscillations. The simplest and most important kind is simple harmonic motion, and it's worth mastering because almost any system nudged slightly from a stable equilibrium oscillates this way. It's also the bridge to waves, the subject of the next two lessons.

## The restoring force

Recall Hooke's law: a spring pulls back with $F = -kx$, proportional to the displacement and opposite to it. Any motion driven by a force of this form is **[[simple harmonic motion]]** (SHM). Newton's second law gives

$$a = -\frac{k}{m}x.$$

The acceleration always points toward equilibrium and is largest at the extremes. The object overshoots equilibrium (it has speed there, and inertia carries it on), slows as the spring stretches the other way, stops, and returns. The cycle repeats forever if there's no friction.

The picture shows three moments in one cycle. At each end the block is momentarily at rest and the acceleration is largest; at equilibrium the block is fastest and the acceleration is zero.

![Three snapshots of a block on a horizontal spring. At x = −A the spring is compressed, the block is at rest, and a large acceleration arrow points right toward equilibrium. At x = 0 the block moves right at maximum speed with zero acceleration. At x = +A the spring is stretched, the block is at rest, and a large acceleration arrow points left. The distance from equilibrium to either end is the amplitude A.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Describing the oscillation

The position follows a sine or cosine curve:

$$x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi).$$

- **[[Amplitude]]** $A$: the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
- **[[Angular frequency]]** $\omega$ (rad/s), related to the period $T$ and frequency $f$ by $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$.
- **[[Phase constant]]** $\phi$: sets where in the cycle the motion starts. Released from rest at $x = A$, $\phi = 0$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 4.2], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "x (m)", "functions": [{"f": "1.2*cos(2*pi*x/2)"}], "labels": [{"at": [1.0, 1.33], "text": "x(t) = A cos(ωt)"}], "points": [{"at": [2, 1.2], "label": "one period T = 2 s"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [0, 1.2], "arrow": true, "label": "A"}], "caption": "SHM with amplitude 1.2 m and period 2.0 s"}
```

For a mass on a spring,

$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac km}, \qquad T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac mk}.$$

A stiffer spring or lighter mass oscillates faster. Remarkably, *the period doesn't depend on the amplitude*: stretch the spring twice as far and the mass travels twice as far, but with twice the force, so it takes the same time. That's what makes oscillators good clocks.

### Example 1

A 0.50 kg block on a frictionless surface is attached to a spring with $k = 200$ N/m. It's pulled 0.10 m from equilibrium and released. Find the period, frequency, maximum speed and maximum acceleration.

$\omega = \sqrt{200/0.50} = 20$ rad/s. $T = 2\pi/20 = 0.314$ s; $f = 3.18$ Hz.

Maximum speed (at equilibrium): $v_{\max} = A\omega = 0.10(20) = 2.0$ m/s.

Maximum acceleration (at the ends): $a_{\max} = A\omega^2 = 0.10(400) = 40$ m/s². Check with force: $kA/m = 200(0.10)/0.50 = 40$ ✓.

## Energy in SHM

With no friction, mechanical energy is conserved and shuttles between kinetic and spring potential energy:

$$E = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac12kx^2 = \tfrac12kA^2.$$

At the turning points ($x = \pm A$) it's all potential; at equilibrium it's all kinetic, so $\tfrac12mv_{\max}^2 = \tfrac12kA^2$, giving $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/m} = A\omega$. At any position, $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.

### Example 2

For the block in Example 1, what is its speed when it's 0.06 m from equilibrium?

$v = 20\sqrt{0.10^2 - 0.06^2} = 20(0.08) = 1.6$ m/s.

*Vertical springs.* Hanging a mass on a vertical spring shifts the equilibrium down by $mg/k$, but measured from the new equilibrium the motion is the same SHM with the same $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$. Gravity just moves the center.

## The simple pendulum

A **[[simple pendulum]]** is a point mass on a light string of length $L$. Displaced by angle $\theta$, gravity's component along the arc is $-mg\sin\theta$. The picture splits the weight into a part along the string, which the tension balances (when the bob is moving, the tension is a little larger, and the extra supplies the centripetal force), and a part along the arc, which pulls the bob back toward the bottom.

![A pendulum of length L hanging from a ceiling, pulled aside by angle θ from the dashed vertical line. The arc from the bottom to the bob is the arc length s = Lθ. Forces on the bob: tension T along the string toward the pivot and weight mg straight down. The weight is split into mg cos θ along the string, away from the pivot, and mg sin θ along the arc, toward equilibrium.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For small angles, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ (in radians; accurate to 1% up to about $14^\circ$), and with arc length $s = L\theta$ the restoring force is $-\dfrac{mg}{L}s$, Hooke's-law form with effective $k = mg/L$. So

$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac gL}, \qquad T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac Lg}.$$

The mass cancels (heavy and light bobs swing together, just as they fall together), and the amplitude doesn't matter as long as it's small. Pendulum clocks are adjusted by moving the bob to change $L$.

### Example 3

How long must a pendulum be to have a period of exactly 2.00 s (a "seconds pendulum," which ticks once per second each way)? Use $g = 9.80$ m/s².

$L = g\left(\dfrac{T}{2\pi}\right)^2 = 9.80\left(\dfrac{2.00}{2\pi}\right)^2 = 0.993$ m.

On the Moon ($g = 1.62$ m/s²) the same pendulum would have $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.993/1.62} = 4.92$ s.

A **[[physical pendulum]]**, any rigid object swinging about a pivot a distance $d$ from its center of mass, has $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the pivot. For a point mass, $I = mL^2$ and $d = L$, recovering the simple pendulum.

## Damping and resonance

Real oscillators lose energy to friction and air drag. With **[[damping]]**, the amplitude shrinks a little with each cycle as mechanical energy turns into thermal energy. Light damping leaves the frequency almost unchanged; heavy damping can stop the oscillation altogether (car shock absorbers are tuned close to **[[critical damping]]**, the amount that returns a system to equilibrium fastest without bouncing; in practice they sit slightly below it, allowing a little overshoot for a softer ride).

A periodic push can feed energy in. When the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$, the amplitude grows large: **[[resonance]]**. You use it pushing a child on a swing at just the right moments. Engineers must avoid it in bridges and buildings (wind or footsteps at the natural frequency can cause dangerous swaying) and exploit it in radios, which tune by resonating with one station's frequency.

## SHM and circular motion

Why does a cosine describe SHM, and where do $v_{\max} = A\omega$ and $a_{\max} = A\omega^2$ come from? Picture a peg moving at constant angular speed $\omega$ around a circle of radius $A$, and look at its shadow on the $x$ axis (light shining from above, or the peg seen edge-on). The peg's angle is $\omega t$, so the shadow is at $x = A\cos(\omega t)$.

- The peg's speed is $A\omega$. The shadow moves with just the $x$ part of that velocity, which is largest (the full $A\omega$) as the shadow passes the center: $v_{\max} = A\omega$.
- The peg's centripetal acceleration, $A\omega^2$, points toward the center of the circle. Its $x$ part is $-\omega^2 x$: always toward equilibrium, proportional to the displacement, and largest ($A\omega^2$) at the ends.

So the shadow's acceleration obeys $a = -\omega^2x$, exactly the SHM rule $a = -\tfrac km x$ with $\omega^2 = k/m$. Any system whose acceleration is $a = -(\text{constant})\,x$ oscillates in SHM with $\omega^2$ equal to that constant, which is a quick way to find the period of a new oscillator. For the pendulum, $a = -\tfrac gL s$, so $\omega^2 = g/L$.

### Example 4

An oscillator's acceleration is $a = -49x$ (SI units) and its amplitude is 0.040 m. Find its period, maximum speed and maximum acceleration.

$\omega^2 = 49$, so $\omega = 7.0$ rad/s and $T = 2\pi/7.0 = 0.898$ s.

$v_{\max} = A\omega = 0.040(7.0) = 0.28$ m/s; $a_{\max} = A\omega^2 = 0.040(49) = 1.96$ m/s².

The chart sums up how to find the period of any oscillator in this lesson.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Finding the period of an oscillator
  accDescr: Start by asking what is oscillating. For a mass on a spring, use T = 2π times the square root of m over k. For a simple pendulum at small angles, use T = 2π times the square root of L over g. For a rigid object swinging on a pivot, use T = 2π times the square root of I over mgd. For anything else, write the acceleration as a = −(constant) times x; the constant is ω squared, and T = 2π/ω.
  A["What is oscillating?"] --> B["Mass on a spring"]
  A --> C["Simple pendulum, small angle"]
  A --> D["Rigid object on a pivot"]
  A --> E["Something else"]
  B --> F["T = 2π √(m/k)"]
  C --> G["T = 2π √(L/g)"]
  D --> H["T = 2π √(I/mgd)"]
  E --> I["Write a = −(constant) × x"]
  I --> J["ω² = constant, so T = 2π/ω"]
```

## Common mistakes

- Thinking a larger amplitude means a longer period.
- Using degrees in $\omega t$ or in $\sin\theta \approx \theta$.
- Putting the mass into the pendulum formula or the length into the spring formula.
- Saying the acceleration is zero at the turning points (it's maximal there; the velocity is zero).
- Confusing $\omega$ (rad/s) with $f$ (Hz): $\omega = 2\pi f$.

## Key points

- SHM arises from a restoring force $F = -kx$: $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$.
- Spring: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. Pendulum (small angles): $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. Period is independent of amplitude.
- $v_{\max} = A\omega$, $a_{\max} = A\omega^2$, $E = \tfrac12kA^2$.
- Damping makes amplitude decay; driving at the natural frequency causes resonance.
- In SHM, $a = -\omega^2x$; $x = A\cos(\omega t)$ is the shadow of uniform circular motion.

lessons.title: Waves and superposition
lessons.body:
## Energy on the move

Flick one end of a rope and a pulse runs along it; drop a stone in a pond and ripples spread out. In both cases the material itself only jiggles in place, yet energy travels across the whole medium. A **[[wave]]** is a disturbance that transfers energy from place to place without transporting matter. This lesson builds on SHM, because a wave is just SHM at every point of a medium, with each point slightly delayed relative to its neighbor.

## Kinds of waves

**[[Mechanical waves]]** need a medium (string, water, air, rock). Electromagnetic waves (light, radio) don't, and come later in the course.

- In a **[[transverse wave]]** the medium moves perpendicular to the direction the wave travels: waves on a string, the "wave" in a stadium.
- In a **[[longitudinal wave]]** the medium moves parallel to the direction of travel, in compressions and rarefactions: sound in air, a pulse along a stretched Slinky.

Water waves are a mix: water parcels move in small circles.

![Top: a transverse wave on a rope, drawn as a sine curve moving right, with three marked bits of rope and double arrows showing that each moves up and down. Bottom: a longitudinal wave drawn as a row of vertical lines (air layers or Slinky coils) that bunch together at compressions, labeled C, and spread apart at rarefactions, labeled R; a double arrow shows that each layer moves back and forth along the direction of travel.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Describing periodic waves

If the source oscillates in SHM, the wave is a repeating sinusoid in both space and time.

- **[[Wavelength]]** $\lambda$: the distance between adjacent crests (one full repeat in space).
- **[[Period]]** $T$ and **[[frequency]]** $f = 1/T$: how often a point in the medium completes an oscillation (set by the source).
- **[[Amplitude]]** $A$: the maximum displacement of the medium.

![A snapshot of a sinusoidal wave drawn across a dashed rest-position line. The highest points are crests and the lowest are troughs. A double arrow from one crest to the next is labeled wavelength λ, and a vertical arrow from the rest line up to a crest is labeled amplitude A.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In one period the wave advances one wavelength, so its speed is

$$v = \frac{\lambda}{T} = f\lambda.$$

This is the master equation for every kind of wave. The speed depends on the medium, the frequency on the source; the wavelength adjusts to fit. When a wave passes into a new medium, its frequency stays the same and its speed and wavelength change.

```plot
{"x": [0, 4.5], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "xLabel": "position x (m)", "yLabel": "displacement y", "functions": [{"f": "sin(2*pi*x/2)", "label": "t = 0"}, {"f": "sin(2*pi*(x - 0.4)/2)", "dashed": true, "label": "a moment later"}], "segments": [{"from": [0.5, 1.2], "to": [2.5, 1.2], "arrow": true, "label": "λ = 2 m"}], "caption": "A sinusoidal wave moving right: the whole pattern shifts while each point moves up and down"}
```

### Example 1

A radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz. Radio waves travel at $3.00\times10^8$ m/s. What is the wavelength?

$\lambda = v/f = (3.00\times10^8)/(98.5\times10^6) = 3.05$ m.

Sound in air at 20°C travels at 343 m/s. Middle A (440 Hz) has $\lambda = 343/440 = 0.780$ m.

## Waves on a string

The speed of a transverse wave on a string depends on the tension $F_T$ and the **[[linear mass density]]** $\mu = m/L$ (kg/m):

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}}.$$

Tighter strings carry waves faster (stronger restoring force); heavier strings slower (more inertia). Guitarists tune by changing tension; the bass strings are thicker to make them slower and lower.

## Superposition and interference

When two waves overlap, the displacement at each point is the sum of the individual displacements. This is the **[[principle of superposition]]**. After they pass through each other, each wave continues unchanged.

- Crest meets crest: the displacements add, **[[constructive interference]]**.
- Crest meets trough: they cancel, **[[destructive interference]]**.

For two waves from sources in step, the result at a point depends on the **[[path difference]]** $\Delta r$ from the two sources: constructive if $\Delta r = m\lambda$ ($m = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$), destructive if $\Delta r = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$. Noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference, producing a sound wave inverted relative to the incoming noise.

### Beats

Two waves of slightly different frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ drift in and out of step: for a moment crests line up (loud), a little later crest meets trough (quiet), and so on. The loudness throbs at the **[[beat frequency]]**

$$f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|,$$

while the tone you hear has the average frequency, $\tfrac12(f_1 + f_2)$. Musicians tune by listening for beats against a reference: as the frequencies approach each other, the beats slow and vanish. A 440 Hz tuning fork and a string at 443 Hz produce 3 beats per second, throbbing on a 441.5 Hz tone.

The graph adds two waves with frequencies far too low to hear (8 Hz and 9 Hz), so that the individual oscillations are visible. The dashed envelope shows the loudness swelling and fading once per second.

```plot
{"x": [0, 2.5], "y": [-2.6, 2.6], "xLabel": "time t (s)", "yLabel": "total displacement", "functions": [{"f": "sin(2*pi*8*x) + sin(2*pi*9*x)", "to": 2}, {"f": "2*cos(pi*x)", "dashed": true, "to": 2}, {"f": "-2*cos(pi*x)", "dashed": true, "to": 2}], "caption": "8 Hz + 9 Hz: loud when the waves are in step (t = 0, 1, 2 s), silent halfway between; beat frequency 1 Hz"}
```

## Reflection and standing waves

A pulse reaching the fixed end of a string reflects upside down; at a free end, it reflects right side up. A continuous wave on a string fixed at both ends reflects back and forth, and the incoming and reflected waves superpose. At certain frequencies the result is a **[[standing wave]]**: a pattern that oscillates in place without traveling. Points that never move are **[[nodes]]**; points of maximum oscillation are **[[antinodes]]**. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.

A string of length $L$ fixed at both ends must have nodes at both ends, so a whole number of half-wavelengths must fit:

$$L = n\frac{\lambda_n}{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lambda_n = \frac{2L}{n}, \qquad f_n = \frac{nv}{2L} = nf_1, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$

These are the string's **[[harmonics]]**. The lowest, $f_1 = v/(2L)$, is the **[[fundamental frequency]]**; the others are integer multiples. A plucked string vibrates in a mix of harmonics, and the mix gives each instrument its tone quality (timbre).

```plot
{"x": [0, 3], "y": [-1.4, 1.4], "xLabel": "position along string", "yLabel": "displacement", "functions": [{"f": "sin(pi*x)"}, {"f": "-sin(pi*x)", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0], "label": "N"}, {"at": [1, 0], "label": "N"}, {"at": [2, 0], "label": "N"}, {"at": [3, 0], "label": "N"}, {"at": [0.5, 1], "label": "A"}], "caption": "Third harmonic on a string fixed at both ends: four nodes (N), three antinodes (A), L = 3λ/2"}
```

### Example 2

A 0.65 m guitar string has mass 3.9 g and is under 80 N tension. Find the wave speed, the fundamental frequency, and the third harmonic.

$\mu = 0.0039/0.65 = 0.0060$ kg/m. $v = \sqrt{80/0.0060} = 115.5$ m/s.

$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L} = \dfrac{115.5}{1.30} = 88.8$ Hz. $f_3 = 3f_1 = 266$ Hz.

Pressing the string against a fret shortens $L$ and raises the pitch; to raise the fundamental an octave (double $f$), halve the length.

## Energy and intensity

A wave's energy is proportional to the square of its amplitude, and the power it carries is too. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the power. For waves spreading out in three dimensions from a point source, the power spreads over a sphere of area $4\pi r^2$, so the **[[intensity]]** (power per area, W/m²) is

$$I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2}.$$

That's another inverse-square law, which we'll use for sound.

## The wave function

A sinusoidal wave moving in the $+x$ direction can be written

$$y(x, t) = A\sin(kx - \omega t),$$

where $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the **[[wave number]]** (rad/m) and $\omega = 2\pi f$ (rad/s). Freeze time and you see a sine curve in space that repeats every $\lambda$; watch one point and you see SHM in time that repeats every $T$. A crest sits where $kx - \omega t$ has a fixed value, so as $t$ grows the crest's $x$ grows at speed $v = \omega/k = f\lambda$. Writing $kx + \omega t$ instead gives a wave moving in the $-x$ direction.

Each point of the string moves in SHM with amplitude $A$ and angular frequency $\omega$, so its maximum transverse speed is $A\omega$ (from the last lesson). That is not the wave speed $v$: one is how fast the string moves up and down, the other how fast the pattern moves along.

Adding a right-moving and a left-moving wave of the same amplitude, a trig identity gives

$$A\sin(kx - \omega t) + A\sin(kx + \omega t) = 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t),$$

a standing wave: a fixed shape $\sin(kx)$ whose size oscillates in time. Nodes are where $\sin kx = 0$, at $x = 0, \lambda/2, \lambda, \ldots$

## Common mistakes

- Thinking the medium travels with the wave.
- Thinking frequency changes when a wave enters a new medium (speed and wavelength change).
- Confusing the wave speed with the speed of the oscillating medium.
- Forgetting that adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, not $\lambda$.
- Using total mass instead of mass per length in $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$.

## Key points

- $v = f\lambda$; speed set by the medium, frequency by the source.
- String: $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$.
- Superposition: displacements add; path difference $m\lambda$ constructive, $(m + \tfrac12)\lambda$ destructive.
- Beats: $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|$.
- Fixed–fixed string: $\lambda_n = 2L/n$, $f_n = nv/(2L)$.
- $y = A\sin(kx - \omega t)$ with $k = 2\pi/\lambda$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.

lessons.title: Sound
lessons.body:
## Waves you can hear

Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave: a vibrating object pushes on neighboring air, creating alternating compressions (slightly higher pressure) and rarefactions (slightly lower), which travel outward. Everything from the last lesson applies, $v = f\lambda$, superposition, beats and standing waves, plus three new ideas specific to how we hear: loudness on the decibel scale, resonance in air columns (how wind instruments work), and the Doppler effect.

## Speed and pitch

The speed of sound depends on the medium: about 343 m/s in air at 20°C, 1480 m/s in water, around 5000 m/s in steel. In air it increases with temperature, roughly $v \approx 331 + 0.6\,T_C$ m/s (where $T_C$ is the Celsius temperature), because faster-moving molecules pass the disturbance along more quickly.

What we perceive as **[[pitch]]** corresponds to frequency. Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Below that is **[[infrasound]]** (used by elephants), above it is **[[ultrasound]]** (used by bats and medical imaging). An octave is a doubling of frequency.

## Intensity and the decibel scale

Sound intensity $I$ (W/m²) is the power per unit area carried by the wave. From a point source radiating equally in all directions, $I = P/(4\pi r^2)$: double the distance, a quarter of the intensity.

The ear responds to an enormous range: from the threshold of hearing, $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m², to the threshold of pain, about 1 W/m², a factor of $10^{12}$. Our perception of loudness is roughly logarithmic, so we use the **[[sound intensity level]]** in **[[decibels]]** (dB):

$$\beta = 10\log_{10}\frac{I}{I_0}.$$

Every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB; doubling the intensity adds $10\log 2 = 3$ dB. Normal conversation is about 60 dB ($10^{-6}$ W/m²), a rock concert 110 dB, and prolonged exposure above about 85 dB damages hearing.

### Example 1

A speaker produces 80 dB at 2.0 m. (a) What is the intensity there? (b) What is the level at 20 m (ignoring reflections)? (c) What is the level if a second identical speaker is added at the 2.0 m spot?

(a) $I = I_0\,10^{\beta/10} = 10^{-12}\times10^{8} = 10^{-4}$ W/m².

(b) Ten times farther means $1/100$ the intensity: $10^{-6}$ W/m², which is 60 dB. (Each factor of 10 in distance subtracts 20 dB.)

(c) Two speakers double the intensity: $80 + 3 = 83$ dB, not 160 dB.

## Standing waves in air columns

Wind instruments and organ pipes work by standing sound waves in a tube. The boundary conditions are about the air's displacement: at a closed end, air can't move, so there's a displacement node; at an open end, air moves freely, so there's an antinode (approximately at the opening).

*Open at both ends* (flute): antinodes at both ends, like a string with the roles swapped. A whole number of half-wavelengths fits:

$$f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$

*Closed at one end* (clarinet, a bottle you blow across): node at the closed end, antinode at the open end, so an odd number of quarter-wavelengths fits:

$$f_n = \frac{nv}{4L}, \qquad n = 1, 3, 5, \ldots \text{ (odd only)}$$

A closed pipe's fundamental is an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length, and it lacks the even harmonics, which gives it a darker sound.

The picture draws the air's displacement pattern for the first two modes of each kind of pipe. Count the quarter-wavelengths: each node-to-antinode stretch is $\lambda/4$.

![Four tubes of the same length, with curves showing how far the air moves along each. Open at both ends, fundamental: antinodes at both ends and one node in the middle, L = λ/2. Open at both ends, second harmonic: antinodes at both ends and the middle, two nodes, L = λ. Closed at the left end, fundamental: a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, L = λ/4. Closed at the left end, third harmonic: node at the closed end, then an antinode, a node and an antinode at the open end, L = 3λ/4.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2

An organ pipe 0.85 m long is closed at one end. With $v = 343$ m/s, find its fundamental and the next two frequencies it can produce. What would the fundamental be if the pipe were open at both ends?

Closed: $f_1 = \dfrac{343}{4(0.85)} = 100.9$ Hz; then $f_3 = 303$ Hz and $f_5 = 504$ Hz.

Open: $f_1 = \dfrac{343}{2(0.85)} = 202$ Hz, an octave higher.

## The Doppler effect

The pitch of an ambulance siren rises as it approaches and drops as it recedes. This is the **[[Doppler effect]]**: relative motion between source and observer changes the observed frequency.

- A moving *source* crowds the waves together ahead of it (shorter wavelength) and spreads them out behind.
- A moving *observer* runs into wave crests more often when approaching, less often when receding.

![Four circular wavefronts sent out by a source moving right at half the speed of sound. Each circle was emitted from an earlier position of the source, so the circles are crowded together on the right, ahead of the source, and spread apart on the left, behind it. An observer ahead receives a shorter wavelength and hears a higher pitch; an observer behind receives a longer wavelength and hears a lower pitch.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

With $v$ the speed of sound, $v_o$ the observer's speed and $v_s$ the source's speed (both relative to the air),

$$f' = f\,\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}.$$

Sign rule: use the upper signs (+ on top, − on the bottom) for motion *toward* the other party, which raises the frequency; lower signs for motion *away*. Check: approaching should always give a higher pitch.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the signs in the Doppler formula
  accDescr: Decide the top and bottom of the fraction separately. Top: if the observer moves toward the source use v + vo; if away, v − vo; if the observer is still, the top is just v. Bottom: if the source moves toward the observer use v − vs; if away, v + vs; if the source is still, the bottom is just v. Then f' = f times top divided by bottom. Check that approaching gives a higher frequency.
  O["Observer moving?"] -->|toward source| O1["Top: v + vo"]
  O -->|away from source| O2["Top: v − vo"]
  S["Source moving?"] -->|toward observer| S1["Bottom: v − vs"]
  S -->|away from observer| S2["Bottom: v + vs"]
  O1 & O2 & S1 & S2 --> R["f' = f × top ÷ bottom. Anything not moving: just v. Check: approaching raises f"]
```

### Example 3

An ambulance's siren emits 800 Hz. It drives at 30 m/s. What frequency does a stationary pedestrian hear (a) as it approaches and (b) after it passes? Use $v = 343$ m/s.

(a) Source toward observer: $f' = 800\dfrac{343}{343 - 30} = 800(1.0958) = 877$ Hz.

(b) Source away: $f' = 800\dfrac{343}{343 + 30} = 736$ Hz.

The pitch drops by about 141 Hz as it passes, which is the familiar "neee-owww."

When a source moves faster than sound, the wavefronts pile up into a cone, a **[[shock wave]]**, heard as a sonic boom. The cone's half-angle satisfies $\sin\theta = v/v_s$; the ratio $v_s/v$ is the Mach number.

Doppler shifts are used in radar speed guns, Doppler ultrasound of blood flow, and (for light) measuring how fast galaxies recede.

## Pressure and displacement

A sound wave can be described in two ways: by how far the air molecules are displaced from their usual positions, or by how much the pressure rises and falls. The two patterns are a quarter wavelength out of step. Where neighboring air moves toward a point from both sides, the air bunches up and the pressure swings are largest, yet the air right at that point barely moves. So a displacement node is a pressure antinode, and vice versa. That's why the closed end of a pipe, where the air can't move (displacement node), is where the pressure swings most (pressure antinode), and the open end, held near atmospheric pressure, is a pressure node.

The speed of sound in a fluid is $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$, where $B$ is the bulk modulus (how hard the fluid is to compress; see the elasticity lesson) and $\rho$ its density: the same "stiffness over inertia" pattern as $\sqrt{F_T/\mu}$ for a string. Water is much denser than air but far harder to compress, so sound travels over four times faster in it.

### Example 4

A pipe closed at one end resonates at 255 Hz and next at 425 Hz, with nothing in between. Is that consistent with a closed pipe, and how long is it? Use $v = 343$ m/s.

A closed pipe's resonances are odd multiples of $f_1$, so neighboring ones differ by $2f_1$: $2f_1 = 425 - 255 = 170$ Hz, giving $f_1 = 85$ Hz. Then $255 = 3(85)$ and $425 = 5(85)$, both odd multiples ✓. Length: $L = \dfrac{v}{4f_1} = \dfrac{343}{4(85)} = 1.01$ m.

## Common mistakes

- Adding decibel levels directly (two 80 dB sources give 83 dB, not 160 dB).
- Using $nv/(2L)$ for a pipe closed at one end, or including even harmonics for it.
- Getting Doppler signs backward (approach must raise the frequency).
- Using $v_s$ and $v_o$ relative to each other instead of relative to the air.

## Key points

- Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave; $v \approx 343$ m/s in air at 20°C.
- $\beta = 10\log(I/I_0)$, $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m²; ×10 in $I$ adds 10 dB; ×2 adds 3 dB.
- Open–open: $f_n = nv/(2L)$, all $n$. Closed–open: $f_n = nv/(4L)$, odd $n$.
- Doppler: $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$, upper signs for approaching.

lessons.title: Damped and driven oscillators
lessons.body:
## Beyond the ideal spring

The simple harmonic motion lesson ended with two short paragraphs: real oscillators lose energy (damping), and a periodic push at the natural frequency builds up a large amplitude (resonance). This lesson puts numbers on both. You'll learn how fast an oscillation dies away, what a single number called the quality factor tells you about any oscillator, how a driven oscillator responds at every driving frequency, and why engineers sometimes add damping on purpose. The results for the motion itself come from solving Newton's second law with calculus; here they are stated and then checked and used with algebra.

## A model of damping

Many damping forces, at least for slow motion, are roughly proportional to the velocity and opposite to it:

$$F_{\text{damp}} = -bv,$$

where the **[[damping constant]]** $b$ (in kg/s, the same as N·s/m) measures how strong the damping is. Air drag on a slow pendulum, oil being pushed through a car's shock absorber and the eddy-current brake of a lab balance all behave roughly this way. (Fast motion through air has drag closer to $v^2$, and sliding friction is roughly constant; the model below is a simplification that works well for many oscillators.)

With this force added to $-kx$, the solution for light damping is

$$x(t) = A_0\,e^{-bt/(2m)}\cos(\omega_d t), \qquad \omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \left(\frac{b}{2m}\right)^2},$$

where $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$ is the undamped (natural) angular frequency. Two things to notice:

- The amplitude $A_0e^{-bt/(2m)}$ decays *exponentially*: it shrinks by the same fraction in every equal time interval, just as a radioactive sample loses the same fraction every half-life. So the amplitude falls by the same fraction each cycle.
- Light damping barely changes the frequency. The correction to $\omega_0$ involves $(b/2m)^2$, which is tiny when the damping is weak.

Since energy is proportional to amplitude squared ($E = \tfrac12kA^2$), the energy decays twice as fast: $E(t) = E_0e^{-bt/m}$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 12.5], "y": [-1.2, 1.2], "xLabel": "time t (s)", "yLabel": "x / A0", "functions": [{"f": "exp(-0.15*x)*cos(2*pi*x)", "to": 10}, {"f": "exp(-0.15*x)", "dashed": true, "to": 10}, {"f": "-exp(-0.15*x)", "dashed": true, "to": 10}], "caption": "Light damping: the oscillation stays inside a shrinking exponential envelope (dashed), losing the same fraction of amplitude each cycle"}
```

## Underdamped, critically damped, overdamped

The formula for $\omega_d$ stops making sense when $b/(2m)$ reaches $\omega_0$. That boundary splits oscillators into three regimes:

- **[[Underdamped]]** ($b < 2\sqrt{mk}$): the system oscillates with shrinking amplitude. Guitar strings, pendulums and tuning forks are underdamped, and very lightly damped (far below critical).
- **[[Critically damped]]** ($b = 2\sqrt{mk}$): the system returns to equilibrium as fast as possible *without* overshooting.
- **[[Overdamped]]** ($b > 2\sqrt{mk}$): the system creeps back to equilibrium without overshooting, more slowly than with critical damping, because the large drag force holds it back.

The critical value $b_c = 2\sqrt{mk} = 2m\omega_0$ comes from setting $b/(2m) = \omega_0$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 7.5], "y": [-0.8, 1.1], "xLabel": "time t (s)", "yLabel": "x / x0", "functions": [{"f": "exp(-0.4*x)*(cos(1.9596*x) + 0.2041*sin(1.9596*x))", "to": 6}, {"f": "(1 + 2*x)*exp(-2*x)", "to": 6}, {"f": "(7.4641*exp(-0.5359*x) - 0.5359*exp(-7.4641*x))/6.9282", "dashed": true, "to": 6}], "caption": "The same oscillator (ω0 = 2 rad/s) released from rest at x0: underdamped (the curve that swings below zero), critically damped (solid, the fastest return without crossing zero) and overdamped (dashed, slower)"}
```

Devices that must settle quickly use damping near critical: analog meter needles, door closers, and car suspensions (which are usually tuned somewhat below critical, accepting a little overshoot for a softer ride).

### Example 1

A 0.50 kg block on a spring with $k = 200$ N/m has damping constant $b = 0.40$ kg/s. (a) Is it underdamped? (b) How long until the amplitude halves, and how many oscillations is that? (c) How much does damping change the frequency?

(a) $b_c = 2\sqrt{mk} = 2\sqrt{0.50 \times 200} = 20$ kg/s. Since $0.40 < 20$, it is underdamped (lightly).

(b) Half amplitude means $e^{-bt/(2m)} = \tfrac12$, so $\dfrac{bt}{2m} = \ln 2$ and

$$t_{1/2} = \frac{2m\ln 2}{b} = \frac{2(0.50)(0.693)}{0.40} = 1.73 \text{ s}.$$

With $\omega_0 = \sqrt{200/0.50} = 20$ rad/s, the period is $T = 2\pi/20 = 0.314$ s, so that's $1.73/0.314 \approx 5.5$ oscillations.

(c) $b/(2m) = 0.40$ s⁻¹, so $\omega_d = \sqrt{20^2 - 0.40^2} = 19.996$ rad/s, a change of 0.02%. Light damping shortens the motion's life, not its rhythm.

## The quality factor

One number summarizes how lightly damped an oscillator is. The **[[quality factor]]** is

$$Q = \frac{m\omega_0}{b} = \frac{\sqrt{mk}}{b}.$$

It is dimensionless, and a large $Q$ means light damping. For the block in Example 1, $Q = (0.50)(20)/0.40 = 25$. Three rules of thumb make $Q$ useful (the first two hold well when $Q$ is large, say above 10):

- **Energy per cycle.** Each cycle loses a fraction of about $2\pi/Q$ of the stored energy. Equivalently, $Q \approx 2\pi \times \dfrac{\text{energy stored}}{\text{energy lost per cycle}}$, which is often used as the definition.
- **Ringing time.** After $Q$ cycles, the amplitude has fallen to $e^{-\pi} \approx 4\%$ of its starting value. (Check: $Q$ cycles take $t = Q\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega_0} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{b}$, and then $\dfrac{bt}{2m} = \pi$.) So $Q$ is roughly "how many times it rings before it's nearly quiet."
- **Regimes.** Critical damping is exactly $Q = \tfrac12$; underdamped means $Q > \tfrac12$.

Very rough typical values: a car suspension well under 1, a playground swing in the tens, a tuning fork in the thousands, and the quartz crystal in a watch (which vibrates at 32 768 Hz) tens of thousands or more. A high $Q$ is what makes a good clock: the oscillator keeps its own rhythm and needs only a tiny push each cycle.

### Example 2

A pendulum's amplitude drops by 2.0% each cycle. (a) What fraction of the amplitude is left after 50 cycles? (b) What fraction of its energy does it lose per cycle? (c) Estimate $Q$.

(a) Each cycle multiplies the amplitude by 0.980, so after 50 cycles: $0.980^{50} = 0.364$, about 36%. (Not $1 - 50(0.02) = 0$: the losses compound, like interest.)

(b) Energy goes as amplitude squared: $0.980^2 = 0.9604$, so it loses $1 - 0.9604 = 0.0396$, about 4.0% per cycle, twice the amplitude percentage (for small losses).

(c) $Q \approx 2\pi/0.0396 \approx 160$.

## Driven oscillations and resonance

Now push the oscillator with a periodic force $F_0\cos(\omega t)$, where $\omega$ is the **[[driving frequency]]**, chosen by whoever is pushing, and $\omega_0$ is the oscillator's own natural frequency. At first the motion is a mess (a mix of the natural oscillation and the forced one), but the natural part dies away with damping. What remains is the **[[steady state]]**: the oscillator moves at the *driving* frequency, with amplitude

$$A = \frac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}.$$

Look at three cases:

- **Slow driving** ($\omega \ll \omega_0$): $A \approx \dfrac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^2} = \dfrac{F_0}{k}$, the stretch a steady force $F_0$ would produce. The spring simply follows the force.
- **Driving at the natural frequency** ($\omega = \omega_0$): the first term vanishes and $A = \dfrac{F_0}{b\omega_0} = Q\,\dfrac{F_0}{k}$. The response is $Q$ times the static stretch, and only the damping limits it.
- **Fast driving** ($\omega \gg \omega_0$): $A \approx \dfrac{F_0}{m\omega^2}$, small. The mass's inertia can't keep up.

```plot
{"x": [0, 2.4], "y": [0, 11], "xLabel": "ω / ω0", "yLabel": "amplitude ÷ (F0/k)", "functions": [{"f": "1/sqrt((1 - x^2)^2 + (x/10)^2)", "to": 2}, {"f": "1/sqrt((1 - x^2)^2 + (x/5)^2)", "to": 2}, {"f": "1/sqrt((1 - x^2)^2 + (x/2)^2)", "to": 2}], "caption": "Resonance curves against driving frequency ω / ω0 for Q = 10 (tallest peak), Q = 5 (middle) and Q = 2 (lowest): the higher the Q, the taller and narrower the peak near ω = ω0", "labels": [{"at": [1.0, 10.3], "text": "Q = 10"}, {"at": [0.93, 1.2], "text": "Q = 2"}]}
```

The peak is not only tall but narrow. The range of driving frequencies over which the oscillator responds strongly (amplitude above about 71% of the peak, which is half the peak energy) has a width of about

$$\Delta\omega \approx \frac{\omega_0}{Q}.$$

A high-$Q$ oscillator is *selective*: it responds strongly to one frequency and ignores its neighbors. That is how a radio tuner picks one station, and why a wine glass (high $Q$) can be shattered by a loud tone held at exactly its pitch.

**Why the peak is at $\omega_0$: the phase.** At steady state the displacement lags behind the force. For slow driving the lag is near zero; at $\omega_0$ it is a quarter cycle ($90^\circ$), and for fast driving it approaches half a cycle. A quarter-cycle lag in position means the *velocity* is exactly in step with the force, so the force pushes forward whenever the mass moves forward and does positive work all the time. That maximizes the power fed in, just like pushing a swing as it moves away from you. (Strictly, the *amplitude* peaks slightly below $\omega_0$, at $\omega_0\sqrt{1 - 1/(2Q^2)}$, and the power peaks exactly at $\omega_0$; for $Q$ above about 3 the difference is under 3%.)

### Example 3

The oscillator of Example 1 ($m = 0.50$ kg, $k = 200$ N/m, $b = 0.40$ kg/s, $Q = 25$) is driven by a force of amplitude $F_0 = 1.0$ N. Find the steady-state amplitude at $\omega = 20$, 18 and 40 rad/s.

The static stretch is $F_0/k = 1.0/200 = 0.0050$ m = 5.0 mm, and $F_0/m = 2.0$ N/kg.

At $\omega = 20$ rad/s (resonance): $A = \dfrac{F_0}{b\omega_0} = \dfrac{1.0}{0.40 \times 20} = 0.125$ m $= 125$ mm, which is $25 \times 5.0$ mm $= Q\times$ static ✓.

At $\omega = 18$ rad/s: $\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 = 400 - 324 = 76$ and $b\omega/m = 0.40(18)/0.50 = 14.4$.
$A = \dfrac{2.0}{\sqrt{76^2 + 14.4^2}} = \dfrac{2.0}{77.4} = 0.0259$ m $\approx 26$ mm.

At $\omega = 40$ rad/s: $400 - 1600 = -1200$ and $b\omega/m = 32$, so $A = 2.0/1200.4 = 0.00167$ m $\approx 1.7$ mm.

Driving just 10% off resonance cuts the response by a factor of about 5: the peak has width $\Delta\omega \approx 20/25 = 0.8$ rad/s.

## Resonance in structures

Resonance is a design problem for anything with a natural frequency that might be driven: machines with rotating parts, bridges under footsteps, buildings in wind and earthquakes. Engineers move the natural frequency away from likely driving frequencies (by changing stiffness or mass) or add damping, which lowers $Q$ and so lowers the peak.

One clever fix is the **[[tuned mass damper]]**: a second, smaller oscillator attached to the structure, tuned to the structure's natural frequency and damped. When the building sways, the damper swings out of step with it and soaks up energy. Taipei 101 has a famous one: a steel sphere of roughly 660 tonnes hung between its upper floors.

Two well-known stories are often told as simple resonance, and both are more subtle:

- **London's Millennium Bridge** (opened June 2000) swayed sideways on its opening weekend and was closed within days. The cause was a feedback loop: as the deck began to sway, walkers adjusted their steps to keep balance, pushing in step with the sway and making it worse. Dampers were fitted, and it reopened in 2002.
- **The Tacoma Narrows Bridge** (collapsed November 1940) is often described as wind "matching its resonant frequency." That's simplified: a steady wind doesn't push at a fixed frequency. Engineers attribute the collapse to aeroelastic flutter, a self-excited oscillation in which the bridge's own twisting changed the wind forces so that they fed energy into the twisting.

### Example 4

A simplified "quarter car" puts 400 kg of a car's mass on one spring with $k = 4.0\times10^4$ N/m. Find the natural frequency and the damping constant that would make the suspension critically damped.

$\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{40\,000/400} = 10$ rad/s, so $f_0 = \omega_0/2\pi = 1.6$ Hz, a typical bounce rate for a car.

$b_c = 2\sqrt{mk} = 2\sqrt{400 \times 40\,000} = 2(4000) = 8000$ kg/s. (Check: $2m\omega_0 = 2(400)(10) = 8000$ ✓.) A shock absorber with $b$ well below this lets the car bounce several times after a bump; one well above it makes the ride feel stiff and slow to recover.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming the amplitude drops by the same *amount* each cycle. It drops by the same *fraction* (exponential decay), so the percentages compound.
- Forgetting that energy goes as amplitude squared: 2% amplitude loss per cycle is about 4% energy loss.
- Thinking a driven oscillator moves at its natural frequency. In steady state it moves at the driving frequency; the natural frequency only sets how strongly it responds.
- Thinking more damping always means faster settling. Overdamped systems settle more slowly than critically damped ones.
- Treating $Q$ rules of thumb ($2\pi/Q$ per cycle, width $\omega_0/Q$) as exact for small $Q$; they are approximations for light damping.

## Key points

- Linear damping $F = -bv$: amplitude $\propto e^{-bt/(2m)}$, energy $\propto e^{-bt/m}$; light damping hardly changes the frequency.
- Critical damping: $b_c = 2\sqrt{mk}$ ($Q = \tfrac12$). Below it, the system oscillates; above it, it creeps back.
- $Q = m\omega_0/b$: about $2\pi/Q$ of the energy lost per cycle; amplitude down to about 4% after $Q$ cycles.
- Driven at $\omega$: the steady state oscillates at $\omega$. Amplitude is $F_0/k$ for slow driving, $QF_0/k$ at resonance, and small for fast driving.
- Resonance width $\Delta\omega \approx \omega_0/Q$; at resonance the velocity is in step with the force.

lessons.title: Harmonics, timbre, and musical scales
lessons.body:
## Why a violin doesn't sound like a flute

The waves lesson said that a plucked string vibrates in a mix of harmonics and that the mix gives each instrument its tone quality; the sound lesson showed that a pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics. Play the same note, say A at 440 Hz, on a violin, a flute and a clarinet, and you hear three different sounds with the same pitch. This lesson explains why, using one of the most useful ideas in all of physics (Fourier's theorem), and then uses harmonics and beats to explain why some pairs of notes sound smooth together, and why a modern piano is, by design, slightly out of tune.

## Fourier's theorem

In his work on heat flow (published in 1822), Joseph Fourier claimed that any repeating pattern can be built from sine waves. In the form used for sound:

> **Fourier's theorem.** Any periodic wave with period $T$ (frequency $f_1 = 1/T$) can be written as a sum of sine waves with frequencies $f_1$, $2f_1$, $3f_1$, $\ldots$, each with its own amplitude and phase.

(Mathematicians later had to make "any" precise, but every wave a musician will meet qualifies.) The sine waves are exactly the harmonics: a repeating wave can contain *only* whole-number multiples of its repetition frequency. Breaking a wave into its harmonics is called **[[Fourier analysis]]**, and a graph of each harmonic's amplitude against its frequency is the wave's **[[spectrum]]**. Building a wave by adding harmonics is Fourier synthesis.

A clean example is the square wave, which jumps between $+1$ and $-1$ every half period. It contains only odd harmonics, with amplitudes falling as $1/n$:

$$\text{square wave} = \frac{4}{\pi}\left[\sin(2\pi f_1t) + \tfrac13\sin(2\pi\cdot3f_1t) + \tfrac15\sin(2\pi\cdot5f_1t) + \cdots\right]$$

```plot
{"x": [0, 2.3], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "xLabel": "t / T", "yLabel": "displacement", "functions": [{"f": "(4/pi)*sin(2*pi*x)", "dashed": true, "to": 2}, {"f": "(4/pi)*(sin(2*pi*x) + sin(6*pi*x)/3 + sin(10*pi*x)/5 + sin(14*pi*x)/7 + sin(18*pi*x)/9)", "to": 2}], "caption": "Adding odd harmonics with amplitudes 1, 1/3, 1/5, … builds a square wave: dashed, the 1st harmonic alone; solid, the sum of the first five odd harmonics (time in periods)"}
```

A sawtooth wave (rising steadily, then dropping) contains *all* harmonics with amplitudes $1/n$. The two waves have the same period and so the same pitch; they differ only in their spectra.

```plot
{"x": [0, 11.5], "y": [0, 1.15], "xLabel": "harmonic n", "yLabel": "amplitude (fundamental = 1)", "bars": [{"x": 1, "height": 1, "width": 0.6}, {"x": 3, "height": 0.3333, "width": 0.6}, {"x": 5, "height": 0.2, "width": 0.6}, {"x": 7, "height": 0.1429, "width": 0.6}, {"x": 9, "height": 0.1111, "width": 0.6}], "caption": "Spectrum of a square wave: odd harmonics only, amplitude 1/n"}
```

## Timbre

**[[Timbre]]** (pronounced "TAM-ber") is the quality that tells two sounds of the same pitch and loudness apart. Its main ingredient is the spectrum: which harmonics are present and how strong. Roughly:

- A flute's tone is close to a pure sine, with weak upper harmonics.
- A clarinet, a pipe effectively closed at one end, has strong odd harmonics and weak even ones in its low register. (Simplified: real clarinets do produce some even harmonics, and the pattern changes in the upper register.)
- A bowed violin string has a rich spectrum with many strong harmonics, close to a sawtooth.

How a sound starts and dies away also matters (a piano note played backward sounds like a different instrument), so the spectrum is the main part of timbre, not all of it.

**Pitch from the pattern.** We hear the pitch of a complex tone at its repetition frequency $f_1$, even if that harmonic is weak or missing. If a sound has components at 600, 800 and 1000 Hz, it repeats 200 times a second (all three are multiples of 200 Hz), and most listeners hear a 200 Hz pitch. This "missing fundamental" effect is why a small phone speaker that can't produce 100 Hz still lets you recognize a deep voice.

### Example 1

A complex tone contains components at 450, 750 and 1050 Hz. (a) What pitch do you expect to hear? (b) Which harmonics are these? (c) Could this tone come from an ideal pipe closed at one end?

(a) The wave repeats at the greatest frequency that divides all three: 450 = 3(150), 750 = 5(150), 1050 = 7(150), so $f_1 = 150$ Hz. (No larger frequency works: 300 Hz, for instance, doesn't divide 450.) The pitch is 150 Hz, even though nothing is present at 150 Hz.

(b) The 3rd, 5th and 7th harmonics.

(c) Yes: all are odd harmonics, which fits a closed pipe (with its fundamental unusually weak).

## Where you pluck matters

For an ideal string, harmonic $n$ has nodes at $L/n$, $2L/n$, …. Plucking (or striking) a point gives that point a large displacement, so harmonics with a node there are not excited at all. Pluck a string exactly in the middle and every even harmonic, which has a node at $L/2$, is missing: the tone is hollow, like a clarinet's. Pluck near the end (as at a guitar's bridge) and many harmonics are present: a bright, twangy tone. This is one reason guitarists move their picking hand to change the sound. (Real strings are stiff and pluck points are not exact, so a "missing" harmonic is in practice just much weaker.)

### Example 2

A string is plucked one-third of the way along. Which of the first nine harmonics are missing?

Harmonic $n$ has a node at $L/3$ if $L/3$ is a whole multiple of $L/n$, which happens when $n$ is a multiple of 3. So harmonics 3, 6 and 9 are missing; 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8 are present.

## Consonance and beats between harmonics

Two notes sound smooth together (consonant) when their frequencies are in a simple whole-number ratio. The main **[[musical intervals]]**:

| Interval | Ratio | Example from A3 = 220 Hz |
|---|---|---|
| Octave | 2 : 1 | 440 Hz |
| Perfect fifth | 3 : 2 | 330 Hz |
| Perfect fourth | 4 : 3 | 293.3 Hz |
| Major third | 5 : 4 | 275 Hz |

One explanation, proposed by Hermann von Helmholtz in the 1860s, uses harmonics. With a simple ratio, many harmonics of the two notes *coincide*: in a 3 : 2 fifth, the 3rd harmonic of the lower note equals the 2nd of the upper. When the ratio is slightly off, those near-coinciding harmonics produce beats, heard as roughness. This is one of the main accounts of the physical side, but the question is not settled: a rival account says listeners prefer combinations whose harmonics together still fit a single harmonic series, and musical training and culture also shape what sounds pleasant.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1600], "y": [0, 1.3], "xLabel": "f (Hz)", "yLabel": "harmonics", "segments": [{"from": [220, 0], "to": [220, 1]}, {"from": [440, 0], "to": [440, 1]}, {"from": [660, 0], "to": [660, 1]}, {"from": [880, 0], "to": [880, 1]}, {"from": [1100, 0], "to": [1100, 1]}, {"from": [1320, 0], "to": [1320, 1]}, {"from": [330, 0], "to": [330, 0.7], "dashed": true}, {"from": [660, 0], "to": [660, 0.7], "dashed": true}, {"from": [990, 0], "to": [990, 0.7], "dashed": true}, {"from": [1320, 0], "to": [1320, 0.7], "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [660, 1.15], "text": "coincide"}, {"at": [1320, 1.15], "text": "coincide"}], "caption": "Harmonics of 220 Hz (solid) and 330 Hz (dashed): in a perfect fifth every 2nd harmonic of the upper note lands on a harmonic of the lower"}
```

Piano tuners use exactly this. To tune a fifth, they listen to the beat between the two nearly coinciding harmonics, which is much easier to hear than the fifth itself.

### Example 3

An A at 220 Hz and an E are played together. (a) If the E is exactly 330 Hz, what is the beat rate between the A's 3rd harmonic and the E's 2nd? (b) If the E is 331 Hz?

(a) $3(220) = 660$ Hz and $2(330) = 660$ Hz: no beats; the fifth is "pure."

(b) $2(331) = 662$ Hz, so $f_{\text{beat}} = 662 - 660 = 2$ Hz. A 1 Hz mistuning of the E shows up as 2 beats per second, because the 2nd harmonic is off by twice as much.

## Equal temperament and cents

A keyboard has 12 notes per octave. If every fifth were a pure 3 : 2, twelve fifths would have to equal seven octaves, but $(3/2)^{12} = 129.7$ while $2^7 = 128$. The small mismatch, about 1.4%, is called the Pythagorean comma, and no fixed tuning can make every interval pure.

The modern compromise is **[[equal temperament]]**: the octave is split into 12 equal frequency *ratios*, called **[[semitones]]**, each

$$r = 2^{1/12} = 1.059\,46.$$

A note $n$ semitones above (or, with $n$ negative, below) a reference has frequency $f = f_{\text{ref}}\cdot 2^{n/12}$. The standard reference is A4 = 440 Hz.

Small pitch differences are measured in **[[cents]]**: 100 cents per equal-tempered semitone, 1200 per octave. For two frequencies,

$$\text{cents} = 1200\log_2\frac{f_2}{f_1}.$$

An equal-tempered fifth is exactly 700 cents, while a pure 3 : 2 fifth is $1200\log_2 1.5 = 702.0$ cents: the tempered fifth is 2 cents narrow, which almost nobody notices. The tempered major third (400 cents) is about 14 cents wider than a pure 5 : 4 (386.3 cents), which is audible as a gentle beating in sustained chords. Equal temperament spreads the error so that every key sounds equally (slightly) impure.

### Example 4

(a) Find middle C (C4), 9 semitones below A4 = 440 Hz. (b) An equal-tempered fifth is played from A3 = 220 Hz. How fast do the A's 3rd harmonic and the E's 2nd harmonic beat?

(a) $f = 440 \cdot 2^{-9/12} = 440(0.5946) = 261.6$ Hz.

(b) The E is 7 semitones up: $220 \cdot 2^{7/12} = 329.63$ Hz. Its 2nd harmonic is 659.26 Hz; the A's 3rd is 660 Hz. Beat rate $= 660 - 659.26 = 0.74$ Hz, a slow wavering about once every 1.3 s. That slow beat is what a tuner listens for when setting tempered fifths.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking the pitch is set by the strongest harmonic. Pitch follows the repetition rate $f_1$, even when that component is missing.
- Expecting a periodic wave to contain frequencies that are not whole multiples of $f_1$. (Real stiff strings, like a piano's, have overtones slightly above exact multiples, so they are only approximately periodic.)
- Adding semitones by adding hertz. Intervals are ratios: each semitone *multiplies* by $2^{1/12}$.
- Forgetting that the $n$th harmonic magnifies a mistuning $n$ times when counting beats between harmonics.
- Using $\log_{10}$ instead of $\log_2$ in the cents formula (or forgetting the 1200).

## Key points

- Fourier: a periodic wave of frequency $f_1$ is a sum of harmonics $nf_1$; the amplitudes form its spectrum.
- Square wave: odd harmonics, amplitudes $1/n$. Sawtooth: all harmonics, $1/n$.
- Timbre is mainly the spectrum (plus how the sound starts and decays); pitch follows $f_1$.
- Plucking at a point removes harmonics that have a node there.
- Simple ratios (2:1, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4) are consonant; near-misses beat between harmonics.
- Equal temperament: semitone ratio $2^{1/12}$, $f = 440\cdot2^{n/12}$; cents $= 1200\log_2(f_2/f_1)$; tempered fifth 700 vs pure 702 cents.

lessons.title: Wave reflection, impedance, and ultrasound imaging
lessons.body:
## Echoes from inside the body

The waves lesson showed that a pulse on a string reflects upside down from a fixed end and right side up from a free end. Most real boundaries are in between: a light rope tied to a heavy one, sound passing from fat into muscle, or from air into skin. Part of the wave goes on and part bounces back. This lesson finds out *how much*, using one number per medium called its impedance, and then applies the result, together with the wave speed and the Doppler effect from the sound lesson, to medical ultrasound, which builds pictures of the inside of the body from echoes.

## Impedance: how hard a medium is to shake

When a wave arrives at a boundary, the two media must move together at the boundary point. If the second medium is "harder to shake" than the first, the boundary moves less than the incoming wave wants, and the difference is sent back as a reflection. The measure of how hard a medium is to shake is its **[[wave impedance]]** $Z$.

- For a string: $Z = \mu v = \sqrt{F_T\mu}$ (units kg/s). A heavier or tighter string is harder to move.
- For sound in a fluid or soft material: the **[[acoustic impedance]]** is $Z = \rho v$, density times speed of sound, in kg/(m²·s), a unit called the rayl.

Only the *ratio* of the two impedances matters. At a boundary hit straight on, the fraction of the wave's intensity (power) that reflects is

$$R = \left(\frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2,$$

and the rest, $T = 1 - R$, is transmitted. (Here and below, "straight on" means the wave hits the boundary perpendicularly; that's the case for imaging along a beam.) The fraction is the same in either direction across the boundary, and $R = 0$ when $Z_1 = Z_2$: matched media let a wave through without any echo, even if their densities and speeds differ.

For displacement on a string, the reflected wave's amplitude is $\dfrac{Z_1 - Z_2}{Z_1 + Z_2}$ times the incoming amplitude. If $Z_2 > Z_1$ this is negative: the reflection is inverted. A fixed end is the limit $Z_2 \to \infty$ (amplitude ratio $-1$, inverted), and a free end is $Z_2 \to 0$ (ratio $+1$, upright), the two cases from the waves lesson.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [0, 1], "xLabel": "impedance ratio Z2 / Z1", "yLabel": "fraction reflected R", "functions": [{"f": "((x - 1)/(x + 1))^2"}], "points": [{"at": [1, 0]}], "caption": "Reflected fraction of intensity against impedance ratio: R = 0 (no echo) when the impedances match (ratio 1), and a ratio of 1/r gives the same R as r", "labels": [{"at": [1.45, 0.2], "text": "no echo"}]}
```

### Example 1

A rope with $\mu_1 = 0.010$ kg/m is tied to one with $\mu_2 = 0.040$ kg/m, both under 100 N tension. A pulse comes along the light rope. Describe the reflected pulse and find the fractions of energy reflected and transmitted.

Impedances: $Z_1 = \sqrt{100 \times 0.010} = 1.0$ kg/s and $Z_2 = \sqrt{100 \times 0.040} = 2.0$ kg/s.

Amplitude ratio: $\dfrac{1.0 - 2.0}{1.0 + 2.0} = -\tfrac13$, so the reflected pulse is inverted with one-third the height.

$R = \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \tfrac19 = 11\%$ of the energy reflects and $T = 89\%$ goes on into the heavy rope (where the wave is slower: $v_2 = \sqrt{100/0.040} = 50$ m/s versus 100 m/s).

## Acoustic impedances in the body

| Medium | Density (kg/m³) | Speed (m/s) | $Z$ (kg/(m²·s)) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Air | 1.2 | 343 | $4.1\times10^{2}$ |
| Water | 1000 | 1480 | $1.48\times10^6$ |
| Fat | 950 | 1450 | $1.38\times10^6$ |
| Soft tissue (average) | 1060 | 1540 | $1.63\times10^6$ |
| Muscle | 1070 | 1580 | $1.69\times10^6$ |
| Bone | 1900 | 4080 | $7.8\times10^6$ |

These are typical values: real tissues vary by a few percent, and bone varies much more. The pattern is what matters. Soft tissues are all close to water, so boundaries between them reflect only about 1% or less; bone is about five times higher; air is about four thousand times *lower*.

### Example 2

(a) What fraction of an ultrasound pulse reflects at a fat–muscle boundary, and at a muscle–bone boundary? (b) Why must the probe be coupled to the skin with gel?

(a) Fat–muscle: $R = \left(\dfrac{1.69 - 1.38}{1.69 + 1.38}\right)^2 = (0.101)^2 = 0.010$, about 1%. Small, but measurable, which is why organ boundaries show up in an image.

Muscle–bone: $R = \left(\dfrac{7.8 - 1.69}{7.8 + 1.69}\right)^2 = (0.644)^2 = 0.41$, about 40%. Bone throws back a strong echo and leaves a "shadow" behind it, which is one reason ultrasound is poor at imaging through bone.

(b) If a thin layer of air is trapped between probe and skin: $R = \left(\dfrac{1.63\times10^6 - 412}{1.63\times10^6 + 412}\right)^2 = 0.999$. Only 0.1% gets in, and of an echo coming back out, only 0.1% gets through again, a round trip of about one part in a million. The gel, whose impedance is close to water's, fills the gap: gel to tissue gives $R \approx \left(\tfrac{1.63 - 1.48}{1.63 + 1.48}\right)^2 = 0.002$.

Inside the probe, a similar problem arises between the **[[transducer]]** (a piezoelectric crystal that converts electrical signals to sound and back, with $Z$ in the tens of millions) and the skin. Probes add one or more **[[matching layers]]** with intermediate impedance; a layer a quarter-wavelength thick with $Z = \sqrt{Z_1Z_2}$ cancels the reflection at one frequency, the same trick as the anti-reflection coatings in the wave optics lesson. (Simplified: real probes use several layers to work over a range of frequencies.)

## Pulse-echo imaging

An ultrasound scanner sends a very short pulse into the body and listens. Each boundary returns a weak echo, and the arrival time tells how deep it is. The pulse travels to the boundary and back, so with speed $v$ and round-trip time $t$,

$$d = \frac{vt}{2}.$$

Scanners assume $v = 1540$ m/s for all soft tissue (a simplification that causes small distance errors in fat, where sound is slower). The strength of the echo sets the brightness of the dot at that depth, and sweeping the beam across builds a two-dimensional image.

![A cross-section of the body below an ultrasound probe. The transducer sits on a thin layer of coupling gel above layers of fat, muscle and bone. A pulse arrow goes down through the layers; a weak echo of about 1% returns from the fat–muscle boundary and a strong echo of about 40% returns from the muscle–bone boundary.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a pulse-echo ultrasound image is made
  accDescr: The transducer sends a short pulse into the body. At each boundary between tissues a small part of the pulse reflects. The echoes travel back and the transducer turns them into electrical signals. The scanner converts each echo's delay into depth using d = vt/2 and its strength into brightness. The beam is then swept sideways and the process repeated, line by line, to build an image.
  A["Transducer sends a short pulse"] --> B["Pulse crosses tissue boundaries"]
  B --> C["Part of the pulse reflects at each boundary"]
  C --> D["Echoes return; transducer turns them into electrical signals"]
  D --> E["Delay gives depth d = vt/2; strength gives brightness"]
  E --> F["Beam sweeps sideways; repeat line by line to build the image"]
```
