So the result is $-3\hat\imath + 6\hat\jmath - 3\hat k$; check: its dot product with $(1, 2, 3)$ is $-3 + 12 - 9 = 0$. The opposite vector is $\vec B\times\vec A$; $-6$ in the middle comes from breaking the cyclic order in the $y$ component; multiplying matching components is not a cross product at all.

questions.stem: Three nonzero vectors have $\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C) = 0$. This tells you that the three vectors
questions.explanation: The absolute value of the triple product is the volume of the box on the three vectors. Zero volume means the box is flat: the vectors are coplanar. They need not be parallel (three vectors in the $xy$ plane pointing different ways also give zero). Mutually perpendicular vectors give the largest volume for their lengths, not zero.

questions.stem: What is the area of the triangle whose two sides from one corner are $\vec A = 2\hat\imath$ m and $\vec B = 3\hat\jmath$ m?
questions.explanation: $\vec A\times\vec B = 6\hat k$ m², so the parallelogram on $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ has area 6 m², and the triangle is half of it: 3 m². (For this right triangle, $\tfrac12 \times 2 \times 3 = 3$ m² agrees.) 6 m² is the whole parallelogram; 1.5 m² halves a second time; 0 is the dot product.

questions.stem: A force $\vec F = 10\hat\imath$ N is described using axes rotated $30^\circ$ counterclockwise from the original ones. What are its new components $(F_{x'}, F_{y'})$?
questions.explanation: $F_{x'} = F_x\cos30^\circ + F_y\sin30^\circ = 8.66$ N and $F_{y'} = -F_x\sin30^\circ + F_y\cos30^\circ = -5.00$ N. The $x'$ axis has turned $30^\circ$ counterclockwise past the force, so the force lies $30^\circ$ below $x'$: its $y'$ component is negative. Check: $\sqrt{8.66^2 + 5^2} = 10$ N. Rotating the vector instead of the axes gives $(8.66, 5.00)$.

questions.stem: Rotating the coordinate axes changes which of these?
choices: The dot product of two vectors
questions.explanation: Components are measured along the axes, so they change when the axes turn. The vector itself doesn't, so its length, the angle between two vectors and their dot product $AB\cos\phi$ are the same in every set of axes.

questions.stem: Which expression is the vector projection of $\vec B$ onto $\vec A$ (the part of $\vec B$ along $\vec A$)?
questions.explanation: The component of $\vec B$ along $\vec A$ is $\vec A\cdot\vec B/A$; multiplying by the unit vector $\vec A/A$ gives $(\vec A\cdot\vec B/A^2)\vec A$. The other two dot-product forms have the wrong length unless $A = 1$, and the cross product points perpendicular to $\vec A$.

questions.stem: The picture shows the parallelogram formed by two vectors from the same point. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A shaded parallelogram. Arrow 1 runs along the bottom edge to the right. Arrow 2 rises up and to the right from the same corner. Line 3 is dotted and drops straight down from the tip of arrow 2 to the bottom edge. Mark 4 is a circle with a dot in the middle of the parallelogram. Mark 5 is an arc at the corner between arrows 1 and 2.

choices: Direction of A × B (out of the page)
Angle φ between A and B
questions.explanation: The base is $\vec A$ (1) and the slanted side is $\vec B$ (2). The dotted height (3) is $B\sin\phi$, so the area is $AB\sin\phi = |\vec A\times\vec B|$. The circle with a dot (4) is an arrow pointing out of the page: curling the fingers from $\vec A$ (right) toward $\vec B$ (up-right) is counterclockwise, so the thumb points out. $\vec B\times\vec A$ would point into the page. The angle $\phi$ (5) is at the shared tail.

questions.stem: Write $\hat\imath\times\hat k$ as a signed unit vector (for example, -i). $\hat\imath\times\hat k =$ ___
questions.explanation: Forward around the cycle, $\hat k\times\hat\imath = \hat\jmath$. Reversing the order flips the sign, so $\hat\imath\times\hat k = -\hat\jmath$. Check with the formula: $(1, 0, 0)\times(0, 0, 1) = (0\cdot1 - 0\cdot0,\ 0\cdot0 - 1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot0 - 0\cdot0) = (0, -1, 0)$.

questions.stem: For $\vec A = 3\hat\imath - \hat\jmath + 2\hat k$ and $\vec B = \hat\imath + 2\hat\jmath$, $\vec A\times\vec B =$ ___ $\hat\imath$ + ___ $\hat\jmath$ + ___ $\hat k$. Give each component as a number.
Which of these are true for all vectors $\vec A$, $\vec B$, $\vec C$? Select all that apply.
choices: $\vec A\times(\vec B\times\vec C) = (\vec A\times\vec B)\times\vec C$
questions.explanation: The cross product is anticommutative (swapping flips the sign), so the third statement is false except when the product is zero. $\vec A\times\vec B$ is perpendicular to $\vec A$, so its dot product with $\vec A$ is 0. $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\phi \le AB$. The cross product is not associative: for example, $\hat\imath\times(\hat\imath\times\hat\jmath) = \hat\imath\times\hat k = -\hat\jmath$, but $(\hat\imath\times\hat\imath)\times\hat\jmath = 0$.

questions.stem: Match each expression to its geometric meaning.
choices: Area of the parallelogram on A and B
Volume of the box on A, B and C
questions.explanation: The cross product's magnitude $AB\sin\phi$ is base times height of the parallelogram. The triple product's absolute value is base area times height of the box. Dividing $\vec A\cdot\vec B$ by $A$ gives the scalar projection of $\vec B$ on $\vec A$. Dividing a vector by its magnitude gives a unit vector. The angle needs an inverse cosine: $\phi = \cos^{-1}[\vec A\cdot\vec B/(AB)]$.

questions.stem: A force $\vec F = 50\hat k$ N acts at $\vec r = 0.40\hat\imath$ m from a pivot. What is the torque $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$?
questions.explanation: $\vec r\times\vec F = (0.40)(50)\,(\hat\imath\times\hat k) = 20(-\hat\jmath) = -20\hat\jmath$ N·m, since $\hat\imath\times\hat k = -\hat\jmath$. Getting $+20\hat\jmath$ means computing $\vec F\times\vec r$ (or $\hat k\times\hat\imath$). A torque is perpendicular to both $\vec r$ and $\vec F$, so it can't point along $\hat k$; it would be zero only if $\vec r$ and $\vec F$ were parallel.

questions.stem: A positive charge moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A region full of × marks. A positive charge sits at the bottom of a circle, with a red arrow pointing right (marker 1) and a blue arrow pointing up toward the circle's center (marker 2). Marker 3 is the center of the circle; marker 4 is one of the × marks in a corner.

choices: Magnetic field out of the page
questions.explanation: The × marks are arrow tails, so the field points into the page (4). The velocity (1) is tangent to the circle, and the magnetic force (2) is perpendicular to it, toward the center (3). Check with the right-hand rule: fingers right along $\vec v$, curl into the page toward $\vec B$, and the thumb points up, toward the center, for a positive charge.

questions.stem: An ion moves in a circle of radius 12 cm in a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is tripled (same field, same ion), the radius becomes ___ cm. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $r = \dfrac{mv}{|q|B}$ is proportional to $v$, so tripling the speed triples the radius: $3 \times 12 = 36$ cm. (The period, $2\pi m/(|q|B)$, stays the same: the ion goes around a bigger circle faster.)

questions.stem: Which statements about the magnetic force on a moving charged particle are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It can speed the particle up if the field is strong enough
It is always perpendicular to the particle's velocity
It is zero when the particle moves parallel to the field
It points the same way for a proton and an electron with the same velocity
It does no work on the particle
questions.explanation: $\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B$ is perpendicular to $\vec v$, so it does no work and never changes the speed (the first statement is false). With $\vec v$ parallel to $\vec B$, $\sin\theta = 0$ and the force vanishes. A proton and an electron have opposite charges, so with the same velocity they feel forces in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a mass spectrometer measurement in order.
choices: Ionize the atoms of the sample
Accelerate the ions through a voltage
Send the ions into a magnetic field perpendicular to their motion
Each ion follows a semicircle whose radius depends on its mass
Ions of different masses land at different spots on a detector
questions.explanation: Only charged particles can be accelerated by a voltage and steered by a magnetic field, so ionizing comes first. The voltage gives the ions their speed; then, in the field, $r = mv/(qB)$ (here $r \propto \sqrt m$), so heavier ions curve less and land farther away.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this simple DC motor.

image.alt: A rectangular coil between two magnet blocks (marker 1 on the left block, marker 2 on the coil). Below, the coil's leads join a split ring (marker 3) touched by two small blocks, one marked 4. Wires lead to a battery symbol (marker 5).

questions.explanation: Field lines run from the magnet's north pole (1) to its south pole. The current-carrying coil (2) feels a torque $\tau = NIAB\sin\phi$. The split ring (3) turns with the coil, and the fixed brushes (4) slide from one half to the other every half turn, reversing the current so the torque keeps turning the coil the same way. The battery (5) supplies the current.

questions.stem: The picture is a cross-section of a solenoid, cut along its axis. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A row of wire cross-sections with dots across the top and a row with crosses across the bottom. Three straight arrows run left to right between the rows; dashed lines loop around outside. Marker 1 is on the straight arrows, 2 at the right end, 3 at the left end, 4 on a dotted wire in the top row and 5 on a dashed outside loop.

choices: Current coming out of the page
questions.explanation: The dots on the top wires mean current out of the page (4); the crosses on the bottom mean current into it. Inside, every turn's field points the same way, giving a strong, uniform field (1) to the right. Field lines leave the north-pole end (2), spread out and return weakly outside (5) into the south-pole end (3). Grip rule check: curl your right fingers out of the page at the top and into it at the bottom, and your thumb points right.

questions.stem: Match each situation to its magnetic field.
left: Distance $r$ from a long straight wire
Center of a circular loop of radius $R$
Inside a long solenoid with $n$ turns per meter
Midway between two long parallel wires with equal currents in the same direction
questions.explanation: A straight wire's field falls as $1/r$; a loop concentrates it at the center, $\mu_0I/(2R)$; a solenoid's interior field is $\mu_0nI$, independent of position. Midway between equal, same-direction currents, the two fields point opposite ways and cancel. The leftover $1/r^2$ form is a common mix-up with a point charge's electric field.

questions.stem: The magnetic field 2.0 cm from a long straight wire is 100 μT. At 8.0 cm from the same wire it is ___ μT. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0I/(2\pi r)$ falls as $1/r$. Four times the distance gives a quarter of the field: $100/4 = 25$ μT. (Using $1/r^2$ would give 6.25 μT, the most common mistake.)

questions.stem: Which changes would double the field inside a long solenoid? Select all that apply.
choices: Doubling both the number of turns and the length
Halving the length while keeping the same number of turns
Doubling the number of turns while keeping the same length
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0nI$ with $n = N/L$. Doubling $I$ doubles $B$. Halving $L$ or doubling $N$ (the other held fixed) doubles $n$, so it doubles $B$. Doubling both $N$ and $L$ leaves $n$ unchanged, and the interior field doesn't depend on the radius at all.

questions.stem: Put these magnetic fields in order from weakest to strongest.
choices: 10 m below a power line carrying 200 A
Inside a 0.40 m solenoid with 2000 turns carrying 3.0 A
questions.explanation: From the lesson: the power line gives $\mu_0I/(2\pi r) = 4.0\times10^{-6}$ T; Earth's field is about $5\times10^{-5}$ T; the solenoid gives $\mu_0nI = 1.9\times10^{-2}$ T; an MRI scanner is 1.5–3 T. Each is at least ten times the one before (the solenoid is a few hundred times Earth's field).

questions.stem: A rod slides along rails in a magnetic field, as in the motional-emf section. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two horizontal rails joined at the left by a zigzag (marker 2). A vertical bar lies across the rails at the right (marker 1). An upward arrow beside the bar (marker 3) and a rightward red arrow to its right (marker 4). Arrows along the rails circulate counterclockwise. Marker 5 is on an × mark in the background.

questions.explanation: The rod (1) moves right (4) in a field into the page (5), so the loop's area and the flux into the page grow. By Lenz's law the induced current (3) makes a field out of the page inside the loop: counterclockwise, up through the rod and through the resistor (2). The force on the rod, $I\vec L\times\vec B$, then points left, opposing the motion; it isn't drawn.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the direction of an induced current with Lenz's law in order.
choices: Find the direction of the external field through the loop
Decide whether the flux through the loop is increasing or decreasing
Choose the induced field direction that opposes that change
Use the right-hand rule for loops to find the current that makes that field
questions.explanation: You can't say whether the flux is growing "into" or "out of" the loop until you know the field's direction; you can't pick the opposing field until you know whether the flux is rising or falling; and the current comes last, from the induced field by the right-hand rule.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer steps 120 V down to 12 V. Its primary coil has 500 turns, so its secondary has ___ turns. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$, so $N_s = 500\cdot\dfrac{12}{120} = 50$ turns. A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns than primary turns.

questions.stem: A wire loop is connected to a sensitive meter. Which of these induce an emf in it? Select all that apply.
choices: A bar magnet is pushed toward the loop
The loop sits still in a strong, steady field
The loop slides sideways while staying entirely inside a uniform field
The loop is rotated in a uniform field
The current in a nearby electromagnet is switched off
questions.explanation: An emf needs a changing flux. Moving the magnet changes $B$ through the loop; rotating the loop changes $\cos\theta$; switching off the electromagnet makes $B$ fall. A steady field through a still loop gives constant flux, and sliding within a uniform field keeps $B$, $A$ and $\theta$ the same, so the flux doesn't change either.

questions.stem: Match each device to the way it uses induction.
choices: A coil rotating in a field has a changing flux
Changing current in one coil induces a voltage in another
A steady current makes a steady field
questions.explanation: All four rely on changing flux. A generator turns a coil so its flux changes continuously. A transformer's alternating primary current makes a changing flux in the shared core. An induction stove's changing field drives eddy currents that heat the pan's metal, and a magnetic brake's fins moving past magnets carry eddy currents whose forces oppose the motion (Lenz). A steady current induces nothing.

questions.stem: A 0.30 H inductor is in series with a 60 Ω resistor and a battery. The time constant is ___ ms. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\tau = L/R = 0.30/60 = 0.0050$ s $= 5$ ms. (Multiplying, $LR = 18$, is the mistake of carrying over the capacitor formula $RC$.)

questions.stem: A component is connected in series with a resistor and a battery. Match each moment to how the component behaves.
left: Inductor at the instant the switch closes
Inductor long after the switch closes
Uncharged capacitor at the instant the switch closes
Capacitor long after the switch closes
questions.explanation: An inductor resists any sudden change in current, so the current starts at zero, but once it is steady there is no emf and the (ideal) inductor is just a wire. A capacitor is the opposite: an uncharged capacitor has no voltage across it, so at first current flows as if it were a wire, but when fully charged no more current flows.

questions.stem: An LC circuit starts with the capacitor fully charged. Put the stages of one cycle in order.
choices: Capacitor fully charged, no current: all the energy is electric
Capacitor empty, current largest: all the energy is magnetic
Capacitor fully charged the opposite way, no current
Capacitor empty, current largest in the reverse direction
questions.explanation: The capacitor discharges through the inductor, building current until all the energy is in the inductor's field. The inductor keeps the current flowing, charging the capacitor the other way. Then the process repeats in reverse. Each stage is a quarter cycle, like a mass on a spring passing through its turning points and its center.

questions.stem: A series RLC circuit is driven at its resonant frequency. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The inductive and capacitive reactances are equal
The current is larger than at any other frequency (same source voltage)
questions.explanation: At resonance $X_L = X_C$, so $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + 0} = R$, the smallest possible impedance, and the current $V/Z$ is at its maximum. Neither reactance is zero; they are equal and cancel. The current is largest, not zero.

questions.stem: A European outlet supplies 230 V (rms). Its peak voltage is ___ V, to the nearest volt. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $V_0 = \sqrt2\,V_{\text{rms}} = 1.414 \times 230 = 325$ V. Rated household voltages are rms values; the peak is about 41% higher.

questions.stem: A proton moves at $4.0\times10^5$ m/s at $60^\circ$ to a 0.20 T field. What is the pitch of its helix? ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C)
questions.explanation: $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} = \dfrac{2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})}{(1.6\times10^{-19})(0.20)} = 3.28\times10^{-7}$ s, and $v_\parallel = v\cos60^\circ = 2.0\times10^5$ m/s, so $p = v_\parallel T = 0.066$ m $= 6.6$ cm. Using $v_\perp = v\sin60^\circ$ gives 11.4 cm; using the full speed gives 13.1 cm; 1.8 cm is the radius, $mv_\perp/(eB)$.

questions.stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field. Its velocity makes an angle of $90^\circ$ with the field. What is the pitch of its path?
choices: Zero: the path is a flat circle
Infinite: the path is a straight line
questions.explanation: At $90^\circ$, $v_\parallel = v\cos90^\circ = 0$, so the particle doesn't advance along the field: the helix flattens into a circle and $p = v_\parallel T = 0$. A straight line (infinite pitch, in a sense) happens at $0^\circ$, when the velocity is along the field and there is no force.

questions.stem: Why can a cyclotron use an accelerating voltage of one fixed frequency, even though the ions speed up on every turn?
choices: The ions' speed stays constant inside the dees
The time for each half circle does not depend on the ion's speed
The magnetic field is increased as the ions speed up
The gap voltage grows on each turn to keep up
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi m/(|q|B)$ has no $v$ in it: a faster ion travels a proportionally bigger semicircle ($r \propto v$) in the same time. So the ion always arrives back at the gap after exactly half a period, in step with the voltage. (Changing the field or frequency is only needed near light speed, in synchrotrons and synchrocyclotrons.)

questions.stem: A proton cyclotron has a 1.2 T field and dees of radius 0.40 m. What kinetic energy do the protons have when they leave? ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.6\times10^{-13}$ J)
questions.explanation: $K = \dfrac{q^2B^2R^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(1.6\times10^{-19})^2(1.2)^2(0.40)^2}{2(1.67\times10^{-27})} = 1.77\times10^{-12}$ J $= 11$ MeV. Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ gives 22 MeV; not squaring $R$ gives 28 MeV; $1.8\times10^{-12}$ is the energy in joules, not MeV.

questions.stem: A cyclotron is rebuilt with dees of twice the radius and the same field. The maximum kinetic energy of its protons
questions.explanation: $K_{\max} = q^2B^2R^2/(2m) \propto R^2$, so doubling $R$ multiplies it by 4 (the exit speed $eBR/m$ doubles, and kinetic energy goes as $v^2$). This assumes the protons stay well below light speed.

questions.stem: Protons circle in a 1.0 T field. Their cyclotron frequency is ___ MHz, to 2 significant figures. ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $f = \dfrac{eB}{2\pi m} = \dfrac{(1.6\times10^{-19})(1.0)}{2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})} = 1.52\times10^7$ Hz $\approx 15$ MHz. (Forgetting the $2\pi$ gives the angular frequency, $9.6\times10^7$ rad/s.)

questions.stem: Electrons pass undeflected through crossed fields $E = 3.0\times10^4$ V/m and $B = 1.5\times10^{-3}$ T. With $E$ switched off, they circle with radius 7.6 cm. What is $e/m$?
questions.explanation: $v = E/B$ and $e/m = v/(Br)$, so $\dfrac em = \dfrac{E}{B^2r} = \dfrac{3.0\times10^4}{(1.5\times10^{-3})^2(0.076)} = 1.75\times10^{11}$ C/kg. Using $B$ instead of $B^2$ gives $2.6\times10^8$; leaving $r$ in centimeters gives $1.75\times10^9$; $5.7\times10^{-12}$ is the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the classroom crossed-fields measurement of $e/m$ in order.
choices: Adjust crossed $E$ and $B$ until the beam goes straight
Measure the radius of the beam's circular path
questions.explanation: The straight beam selects the speed $v = E/B$, which needs both fields on. Only after switching off $E$ does the beam circle in $B$ alone, so you can measure $r$; the formula needs $E$, $B$ and $r$, so the calculation comes last.

questions.stem: A silver strip 1.0 cm wide and 0.20 mm thick carries 5.0 A in a 0.80 T field perpendicular to its face. Silver has $n = 5.9\times10^{28}$ m⁻³. What is the Hall voltage? ($e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C)
questions.explanation: $V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt} = \dfrac{(5.0)(0.80)}{(5.9\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})(2.0\times10^{-4})} = 2.1\times10^{-6}$ V. Using the width (1.0 cm) instead of the thickness gives $4.2\times10^{-8}$ V; leaving out $B$ gives $2.6\times10^{-6}$ V; $2.1\times10^{-9}$ V comes from using 0.20 (the thickness in millimeters) as if it were meters.

questions.stem: Which can be found from a Hall-effect measurement on a strip of known thickness carrying a known current? Select all that apply.
choices: The mass of the charge carriers
The sign of the charge carriers
The number of carriers per cubic meter, if $B$ is known
The magnetic field, if the carrier density is known
The speed of light in the material
questions.explanation: $V_H = IB/(nqt)$: its sign tells which edge the carriers pile up on, and so their sign; its size gives $n$ when $B$ is known, or $B$ when $n$ is known (that's how Hall sensors work). Mass doesn't appear in the formula, and the measurement says nothing about light.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this cyclotron (top view).

image.alt: Two D-shaped regions side by side with a narrow vertical gap between them (marker 1 on the left D, marker 2 in the gap near the bottom). A spiral path starts at a central dot (marker 3). Below, the two Ds connect to a circle with a wave symbol (marker 4). An arrow leaves the outermost turn to the right (marker 5).

questions.explanation: Ions start at the source (3) at the center. The alternating source (4) makes the voltage across the gap (2) reverse every half orbit, so the ions are pushed forward each time they cross. Inside each hollow dee (1) there is only the magnetic field, which bends them into semicircles. When the orbit reaches the rim, the beam (5) is steered out.

questions.stem: Match each device or phenomenon to the physics behind it.
choices: Charged particles spiral along field lines into the upper atmosphere
The orbit period does not depend on speed
Electric and magnetic forces cancel at one speed
Carriers pushed to one edge build a sideways voltage
The path radius depends on the ion's mass
questions.explanation: The aurora: particles follow Earth's field lines in helices toward the poles. The cyclotron: $T = 2\pi m/(|q|B)$ is speed-independent. The velocity selector: $qE = qvB$ only at $v = E/B$. The Hall sensor: the magnetic force on drifting carriers piles charge on one edge until $qE_H = qv_dB$. The mass spectrometer: $r = mv/(qB)$ sorts ions by mass.

questions.stem: Why are practical Hall sensors made of semiconductors rather than metals?
choices: Semiconductors have far fewer charge carriers, so each drifts faster and the Hall voltage is much larger
Metals have no Hall effect because their carriers are electrons
Semiconductors conduct better, so the current is larger
The Hall voltage in a metal is too large to measure safely
questions.explanation: $V_H = IB/(nqt)$ is inversely proportional to the carrier density $n$. A doped semiconductor has millions of times fewer carriers than copper, so for the same current each carrier drifts much faster and the voltage is far larger. Metals do show a Hall effect (that's how Hall discovered it), just a tiny one, microvolts in the lesson's copper example.

questions.stem: Why does a fixed-frequency cyclotron stop working once its particles approach the speed of light?
choices: The magnetic force stops acting on fast particles
The particles start to radiate all their energy away instantly
Their orbit period grows (a relativistic effect), so they fall out of step with the voltage
The dees become too hot to hold a voltage
questions.explanation: The speed-independent period $2\pi m/(|q|B)$ is only true well below light speed. Near it, special relativity makes the period grow with energy, so the ions arrive at the gap later and later and are no longer accelerated. Synchrocyclotrons lower the frequency to keep in step; synchrotrons raise the field (and adjust the frequency) as the particles gain energy. (Fast particles do radiate in magnetic fields, but that isn't what limits a cyclotron.)

questions.stem: An AC voltage is applied across an ideal inductor alone. Compared with the voltage, the current
choices: leads it by a quarter cycle
is half a cycle out of step with it
lags it by a quarter cycle
questions.explanation: The inductor's voltage is proportional to how fast the current changes, so it is largest when the current crosses zero, a quarter cycle before the current peaks. The current lags by $90^\circ$ ("ELI": E before I in an inductor). Leading by a quarter cycle is the capacitor's behavior.

questions.stem: Match each AC circuit to how its current compares with the source voltage.
questions.explanation: A resistor follows $V = IR$ instant by instant. An inductor's current lags by $90^\circ$ and a capacitor's leads by $90^\circ$. At resonance $X_L = X_C$, so $\tan\varphi = (X_L - X_C)/R = 0$ and the circuit acts like a pure resistance: in phase.

questions.stem: A series circuit has $R = 40\ \Omega$, $X_L = 80\ \Omega$ and $X_C = 50\ \Omega$. What is the phase angle, and does the current lead or lag the voltage?
questions.explanation: $\tan\varphi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R} = \dfrac{30}{40} = 0.75$, so $\varphi = 36.9^\circ$. $X_L > X_C$ makes the circuit inductive, so the current lags. $53.1^\circ$ comes from inverting the ratio ($40/30$).

questions.stem: The circuit with $R = 40\ \Omega$, $X_L = 80\ \Omega$ and $X_C = 50\ \Omega$ is driven by 100 V (rms). What average power does it use?
questions.explanation: $Z = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50\ \Omega$, so $I_{\text{rms}} = 100/50 = 2.0$ A. $P = I_{\text{rms}}^2R = (2.0)^2(40) = 160$ W, the same as $I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\varphi = (2.0)(100)(0.80)$. 200 W leaves out the power factor; 250 W is $V^2/R$, as if the reactances were absent; 120 W uses $\sin\varphi$ instead of $\cos\varphi$.

questions.stem: A series AC circuit has a resistance of 30 Ω and an impedance of 50 Ω. Its power factor is ___. Give it as a decimal.
questions.explanation: From the phasor triangle, $\cos\varphi = R/Z = 30/50 = 0.60$. The circuit uses 60% of the product $I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}$ as real power.

questions.stem: An ideal inductor is connected to an AC source. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It heats up because current flows through it
Its current lags its voltage by $90^\circ$
questions.explanation: An ideal inductor stores energy in its field for a quarter cycle and returns it the next, so its average power is zero and it doesn't heat up (real coils do, a little, through their wire's resistance). $X_L = \omega L$ rises with frequency, and the current lags by $90^\circ$, so its power factor is $\cos90^\circ = 0$, not 1.

questions.stem: In a series RLC circuit the rms voltages are $V_R = 60$ V, $V_L = 160$ V and $V_C = 80$ V. What is the source voltage (rms)?
questions.explanation: The voltages add as phasors: $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + 80^2} = 100$ V. Adding them as numbers gives 300 V; adding $V_R$ and $V_L - V_C$ as plain numbers ($60 + 80$) gives 140 V; squaring all three separately gives 189 V. The inductor's 160 V really is larger than the source's 100 V, because $V_L$ and $V_C$ partly cancel.

questions.stem: This phasor diagram for a series RLC circuit draws the current along the horizontal axis. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A dashed horizontal axis. From one point, a short arrow points right along the axis (marker 1), an arrow points straight up (marker 2), a longer arrow points straight down (marker 3), and an arrow points down and to the right (marker 4). Marker 5 is on a small arc between the rightward arrow and the down-right arrow.

questions.explanation: The resistor's voltage (1) is in phase with the current, along the axis. The inductor's voltage (2) is $90^\circ$ ahead (up) and the capacitor's (3) $90^\circ$ behind (down). Their vector sum is the source voltage (4), and the angle between it and the current is the phase angle (5). Here $V_C > V_L$, so the source voltage lies below the axis: the circuit is capacitive and the current leads.

questions.stem: The same power is sent through the same line at 115 kV instead of 345 kV. The power lost in the line is
questions.explanation: $P_{\text{loss}} = (P/V)^2R_{\text{line}}$. Cutting $V$ to a third triples the current, and the loss goes as $I^2$: $3^2 = 9$ times larger. "3 times" forgets to square; "9 times smaller" uses $V^2/R$ with the transmission voltage.

questions.stem: A plant sends 2.0 MW at 10 kV through lines with a total resistance of 4.0 Ω. The power lost in the lines is ___ kW. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $I = P/V = 2.0\times10^6/1.0\times10^4 = 200$ A, so $P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R = (200)^2(4.0) = 1.6\times10^5$ W $= 160$ kW, 8% of the power sent.

questions.stem: Put the stages of delivering electric power from a power plant to a house in order.
choices: Pole or pad transformer near the house
questions.explanation: The generator's output (about 10–25 kV) is stepped up to hundreds of kilovolts for the long trip, because a higher voltage means less current and much less $I^2R$ loss. A substation steps it down for local distribution lines (several to tens of kV), and a final transformer near the house brings it to household voltage.

questions.stem: What was the main technical reason AC won out over DC for power grids in the 1890s?
choices: AC carries more energy per electron
Transformers could easily step AC voltage up for transmission and down for use
AC wires have lower resistance than DC wires
AC cannot give an electric shock
questions.explanation: Low losses need high transmission voltages, but safe use needs low voltages. Transformers change AC voltage efficiently; with the technology of the time, DC could not be transformed, so DC plants had to sit close to their customers. The wire's resistance is the same either way, and AC is certainly dangerous.

questions.stem: A factory's motors give it a power factor of 0.70 (current lagging). Why does adding capacitors help?
choices: The capacitors store energy that runs the motors for free
The capacitors raise the supply voltage
The capacitors increase the motors' real power output
The capacitors' leading current offsets the motors' lagging current, so less current is needed for the same real power
questions.explanation: Real power is $I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\varphi$. At a power factor of 0.70 the wiring carries $1/0.70 = 1.43$ times the current needed at power factor 1, and loses about twice as much power in it ($1/0.70^2$). Capacitors draw current that leads, canceling much of the motors' lagging current, so the power factor rises toward 1. They don't supply real energy or change the motors' output.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of three-phase power for a balanced load?
choices: The total power delivered is steady instead of pulsing
It doubles the frequency of the supply
questions.explanation: With three voltages a third of a cycle apart, the three currents in a balanced load add to zero at every instant (so no heavy return wire is needed), and the total power stays constant, which lets big motors run smoothly. Three-phase systems still use transformers, still carry AC, and run at the ordinary 50 or 60 Hz.

questions.stem: Diamond has $n = 2.42$. The critical angle for light inside diamond reaching a diamond–air surface is ___ degrees, to the nearest degree. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1 = 1.00/2.42 = 0.413$, so $\theta_c = 24.4^\circ \approx 24^\circ$. The small critical angle traps light inside a cut diamond for many reflections, which is why diamonds sparkle.

questions.stem: Put these kinds of electromagnetic waves in order from lowest frequency to highest frequency.
questions.explanation: All travel at $c$, so $f = c/\lambda$: the longer the wavelength, the lower the frequency. Radio waves are longest (over a meter), then microwaves (mm to m), infrared, visible (400–700 nm), ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays (shortest, highest frequency).

questions.stem: Which statements about electromagnetic waves in vacuum are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
All frequencies travel at the same speed, $3.00\times10^8$ m/s
They need a medium such as air to travel through
The field magnitudes are related by $E = cB$
questions.explanation: EM waves are transverse, with $\vec E$, $\vec B$ and the direction of travel all mutually perpendicular, and in vacuum every frequency moves at $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$, with $E = cB$. They need no medium: light crosses empty space from the Sun. Their speed doesn't depend on frequency in vacuum; only in materials does the speed vary slightly with wavelength (dispersion).

questions.stem: The picture is a snapshot of an electromagnetic wave. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A wave traveling along a horizontal axis with an arrowhead at the right end, marked 4. One wave of vertical arrows has a trough marked 2. A second wave of slanted arrows, perpendicular to the first, is marked 3. A bracket between two crests of the vertical wave is marked 1.

questions.explanation: The wave travels along the axis (4). The electric field (2) oscillates in one plane and the magnetic field (3) in the perpendicular plane, in step with it, so both peak at the same places. The distance from one crest to the next (1) is the wavelength. The amplitude would be the height of a crest above the axis, not the crest-to-crest distance.

questions.stem: Match each everyday observation to the effect behind it.
left: A prism spreads white light into colors
An optical fiber carries light around bends
A straw looks bent where it enters water
Polarized sunglasses cut glare from a road
You see the trees reflected in a still pond
questions.explanation: A prism's index depends slightly on wavelength (dispersion), so colors bend by different amounts. A fiber keeps light inside because it hits the wall beyond the critical angle (total internal reflection). Light from the underwater part of the straw bends at the surface (refraction), so it seems to come from a different place. Glare is partly polarized horizontally, and the glasses' vertical axis blocks it (polarization). A smooth surface gives a mirror image (reflection). Diffraction needs openings comparable to the wavelength and explains none of these.

questions.stem: An object is 12 cm from a converging lens with a focal length of 8.0 cm. The image is ___ cm from the lens. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f - \dfrac1{d_o} = \dfrac18 - \dfrac1{12} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{24} = \dfrac1{24}$, so $d_i = 24$ cm. It is positive, so the image is real, on the far side of the lens; $m = -24/12 = -2$, inverted and twice as tall (the object is between $f$ and $2f$).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this ray diagram for a concave mirror.

image.alt: A curved mirror on the right, marked 6, with a dashed horizontal axis marked 5. Two dots on the axis are marked 1 (farther from the mirror) and 2 (closer). An upright arrow on the left, beyond dot 1, is marked 3. Rays from its tip reflect and meet at a short inverted arrow between dots 1 and 2, marked 4.

questions.explanation: The focal point (2) is halfway between the mirror (6) and the center of curvature (1), since $f = R/2$. The object (3) stands beyond C, so the reflected rays really meet in front of the mirror, between C and F, forming a real, inverted, smaller image (4): here $d_o = 3f$ gives $d_i = 1.5f$ and $m = -0.5$. All of this is measured along the principal axis (5).

questions.stem: An object starts far from a converging lens and moves steadily toward it, ending very close to the lens. Put the images it produces in the order they appear.
choices: Real, inverted and smaller than the object
Real, inverted and the same size
Real, inverted and larger than the object
No image (rays leave the lens parallel)
Virtual, upright and larger than the object
questions.explanation: Beyond $2f$ the image is real, inverted and reduced; at exactly $2f$ it is the same size; between $f$ and $2f$ it is enlarged (a projector); at $f$ the rays emerge parallel, so no image forms; inside $f$ the image is virtual, upright and enlarged (a magnifying glass).

questions.stem: For a real object at any distance, which of these always form a virtual, upright image that is smaller than the object? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors and diverging lenses have $f < 0$, and with $d_o > 0$ the lens equation always gives $-|f| < d_i < 0$, so the image is virtual, upright and reduced. A plane mirror's image is virtual and upright but the same size. Concave mirrors and converging lenses give real inverted images for objects beyond $f$ and enlarged virtual images inside $f$, so they never give a reduced upright image.

questions.stem: Match each optical element to the sign of its focal length in the thin-lens and mirror equation.
choices: No focal point (parallel rays stay parallel)
questions.explanation: Optics that bring parallel rays to a real focus (converging lenses, concave mirrors) have $f > 0$. Optics that spread parallel rays as if from a point behind or in front of them (diverging lenses, convex mirrors) have $f < 0$. A plane mirror reflects parallel rays as parallel rays, so it has no focal point; you can think of its focal length as infinite, which makes the mirror equation give $d_i = -d_o$.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the eye.

image.alt: A cross-section of an eye with parallel rays entering from the left. Marker 1 is on the curved, clear front bulge. Marker 2 is on a dark bar beside the opening the rays pass through. Marker 3 is on the oval just behind that opening. Marker 4 is on the thick curved layer lining the back of the eye, where the rays meet. Marker 5 is on the band leaving the back of the eye.

questions.explanation: Light first bends at the curved cornea (1), which does most of the focusing. The iris (2) is the colored ring of tissue; the pupil is the opening in it, not the tissue itself. The lens (3) changes shape to fine-tune the focus (accommodation). The image forms on the retina (4), and the optic nerve (5) carries the signals to the brain. An eyepiece belongs to a microscope or telescope.

questions.stem: A nearsighted person's far point is 40 cm. Treating the lens as right at the eye, the contact lens they need has a power of ___ diopters. Give only the number, with its sign.
questions.explanation: The lens must make a distant object's image at the far point on the object's side, so $f = -40$ cm $= -0.40$ m and $P = 1/f = 1/(-0.40\text{ m}) = -2.5$ D. The negative sign means a diverging lens; $+2.5$ would be the farsighted (converging) correction, and $-0.025$ comes from using centimeters instead of meters.

questions.stem: Match each instrument to its angular magnification ($f$ is a focal length; near point 25 cm).
left: Magnifier, image at the near point
choices: Minus objective focal length over eyepiece focal length
Objective focal length plus eyepiece focal length
questions.explanation: A magnifier gives $M = 25\text{ cm}/f$ with the object at its focal point (relaxed eye) and $1 + 25\text{ cm}/f$ with the image at the near point. A microscope multiplies the objective's lateral magnification by the eyepiece's angular magnification. A telescope gives $M = -f_o/f_e$. The sum $f_o + f_e$ is the telescope's length, not a magnification.

questions.stem: A telescope's objective is replaced by one with the same focal length but twice the diameter. Which of these change? Select all that apply.
choices: It collects about four times as much light
It can resolve details about half as far apart in angle
questions.explanation: Light collected is proportional to the objective's area, which grows as $D^2$: four times as much. The smallest resolvable angle is proportional to $\lambda/D$, so it halves. Magnification $f_o/f_e$ and length $f_o + f_e$ depend only on focal lengths, which haven't changed.

questions.stem: Put the stages of image formation in a compound microscope in order, starting with the specimen.
choices: Specimen placed just outside the objective's focal point
Real, inverted, enlarged image forms inside the tube
Eyepiece acts as a magnifier for that image
Eye views a final image at infinity
questions.explanation: The objective makes a real, enlarged intermediate image of a specimen placed just beyond its focal point. That image sits at the eyepiece's focal point, so the eyepiece, working as a magnifier, sends parallel rays to a relaxed eye. The overall magnification is the product of the two stages.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this double-slit setup.

image.alt: A box on the left, marked 1, sends a wide beam to a dark vertical barrier with two narrow openings, marked 2. A short bracket beside the openings is marked 3. A tall strip on the right with evenly spaced bright patches is marked 4, and its middle patch, straight ahead of the openings, is marked 5. A long bracket along the bottom from the barrier to the strip is marked 6.

questions.explanation: A laser (1) provides coherent light, which passes through the double slit (2), two openings a distance $d$ apart (3). On the screen (4) at distance $L$ (6), bright fringes appear where $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$; the central one, $m = 0$ (5), is straight ahead, where the two paths are equal. A grating would have thousands of slits, not two.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, $\lambda = 600$ nm, the slits are 0.30 mm apart and the screen is 1.5 m away. The bright fringes are ___ mm apart. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d} = \dfrac{(600\times10^{-9}\text{ m})(1.5\text{ m})}{0.30\times10^{-3}\text{ m}} = 3.0\times10^{-3}$ m $= 3.0$ mm.

questions.stem: Each condition locates fringes in a pattern. Match each one to whether it gives a bright or a dark fringe ($m$ is a whole number).
left: Soap film in air (one flip), in reflection: $2nt = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$
Coating on glass (two flips), in reflection: $2nt = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$
questions.explanation: For two slits, a whole number of wavelengths of path difference gives a bright fringe and a half-integer number gives a dark one. The single-slit formula looks the same but marks dark fringes: pairing waves from the two halves of the slit, they cancel. In thin films the phase flips decide: with one flip the half-integer condition is bright; with two flips (which cancel each other) it is dark, the condition anti-reflection coatings use.

questions.stem: Which changes make the bright fringes in a double-slit pattern farther apart? Select all that apply.
choices: Using red light instead of blue
Moving the screen farther from the slits
Using a brighter laser of the same color
questions.explanation: The spacing is $\Delta y = \lambda L/d$. It grows with a longer wavelength (red is longer than blue), a larger screen distance $L$, and a smaller slit spacing $d$. Brightness changes how bright the fringes are, not where they are, and moving the slits apart (larger $d$) squeezes the fringes together.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the thinnest anti-reflection coating (index $n$) on a glass lens in order.
choices: Count the reflections onto a higher index: two, at the top and bottom of the coating
Note that the two phase flips cancel, so only the extra path $2t$ in the film matters
For cancellation, set the extra path to half a wavelength in the film: $2nt = \tfrac12\lambda$
questions.explanation: You can't choose the interference condition until you know how many flips there are, and you can't solve for $t$ until you have the condition. With $n = 1.38$ and $\lambda = 550$ nm this gives $t = 550/(4 \times 1.38) = 99.6$ nm.

questions.stem: Light in air reflects from flint glass ($n = 1.66$). At what angle of incidence is the reflected light completely polarized?
questions.explanation: $\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1 = 1.66$, so $\theta_B = 58.9^\circ$. $37.0^\circ$ comes from $\sin\theta = 1/1.66$ (the critical-angle formula, which doesn't even apply going into a denser medium); $31.1^\circ$ is the refraction angle at Brewster's angle, $90^\circ - 58.9^\circ$; $53.0^\circ$ uses $\cos\theta = 1/1.66$.

questions.stem: Unpolarized light reflects from a lake at Brewster's angle. The reflected light is
choices: polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is horizontal (parallel to the lake)
polarized in the plane of incidence, partly vertical
unpolarized but much weaker than the incident light
questions.explanation: At Brewster's angle the p part (field in the plane of incidence) does not reflect at all, so only the s part, perpendicular to the plane of incidence, remains. For a horizontal surface that field is horizontal, which is why vertical-axis polarized sunglasses block this glare.

questions.stem: Why does no p-polarized light reflect at Brewster's angle?
choices: The p light is totally internally reflected inside the glass
The glass absorbs all of the p light at that angle
The electrons that would produce it oscillate along the direction the reflected ray would travel, and they cannot radiate along that line
The s and p reflections cancel each other by interference
questions.explanation: The refracted wave drives electrons along its field. For p light that field lies in the plane of incidence, perpendicular to the refracted ray. When the reflected direction is perpendicular to the refracted ray, it points along that oscillation, and an oscillating charge radiates nothing along its own line. Total internal reflection doesn't occur going into a denser medium, glass barely absorbs visible light, and s and p are perpendicular polarizations that don't cancel each other.

questions.stem: Light under water ($n = 1.33$) reaches the water–air surface. Its Brewster's angle there is ___ degrees, to the nearest 0.1°. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Now $n_1 = 1.33$ and $n_2 = 1.00$: $\tan\theta_B = 1.00/1.33 = 0.752$, so $\theta_B = 36.9^\circ$. It is the complement of the air-to-water value ($53.1^\circ$) and smaller than the critical angle, $48.8^\circ$, as Brewster's angle always is.

questions.stem: Which of these are caused by Rayleigh scattering of sunlight by air molecules? Select all that apply.
choices: The blue color of the clear sky
The red color of the setting Sun
The strong polarization of skylight $90^\circ$ from the Sun
questions.explanation: Molecules are much smaller than the wavelength, so they scatter as $1/\lambda^4$: blue is scattered across the sky, leaving the long sunset path reddened, and scattering at $90^\circ$ is strongly polarized. Cloud droplets are larger than the wavelength and scatter all colors about equally (white), and rainbows come from refraction and dispersion inside raindrops.

questions.stem: By what factor is 450 nm light scattered more strongly than 600 nm light by air molecules?
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering goes as $1/\lambda^4$: $(600/450)^4 = 1.333^4 = 3.16$. The other choices use the first, second and third powers of the ratio.

questions.stem: A photographer rotates a polarizing filter to darken a clear blue sky. In which part of the sky does the filter have the strongest effect?
questions.explanation: Sunlight shakes the molecules' electrons perpendicular to the sunbeam. Looking $90^\circ$ from the Sun, the part of that motion along your line of sight sends you nothing, so you receive light polarized in one direction, which the filter can block. Near the Sun or directly opposite it, the scattering angle is small or near $180^\circ$ and the light is only weakly polarized.

questions.stem: A clear calcite crystal laid on a printed page shows every letter twice because calcite
choices: reflects light from both its top and bottom faces
has two indices of refraction, one for each of two perpendicular polarizations
spreads white light into colors more strongly than glass
diffracts light from its regular rows of atoms
questions.explanation: Calcite is birefringent: light polarized one way travels with $n_o = 1.658$ and light polarized at right angles with $n_e = 1.486$ (at 589 nm), so the two polarizations refract differently and form two images. A polarizer over the crystal can make either image vanish, which proves the two are polarized at right angles. Reflections and dispersion don't make two distinct images, and the atomic rows are far too close together to diffract visible light noticeably.

questions.stem: Quartz has $|n_e - n_o| = 0.0091$. The thinnest quartz quarter-wave plate for 632.8 nm light is ___ μm thick, to 3 significant figures. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: A quarter-wave plate delays one polarization by $\lambda/4$: $t\,|n_e - n_o| = \lambda/4$, so $t = \dfrac{632.8\text{ nm}}{4(0.0091)} = 17\,400$ nm $= 17.4$ μm.

questions.stem: Linearly polarized light enters a half-wave plate with its polarization at $20^\circ$ to the plate's fast axis. What comes out?
questions.explanation: A half-wave plate flips the component along one axis relative to the other, which mirrors the polarization across the fast axis: from $+20^\circ$ to $-20^\circ$, a rotation of $2(20^\circ) = 40^\circ$. Circular polarization comes from a quarter-wave plate with the light at $45^\circ$, and light is unchanged only if it is polarized along one of the axes.

questions.stem: Match each optical element to what it does to polarized light.
left: Quarter-wave plate, light at $45^\circ$ to its axes
choices: Transmits only the field component along its axis
Rotates linear polarization by twice its angle to the fast axis
Reflects only light polarized parallel to the surface
Doubles the frequency of the light
questions.explanation: A polarizer absorbs the field component across its axis. Wave plates absorb nothing; they delay one component: a quarter-wave delay with equal components gives circular light, and a half-wave delay mirrors the polarization across the fast axis. At Brewster's angle only s light, polarized parallel to the surface, reflects. None of these changes the light's frequency.

questions.stem: In the simplified LCD model, a pixel between crossed polarizers turns the polarization by $\phi = 60^\circ$. What fraction of the unpolarized backlight $I_0$ gets through?
questions.explanation: The first polarizer passes $\tfrac12I_0$. The light is then at $60^\circ$ to the first axis, so at $30^\circ$ to the crossed second one: $I = \tfrac12I_0\cos^2 30^\circ = \tfrac12I_0\sin^2 60^\circ = 0.375I_0$. $0.125I_0$ uses $\cos^2 60^\circ$ (the angle to the wrong polarizer), $0.75I_0$ forgets the first polarizer's half, and $0.433I_0$ forgets to square.

questions.stem: Put the stages of light passing through a bright (switched-off) twisted nematic LCD pixel in order.
choices: The first polarizer passes half of it, polarized along its axis
The twisted liquid crystal rotates the polarization by 90°
The crossed second polarizer, now aligned with the light, lets it through
questions.explanation: The polarization must be set by the first polarizer before the liquid crystal can rotate it, and it must be rotated before it can pass the crossed second polarizer. With a voltage applied, the twist disappears and the third step no longer happens, so the second polarizer blocks the light.

questions.stem: Light reflects from glass at Brewster's angle. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A horizontal air–glass surface with a dashed vertical line (marker 4). A ray from the upper left (marker 1), with dots and double arrows along it, reaches the surface. A ray leaving to the upper right (marker 2) has only dots. A ray going down into the glass (marker 3) has mostly double arrows and one dot. Marker 5 is on an arc between the dashed line and the upper-left ray; marker 6 is on a square corner between the two outgoing rays.

choices: Reflected light polarized parallel to the surface
questions.explanation: Dots show the field perpendicular to the page (the s direction, parallel to the surface) and double arrows the field in the page (p). The incident light (1) has both. The reflected light (2) has only dots, because at Brewster's angle (5, measured from the normal, 4) no p light reflects. The refracted light (3) keeps all the p light and most of the s, so it is only partly polarized. The reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular (6), the condition that defines Brewster's angle. The critical angle applies only to light going toward a lower index.

questions.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity 800 W/m² hits glass at Brewster's angle, where the s part has a reflectance of 15.7% and the p part 0. What is the reflected intensity?
questions.explanation: Unpolarized light is half s and half p: 400 W/m² each. Only s reflects, so $I_r = 0.157 \times 400 = 63$ W/m², all s-polarized. 126 W/m² applies 15.7% to the full 800 W/m², forgetting that only half the light is s; 0 confuses "no p reflection" with no reflection at all; 400 W/m² is the whole s part.

questions.stem: Two glass plates touching along one edge enclose a thin air wedge. In reflected light, the line where they touch is dark because
choices: the gap is zero there and exactly one of the two reflections is flipped, so they cancel
both reflections are flipped there, so they cancel
the glass absorbs light where the plates touch
questions.explanation: The reflection from glass into air (top plate's lower surface) has no flip; the reflection from air onto glass (bottom plate) has one. With zero gap there is no extra path, so the single half-wavelength flip makes the two reflections cancel. Two flips would cancel each other and give a bright line.

questions.stem: An air wedge is lit with 600 nm light. The spacer at the far end is 30 μm thick. How many dark fringes appear, counting the one at the touching edge?
questions.explanation: Dark fringes occur where $2t = m\lambda$, so $m$ runs from 0 to $2D/\lambda = 2(30\times10^{-6})/(600\times10^{-9}) = 100$: that's 101 dark fringes. 100 forgets the dark line at the touching edge; 50 and 51 use $D/\lambda$, forgetting that the light crosses the gap twice.

questions.stem: An air wedge 5.0 cm long has a 25 μm spacer at its far end and is lit with 500 nm light. The dark fringes are ___ mm apart. Give only the number.

An optical flat on a test surface shows straight fringes, except that one fringe bends aside by half the fringe spacing over a small region. With 600 nm light, about how high is the bump or dip there?
questions.explanation: Neighboring fringes are contour lines a height $\lambda/2 = 300$ nm apart. A shift of half a fringe spacing means half that height: $\lambda/4 = 150$ nm. 300 nm would be a full fringe of shift; 600 nm treats a full fringe as a height step of $\lambda$, forgetting that the light crosses the gap twice; 75 nm halves the answer one time too many.

questions.stem: A lens surface with radius of curvature 2.0 m rests on a flat plate and is lit with 550 nm light. What is the radius of the fourth dark ring (not counting the dark center)?
questions.explanation: $r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R} = \sqrt{4(550\times10^{-9})(2.0)} = \sqrt{4.4\times10^{-6}}$ m $= 2.10$ mm. 1.48 mm uses $t = r^2/R$ instead of $r^2/(2R)$; 2.97 mm uses $t = m\lambda$, forgetting that the light crosses the gap twice; 1.05 mm is the first ring.

questions.stem: Which statements about Newton's rings seen in reflected light are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The center, where the lens touches the plate, is dark
The rings get closer together farther from the center
The radius of the $m$th dark ring is proportional to $\sqrt m$
A flatter lens surface (larger $R$) gives smaller rings
questions.explanation: With one phase flip and zero gap, the center is dark. The gap grows as $r^2/(2R)$, so dark rings sit at $r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R}$: proportional to $\sqrt m$ and crowding together outward, not equally spaced. A larger $R$ makes every $r_m$ larger, not smaller.

questions.stem: The movable mirror of a Michelson interferometer lit with 632.8 nm light moves 0.200 mm. About ___ fringes pass the detector, to the nearest whole fringe. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $N = \dfrac{2\Delta d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2(0.200\times10^{-3})}{632.8\times10^{-9}} = 632.1$, about 632 fringes. Forgetting the factor of 2 (the light goes out and back) gives 316.

questions.stem: A Michelson interferometer shows a bright spot at the center of its pattern. The movable mirror is then moved by a quarter of a wavelength. The center becomes
choices: dark, because the path difference changed by half a wavelength
bright again, because the path difference changed by a whole wavelength
unchanged, because a quarter wavelength is too small to matter
bright again after two fringes have passed
questions.explanation: Moving the mirror by $\lambda/4$ lengthens that arm's round trip by $2(\lambda/4) = \lambda/2$, turning constructive interference into destructive. A whole wavelength of path change needs a mirror motion of $\lambda/2$.

questions.stem: A 4.00 cm cell in a Michelson interferometer is filled with helium ($n - 1 = 3.5\times10^{-5}$) while lit with 632.8 nm light. About how many fringes pass?
questions.explanation: $N = \dfrac{2L(n - 1)}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2(0.0400)(3.5\times10^{-5})}{632.8\times10^{-9}} = 4.4$. 2.2 counts only one pass through the cell; 44 uses 40 cm for 4.00 cm; $1.3\times10^5$ uses $n$ instead of $n - 1$ (that is the total number of wavelengths in the cell, not the change).

questions.stem: Put the path of light through a Michelson interferometer in order.
choices: The beam splitter divides it into two beams
Each beam reflects from its mirror and returns
The beam splitter recombines the two beams
The combined light reaches the detector, where it interferes
questions.explanation: The beams must be split before they can travel separate arms, and they must return before they can be recombined. Any difference in the two round trips shows up as a shift in the fringes at the detector.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this Michelson interferometer.

image.alt: A box on the left, marked 1, sends a beam to a tilted plate at the center, marked 2. One beam goes right to a vertical plate with a double arrow beside it, marked 3, and back. Another goes up to a horizontal plate, marked 4, and back. The recombined beam goes down to a striped strip, marked 5.

questions.explanation: Light from the source (1) is split at the half-silvered beam splitter (2). One beam returns from the movable mirror (3, the double arrow shows it slides along the beam) and the other from the fixed mirror (4). The beam splitter recombines them and they interfere at the detector or screen (5). There is no grating: the two paths are separated by the beam splitter, not by diffraction.

questions.stem: With white light, a Michelson interferometer shows colored fringes only when its two arms are equal to within about a micrometer. Why?
choices: The beam splitter absorbs white light unless the arms are equal
White light is not an electromagnetic wave
White light's coherence length is only about a micrometer
White-light fringes are too close together to see unless the arms are equal
questions.explanation: White light spans about 300 nm of wavelengths, so its coherence length is roughly $\lambda^2/\Delta\lambda \approx (550\text{ nm})^2/300\text{ nm} \approx 1$ μm. Fringes form only when the path difference is shorter than that. (Laser light, with a far narrower spread of wavelengths, gives fringes over much larger path differences.)

questions.stem: A light source has $\lambda = 600$ nm and a wavelength spread of $\Delta\lambda = 0.10$ nm. Estimate its coherence length.
questions.explanation: $\ell_c \approx \dfrac{\lambda^2}{\Delta\lambda} = \dfrac{(600\times10^{-9}\text{ m})^2}{0.10\times10^{-9}\text{ m}} = 3.6\times10^{-3}$ m $= 3.6$ mm, or about 6000 wavelengths. 0.60 μm is just one wavelength; 3.6 μm and 36 cm come from slipping powers of ten when converting nanometers to meters.

questions.stem: Match each interference measurement to what it measured or showed.
left: Gas cell in a Michelson interferometer
choices: No sign of Earth's motion through an ether
Gravitational waves stretching and squeezing its arms
The thickness of a thin wire or hair
The index of refraction of a gas
The radius of curvature of a lens surface
The speed of sound in air
questions.explanation: Michelson and Morley expected a shift of about 0.4 fringe from an ether wind and saw almost none. LIGO's 4 km arms changed length by a few times $10^{-18}$ m. An air wedge's fringe spacing gives the spacer thickness, a filling gas cell's fringe count gives $n - 1$, and the ring radii $r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R}$ give $R$. None of these involves sound.

questions.stem: Michelson and Morley expected their rotating interferometer to show a fringe shift of about 0.4 fringe from Earth's motion through the ether. What did they observe?
choices: A shift of about 0.4 fringe, confirming the ether
A shift of about 0.8 fringe, twice the prediction
A shift that changed with the time of day exactly as predicted
At most a few hundredths of a fringe, consistent with no shift at all
questions.explanation: The "null result" of 1887 found far less than the predicted shift, consistent with zero. It stayed a puzzle until special relativity explained it: the speed of light is the same for every inertial observer, so there is no ether wind to detect.

questions.stem: The picture shows a light clock at rest (left) and the same clock moving to the right (right). Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Left: two horizontal mirrors one above the other with a pulse arrow going straight up and another straight down between them, and a double arrow (5) beside them spanning the gap. Marker 1 is on the top mirror and marker 2 on the vertical arrows. Right: the same pair of mirrors drawn at three positions moving right; a diagonal arrow (3) goes from the first bottom mirror up to the middle top mirror and another goes down to the last bottom mirror. A double arrow (4) along the bottom spans the sideways distance from the first position to the middle one.

choices: Light path in the clock's own frame
Light path seen by an observer the clock passes
Distance the clock moves in half a tick
Distance light travels in a full tick
questions.explanation: In its own frame (left) the pulse (2) goes straight between the mirrors (1), a distance $D$ (5) apart, so a tick takes $2D/c$. An observer the clock passes sees the pulse follow the diagonal (3) while the clock moves sideways (4). The diagonal is longer than $D$, and light still moves at $c$, so the moving clock's tick takes longer: $\Delta t = \gamma\,\Delta t_0$.

questions.stem: A spaceship moves at $0.60c$ relative to Earth. Its Lorentz factor is $\gamma =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.60^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.64}} = \dfrac{1}{0.80} = 1.25$. So a 1.00 s tick of the ship's clock lasts 1.25 s by Earth clocks, and the ship is shortened to $1/1.25 = 80\%$ of its proper length.

questions.stem: Match each formula to what it describes.
questions.explanation: Moving clocks run slow ($\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0$) and moving lengths shrink ($L = L_0/\gamma$). Velocities combine with the denominator $1 + u'v/c^2$, which keeps every result below $c$. Kinetic energy is total energy minus rest energy, $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$, and $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$ links energy, momentum and mass. Classical kinetic energy, $\tfrac12mv^2$, is none of these; it is the low-speed limit of $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$.

questions.stem: A spaceship passes Earth at $0.80c$. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Earth observers measure the ship's clocks running slow
Astronauts on the ship measure Earth's clocks running slow
The astronauts notice their own clocks ticking slowly
Earth observers measure the ship as shorter along its direction of motion
Earth observers measure the ship as narrower across its direction of motion
questions.explanation: The effects are symmetric: each frame measures the other's clocks running slow, because by the first postulate neither frame is special. Nobody notices anything odd about their own clocks; in the ship's own frame its clocks tick normally. Length contraction happens only along the direction of motion, so the ship is shorter but not narrower.

questions.stem: A ship moving at $0.60c$ relative to Earth fires a probe forward at $0.60c$ relative to the ship. The probe's speed relative to Earth is ___ $c$. Give the number to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $u = \dfrac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2} = \dfrac{0.60c + 0.60c}{1 + 0.36} = \dfrac{1.20c}{1.36} = 0.882c$. Adding classically would give $1.20c$, faster than light, which is impossible.

questions.stem: The diagram shows energy levels of hydrogen (spacing not to scale) with downward transitions. Name the numbered features.

image.alt: Horizontal energy levels at −13.60 eV (marker 1, the lowest), −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV and −0.85 eV, and a dashed line at 0 eV (marker 2, the top). Three downward arrows end on the −13.60 eV level (marker 3), two end on the −3.40 eV level (marker 4), and one short arrow goes from −0.85 eV to −1.51 eV (marker 5).

questions.explanation: The lowest level, $-13.6$ eV, is the ground state (1); at 0 eV (2) the electron is free, so 13.6 eV ionizes the atom. Each series is named for the level it ends on: Lyman at $n = 1$ (3, the biggest drops, ultraviolet), Balmer at $n = 2$ (4, visible), Paschen at $n = 3$ (5, small drops, infrared).

questions.stem: Put these hydrogen transitions in order of the emitted photon's wavelength, from longest to shortest.
questions.explanation: Wavelength is longest for the smallest energy drop. With $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV the drops are: $4\to3$: 0.66 eV (1880 nm, infrared); $3\to2$: 1.89 eV (656 nm); $4\to2$: 2.55 eV (486 nm); $2\to1$: 10.2 eV (122 nm); $4\to1$: 12.75 eV (97 nm).

questions.stem: Which photoelectric observations could the wave theory of light NOT explain? Select all that apply.
choices: Below a threshold frequency no electrons come out, however bright the light
Electrons come out at once, even in very dim light
Light reflects off the polished metal surface
The electrons' maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not brightness
questions.explanation: A wave spreads its energy smoothly, so bright enough light of any color should eventually free electrons, dim light should need time to build up energy, and brighter light should give faster electrons. All three predictions fail; one photon giving all its energy $hf$ to one electron explains each of them. Reflection is ordinary wave behavior and no puzzle at all.

questions.stem: A photon of wavelength 310 nm has energy ___ eV. Use $hc = 1240$ eV·nm and give only the number.
questions.explanation: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240\text{ eV·nm}}{310\text{ nm}} = 4.0$ eV, an ultraviolet photon.

questions.stem: Match each experiment or observation to what it showed.
choices: Light's energy arrives in packets of hf
Planck's quanta remove the classical short-wavelength runaway
Light has the same speed for all observers
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect showed light's energy comes in photons of $hf$; Compton's X-ray shift showed photons carry momentum $h/\lambda$; electron diffraction from crystals (Davisson and Germer, 1927) confirmed de Broglie's matter waves; sharp spectral lines reveal discrete levels; and Planck's quantum assumption fixed the blackbody curve, where classical theory predicted power growing without limit at short wavelengths. The constancy of light's speed is a postulate of relativity, not one of these quantum results.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this X-ray tube.

image.alt: A long rounded glass tube. At the left end, a zigzag wire (1) is connected by leads to an external circuit. A dashed arrow of dots (2) runs right to an angled metal block (3) at the right end. Two wavy arrows (4) leave the block downward through the tube wall. Above the tube, a battery symbol (5) with minus on the left and plus on the right connects the zigzag wire to the metal block.

questions.explanation: The hot filament (1) releases electrons, which the high voltage (5), often tens of kilovolts, accelerates across the tube (2) to the positive target (3). There each electron's kinetic energy $eV$ turns partly into X-rays (4): bremsstrahlung up to $hf_{\max} = eV$ plus the target's characteristic lines.

questions.stem: Put these subshells in the order in which they fill as atoms get more electrons.
questions.explanation: The filling order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, … The 4s subshell fills before 3d because its electrons spend time close to the nucleus, where they are less screened, and so are more tightly bound. That is why the third row of the periodic table stops at argon and the 3d elements (scandium to zinc) appear in the fourth row.

questions.stem: The $n = 4$ shell can hold at most ___ electrons. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $l$ runs from 0 to 3 (4s, 4p, 4d, 4f), with $2l + 1 = 1, 3, 5, 7$ orbitals: 16 orbitals. Two spin states each give 32 electrons, matching $2n^2 = 2(16) = 32$.

questions.stem: Which are properties of laser light? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Stimulated emission makes each new photon a copy of the one that triggered it (same energy, direction and phase), so laser light is monochromatic, coherent and directional. Spontaneous emission, with random directions and phases, is how ordinary lamps glow and why their light spreads in all directions.

questions.stem: Match each quantum number to what it describes.
choices: Size of the orbital and most of its energy
Shape of the orbital (s, p, d, f)
Number of protons in the nucleus
questions.explanation: The principal number $n$ sets the shell (size, and mostly energy); $l$ from 0 to $n - 1$ sets the subshell shape; $m_l$ from $-l$ to $l$ sets the orientation; $m_s = \pm\tfrac12$ is the spin. The number of protons is the atomic number $Z$, a property of the nucleus, not a quantum number of an electron.

questions.stem: A source emits three kinds of radiation toward three absorbers. Name the numbered beams and absorbers.

image.alt: A source on the left emits three beams to the right. Beam 1 (top) stops at a thin white sheet (4). Beam 2 (middle) passes the white sheet and stops at a thicker gray sheet (5). Beam 3 (bottom) passes both sheets and reaches a thick dark block (6), with only a faint dashed continuation beyond it.

questions.explanation: Alpha particles (1) are heavy and doubly charged, so they ionize densely and stop in a sheet of paper (4). Beta particles (2) get through paper but stop in a few millimeters of aluminum (5). Gamma rays (3) are uncharged photons; even thick lead (6) only weakens them.

questions.stem: Put the steps of carbon-14 dating in order.
choices: Measure the sample's carbon-14 activity per gram of carbon
Divide by the activity per gram of living material to get the fraction remaining
questions.explanation: You need the measured activity before you can compare it with living material, the fraction before you can write the decay law, and the equation before you can take logs: $t = 5730\,\dfrac{\ln(\text{fraction})}{\ln 0.5}$ years.

questions.stem: Thorium-234 ($^{234}_{90}\text{Th}$) undergoes beta-minus decay. The daughter nucleus has atomic number ___ and mass number ___.
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron (plus an antineutrino) is emitted: $Z$ rises by 1 and $A$ is unchanged. $^{234}_{90}\text{Th} \to {}^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} + e^- + \bar\nu$ (protactinium-234).

questions.stem: Which quantities are conserved in every nuclear reaction and decay? Select all that apply.
choices: Total number of nucleons (sum of the mass numbers)
questions.explanation: Charge, nucleon number and total energy (with rest energy counted, $E_0 = mc^2$) always balance. Protons and neutrons can change into each other: beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton, and beta-plus does the reverse, so their separate numbers are not conserved.

questions.stem: Match each type of decay to how it changes the nucleus.
choices: Z falls by 2 and A falls by 4
Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged
Z falls by 1 and A is unchanged
Z and A are both unchanged
Z rises by 2 and A rises by 4
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons). Beta minus turns a neutron into a proton; beta plus turns a proton into a neutron; neither changes the nucleon count. A gamma ray is a photon, carrying away energy only. No spontaneous decay adds nucleons.

questions.stem: On a spacetime diagram with position across and time up, what does the worldline of an object at rest look like?
questions.explanation: An object at rest keeps the same $x$ as time goes on, so its worldline runs straight up. A horizontal line would mean many places at one instant (a line of simultaneity), a 45° line is a light pulse (with $c = 1$ ly/yr), and a single point is one event, not a history.

questions.stem: Two events are 5.0 years apart in time and 3.0 light-years apart in space. How much time passes for a traveler who goes from one to the other at constant velocity?
questions.explanation: The traveler's proper time is $\Delta s/c$: $(\Delta s)^2 = 5.0^2 - 3.0^2 = 16$, so 4.0 yr. (Check: the speed is $0.60c$, $\gamma = 1.25$, and $5.0/1.25 = 4.0$.) Adding the squares gives 5.8 yr, the wrong sign; 5.0 yr is the time in the frame where the events are 3 ly apart, not the traveler's.

questions.stem: Event B happens 2.0 years after event A and 3.0 light-years away. How is the pair classified?
questions.explanation: $(c\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x)^2 = 2.0^2 - 3.0^2 = -5$ (ly)², negative, so spacelike: light from A has gone only 2 ly when B happens. The classification can't depend on the observer, because every inertial observer gets the same interval.

questions.stem: Two events have a spacelike separation. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Some inertial observer measures them as simultaneous
Different observers can disagree about which happened first
One of them could have caused the other
All inertial observers get the same value of $(c\,\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x)^2$
A clock can travel from one event to the other
questions.explanation: For a spacelike pair, $|\Delta x| > c|\Delta t|$, so reaching one from the other would need a speed above $c$: no clock can make the trip and no cause can connect them. That's why it is harmless that their order depends on the frame, and there is a frame (moving at $v = c^2\Delta t/\Delta x$) where they are simultaneous. The interval itself is the same for everyone.

questions.stem: With time in years and distance in light-years, a light pulse's worldline makes an angle of ___ degrees with the time axis. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: In these units $c = 1$ ly/yr, so light moves one unit across for each unit up: a 45° line. Every material object moves slower, so its worldline is steeper (closer to the time axis) than 45°.

questions.stem: Blair flies to a star 4.0 ly away at $0.80c$ and straight back, sending a light signal home on each of Blair's birthdays. Put these events in order of Earth time.
choices: Alex receives the signal from Blair's first birthday on the trip
Blair turns around at the star
Alex first sees Blair turn around
questions.explanation: Earth times: departure 0. Blair's first birthday on the trip comes when Earth time $\gamma(1\text{ yr}) = 1.67$ yr has passed, at $x = 0.80(1.67) = 1.33$ ly, so its signal reaches Earth at $1.67 + 1.33 = 3.0$ yr. Turnaround at 5.0 yr; its light needs 4.0 yr more, arriving at 9.0 yr; Blair is home at 10.0 yr.

questions.stem: This spacetime diagram shows the twin paradox trip (time in years up, distance in light-years across). Name the numbered features.

image.alt: Axes: x from 0 to 5 light-years across, t from 0 to 10 years up. A thick vertical line along the t axis (1). A line from the origin up to the point x = 4, t = 5 (2), a dot at that point (4), and a line from there back to x = 0, t = 10 (3). A dashed arrow at 45 degrees (5) runs from the dot back to the t axis, arriving at t = 9. A faint dashed 45-degree line also runs from the origin.

questions.explanation: The Earth twin stays at $x = 0$, so that worldline (1) is vertical and straight. The traveler goes out at $0.8c$ (2, rising 5 yr while moving 4 ly), turns around at the event (4), and returns (3). The dashed 45° line (5) is light from the turnaround reaching Earth at $t = 9$ yr. Each straight leg has $(\Delta s)^2 = 5^2 - 4^2 = 9$, so the traveler ages 3 + 3 = 6 years against Alex's 10.

questions.stem: Two firecrackers 1200 m apart explode simultaneously in the ground frame. A rocket moves along the line joining them at $0.80c$. By how much do the explosion times differ in the rocket's frame? ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s)
questions.explanation: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.64} = 5/3$. $|\Delta t'| = \gamma\dfrac{v\,\Delta x}{c^2} = \dfrac53 \cdot \dfrac{0.80(1200)}{3.00\times10^8} = \dfrac53(3.2\times10^{-6}) = 5.3\times10^{-6}$ s. Leaving out $\gamma$ gives 3.2 μs, dividing by it gives 1.9 μs, and 4.0 μs is just the light travel time $\Delta x/c$.

questions.stem: In the previous situation, which explosion happens first according to the rocket?
choices: The one farther along the rocket's direction of motion
The one behind the rocket's direction of motion
They are simultaneous for the rocket too
