questions.stem: What mass ratio $m_0/m_f$ does a rocket need to reach a delta-v equal to twice its exhaust speed?
questions.explanation: $m_0/m_f = e^{\Delta v/u} = e^2 = 7.39$. The ratio grows exponentially, not in proportion: 2 or 4 assume it grows linearly or as a square. 0.14 is $m_f/m_0$, the upside-down ratio.

questions.stem: For a rocket in free space, which changes increase the delta-v it can reach? Select all that apply.
choices: A larger fraction of its starting mass as propellant
Dropping empty tanks and engines partway through (staging)
Burning the same propellant faster, for more thrust
questions.explanation: $\Delta v = u\ln(m_0/m_f)$ depends only on the exhaust speed and the mass ratio. A higher $u$, more propellant, and staging (which lowers the mass the later burns must push) all raise it. Burning faster changes the thrust and the burn time but not $u$ or the mass ratio, so in free space the final $\Delta v$ is the same. A heavier payload raises $m_f$ and lowers the mass ratio.

questions.stem: Put the events of a two-stage launch in order, for the usual sequence shown in the lesson, where the second stage ignites after separation.
choices: The first-stage engines ignite at liftoff
The first stage runs out of propellant
The empty first stage separates and falls away
The second stage burns out with the payload at its final speed
questions.explanation: The first stage burns until it is empty; only then is it dropped, so its dead weight is no longer carried. The second stage then ignites and burns the rest of the way. (Some rockets "hot stage", lighting the second stage a moment before separation; this question asks about the usual sequence.)

questions.stem: A 50 t two-stage rocket ($u = 3000$ m/s) burns 30 t of propellant in its first stage, drops the 5 t empty first stage, and then burns 10 t of propellant in its second stage. What total delta-v does it reach in free space?
questions.explanation: Stage 1: 50 t to 20 t, $3000\ln 2.5 = 2749$ m/s. Drop 5 t, leaving 15 t. Stage 2: 15 t to 5 t, $3000\ln 3 = 3296$ m/s. Total 6045 m/s. 4830 m/s keeps the empty stage the whole way ($3000\ln(50/10)$); 6910 m/s treats the dropped 5 t as if it were burned propellant ($3000\ln(50/5)$); 2750 m/s is stage 1 only.

questions.stem: Sand falls straight down onto a conveyor belt at 30 kg/s. How much extra horizontal force must the motor supply to keep the belt moving at a steady 2.0 m/s?
questions.explanation: Each second, 30 kg of sand gains horizontal momentum $30(2.0) = 60$ kg·m/s, so $F = Rv = 60$ N. 30 N comes from setting the motor's power equal to only the sand's kinetic energy gain, $\tfrac12Rv^2$; 120 N multiplies by $v^2$.

questions.stem: For sand dropped onto a steadily moving conveyor belt, what fraction of the motor's extra power ends up as kinetic energy of the sand?
choices: One half, whatever the roughness of the belt
All of it, because the belt does no work against friction
It depends on how rough the belt is
questions.explanation: The motor supplies $P = Fv = Rv^2$, but the sand gains only $\tfrac12Rv^2$ of kinetic energy per second. The other half becomes heat as the sand skids before catching up. A rougher belt makes the sand catch up sooner but with a larger friction force, and the two effects cancel, so the split is always half and half.

questions.stem: An open 18 000 kg rail car coasts at 4.0 m/s on a level track with negligible friction. Rain falling straight down adds 2000 kg of water. The car's new speed is ___ m/s. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: The rain brings no horizontal momentum and no horizontal external force acts, so horizontal momentum is conserved: $18\,000(4.0) = 20\,000v$, giving $v = 3.6$ m/s.

questions.stem: A rail car full of sand coasts on a level, frictionless track while sand drains straight down through a hole in its floor. What happens to the car's speed?
choices: It increases, like a rocket losing mass
It decreases, because sand is being lost
It increases at first, then decreases
questions.explanation: The sand leaves with the car's own horizontal velocity, so it carries away exactly its share of the momentum, and no horizontal force acts on the car. Unlike rocket exhaust, the sand is not pushed backward relative to the car, so the car neither speeds up nor slows down.

questions.stem: Match each rocket quantity to its meaning.
choices: Speed of the gas relative to the rocket
Mass of propellant expelled per second
Mass at the start of a burn divided by mass at the end
Forward force on the rocket from expelling gas
Weight of the rocket at liftoff
questions.explanation: The exhaust speed $u$ is measured relative to the rocket. The mass flow rate $R$ is kilograms per second. The mass ratio $m_0/m_f$ goes into the rocket equation. Thrust is $T = uR$; the weight is a separate force that thrust must beat at liftoff.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this rocket.

image.alt: A rocket standing upright: a pointed nose section, two tank sections below it, a bell-shaped piece at the bottom, a flame-shaped region below that, a downward arrow beside the flame and an upward arrow to the right of the rocket. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The payload (1) rides under the nose cone. Below it are the propellant tanks (2), holding fuel and oxidizer. The engine's nozzle (3) directs the exhaust gas (4) backward; the reaction to pushing that gas backward is the upward thrust (5).

questions.stem: An ion thruster has an exhaust speed about ten times that of a chemical rocket but a thrust of only a fraction of a newton. Which statement is correct?
choices: It reaches a much larger delta-v for the same mass ratio, but it accelerates very slowly
It reaches the same delta-v as a chemical rocket, only sooner
Its high exhaust speed lets it lift off from Earth easily
Its low thrust means it can never reach a large delta-v
questions.explanation: $\Delta v = u\ln(m_0/m_f)$, so ten times the exhaust speed gives ten times the delta-v for the same mass ratio. The tiny thrust means the acceleration is small, far below $g$, so it can't lift off, but over months in space the small push adds up.

questions.stem: A ball dropped from 2.00 m rebounds to 1.28 m. What is the coefficient of restitution between the ball and the floor?
questions.explanation: The rebound speed is $e$ times the impact speed, and height is proportional to speed squared, so $h_{\text{after}}/h_{\text{before}} = e^2 = 1.28/2.00 = 0.64$ and $e = 0.80$. 0.64 is the height ratio, not $e$; 0.36 is $1 - e^2$.

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg cart moving at 6.0 m/s hits a 2.0 kg cart at rest head-on. The coefficient of restitution is 0.50. What are the final velocities?
questions.explanation: Momentum: $v_1 + 2.0v_2 = 6.0$. Restitution: $v_2 - v_1 = 0.50(6.0) = 3.0$. Substituting $v_2 = v_1 + 3.0$: $3.0v_1 + 6.0 = 6.0$, so $v_1 = 0$ and $v_2 = 3.0$ m/s. The (2.0, 2.0) choice is the perfectly inelastic result ($e = 0$), and (−2.0, 4.0) is the elastic one ($e = 1$). (1.0, 2.5) conserves momentum but separates at only 1.5 m/s.

questions.stem: In a collision with coefficient of restitution 0.60, ___ % of the relative kinetic energy (the kinetic energy in the center-of-mass frame) is lost. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: In the center-of-mass frame every speed is multiplied by $e$, so every kinetic energy is multiplied by $e^2 = 0.36$. The fraction lost is $1 - e^2 = 0.64$, or 64%. (Not 40%: $e$ scales speeds, not energies.)

questions.stem: What is the reduced mass of a 2.0 kg object and a 3.0 kg object?
questions.explanation: $\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{6.0}{5.0} = 1.2$ kg, less than either mass. 5.0 kg is the total mass and 2.5 kg the average; 0.83 kg is $\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1m_2}$, the upside-down fraction.

questions.stem: Which statements about a head-on collision, viewed in the center-of-mass frame, are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The total momentum is zero before and after
Each object's velocity reverses and is multiplied by $e$
The kinetic energy $\tfrac12Mv_{\text{cm}}^2$ of the center of mass cannot be lost
Both objects always end at rest
The relative speed is the same after as before
questions.explanation: In the CM frame the total momentum is zero by definition and stays zero, so the objects must leave with opposite momenta, each velocity reversed and scaled by $e$. The CM's own kinetic energy can't change because momentum is conserved. The objects end at rest only when $e = 0$, and the relative speed is unchanged only when $e = 1$.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from 1.0 m with $e = 0.50$. Ignoring air resistance, what total distance does it travel before it comes to rest?
questions.explanation: $D = h_0\dfrac{1 + e^2}{1 - e^2} = 1.0\cdot\dfrac{1.25}{0.75} = 1.67$ m: down 1.0 m, then up and down $0.25 + 0.0625 + \dots = 0.333$ m each way. 1.33 m counts each bounce only once; 3.0 m uses $e$ instead of $e^2$ for the height ratio; 2.0 m is $h_0/(1 - e)$, which also uses $e$ in place of $e^2$.

questions.stem: A tennis ball dropped from 254 cm onto concrete rebounds to 140 cm. Ignoring air resistance, what is its coefficient of restitution?
questions.explanation: $e = \sqrt{h_{\text{after}}/h_{\text{before}}} = \sqrt{140/254} = \sqrt{0.551} = 0.74$, inside the 0.73–0.76 range implied by the tennis rules. 0.55 is the height ratio without the square root; 0.45 is $1 - 0.55$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding a spacecraft's speed after an idealized head-on gravity assist in order.
choices: Subtract the planet's velocity to find the craft's velocity in the planet's frame
Reverse that velocity, keeping its speed, because the flyby is elastic in the planet's frame
Add the planet's velocity back to return to the Sun's frame
Compare the new speed with the original speed
questions.explanation: The flyby is simple only in the planet's frame, so change frames first, apply the elastic "bounce" there, change back, and only then compare speeds in the Sun's frame. For a craft at $v$ meeting a planet at $U$ head-on, the speed goes from $v$ to $v + 2U$.

questions.stem: A spacecraft moving at 8 km/s meets a planet moving at 12 km/s in the idealized head-on geometry, and swings around behind it. What is the craft's speed afterward (in the Sun's frame)?
questions.explanation: In the planet's frame the craft approaches at $8 + 12 = 20$ km/s and leaves at 20 km/s. Adding the planet's 12 km/s gives $v + 2U = 32$ km/s. 20 km/s forgets to change back to the Sun's frame; 24 km/s is just $2U$.

questions.stem: Where does the extra kinetic energy a spacecraft gains in a gravity assist come from?
choices: From the spacecraft's fuel, burned during the flyby
From the planet's motion: the planet slows down by an extremely small amount
Nowhere: in the Sun's frame the craft's speed doesn't really change
From the planet's gravitational potential energy, which is used up
questions.explanation: The flyby is an elastic interaction between craft and planet. Momentum conservation means the planet's momentum changes by the opposite amount, so the planet slows very slightly and loses exactly the kinetic energy the craft gains. Because the planet is so massive, its change in speed is far too small to measure.

questions.stem: Match each coefficient of restitution to the kind of collision.
questions.explanation: $e = 1$ means the objects separate as fast as they approached, so no kinetic energy is lost: elastic. $e = 0$ means they don't separate at all: perfectly inelastic. Anything in between is inelastic, losing the fraction $1 - e^2$ of the relative kinetic energy. An explosion releases stored energy, which would correspond to $e > 1$.

questions.stem: This picture shows an idealized head-on gravity assist in the Sun's frame. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A planet with an arrow pointing left from it, and a dashed spacecraft path that comes in from the left along the top moving right, loops around the right side of the planet, and goes back out to the left along the bottom. Arrows along the path show the craft moving right at the top and left at the bottom. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The circle is the planet (1), moving left at $U$ (2). The craft comes in moving right at $v$ (3), swings around the planet's trailing side, and leaves moving left (4). In the planet's frame its speed is $v + U$ both in and out; adding the planet's velocity back gives $v + 2U$ in the Sun's frame, not the original $v$.

questions.stem: A ball arrives at 30 m/s and meets a very heavy bat moving toward it at 20 m/s. With $e = 0.50$, how fast does the ball leave the bat (treating the bat's speed as unchanged)?
questions.explanation: In the bat's frame the ball comes in at $30 + 20 = 50$ m/s and leaves at $0.50(50) = 25$ m/s. Back in the ground frame: $25 + 20 = 45$ m/s. 70 m/s is the elastic result $v + 2V$; 25 m/s forgets to add the bat's velocity back; 35 m/s applies $e$ to the ball's speed alone.

questions.stem: A ball dropped from 4.9 m takes 1.0 s to reach the floor. If $e = 0.50$ and air resistance is ignored, how long after release does it stop bouncing?
choices: It never stops: the bounces go on forever
questions.explanation: $T = t_0\dfrac{1 + e}{1 - e} = 1.0 \times \dfrac{1.5}{0.5} = 3.0$ s. The first fall takes 1.0 s; each later bounce lasts $2e^n t_0$: 1.0 s, 0.5 s, 0.25 s, …, adding to 2.0 s more. Infinitely many bounces fit in a finite time because the times form a geometric series. 2.0 s counts each bounce's flight only once.

questions.stem: A point on the rim of a wheel is 0.50 m from the axle. The wheel turns at 12 rad/s. The point's speed is ___ m/s. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $v = r\omega = 0.50(12) = 6.0$ m/s. This works because $\omega$ is in rad/s.

questions.stem: Match each quantity for straight-line motion to its rotational counterpart.
questions.explanation: The rotational equations mirror the linear ones symbol by symbol: $\theta$ for $x$, $\omega$ for $v$, $\alpha$ for $a$, $I$ for $m$ and $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ for $\tfrac12mv^2$. Torque is the counterpart of force, which isn't listed.

questions.stem: In which of these must $\omega$ be in rad/s (not rpm or rev/s) to get the right answer? Select all that apply.
choices: The ratio $\omega_2/\omega_1$ of two angular speeds
questions.explanation: The relations $v = r\omega$, $a_c = r\omega^2$ and $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ come from $s = r\theta$, which holds only with $\theta$ in radians. A ratio of two angular speeds has the same value in any unit, because the unit cancels.

questions.stem: A disk turns counterclockwise about its axis. Name the numbered parts of the picture for the point on its rim.

image.alt: A disk turning counterclockwise with four numbered parts: the center of the disk, the curved arc along the rim from a dashed reference line to the point, an arrow at the point pointing along the rim, and an arrow at the point pointing toward the center.

questions.explanation: The disk turns about its axis (1). The arc (2) swept from the reference line to the point has length $s = r\theta$. The velocity (3) is tangent to the rim, $v = r\omega$, and the centripetal acceleration (4) points along the radius toward the axis, $a_c = r\omega^2$. The radius itself is the line the acceleration lies along, not an arrow.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg uniform solid disk of radius 0.30 m rotates about an axis through its rim, parallel to its central axis. Its moment of inertia is ___ kg·m². (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Parallel-axis theorem with $d = R$: $I = \tfrac12MR^2 + MR^2 = \tfrac32(2.0)(0.30)^2 = 0.27$ kg·m².

questions.stem: A 50 N force pushes perpendicular to a 0.40 m wrench at its end. The torque about the bolt is ___ N·m. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Perpendicular force: $\tau = rF = 0.40(50) = 20$ N·m.

questions.stem: Each force acts at the end of the same 0.30 m wrench, at the given angle to the handle. Put them in order of torque, smallest first.
questions.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$ with $r = 0.30$ m: $200\sin 0^\circ$ gives 0 (aimed along the handle); $0.30(100)\sin 15^\circ = 7.8$; $0.30(80)\sin 30^\circ = 12.0$; $0.30(50) = 15.0$; $0.30(60)\sin 60^\circ = 15.6$ N·m.

questions.stem: A bucket hangs from a rope wound on a heavy solid cylinder that turns on a frictionless axle. The bucket is released. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The rope tension is less than the bucket's weight
The bucket's acceleration is less than $g$
The tension equals the bucket's weight because the rope is light
A heavier cylinder gives the bucket a smaller acceleration
questions.explanation: The bucket accelerates down, so $mg - T = ma > 0$ and $T < mg$. Since $a = mg/(m + \tfrac12M)$, $a < g$ and a heavier cylinder (larger $M$) gives a smaller $a$. A light rope doesn't make $T = mg$; that would need zero acceleration.

questions.stem: A bucket hangs from a rope wound on a solid cylinder. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A cylinder on a fixed axle with a rope hanging from its right side to a bucket. Five numbered parts: the center of the cylinder, a dashed line from the center to the rim, a downward arrow at the cylinder's rim beside the rope, an upward arrow on the bucket beside the rope, and a downward arrow below the bucket.

questions.explanation: The cylinder turns about its axle (1). The rope leaves the rim at a distance equal to the radius (2), which is the lever arm of the tension. The rope pulls down on the cylinder (3) and up on the bucket (4); the bucket's weight (5) pulls down. The axle is frictionless and nothing pushes on the bucket from below.

questions.stem: A motor delivers a torque of 200 N·m while turning at 300 rad/s. Its power output is ___ kW. (Give only the number.)
A wheel rolls to the right without slipping; its center moves at speed $v$. Choose the motion of each numbered point.

image.alt: A wheel rolling to the right on the ground, with arrows showing velocities. Four numbered points: the arrow at the top of the wheel, the arrow at the center, the point touching the ground, and the slanted arrow at the front of the wheel level with the center.

questions.explanation: Rolling is the center's motion plus rotation about the center. At the top the two add: $v + R\omega = 2v$ (1). The center moves at $v$ (2). At the bottom they cancel, so the contact point is at rest (3). The front point adds $v$ forward and $R\omega = v$ downward, giving $\sqrt2v \approx 1.41v$ slanting down (4). No point of a wheel rolling forward moves backward at $v$.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping with its center moving at 5.0 m/s. The top of the ball moves at ___ m/s relative to the ground. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: The top moves at $v + R\omega = 2v = 10$ m/s.

questions.stem: Writing $I_{\text{cm}} = cMR^2$, match each rolling object to its shape factor $c$.
questions.explanation: From the moment-of-inertia table: hoop $MR^2$, solid cylinder $\tfrac12MR^2$, solid sphere $\tfrac25MR^2$, spherical shell $\tfrac23MR^2$. $\tfrac13$ belongs to a rod about one end, which doesn't roll.

questions.stem: All start from rest at the top of the same ramp: a block sliding without friction, and four objects rolling without slipping. Put them in the order they reach the bottom, first to last.
questions.explanation: $a = g\sin\theta/(1 + c)$, so smaller $c$ is faster: block $c = 0$, solid sphere 0.4, solid cylinder 0.5, hollow sphere 0.667, hoop 1.

questions.stem: In which situations is angular momentum (about the stated axis) conserved? Select all that apply.
choices: A skater on frictionless ice pulls in her arms (axis: her spin axis)
A disk is dropped onto another disk spinning on a frictionless axle (axis: the axle)
A motor spins up a fan from rest (axis: the fan's shaft)
A diver somersaults in a tuck during the dive (axis: through her center of mass)
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved when the net external torque is zero. The skater's arms and the dropped disk exert only internal forces; gravity on the diver acts at her center of mass, so it has no torque about it. The motor exerts an external torque on the fan, so the fan's angular momentum grows.

questions.stem: A uniform ladder leans against a smooth wall. Name the numbered forces acting on it.

image.alt: A ladder leaning against a wall with four numbered force arrows: a horizontal arrow at the top pointing away from the wall, a downward arrow at the middle of the ladder, an upward arrow at the foot, and a horizontal arrow along the floor at the foot pointing toward the wall.

questions.explanation: A smooth wall can only push perpendicular to itself (1). The weight of a uniform ladder acts at its middle (2). The floor pushes up (3) and its static friction (4) acts toward the wall, balancing the wall's push. A smooth wall gives no friction, and nothing here is a rope.

questions.stem: A 20 kg child sits 2.4 m from the pivot of a uniform seesaw pivoted at its center. A 40 kg child balances it by sitting ___ m from the pivot on the other side. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Equal torques about the pivot: $20g(2.4) = 40g\,x$, so $x = 1.2$ m.

questions.stem: Match each problem to the best point about which to take torques.
left: Beam on supports A and B: find the force at B
Beam hinged to a wall and held by a cable: find the cable tension
Ladder against a smooth wall: find the wall's push
Seesaw: where should the second child sit?
questions.explanation: Pick the point where unknown forces you don't want act, so they drop out: support A removes $F_A$; the hinge removes both hinge components; the foot removes floor friction and the floor's normal force; the pivot removes the pivot force (and a uniform seesaw's weight). The top of the ladder would remove the very wall force you want.

questions.stem: Which conditions are required for a rigid object to be in static equilibrium? Select all that apply.
choices: Every individual force on it is zero
Its center of gravity is directly above its pivot
questions.explanation: Zero net force and zero net torque are both needed (and with zero net force, zero torque about one point means zero about all). The forces need not be zero individually, and a balanced seesaw with two children doesn't need its own center of gravity over the pivot to balance by itself.

questions.stem: A uniform 6.0 m beam weighing 300 N rests on supports at its ends A and B. A 600 N load sits 2.0 m from A. The force from support B is ___ N. (Give only the number.)
Each block is deformed by the forces shown (the dashed outlines are the original shapes). Name each kind of deformation.

image.alt: Three blocks with dashed outlines of their original shapes. Block 1 is pulled outward at both ends and is longer. Block 2 has a force to the right along its top face and to the left along its bottom face and is slanted. Block 3 is pushed inward on all four sides and is smaller.

questions.explanation: Pulling along the length stretches the bar: tension, described by Young's modulus (1). Forces along opposite faces slant the block: shear, described by the shear modulus (2). Pressure on all sides shrinks the volume: bulk compression, described by the bulk modulus (3).

questions.stem: A wire 2.0 m long stretches by 1.0 mm under a load. Its strain is ___ (a plain number with no units).
questions.explanation: Strain $= \Delta L/L_0 = 0.0010\text{ m}/2.0\text{ m} = 5.0\times10^{-4}$. Convert both lengths to the same unit first.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: Largest stress the material fully recovers from
Greatest stress the material can withstand
questions.explanation: Below the elastic limit the material springs back; beyond it, deformation is plastic (permanent). The ultimate strength is the top of the stress–strain curve. Strain is $\Delta L/L_0$, a ratio with no units; stress is force per unit area, not per unit length.

questions.stem: Which of these have no shear modulus (they cannot hold a sideways shear strain)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Fluids flow when sheared, so liquids and gases have no shear modulus. Steel and rubber are solids: steel's shear modulus is about $8\times10^{10}$ Pa and rubber's is small but not zero.

questions.stem: A metal rod is pulled with a steadily increasing load until it breaks. Put the stages in order.
choices: Stretches in proportion to the load (Hooke's law)
questions.explanation: The stress–strain curve is straight up to about the elastic limit, then the metal flows plastically up to the curve's peak (ultimate strength). After that it necks at one spot and breaks.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this planetary orbit.

image.alt: An ellipse with a large dot near its right end, two dots at the ends of the long axis, a dot at the middle, and a bar above the left half of the long axis. Five numbers: the large dot near the right end, the dot at the right end, the dot at the left end, the bar, and the middle dot.

questions.explanation: The Sun sits at a focus (1), not the center (5). The planet is closest at perihelion (2), the end of the long axis nearest the Sun, and farthest at aphelion (3). The semimajor axis (4) is half the long axis, from the center to either end.

questions.stem: The distance between two masses is tripled. The gravitational force between them becomes 1/___ of its original value. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Inverse square: $F \propto 1/r^2$, so tripling $r$ divides $F$ by $3^2 = 9$.

questions.stem: Put these Earth orbits in order of period, shortest first.
choices: The International Space Station (about 400 km up)
The Moon (about 384 000 km from Earth's center)
questions.explanation: $T^2 \propto r^3$: higher orbits take longer. The ISS takes about 92 minutes, GPS satellites about 12 hours, geostationary satellites 24 hours, and the Moon about 27 days.

questions.stem: Which statements about a satellite in a circular orbit around Earth are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its orbital speed does not depend on its own mass
A lower orbit has a higher speed
Astronauts aboard float because there is no gravity at that height
Its total mechanical energy is negative
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ has no satellite mass in it and grows as $r$ shrinks. $E = -GMm/(2r) < 0$: the satellite is bound. Gravity at the ISS is still about 89% of its surface value; astronauts float because they and the station fall together.

questions.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun with a semimajor axis of 4.0 AU. Its orbital period is ___ years. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Kepler's third law as a ratio with Earth (1 AU, 1 yr): $T = a^{3/2} = 4.0^{3/2} = 8.0$ yr.

questions.stem: Match each of Kepler's laws to its statement.
choices: Orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus
A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times
Period squared is proportional to semimajor axis cubed
Gravity falls off as the inverse square of distance
questions.explanation: Kepler's three laws describe the orbits; the inverse-square law of gravitation is Newton's, and it explains all three.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping down a ramp. Which way does static friction on the ball point, and why?
choices: Down the slope, because it helps the ball speed up
Up the slope, because its torque about the center spins the ball up
There is no friction, because the contact point is at rest
Perpendicular to the slope, because it adds to the normal force
questions.explanation: Gravity and the normal force have no torque about the center, so only friction can spin the ball up. To give a forward spin for downhill rolling, it must point up the slope. The contact point being at rest means friction does no work, not that it is zero.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg solid sphere rolls without slipping down a $30^\circ$ slope. What is the static friction force on it? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $f = \dfrac{c}{1 + c}Mg\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.4}{1.4}(2.0)(9.8)(0.5) = 2.8$ N. 9.8 N is the whole $Mg\sin\theta$; 7.0 N uses $\tfrac{1}{1 + c}$ (that's the fraction going into acceleration); 3.9 N multiplies by $c$ without dividing by $1 + c$.

questions.stem: A thin hoop rolls without slipping down a $45^\circ$ slope. The smallest coefficient of static friction that allows this is ___. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $\mu_s \ge \dfrac{c}{1 + c}\tan\theta = \dfrac12\tan 45^\circ = 0.50$.

questions.stem: A slope is at $40^\circ$ and $\mu_s = 0.30$. Which of these objects can roll down it without slipping? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Rolling needs $\mu_s \ge \tfrac{c}{1 + c}\tan 40^\circ$, with $\tan 40^\circ = 0.839$: solid sphere 0.24, solid cylinder 0.28, hollow sphere 0.34, hoop 0.42. Only the first two need less than 0.30.

questions.stem: A bowling ball (a solid sphere) is released sliding at 6.3 m/s with no spin. What is its speed once it rolls without slipping?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about a point on the lane is conserved: $v_1 = v_0/(1 + c) = 6.3/1.4 = 4.5$ m/s. 6.3 m/s ignores friction; 3.2 m/s is $v_0/2$ (a hoop's answer); 5.3 m/s divides by 1.2.

questions.stem: A solid sphere released sliding with no spin skids until it rolls. To the nearest whole percent, ___ percent of its initial kinetic energy is lost while it skids.
questions.explanation: Final energy is $\tfrac{1}{1 + c}$ of the initial, so the fraction lost is $\tfrac{c}{1 + c} = \tfrac{0.4}{1.4} = \tfrac27 = 28.6\% \approx 29\%$.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a bowling ball's trip down the lane in order.
choices: Released sliding fast, with no spin
Kinetic friction slows the center and spins the ball up
questions.explanation: While the bottom skids, kinetic friction lowers $v$ and raises $R\omega$. When $R\omega = v$ the contact point stops skidding, so kinetic friction switches off and the ball rolls on at constant speed (ignoring small rolling resistance).

questions.stem: Why is the skidding ball's angular momentum conserved about a fixed point on the lane, but not about the ball's center?
choices: Friction is too small to matter about either point
Gravity has a torque about the center but not about the lane
Friction acts along the lane, so it has no torque about a point on the lane, but it does have a torque about the center
The normal force has a torque about the lane point that cancels friction's
questions.explanation: About a point on the lane, friction's line of action passes through the point, and gravity and the normal force cancel each other's torques (they are equal, opposite and on the same vertical line). About the center, friction has lever arm $R$, which is exactly what spins the ball up.

questions.stem: A thin hoop is launched sliding along a level floor at 6.0 m/s with no spin. What is its speed once it rolls without slipping?
questions.explanation: $v_1 = v_0/(1 + c)$ with $c = 1$: $6.0/2 = 3.0$ m/s. 4.3 m/s uses the solid sphere's $c = 0.4$; 2.0 m/s divides by 3.

questions.stem: A uniform rod 0.90 m long hangs from a pivot at its top end. To give the pivot no jolt when the rod is struck, it should be hit ___ m below the pivot. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: The center of percussion of a uniform rod pivoted at one end is at $\tfrac23L = \tfrac23(0.90) = 0.60$ m.

questions.stem: A uniform rod hanging from a pivot at its top is struck horizontally at its very bottom with impulse $J$. What impulse does the pivot give the rod?
choices: $\tfrac12J$, in the direction of the blow
questions.explanation: About the pivot: $JL = \tfrac13ML^2\omega$, so $\omega = 3J/(ML)$ and $Mv_{\text{cm}} = M\omega L/2 = \tfrac32J$. Linear impulse: $J + J_p = \tfrac32J$, so $J_p = +\tfrac12J$, the same direction as the blow. Below the center of percussion the pivot pushes forward; above it, back.

questions.stem: A gyroscope with $I = 0.0050$ kg·m² spins at 200 rad/s. Its axle is horizontal, supported at one end, and its 0.40 kg mass is centered 0.050 m from the support. What is its precession rate? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $\tau = Mgr = 0.40(9.8)(0.050) = 0.196$ N·m; $L = I\omega = 1.0$ kg·m²/s; $\Omega = \tau/L = 0.20$ rad/s. 5.1 is $L/\tau$ (upside down); 3.9 leaves out $r$ (uses $Mg$ as the torque); 39 multiplies $\tau$ by $\omega$.

questions.stem: A gyroscope precesses with its axle horizontal. Match each change (everything else the same) to its effect on the precession rate $\Omega = Mgr/(I\omega)$.
left: Distance from support to wheel's center doubled
Wheel replaced by one of the same shape and size but twice the mass
questions.explanation: $\Omega \propto r/\omega$. Doubling the mass doubles both the torque $Mgr$ and $I$, so they cancel.

questions.stem: The formula $\Omega = \tau/L$ for a gyroscope's precession is a simplification. Which assumptions does it make? Select all that apply.
choices: The spin is fast, so the precession rate is much smaller than the spin rate
The bobbing (nutation) of a just-released gyroscope is ignored
The wheel is a solid disk
questions.explanation: The derivation treats the extra angular momentum of the precession and the initial nutation as negligible, which needs fast spin. The wheel's shape enters only through $I$. An axle pointing straight up is not assumed: there gravity would have no torque about the support at all. (For a tilted axle, the rate $Mgr/(I\omega)$ still holds, because the torque and the horizontal part of $\vec L$ it turns both shrink by the same factor.)

questions.stem: In an ideal pin-jointed truss loaded only at its joints, the force each member exerts on a pin is
choices: along the member, either pulling or pushing
zero, since the members are weightless
questions.explanation: Each member is a two-force member: the two pin forces on it must be equal, opposite and on the same line, and the only line through both pins is the member. So it pulls (tension) or pushes (compression) along its length.

questions.stem: An A-frame has rafters at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal and a 10 kN load at its peak. Each rafter carries a compression of ___ kN. (Give the number to 3 significant figures.)
questions.explanation: At the peak: $2F\sin 45^\circ = 10$ kN, so $F = 10/(2 \times 0.7071) = 7.07$ kN.

questions.stem: For the same $45^\circ$ A-frame with a 10 kN peak load, what is the tension in the horizontal tie joining the rafters' feet?
questions.explanation: At a foot, the rafter's horizontal push $F\cos 45^\circ = 7.07(0.7071) = 5.0$ kN is balanced by the tie. 7.1 kN is the rafter force; 10 kN is the load; 3.5 kN is half the rafter force.

questions.stem: In the lesson's bridge truss (equilateral triangles, load at bottom joint C, supports at A and E), is each member in tension or compression?
questions.explanation: Joint A gave $F_{AB} = -17.3$ kN (compression) and $F_{AC} = +8.66$ kN (tension); joint B gave $F_{BC} = +17.3$ kN (tension) and $F_{BD} = -17.3$ kN (compression). As in a bent beam, the top chord is squeezed and the bottom stretched.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the method of joints in order.
choices: Find the support forces, treating the whole truss as one body
Pick a joint with at most two unknown member forces
Assume those members are in tension and write $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$ there
Solve; a negative answer means compression
Move on to the next joint with at most two unknowns
questions.explanation: The supports must come first, since every joint at a support involves them. Each joint gives only two equations, so you can solve only a joint with at most two unknowns, then use those results at the next joint.

questions.stem: A truss joint has three unknown member forces and no known ones. Why can't the method of joints solve it yet?
choices: Torques about the joint are needed and they are all zero
The forces at a joint are never in equilibrium
Two-force members can only be in tension
A joint gives only two equations ($\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$), too few for three unknowns
questions.explanation: All the forces at a pin pass through it, so the torque equation says nothing new. Two equations can't fix three unknowns; solve a neighboring joint first.

questions.stem: A uniform ladder leans against a smooth wall; $\mu_s = 0.50$ at the floor. The smallest angle above the floor at which it can stand is ___ degrees. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $\tan\theta \ge \dfrac{1}{2\mu_s} = \dfrac{1}{1.0} = 1$, so $\theta \ge 45^\circ$.

questions.stem: A uniform 20 kg ladder leans at $65^\circ$ above the floor against a smooth wall. How much static friction must the floor supply? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $f = N_w = \dfrac{W}{2\tan\theta} = \dfrac{196}{2\tan 65^\circ} = 45.7 \approx 46$ N. 91 N forgets the factor 2 (the weight acts at the middle); 196 N is the weight; 210 N uses $\tan$ instead of dividing by it.

questions.stem: A ladder rests against a smooth wall. Which changes make it more likely to slip? Select all that apply.
choices: Setting it at a smaller angle to the floor
A person climbing higher on it
Using a longer ladder of the same material at the same angle
questions.explanation: The friction needed is $W/(2\tan\theta)$ for an empty ladder, so a smaller angle needs more; a climber's lever arm about the foot grows as she goes up; a smaller $\mu_s$ lowers the friction available. Length cancels: the condition $\tan\theta \ge 1/(2\mu_s)$ doesn't involve it.

questions.stem: A uniform crate 0.50 m wide and 1.0 m tall sits on a board with $\mu_s = 0.60$. The board is slowly tilted. What happens first?
questions.explanation: Tipping when $\tan\theta = w/h = 0.50$, at $26.6^\circ$; sliding when $\tan\theta = \mu_s = 0.60$, at $31^\circ$. Tipping comes first, since $w/h < \mu_s$.

questions.stem: A uniform box 0.80 m deep (in the direction of the push) sits on a floor with $\mu_s = 0.40$. Pushed horizontally above a height of ___ m, it tips before it slides. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: It tips first when $\dfrac{w}{2H} < \mu_s$, i.e. above $H = \dfrac{w}{2\mu_s} = \dfrac{0.80}{0.80} = 1.0$ m.

questions.stem: A uniform 60 kg cabinet is 0.60 m deep. You push horizontally on its front face 1.5 m above the floor. What force starts it tipping (if it doesn't slide first)? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Torques about the bottom edge it tips over (the far edge from you): $FH = mg\tfrac w2$, so $F = \dfrac{60(9.8)(0.30)}{1.5} = 118$ N. 235 N uses the full depth instead of half; 588 N is the weight; 735 N swaps the two lever arms ($mgH/(2w)$).

questions.stem: A bridge truss supported at its ends carries a load in the middle. In general, its top chord is in ___ and its bottom chord in ___.
questions.explanation: Like a beam bending under a load, the top is squeezed and the bottom stretched. In the lesson's example BD was in compression and AC, CE in tension.

questions.stem: An A-frame roof is made steeper while the load at its peak stays the same. What happens to the force in each rafter?
choices: It increases, because the rafters are longer
It stays the same, because the load is the same
It decreases, because more of each rafter's force is vertical
It becomes tension instead of compression
questions.explanation: $F = P/(2\sin\theta)$: a larger $\theta$ means a larger vertical part per unit of rafter force, so less force is needed (12 kN at $30^\circ$, 6.93 kN at $60^\circ$ for a 12 kN load). The rafters still push, so they stay in compression.

questions.stem: A satellite's perigee is 8000 km and its apogee 12 000 km from Earth's center. Its semimajor axis is ___ km. (Give only the number.)
A comet moves at 9.0 km/s at perihelion, 0.70 AU from the Sun. Its aphelion is 2.1 AU from the Sun. How fast does it move at aphelion?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum: $r_pv_p = r_av_a$, so $v_a = 9.0 \times \dfrac{0.70}{2.1} = 3.0$ km/s. 27 km/s multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing; 1.0 km/s uses the square of the ratio; 5.2 km/s uses its square root.

questions.stem: Two satellites of equal mass orbit Earth. One is in a circle of radius 20 000 km; the other in an ellipse with perigee 10 000 km and apogee 30 000 km. Compare their total energies and periods.
choices: They have the same energy and the same period
The ellipse has more energy and a longer period
The ellipse has less energy and a shorter period
The circle has more energy but the same period
questions.explanation: The ellipse has $a = \tfrac12(10\,000 + 30\,000) = 20\,000$ km, the same as the circle. Both $E = -GMm/(2a)$ and $T^2 \propto a^3$ depend only on $a$.

questions.stem: By the vis-viva equation, at the points of any orbit where the distance $r$ equals the semimajor axis $a$, the speed satisfies $v^2 = GM/$___. (Give the letter.)
questions.explanation: $v^2 = GM(2/r - 1/a)$ with $r = a$ gives $GM/a$, the circular-orbit speed for radius $a$ (and here $r = a$, so $GM/r$ is the same thing).

questions.stem: A satellite's orbit has semimajor axis $8.0\times10^6$ m. How fast is it moving when it is $6.8\times10^6$ m from Earth's center? ($GM_E = 3.98\times10^{14}$ m³/s²)
questions.explanation: $v^2 = 3.98\times10^{14}\left(\dfrac{2}{6.8\times10^6} - \dfrac{1}{8.0\times10^6}\right) = 6.73\times10^7$, so $v = 8.20$ km/s. 7.65 km/s is the circular speed at $6.8\times10^6$ m; 7.05 km/s is the circular speed at $a$; 10.8 km/s is the escape speed at $6.8\times10^6$ m.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a Hohmann transfer to a higher circular orbit in order.
choices: Coast in the inner circular orbit
Burn forward to the transfer ellipse's periapsis speed
Burn forward to the outer orbit's circular speed
Coast in the outer circular orbit
questions.explanation: The first burn puts the craft on an ellipse touching both orbits. Half an ellipse later it reaches apoapsis on the outer orbit, moving too slowly to stay there, and the second burn brings it up to circular speed.

questions.stem: After a Hohmann transfer from a low circular orbit to a high circular orbit, the spacecraft's speed compared with its starting speed is
choices: higher, since both burns sped it up
lower, since circular speed $\sqrt{GM/r}$ is smaller farther out
the same, since the burns cancel
questions.explanation: Both burns add speed, but the coast up the ellipse turns kinetic energy into potential energy. The final speed is the outer circular speed, which is lower (3.07 km/s at geostationary radius versus 7.72 km/s at 300 km).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this Hohmann transfer around Earth.

image.alt: Earth with a small circular orbit and a large circular orbit around it, joined by a dashed half ellipse over the top. Five numbers: the dot where the half ellipse meets the small circle, the dot where it meets the large circle, the small circle, the large circle, and the dashed half ellipse.

questions.explanation: The craft starts on the inner orbit (3) and burns (1) where the transfer ellipse (5) touches it, at the ellipse's periapsis. It coasts to the far side and burns again (2) where the ellipse touches the outer orbit (4). A path that escapes would not close, and none is drawn.

questions.stem: A probe goes by Hohmann transfer from Earth's orbit (1.0 AU) to an asteroid orbiting the Sun at 4.0 AU. About how long does the trip take?
questions.explanation: $a_t = \tfrac12(1.0 + 4.0) = 2.5$ AU; full period $2.5^{3/2} = 3.95$ yr; the trip is half of it, about 2.0 yr. 4.0 yr is roughly the full period, and 8.0 yr is the asteroid's own period.

questions.stem: Two stars orbit each other with a separation whose semimajor axis is 8.0 AU, and a period of 16 years. Their total mass is ___ solar masses. (Give only the number.)
Jupiter's moon Europa orbits at $a = 6.71\times10^8$ m with a period of 3.551 days. What mass does this give for Jupiter? ($G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²)
questions.explanation: $T = 3.551(86\,400) = 3.068\times10^5$ s; $M = \dfrac{4\pi^2a^3}{GT^2} = 1.90\times10^{27}$ kg, matching the value from Io. $1.42\times10^{37}$ kg leaves $T$ in days; $4.80\times10^{22}$ kg is Europa's own mass, which the method can't give; $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg is Earth's.

questions.stem: Using $M = 4\pi^2a^3/(GT^2)$ with a measured orbit, what can you find? Select all that apply.
choices: The mass of a planet, from a small moon's orbit around it
The mass of the small moon itself
The total mass of a binary star pair, from their orbit
questions.explanation: The orbiting body's own mass cancels when it is small, so the moon's mass can't be found this way; the formula gives the central mass. For a binary it gives the sum $M_1 + M_2$. The planet's size doesn't enter at all.

questions.stem: Match each orbital term to its meaning.
choices: Closest point to the central body
Farthest point from the central body
Half the long axis of the ellipse
Change in velocity from an engine burn
questions.explanation: Periapsis and apoapsis are the ends of the long axis; perigee/apogee and perihelion/aphelion are the names around Earth and the Sun. The semimajor axis is $\tfrac12(r_p + r_a)$. The time for one orbit is the period.

questions.stem: A 500 kg satellite orbits Earth on an ellipse with semimajor axis $1.0\times10^7$ m. What is its total orbital energy? ($GM_E = 3.98\times10^{14}$ m³/s²)
questions.explanation: $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a} = -\dfrac{(3.98\times10^{14})(500)}{2(1.0\times10^7)} = -9.95\times10^9$ J. $-1.99\times10^{10}$ J forgets the 2 (it is the potential energy at $r = a$); a bound orbit's energy is negative, never positive.

questions.stem: A 0.40 kg mass on a spring with $k = 160$ N/m oscillates. Its angular frequency is ___ rad/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{160/0.40} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ rad/s. (The period is $2\pi/20 = 0.314$ s.)

questions.stem: A block on a horizontal spring is released from rest at $x = +A$. Put these moments of its first cycle in order.
choices: Released at rest at $x = +A$, with maximum acceleration toward equilibrium
Passes equilibrium moving toward $-A$ at maximum speed
Passes equilibrium moving toward $+A$ at maximum speed
Back at rest at $x = +A$, one period after release
questions.explanation: The block accelerates toward equilibrium, overshoots at top speed, slows to a stop at $-A$, and comes back the same way. Each step takes a quarter period.

questions.stem: A block oscillates on a horizontal spring with no friction. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The acceleration has its largest magnitude at the turning points.
The kinetic energy is largest at equilibrium.
Doubling the amplitude doubles the period.
The acceleration is zero at the turning points.
questions.explanation: At the turning points the spring force, and so the acceleration, is largest while the speed is zero; at equilibrium the force is zero and the speed (and kinetic energy) is largest. $E = \tfrac12kA^2$ throughout. The period $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ doesn't depend on amplitude, and the acceleration is zero at equilibrium, not at the turning points.

questions.stem: The picture shows the forces on a pendulum bob pulled aside from the vertical. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A pendulum hanging from a ceiling, pulled aside from a dashed vertical line. Arrows start at the bob: one along the string toward the pivot, one straight down, one along the arc toward the bottom, and a dashed one along the string away from the pivot. An angle at the pivot and a dashed arc near the bottom are also marked. Six parts are numbered.

choices: Restoring part of the weight (mg sin θ)
Part of the weight along the string (mg cos θ)
questions.explanation: The tension (1) pulls along the string toward the pivot and the weight (2) acts straight down. Splitting the weight, the part along the arc, $mg\sin\theta$ (3), pulls the bob back toward the bottom; the part along the string, $mg\cos\theta$ (4), is balanced by the tension. The angle $\theta$ (5) is measured at the pivot from the vertical, and the arc (6) is $s = L\theta$. There is no surface, so no normal force or friction.

questions.stem: Match each change to its effect on the period.
left: Mass on a spring: mass made 4 times larger
Mass on a spring: spring constant made 4 times larger
Simple pendulum: taken where $g$ is 4 times smaller
questions.explanation: Spring: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, so $4m$ gives $2T$ and $4k$ gives $T/2$. Pendulum: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ has no mass in it, and $g/4$ gives $2T$. Because of the square roots, a factor of 4 never changes the period by a factor of 4.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this snapshot of a wave.

image.alt: A sine-shaped wave drawn across a dashed horizontal line. A double arrow spans from one high point to the next, and a vertical arrow runs from the dashed line up to a high point. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The crest (1) and trough (2) are the highest and lowest points. One wavelength (3) is the distance from one crest to the next; the amplitude (4) is measured from the rest position (5) to a crest, not from trough to crest. A node belongs to a standing wave, and the period is a time, which a snapshot in space can't show.

questions.stem: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4.0 m. Its speed is ___ m/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 4.0 = 200$ m/s.

questions.stem: Match each wave to the way the medium moves.
left: A wave on a guitar string
A pulse pushed along the length of a Slinky
questions.explanation: In sound and in a pushed Slinky, the medium moves back and forth along the direction of travel (longitudinal). A guitar string moves sideways to the travel (transverse). Water parcels in a surface wave move in small circles, a mix of both.

questions.stem: A wave passes from one medium into another in which it travels more slowly. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The frequency (and so the period) is set by the source and doesn't change at the boundary. With $\lambda = v/f$, a lower speed at the same frequency means a shorter wavelength.

questions.stem: Put these strings in order of wave speed, slowest first.
Each tube shows the air's displacement pattern for one resonance. The thick bar marks a closed end; the other ends are open. Name each numbered mode.

image.alt: Four tubes of equal length, each with curves showing how far the air moves. Tube 1, open at both ends: largest at both ends, zero in the middle. Tube 2, open at both ends: largest at both ends and in the middle, zero at two points. Tube 3, closed at the left: zero at the closed end, rising to largest at the open end. Tube 4, closed at the left: zero at the closed end, then largest, zero, and largest again at the open end. The four tubes are numbered.

choices: Open at both ends, second harmonic
Closed at one end, third harmonic
Closed at one end, second harmonic
Open at both ends, third harmonic
questions.explanation: Open ends are displacement antinodes and closed ends are nodes. Tube 1 fits half a wavelength ($L = \lambda/2$, one node); tube 2 fits a whole wavelength (two nodes), the second harmonic. Tube 3 fits a quarter wavelength (the fundamental, $f_1 = v/4L$) and tube 4 three quarters (the third harmonic). A pipe closed at one end has no second harmonic, and an open pipe's third harmonic would show three nodes.

questions.stem: Two identical machines each produce 60 dB at a certain spot. With both running, the level there is ___ dB (to the nearest decibel). Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Intensities add: twice the intensity adds $10\log_{10}2 = 3.0$ dB, so 63 dB, not 120 dB.

questions.stem: Match each situation (in still air) to the pitch the listener hears compared with the pitch the source emits.
left: A siren drives toward a listener standing still
A listener drives away from a siren that is standing still
A siren drives away from a listener standing still
A listener and a siren move in the same direction at the same speed
questions.explanation: Approaching raises the pitch and receding lowers it, whichever one moves. With equal velocities in the same direction, the listener moving away ($v - u$ on top) and the source moving toward the listener ($v - u$ on the bottom) cancel exactly: no relative motion, no shift.

questions.stem: Which of these would raise the fundamental frequency of an organ pipe? Select all that apply.
choices: Opening the closed end of a pipe that was closed at one end
Warming the air inside the pipe
Closing one end of a pipe that was open at both ends
questions.explanation: $f_1 = v/(2L)$ for an open pipe and $v/(4L)$ for a closed one. A shorter pipe raises $f_1$; opening the closed end changes $v/4L$ to $v/2L$, doubling it; warmer air raises $v$. Closing one end halves $f_1$, and a longer pipe lowers it.

questions.stem: Put these sounds in order from quietest to loudest. ($I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m²)
questions.explanation: Convert all to decibels with $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$: $10^{-9}$ W/m² is 30 dB, $10^{-4}$ W/m² is 80 dB, and 1 W/m² is 120 dB. So 30, 50, 80, 95, 120 dB.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass on a spring with $k = 800$ N/m has damping constant $b = 0.50$ kg/s. What is its quality factor?
questions.explanation: $Q = \sqrt{mk}/b = \sqrt{1600}/0.50 = 40/0.50 = 80$. 40 is $\sqrt{mk}$ without dividing by $b$; 20 rad/s is $\omega_0$; 160 uses $2\sqrt{mk}$, the critical damping constant, in place of $\sqrt{mk}$.

questions.stem: A lightly damped oscillator loses 5.0% of its amplitude each cycle. About what percentage of the starting amplitude is left after 20 cycles?
questions.explanation: The amplitude is multiplied by 0.95 each cycle: $0.95^{20} = 0.36$, so about 36%. Subtracting $20 \times 5\%$ gives 0%, but the losses compound; 64% is the fraction lost, not the fraction left.

questions.stem: A 4.0 kg mass hangs on a spring with $k = 100$ N/m. The damping constant that makes it critically damped is ___ kg/s. Give only the number.
Which statements about a lightly damped oscillator (damping force $-bv$) are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its amplitude decreases by the same fraction each cycle.
Its frequency is almost the same as without damping.
Its amplitude decreases by the same amount each cycle.
Its energy decays faster than its amplitude.
Its period grows steadily as the amplitude shrinks.
questions.explanation: The amplitude goes as $e^{-bt/(2m)}$: the same fraction each cycle, not the same amount. Energy goes as amplitude squared, $e^{-bt/m}$, so it decays twice as fast. $\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - (b/2m)^2}$ is almost $\omega_0$ for light damping and doesn't change as the amplitude shrinks.

questions.stem: Match each amount of damping to how the system behaves after being displaced and released.
questions.explanation: $2\sqrt{mk}$ is the critical damping constant. Below it the system is underdamped and oscillates; at it the return is fastest with no overshoot; above it (overdamped) the large drag slows the return. Constant amplitude needs no damping at all.

questions.stem: An oscillator with $Q = 50$ stretches 2.0 mm under a steady force $F_0$. About what steady-state amplitude does it reach when driven at its natural frequency by a force of amplitude $F_0$?
questions.explanation: At resonance $A = QF_0/k = 50 \times 2.0$ mm $= 100$ mm. 2.0 mm is the static response (slow driving); 25 mm divides $Q$ by 2; 0.040 mm divides by $Q$ instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring with natural frequency 4.0 Hz is driven by a force at 2.5 Hz. Once the start-up motion has died away, it oscillates at
questions.explanation: In steady state a driven oscillator moves at the driving frequency. The natural frequency only sets how large the response is. 6.5 and 1.5 Hz are the sum and difference, which are not motions of the mass.

questions.stem: An oscillator with $\omega_0 = 1000$ rad/s and $Q = 200$ is driven at various frequencies. About how wide is the band of driving frequencies over which it responds strongly?
questions.explanation: $\Delta\omega \approx \omega_0/Q = 1000/200 = 5$ rad/s: a sharp, selective resonance. 200 rad/s is $Q$ itself and 0.2 rad/s is $Q/\omega_0$.

questions.stem: An oscillator is driven exactly at its natural frequency. In steady state, how is its motion timed relative to the driving force?
choices: The displacement is in step with the force.
The displacement is half a cycle behind the force.
The displacement lags a quarter cycle, so the velocity is in step with the force.
The velocity is half a cycle behind the force.
questions.explanation: At resonance the displacement lags by $90^\circ$, which puts the velocity in step with the force, so the force does positive work throughout the cycle. In step is the slow-driving limit; half a cycle behind is the fast-driving limit.

questions.stem: An oscillator has $\omega_0 = 10$ rad/s and $Q = 20$. Put these driving frequencies in order of steady-state amplitude, largest first.
questions.explanation: In units of $F_0/k$ the amplitude is $1/\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (r/Q)^2}$ with $r = \omega/\omega_0$: 20 at $r = 1$, 5.1 at $r = 0.9$, 4.6 at $r = 1.1$, 1.33 at $r = 0.5$ and 0.33 at $r = 2$. The peak leans slightly toward low frequencies, which approach the static response $F_0/k$, while high frequencies fall toward zero.

questions.stem: Why did London's Millennium Bridge sway sideways when it opened in 2000?
choices: Walkers adjusted their steps to the sway and ended up pushing in step with it.
The wind gusted at exactly the bridge's natural frequency.
Soldiers marched across it in step.
An earthquake shook its supports at resonance.
questions.explanation: It was a feedback loop: a small sway made walkers adjust their gait for balance, and their sideways pushes fell into step with the sway, feeding it more energy. Dampers fixed it, and the bridge reopened in 2002.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how engineers explain the 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
choices: The wind gusted at exactly the bridge's natural frequency.
Traffic crossing in step drove it at resonance.
Steel fatigue from years of small earthquakes.
Flutter: the twisting changed the wind forces so that they fed energy into the twisting.
questions.explanation: A steady wind doesn't push at a fixed frequency, so "wind matching the natural frequency" is a simplification. The accepted explanation is aeroelastic flutter, a self-excited oscillation in which the structure's own motion controls the forces that drive it.

questions.stem: A lightly damped oscillator loses 0.50% of its stored energy each cycle. Using $Q \approx 2\pi / (\text{fraction lost per cycle})$, its $Q$ is about ___ . Give the number to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $Q \approx 2\pi/0.0050 = 1257 \approx 1300$. (A tuning fork is in this range.)

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg oscillator has damping constant $b = 0.20$ kg/s. How long does its amplitude take to fall to half?
questions.explanation: $t_{1/2} = 2m\ln 2/b = 2(1.0)(0.693)/0.20 = 6.9$ s. 3.5 s ($m\ln 2/b$) is when the energy halves; 10 s is $2m/b$, forgetting the $\ln 2$; 14 s doubles the answer.

questions.stem: A sound contains components at 300, 500 and 700 Hz only. What pitch do most listeners hear?
questions.explanation: All three are multiples of 100 Hz (the 3rd, 5th and 7th harmonics), so the wave repeats 100 times a second and that's the pitch: the missing fundamental. 200 Hz is the spacing between components, but 300 Hz isn't a multiple of 200 Hz.

questions.stem: Which harmonics does a square wave contain?
choices: Odd harmonics only, amplitudes falling as $1/n$
Even harmonics only, amplitudes falling as $1/n$
questions.explanation: Square wave $= \tfrac4\pi[\sin(\omega t) + \tfrac13\sin(3\omega t) + \tfrac15\sin(5\omega t) + \cdots]$: odd harmonics with amplitudes $1/n$. A sawtooth has all harmonics with amplitudes $1/n$.

questions.stem: In equal temperament, the note 12 semitones above 220 Hz has frequency ___ Hz. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: 12 semitones is an octave: $220 \times 2^{12/12} = 440$ Hz.

questions.stem: With A4 = 440 Hz, what is the equal-tempered frequency of the note 9 semitones below A4 (middle C)?
questions.explanation: $f = 440 \cdot 2^{-9/12} = 440(0.5946) = 261.6$ Hz. 293.7 Hz is 7 semitones down and 246.9 Hz is 10 down; 110 Hz subtracts $\tfrac{9}{12}$ of 440 Hz, treating semitones as equal steps in hertz instead of equal ratios.

questions.stem: The interval from 300 Hz to 600 Hz is ___ cents. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: cents $= 1200\log_2(600/300) = 1200\log_2 2 = 1200$: every octave is 1200 cents.

questions.stem: An ideal string is plucked exactly at its midpoint. Which of these harmonics are present in its sound? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The even harmonics all have a node at the midpoint, so plucking there doesn't excite them. The odd harmonics have an antinode there and are present.

questions.stem: Match each musical interval to its pure frequency ratio.
questions.explanation: From 220 Hz: octave 440, fifth 330, fourth 293.3, major third 275 Hz. (6:5 is a minor third.)

questions.stem: A 200 Hz note is played with a note of 301 Hz, meant as a pure fifth. At what rate do the nearly coinciding harmonics beat?
questions.explanation: The lower note's 3rd harmonic is 600 Hz and the upper note's 2nd is 602 Hz, so they beat at 2 Hz. The 1 Hz mistuning is doubled in the 2nd harmonic. 101 Hz is just the difference of the two notes, which is not heard as a beat.

questions.stem: How does an equal-tempered perfect fifth compare with a pure 3:2 fifth?
choices: It is a whole semitone narrower.
questions.explanation: Tempered fifth: 7 semitones = 700 cents. Pure fifth: $1200\log_2 1.5 = 702.0$ cents. The 14-cent difference belongs to the major third (400 vs 386.3 cents).

questions.stem: A flute and a violin play the same note at the same loudness, yet they sound different. The main physical reason is that they differ in
choices: the relative strengths of their harmonics
the speed of sound they produce
questions.explanation: Same note means same fundamental, and therefore the same wavelength and speed in air. Timbre comes mainly from the spectrum, plus how each sound starts and decays.

questions.stem: Put these intervals in order of frequency ratio, smallest first.
questions.explanation: Ratios: semitone $2^{1/12} \approx 1.06$, major third 1.25, fourth 1.33, fifth 1.5, octave 2.

questions.stem: Why can't a 12-note keyboard have every fifth tuned to a pure 3:2?
choices: Pure fifths would make every octave pure as well.
Pure fifths cannot be produced by strings.
Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by about 1.4%.
The ear cannot hear a pure fifth.
questions.explanation: Going up 12 fifths should land 7 octaves up, but $(3/2)^{12} = 129.7$ while $2^7 = 128$, a mismatch of about 1.4% (the Pythagorean comma). Equal temperament narrows each fifth by 2 cents to close the gap.

questions.stem: A periodic sound contains components at 240, 400 and 560 Hz. It repeats ___ times per second, which is the pitch heard. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The largest frequency that divides all three is 80 Hz: $240 = 3(80)$, $400 = 5(80)$, $560 = 7(80)$. So these are the 3rd, 5th and 7th harmonics of 80 Hz.

questions.stem: A material has density 1200 kg/m³ and sound speed 1500 m/s. What is its acoustic impedance?
questions.explanation: $Z = \rho v = 1200 \times 1500 = 1.8\times10^6$ kg/(m²·s). 0.80 and 1.25 divide instead of multiplying; 2700 adds.

questions.stem: Sound hits a boundary straight on where $Z_2 = 3Z_1$. What fraction of the intensity is reflected?
questions.explanation: $R = \left(\dfrac{3 - 1}{3 + 1}\right)^2 = (0.5)^2 = 25\%$. 50% is the amplitude ratio without squaring; 75% is the transmitted fraction; 6.25% squares twice.

questions.stem: An ultrasound echo returns 130 μs after the pulse was sent. Using $v = 1540$ m/s, the boundary is ___ cm deep. Give only the number, to the nearest centimeter.
questions.explanation: $d = vt/2 = 1540 \times 130\times10^{-6}/2 = 0.100$ m $= 10$ cm. Forgetting to halve the round trip gives 20 cm.

questions.stem: Which statements about the fraction of a wave's intensity reflected straight on at a boundary are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It is zero when the two impedances are equal.
It is the same whichever side the wave comes from.
It depends only on the two densities.
It is close to 100% at a tissue–air boundary.
It is largest when the two impedances are nearly equal.
questions.explanation: $R = \left(\dfrac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$ is zero for $Z_1 = Z_2$, unchanged if $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ swap, and about 0.999 for tissue and air. It depends on $Z = \rho v$, not density alone, and it is smallest, not largest, for nearly equal impedances.

questions.stem: Match each boundary to the approximate fraction of ultrasound intensity it reflects.
questions.explanation: With $Z$ in units of $10^6$ kg/(m²·s): fat–muscle $\left(\tfrac{1.69 - 1.38}{3.07}\right)^2 = 0.010$; muscle–bone $\left(\tfrac{7.8 - 1.69}{9.49}\right)^2 = 0.41$; tissue–air 0.999; gel (1.48) to tissue (1.63) 0.002.

questions.stem: This cross-section shows an ultrasound probe on the body, with a pulse going down and two echoes coming back (a thin one and a thick one). Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A probe sits on a thin layer above three horizontal bands of tissue. A downward arrow passes through the top two bands; a thin upward arrow returns from the boundary between the first two bands and a thick upward arrow from the boundary between the second and third bands. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The transducer (1) sends the pulse and hears the echoes; the gel (2) keeps air out. The fat–muscle boundary (between 3 and 4) gives a weak echo of about 1%, and the muscle–bone boundary (between 4 and 5) a strong one of about 40%, which is why the deepest band is bone. An air gap would reflect nearly everything at the surface.

questions.stem: Put these steps in making one line of an ultrasound image in order.
choices: The transducer sends a short pulse into the body
The pulse reaches a boundary between two tissues
Part of the pulse reflects as an echo
The echo returns and the transducer turns it into an electrical signal
The scanner converts the delay to depth and the strength to brightness
questions.explanation: Pulse out, reflection at a boundary, echo back, then the scanner uses $d = vt/2$ for depth and the echo's strength for brightness. Sweeping the beam sideways repeats this line by line.

questions.stem: A pulse on a light rope reaches a knot joining it to a heavier rope under the same tension. The reflected pulse is
choices: upright and larger than the incoming pulse
inverted and smaller than the incoming pulse
upright and smaller than the incoming pulse
absent: all of it passes into the heavy rope
questions.explanation: The heavy rope has higher impedance ($Z = \sqrt{F_T\mu}$), so the amplitude ratio $(Z_1 - Z_2)/(Z_1 + Z_2)$ is negative with magnitude less than 1: inverted and smaller, partway toward the fixed-end case. An upright reflection happens going from heavy to light.

questions.stem: A 4.0 MHz ultrasound beam points straight along an artery in which blood moves toward the probe at 0.60 m/s. About what Doppler shift is measured? (Sound speed in tissue 1540 m/s.)
questions.explanation: $\Delta f = 2fu/v = 2(4.0\times10^6)(0.60)/1540 = 3.1\times10^3$ Hz. 1.6 kHz leaves out the factor 2 (the shift happens twice); 14 kHz uses the speed of sound in air; 0.31 kHz is a power-of-ten slip.

questions.stem: Why are deep organs scanned at lower ultrasound frequencies than shallow tendons?
choices: Low frequencies reflect more strongly at boundaries.
Low frequencies travel faster in tissue.
Low frequencies are absorbed less, so echoes from deep tissue are still strong enough.
questions.explanation: Absorption rises roughly in proportion to frequency (about 0.5 dB per cm per MHz in soft tissue), so high frequencies die out before reaching deep organs. Low frequencies give coarser detail, not finer; the speed and the reflected fraction don't depend much on frequency.

questions.stem: The wavelength of 7.7 MHz ultrasound in soft tissue ($v = 1540$ m/s) is ___ mm. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\lambda = v/f = 1540/(7.7\times10^6) = 2.0\times10^{-4}$ m $= 0.20$ mm, which sets the scale of the finest detail.

questions.stem: A Doppler ultrasound beam is held exactly perpendicular to a blood vessel. What Doppler shift does it measure?
choices: The usual shift, since angle doesn't matter
A shift that depends only on the beam frequency
questions.explanation: $\Delta f \approx 2fu\cos\theta/v$, and the blood has no velocity component along a perpendicular beam. Operators tilt the probe along the vessel to get a signal.

questions.stem: Two materials have different densities and different sound speeds, but the same product $\rho v$. Sound crossing straight from one into the other
choices: reflects an amount set by the density ratio
questions.explanation: Reflection depends only on the impedances $Z = \rho v$. Equal impedances give $R = 0$, even though the wave's speed and wavelength change at the boundary.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this hydraulic lift.

image.alt: A hydraulic lift with five numbered parts: a downward arrow pushing on the narrow left column, the plate at the top of the narrow column, the plate at the top of the wide right column, the box resting on that plate, and the liquid in the channel joining the two columns.

questions.explanation: You push down (1) on the small piston (2). The pressure $F_1/A_1$ spreads undiminished through the hydraulic fluid (5) to the large piston (3), which pushes up on the load (4) with the larger force $F_2 = F_1A_2/A_1$. There is no valve or spring in this simple lift.

questions.stem: The large piston of a hydraulic lift has 50 times the area of the small piston. A 120 N push on the small piston can hold up a load of ___ N. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Pascal's principle: the pressure is the same on both pistons, so $F_2 = F_1\dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = 120(50) = 6000$ N. The small piston must move 50 times as far as the large one, so no energy is created.

questions.stem: Which of these change the buoyant force on an object that is completely under the surface of a liquid? Select all that apply.
choices: How deep below the surface the object is
questions.explanation: Archimedes: $F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$. A fully submerged object displaces its own volume, so the fluid's density and the object's volume matter. The object's own density decides whether it sinks or floats, but not the size of $F_B$. Depth doesn't matter in a liquid: the pressure at the top and bottom both grow with depth, and their difference stays the same.

questions.stem: Put these places in order from lowest to highest absolute pressure. (Fresh water 1000 kg/m³, seawater 1025 kg/m³, the same air pressure at both surfaces.)
choices: At the surface of a pond
questions.explanation: $P = P_{\text{atm}} + \rho gh$: 101.3 kPa at the surface; $101.3 + 19.6 = 120.9$ kPa at 2.0 m in fresh water; $101.3 + 20.1 = 121.4$ kPa at 2.0 m in the denser seawater; $101.3 + 49.0 = 150.3$ kPa at 5.0 m.

questions.stem: Match each device or fact to the idea that explains it.
left: A dam built thicker at its base
choices: Air pressure balancing the weight of a liquid column
questions.explanation: A lift transmits pressure through an enclosed fluid (Pascal). A ship floats because it displaces its own weight of water (Archimedes). In a barometer the atmosphere holds up a column with $P_{\text{atm}} = \rho gh$. The water pushes hardest near the bottom of a dam, where it is deepest. The Bernoulli effect is about moving fluids, and none of these involve flow.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this Venturi tube, which has water flowing through it.

image.alt: A horizontal pipe that narrows in the middle, with five numbered parts: an arrow at the left outside the pipe, one of the lines running along the pipe on the right, the narrow middle section, the tall column of liquid in the tube above the wide left section, and the short column in the tube above the narrow section.

questions.explanation: The arrow (1) shows the flow direction, and the lines (2) are streamlines, the paths the fluid follows. In the constriction (3) the streamlines crowd together because the fluid moves faster ($A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$). Faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli), so the column above the narrow section (5) is shorter than the one above the wide section (4).

questions.stem: Water flows at 3.0 m/s in a pipe that narrows to half its diameter. In the narrow part it flows at ___ m/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Half the diameter means a quarter of the area ($A \propto D^2$), so by continuity the speed is 4 times as large: $4(3.0) = 12$ m/s. Doubling the speed (6 m/s) is the mistake of scaling with diameter instead of diameter squared.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe made of sections with these inside diameters. Put the sections in order from highest to lowest pressure.
questions.explanation: The narrower the section, the faster the water ($v \propto 1/D^2$), and in a horizontal pipe $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2$ is constant, so faster means lower pressure. The widest section (4.0 cm) has the slowest flow and the highest pressure; the 1.5 cm section has the lowest.

questions.stem: Which of these are explained, at least in part, by the Bernoulli effect (faster flow, lower pressure)? Select all that apply.
choices: A perfume atomizer drawing liquid up a tube into a fast air stream
A roof lifting off in a strong wind
A hydraulic jack lifting a car
An iceberg floating with most of its volume under water
questions.explanation: In the atomizer, fast air across the top of the tube lowers the pressure there, so the higher air pressure on the liquid pushes it up the tube; fast wind over a roof lowers the pressure above it, so the still air inside pushes the roof up. A hydraulic jack works by Pascal's principle and an iceberg floats by Archimedes' principle; both are fluids at rest.

questions.stem: Match each equation to what it describes.
choices: Conservation of mass in steady flow
Conservation of energy along a streamline
Speed of liquid leaving a hole in a tank
Buoyant force on a submerged object
questions.explanation: Continuity says the volume flow rate is the same everywhere in a pipe; Bernoulli's equation is energy per unit volume; Torricelli's theorem gives the leak speed; Poiseuille's law gives viscous flow. The buoyant force is $\rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ from the previous lesson.

questions.stem: A pot of water sits on a gas burner. Name the numbered parts: the three ways heat moves, and where the heat comes from.

image.alt: A pot of water on a burner with four numbered parts: an arrow running along the pot's metal handle, a loop of arrows circulating in the water, wavy arrows leaving the flames to the left, and the burner under the pot.

questions.explanation: The handle (1) warms by conduction, molecule to molecule through the metal. Warm water rises and cool water sinks in loops (2): convection, which needs a moving fluid. The wavy arrows (3) are radiation, electromagnetic waves that need no medium. The burner (4) is the heat source.

questions.stem: Water has a specific heat of 4186 J/(kg·K). Heating 0.50 kg of water from 20°C to 60°C takes ___ J. Give only the exact number.
questions.explanation: $Q = mc\Delta T = 0.50(4186)(60 - 20) = 0.50(4186)(40) = 83\,720$ J. A temperature change of 40°C is a change of 40 K, so no conversion is needed.

questions.stem: Heat is added steadily to 1 kg of ice at −20°C until it becomes steam at 120°C. Put the stages in order.
questions.explanation: The temperature rises only between phase changes. It stays flat at 0°C while the ice melts ($Q = mL_f$) and at 100°C while the water boils ($Q = mL_v$), which is the longest stage because $L_v$ is so large. That is the shape of the heating curve in the lesson.

questions.stem: In which of these calculations must temperatures be in kelvins, not degrees Celsius? Select all that apply.
choices: Pressure from the ideal gas law, $PV = nRT$
Power radiated by a hot surface, $P = e\sigma AT^4$
Heat to warm water, $Q = mc\Delta T$
Thermal expansion of a rod, $\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T$
questions.explanation: The gas law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law use the temperature itself, so they need the absolute (kelvin) scale. $Q = mc\Delta T$ and $\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T$ use only a temperature difference, which is the same in kelvins and Celsius degrees.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the main way heat is transferred.
left: A metal spoon handle heating up in hot soup
Warm air from a heater spreading around a room
Heat leaking through a single pane of window glass
questions.explanation: Heat moves through a solid (the spoon, the glass) by conduction. A moving fluid carrying heat with it (warm air rising and circulating) is convection. Sunlight crosses the vacuum of space, so it can only be radiation.

questions.stem: At constant temperature, a gas at 2.0 atm is compressed from 9.0 L to 3.0 L. Its new pressure is ___ atm. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$, so $P_2 = 2.0(9.0/3.0) = 6.0$ atm. A third of the volume means three times the pressure.

questions.stem: For a fixed amount of gas, match each law to the condition it needs.
questions.explanation: Boyle: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$ at constant $T$. Charles: $V/T$ constant at constant $P$. Gay-Lussac: $P/T$ constant at constant $V$. The combined law $P_1V_1/T_1 = P_2V_2/T_2$ covers any change of a fixed amount of gas. None of them allows the amount of gas to change; for that you need $PV = nRT$ with the new $n$.

questions.stem: Helium and nitrogen are held at the same temperature. Which of these are the same for both gases? Select all that apply.
choices: The average translational kinetic energy per molecule
The rms speed of the molecules
questions.explanation: $\tfrac12m\overline{v^2} = \tfrac32k_BT$ depends only on temperature, and $PV/(nT) = R$ for every ideal gas. Helium atoms are 7 times lighter than N₂ molecules, so with the same kinetic energy they move faster: $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$ is larger for helium.

questions.stem: Put these gases in order from slowest to fastest rms molecular speed, all at the same temperature.
questions.explanation: At the same temperature, $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$, so the heaviest molecules are slowest. Ordering by molar mass from largest to smallest gives CO₂, O₂, N₂, He.

questions.stem: The absolute temperature of a gas is multiplied by 4. Its rms molecular speed becomes ___ times as large. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M} \propto \sqrt T$, and $\sqrt4 = 2$. The average kinetic energy is 4 times as large, but speed goes as the square root of energy.

questions.stem: A gas in a cylinder is heated and lifts a weight. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A cylinder on a hot plate, with five numbered parts: the space inside the cylinder, the movable plate near the top of the cylinder, the block held up on a rod above it, an upward arrow beside the cylinder, and one of the upward arrows rising from the hot plate into the cylinder.

questions.explanation: The gas (1) is the system. Heat $Q$ flows into it from the hot plate (5). As it expands it pushes the piston (2) up and lifts the weight (3), doing positive work $W$ on its surroundings (4). Then $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$.
