questions.stem: A gas absorbs 650 J of heat and does 250 J of work on its surroundings. Its internal energy changes by ___ J. Give only the number, with a minus sign if it decreases.
questions.explanation: $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W = 650 - 250 = +400$ J: the energy that came in as heat and did not leave as work stays in the gas. (Adding them, 900 J, is the sign mistake.)

questions.stem: Match each process to the statement that is true of it for an ideal gas.
choices: The internal energy does not change
No heat flows in or out
The entropy of the universe decreases
questions.explanation: Isobaric means constant pressure. Isochoric means constant volume, so $W = 0$. Isothermal means constant temperature, and an ideal gas's internal energy depends only on $T$, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$. Adiabatic means $Q = 0$. No real process decreases the entropy of the universe.

questions.stem: An ideal gas expands isothermally. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The gas does positive work on its surroundings
The internal energy of the gas increases
The pressure of the gas stays constant
questions.explanation: Expanding, the gas does positive work. Its temperature is fixed, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$, and the first law gives $Q = W > 0$: it absorbs exactly as much heat as the work it does. With $T$ fixed, $PV$ is constant, so the pressure falls as the volume grows.

questions.stem: Samples of the same ideal gas start in the same state and expand to the same final volume by three different processes. Put the processes in order from least to most work done by the gas.
questions.explanation: Work is the area under each path on the PV diagram. At constant pressure the path stays at the starting pressure (most area). On an isotherm the pressure falls as $1/V$. On an adiabat it falls faster still, because the gas also cools, so it has the least area under it.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this energy-flow diagram of a heat engine.

image.alt: An energy-flow diagram with five numbered parts: a box at the top, a box at the bottom, a thick arrow from the top box down into a circle, a thinner arrow leaving the circle to the right, and an arrow from the circle down to the bottom box.

choices: Heat taken in from the hot reservoir
Heat exhausted to the cold reservoir
questions.explanation: An engine takes heat $Q_H$ (3) from the hot reservoir (1), turns part of it into work $W$ (4), and exhausts the rest, $Q_C$ (5), to the cold reservoir (2), so $W = Q_H - Q_C$. Work goes in only for a refrigerator or heat pump.

questions.stem: A Carnot engine runs between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is ___ %. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - T_C/T_H = 1 - 300/500 = 0.40$, or 40%. No engine working between these temperatures can do better.

questions.stem: Put the four steps of a Carnot cycle in order, starting with the step in which the gas absorbs heat.
choices: Isothermal expansion at the hot temperature
Adiabatic expansion, cooling the gas to the cold temperature
Isothermal compression at the cold temperature
Adiabatic compression, warming the gas to the hot temperature
questions.explanation: Heat enters only during the hot isothermal expansion. The gas then expands adiabatically and cools to $T_C$, gives up $Q_C$ while being compressed at $T_C$, and is compressed adiabatically back up to $T_H$, ready to start again.

questions.stem: Which statements agree with the second law of thermodynamics? Select all that apply.
choices: No cyclic device can turn heat completely into work
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases
The entropy of any object can never decrease
A refrigerator's coefficient of performance can never be more than 1
questions.explanation: The first is the Kelvin–Planck statement and the second the entropy statement. An object's entropy can decrease (water freezing in a freezer) as long as the total increases. A refrigerator's COP is often 2 to 6, because it moves heat rather than converting it; only an engine's efficiency is limited to below 1.

questions.stem: Match each expression to what it gives.
choices: Highest possible efficiency of an engine
Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator
Entropy change for heat transferred at constant temperature
Work done by an engine in one cycle
Heat absorbed from the cold reservoir by an engine
questions.explanation: $1 - T_C/T_H$ is the Carnot limit (kelvins). A refrigerator's COP is the heat removed per unit of work, $Q_C/W$. $\Delta S = Q/T$ at constant $T$. The first law over a cycle gives $W = Q_H - Q_C$. An engine rejects heat to the cold reservoir; it does not absorb heat from it.

questions.stem: A flat plate of area 0.10 m² slides at 0.50 m/s on a 1.0 mm layer of oil with viscosity 0.20 Pa·s. What force keeps it moving at constant speed?
questions.explanation: $F = \eta Av/d = (0.20)(0.10)(0.50)/(1.0\times10^{-3}) = 10$ N. Leaving the thickness in millimeters gives 0.010 N; dividing by $v$ instead of multiplying gives 40 N; using 10 mm for the film gives 1.0 N.

questions.stem: Plaque narrows an artery's radius by 10%. If the pressure difference along it stays the same and the flow is laminar, the blood flow becomes about
questions.explanation: Poiseuille: $Q \propto R^4$, and $0.9^4 = 0.66$. A 10% narrower vessel carries about a third less blood. (81% and 73% come from $0.9^2$ and $0.9^3$.) In practice the body partly compensates by raising blood pressure.

questions.stem: A needle is replaced by one of the same length with half the inner radius. To keep the same flow rate of medicine, the pressure difference must be multiplied by
questions.explanation: $\Delta P = Q\,\dfrac{8\eta L}{\pi R^4}$. Halving $R$ multiplies $1/R^4$ by $2^4 = 16$, so the same $Q$ needs 16 times the pressure difference.

questions.stem: Water (density 1000 kg/m³, viscosity $1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s) flows at 0.50 m/s through a pipe 2.5 cm in diameter. What is the Reynolds number, and what kind of flow is it?
questions.explanation: $\text{Re} = \rho vD/\eta = (1000)(0.50)(0.025)/(1.0\times10^{-3}) = 12\,500$, well above about 4000, so the flow is turbulent. 12.5 comes from taking the viscosity as 1.0 instead of $1.0\times10^{-3}$; 1250 from converting 2.5 cm to 0.0025 m.

questions.stem: Two water droplets fall through still air, both slowly enough for Stokes's law to apply. One has 3 times the radius of the other. Its terminal speed is
questions.explanation: $v_T = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{9\eta} \propto r^2$, so tripling $r$ gives $3^2 = 9$ times the speed. Weight grows as $r^3$ but Stokes drag only as $r$, so bigger drops fall faster.

questions.stem: Water rises 3.0 cm in a clean glass tube. In a tube with half the inner radius, it rises
questions.explanation: $h = 2\gamma\cos\theta/(\rho gr) \propto 1/r$, so half the radius gives twice the rise: 6.0 cm. The upward pull grows with the circumference ($\propto r$) but the weight to hold up grows with the area ($\propto r^2$).

questions.stem: How high does water (surface tension 0.073 N/m, contact angle 0°) rise in a clean glass tube of inner radius 0.50 mm? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $h = \dfrac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{\rho gr} = \dfrac{2(0.073)(1)}{(1000)(9.8)(5.0\times10^{-4})} = 0.030$ m $= 3.0$ cm. Dropping the 2 gives 1.5 cm; using 0.05 mm for the radius gives 30 cm; using $4\gamma$ (as for a bubble) gives 6.0 cm.

questions.stem: A soap bubble of radius 2.0 cm is made from a solution with surface tension 0.025 N/m. How much higher is the pressure inside than outside?
questions.explanation: A soap film has two surfaces, so $\Delta P = 4\gamma/r = 4(0.025)/0.020 = 5.0$ Pa. Using $2\gamma/r$ (a drop, one surface) gives 2.5 Pa; leaving $r$ in centimeters gives 0.050 Pa.

questions.stem: The dimensionless quantity $\rho vD/\eta$, which predicts whether flow in a pipe is laminar or turbulent, is called the ___ number.
questions.explanation: The Reynolds number, named for Osborne Reynolds, who studied the change from smooth to turbulent pipe flow in the 1880s. Pipe flow is usually laminar below about 2000 and turbulent above about 4000.

questions.stem: Put these fluids in order from least to most viscous, all at about room temperature.
questions.explanation: Roughly: air $1.8\times10^{-5}$ Pa·s, water $1.0\times10^{-3}$, olive oil 0.08 and honey several Pa·s. Each step is a factor of about 25 to 100 or more.

questions.stem: Which changes make flow through a pipe more likely to be laminar? Select all that apply.
choices: Using a wider pipe at the same speed
Using a denser fluid with the same viscosity
questions.explanation: Flow is laminar when $\text{Re} = \rho vD/\eta$ is small. Larger $\eta$ or smaller $v$ lowers Re. A wider pipe or a denser fluid raises Re, making turbulence more likely.

questions.stem: Narrow glass tubes stand in water (left) and mercury (right). Name the numbered features.

image.alt: Two beakers with a narrow tube in each, with four numbered features: the curved top of the liquid in the left tube, the curved top of the liquid in the right tube, the arrow measuring how far the left liquid stands above the outside level, and the arrow measuring how far the right liquid stands below the outside level.

questions.explanation: Water wets glass (contact angle near 0°): its meniscus curves down in the middle (concave, 1) and it rises in the tube (3). Mercury doesn't wet glass (about 140°): its meniscus bulges up (convex, 2) and it sits below the outside level (4), since $h = 2\gamma\cos\theta/(\rho gr)$ is negative when $\theta > 90°$.

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its meaning.
choices: Internal friction between layers of a moving fluid
Force per unit length along a liquid surface
Compares a fluid's inertia with its viscous friction
Angle at which a liquid surface meets a solid wall
Pressure difference per unit length of pipe
questions.explanation: Viscosity $\eta$ resists layers sliding past each other; surface tension $\gamma$ is in N/m (or J/m²); the Reynolds number $\rho vD/\eta$ predicts laminar versus turbulent flow; the contact angle $\theta$ decides whether a liquid rises or falls in a narrow tube.

questions.stem: Why can fog hang in the air for hours?
choices: Its droplets are so small that their terminal speed is only about a centimeter per second or less
The droplets are less dense than air
Surface tension holds the droplets up
Air has no viscosity at the scale of a droplet
questions.explanation: By Stokes's law $v_T \propto r^2$; a 10 µm droplet settles at about 1.2 cm/s, so gentle air currents keep it aloft. Water is about 800 times denser than air, surface tension only shapes the drop, and it is air's viscosity that slows the fall.

questions.stem: A monatomic ideal gas runs a rectangular cycle: A (100 kPa, 2.0 L) → B (200 kPa, 2.0 L) → C (200 kPa, 5.0 L) → D (100 kPa, 5.0 L) → A. What is its efficiency? (1 kPa·L = 1 J)
questions.explanation: Net work = area $= (100)(3.0) = 300$ J. Heat in: A → B, $\tfrac32V\Delta P = 1.5(2.0)(100) = 300$ J; B → C, $\tfrac52P\Delta V = 2.5(200)(3.0) = 1500$ J; total 1800 J. $e = 300/1800 = 17\%$. Dividing by the B → C heat alone gives 20%; 80% is the Carnot limit between the hottest point C and the coldest point A ($PV$ = 1000 and 200); 100% comes from dividing by the net heat, which equals the net work.

questions.stem: Why is an engine's efficiency computed as net work divided by the heat taken in, rather than by the net heat?
choices: The net heat is always negative
Over a full cycle the net heat equals the net work, so the ratio would always be 100%
The net heat cannot be measured
The heat taken in includes the work done on the gas
questions.explanation: Over a cycle $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$, so $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}}$. Efficiency asks what fraction of the heat you had to supply came out as work, so the denominator is the heat taken in, $Q_{\text{in}}$.

questions.stem: What is the ideal Otto-cycle efficiency for a compression ratio of 8, with $\gamma = 1.4$?
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - 1/r^{\gamma - 1} = 1 - 8^{-0.4} = 1 - 0.435 = 0.565$, about 56%. 88% is $1 - 1/8$ (forgot the exponent), 95% uses $r^\gamma$, and 44% is the fraction of the heat rejected.

questions.stem: Air ($\gamma = 1.4$) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-ninth of its volume. Its temperature becomes about
questions.explanation: $TV^{\gamma - 1}$ is constant, so $T_2 = 300(9)^{0.4} = 722$ K. 2700 K multiplies by the full compression ratio, 900 K uses an exponent of 0.5, and 6500 K uses $9^{1.4}$.

questions.stem: A diesel engine has no spark plugs. What ignites its fuel?
choices: A glowing catalyst in the cylinder head
Air heated by rapid, nearly adiabatic compression to well above the fuel's ignition temperature
Friction between the piston and the cylinder wall
questions.explanation: With a compression ratio near 18, adiabatic compression heats the air to roughly 900 K or more, far above the temperature at which diesel fuel ignites by itself, so the fuel catches fire as soon as it is injected. (Some diesels use glow plugs only to help cold starts.)

questions.stem: A higher compression ratio would raise a gasoline engine's ideal efficiency. What mainly limits how high it can be?
choices: The fuel-air mixture would ignite by itself before the spark (knock)
The second law forbids ratios above 10
The gas would be cooled too much by compression
Higher ratios lower the ideal Otto efficiency
questions.explanation: Compression heats the mixture; too much and it ignites on its own, an uncontrolled burn called knock that can damage the engine. Diesel engines avoid this by compressing air alone. Compression heats a gas, and the Otto efficiency rises with $r$.

questions.stem: Why does a real gasoline engine reach well below its ideal Otto efficiency? Select all that apply.
choices: Heat leaking out through the cylinder walls during the cycle
The first law of thermodynamics does not apply to real engines
A real engine has no cold reservoir to reject heat to
questions.explanation: Friction and heat leaks (along with burning that takes time and real-gas effects) waste energy. The first law always applies, and a real engine does reject heat, to the outside air through the exhaust and radiator.

questions.stem: Put the four strokes of a gasoline engine in order, starting with the intake stroke.
questions.explanation: Intake draws in fuel and air, compression squeezes it, the spark fires and the power stroke pushes the piston down, and exhaust clears the cylinder for the next intake.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this refrigerator loop.

image.alt: A closed loop of tubing with four numbered parts: zigzag coils along the top in a warm-colored region with a heat arrow leaving upward, a round unit on the right side with an arrow of work going in, a small bow-tie shaped part on the left side, and zigzag coils along the bottom in a cool-colored region with a heat arrow entering from below.

questions.explanation: The compressor (2) takes in work and squeezes the refrigerant vapor, making it hot. In the condenser (1) it gives heat $Q_H$ to the room and liquefies. The expansion valve (3) drops its pressure, chilling it, and in the evaporator (4) inside the fridge it absorbs $Q_C$ from the food and boils.

questions.stem: Refrigerant leaves the evaporator as a cool, low-pressure vapor. Put what happens to it next in order.
choices: It is compressed into a hot, high-pressure vapor
It gives off heat to the room and condenses to a liquid
It passes through a narrow valve and its pressure drops, chilling it
It absorbs heat from inside the fridge and evaporates
questions.explanation: Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator, and back to the compressor. Heat leaves at the condenser (high temperature) and enters at the evaporator (low temperature), which is possible only because the compressor does work.

questions.stem: The ideal Otto efficiency is $1 - 1/r^{\gamma - 1}$, where $r = V_{\max}/V_{\min}$ is called the ___ ratio.
questions.explanation: The compression ratio compares the cylinder's volume with the piston at the bottom of its stroke to the volume at the top. Most gasoline car engines use about 9 to 14, diesels about 15 to 22.

questions.stem: Match each step of the ideal Otto cycle to what happens in it.
choices: No heat flow; work is done on the gas
Heat is absorbed; no work is done
No heat flow; the gas does work
Heat is rejected; no work is done
Heat is absorbed at constant temperature
questions.explanation: Adiabatic steps have $Q = 0$; compression takes work in and expansion (the power stroke) gives work out. Constant-volume steps do no work; heat enters when the fuel burns (2 → 3) and leaves with the exhaust (4 → 1). Heat absorbed at constant temperature belongs to the Carnot cycle.

questions.stem: A refrigerator with a coefficient of performance of 3.0 removes 90 kJ of heat from its interior. How much electrical energy does it use, and how much heat does it release into the kitchen?
questions.explanation: $W = Q_C/K = 90/3.0 = 30$ kJ, and $Q_H = Q_C + W = 120$ kJ. Subtracting the work instead of adding gives 60 kJ; multiplying by the COP gives 270 kJ.

questions.stem: According to the ideal Otto-cycle formula, which would raise the efficiency? Select all that apply.
choices: A working gas with a larger $\gamma$
Burning more fuel in each cycle
A larger engine with the same compression ratio
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - 1/r^{\gamma - 1}$ depends only on $r$ and $\gamma$, and grows with both. More fuel or a bigger engine gives more work per cycle, but at the same efficiency in this model.

questions.stem: A 12 m² wall has two layers with thermal resistances 0.50 and 2.0 m²·K/W. The temperature difference across it is 20 K. At what rate does heat flow through it?
questions.explanation: The layers are in series, so $R = 0.50 + 2.0 = 2.5$ m²·K/W and $Q/t = A\Delta T/R = (12)(20)/2.5 = 96$ W. Combining them like parallel resistors ($R = 0.40$) gives 600 W; using only the 2.0 layer gives 120 W, and only the 0.50 layer, 480 W.

questions.stem: What is the thermal resistance per unit area of a 5.0 cm layer of foam with thermal conductivity 0.025 W/(m·K)?
questions.explanation: $R = L/k = 0.050/0.025 = 2.0$ m²·K/W. Using 5.0 instead of 0.050 m gives 200; computing $k/L$ gives 0.50; $kL$ gives 0.0013.

questions.stem: An object of area 0.50 m² and emissivity 0.90 is at 400 K in surroundings at 300 K. What net power does it lose by radiation? ($\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴))
questions.explanation: $P = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_s^4) = (0.90)(5.67\times10^{-8})(0.50)(400^4 - 300^4) = 2.55\times10^{-8}(1.75\times10^{10}) = 450$ W. Using $(400 - 300)^4$ gives 2.6 W; forgetting the absorbed radiation (using $400^4$ alone) gives 650 W; leaving out the emissivity gives 496 W.

questions.stem: If a star's surface temperature (in kelvins) were doubled with its size unchanged, the power it radiates would be multiplied by
questions.explanation: $P = e\sigma AT^4$, and $2^4 = 16$. The fourth power makes radiation extremely sensitive to temperature.

questions.stem: Mars is 1.52 times as far from the Sun as Earth. The solar constant at Earth is 1361 W/m². About how intense is sunlight at Mars?
questions.explanation: Intensity falls as $1/d^2$: $1361/1.52^2 = 590$ W/m². Dividing by 1.52 only gives 895 W/m²; multiplying by $1.52^2$ gives 3140 W/m².

questions.stem: In the equilibrium-temperature formula $T_e = [(1 - a)S/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}$, where does the factor of 4 come from?
choices: The fourth power in the Stefan–Boltzmann law
The planet absorbs sunlight over a disk of area $\pi R^2$ but radiates from a sphere of area $4\pi R^2$
Only a quarter of sunlight is visible light
questions.explanation: Setting $(1 - a)S\pi R^2 = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$ leaves $(1 - a)S/4$ on the left: averaged over the whole sphere, each square meter gets a quarter of the solar constant. The fourth power is why the result has a fourth root, not why there is a 4 in the denominator.

questions.stem: Earth's equilibrium temperature is 255 K with an albedo of 0.30. If the albedo rose to 0.35 with the same sunlight, the equilibrium temperature would be about
questions.explanation: $T_e \propto (1 - a)^{1/4}$, so $T = 255(0.65/0.70)^{1/4} = 250$ K. A brighter (more reflective) planet absorbs less sunlight and is cooler. 237 K would follow from $T \propto 1 - a$, forgetting the fourth root; 260 K has the change going the wrong way.

questions.stem: In the one-layer greenhouse model, why is the surface warmer than the equilibrium temperature?
choices: The atmosphere absorbs sunlight before it reaches the ground
The surface receives infrared radiated down by the atmosphere in addition to sunlight
The planet absorbs more energy than it radiates to space
The atmosphere reflects sunlight back onto the surface
questions.explanation: The layer absorbs the surface's infrared and radiates half of its emission back down, so the surface absorbs $2F$ instead of $F$ and must reach $2^{1/4}T_e$. The planet as a whole still sends out exactly what it absorbs; in this model the layer is transparent to sunlight.

questions.stem: The fraction of incoming sunlight that a planet reflects straight back to space is called its ___.
questions.explanation: Earth's albedo is about 0.30: clouds, ice, snow and deserts reflect strongly, oceans and forests weakly. It enters the energy balance as the factor $1 - a$.

questions.stem: In the one-layer greenhouse model the surface temperature is $2^{1/4}$ times the equilibrium temperature. For $T_e = 255$ K, the surface temperature is ___ K. Give only the number, to the nearest kelvin.
questions.explanation: $2^{1/4} = 1.189$, and $1.189 \times 255 = 303$ K. The real average surface temperature, about 288 K, is lower, because the real atmosphere absorbs only part of the infrared and convection also carries heat upward.

questions.stem: A wall is made of 1.2 cm of drywall ($k = 0.17$ W/(m·K)), 9.0 cm of fiberglass ($k = 0.040$) and 2.0 cm of wood ($k = 0.12$). Put the layers in order from largest to smallest temperature drop across them.
questions.explanation: The same heat flows through each layer, so each takes a share of the temperature drop proportional to its resistance $R = L/k$: fiberglass 2.25, wood 0.167, drywall 0.071 m²·K/W.

questions.stem: Using the simple equilibrium-temperature model (no greenhouse effect), which changes would make a planet's equilibrium temperature higher? Select all that apply.
choices: Moving the planet closer to its star
questions.explanation: $T_e = [(1 - a)S/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}$. Closer means larger $S$; lower albedo means more sunlight absorbed. The radius cancels: a bigger planet absorbs more but also radiates more, in the same proportion.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: A layer's thickness divided by its thermal conductivity
Intensity of sunlight at Earth's distance from the Sun
How well a surface radiates compared with a perfect blackbody
Total power the Sun radiates in all directions
questions.explanation: $R = L/k$ (m²·K/W); albedo $a$ is about 0.30 for Earth; the solar constant is about 1361 W/m²; emissivity $e$ runs from 0 to 1. The Sun's total power, about $3.8\times10^{26}$ W, is its luminosity.

questions.stem: Sunlight peaks near 0.5 µm and Earth's surface radiates most strongly near 10 µm. Why does that difference matter for the greenhouse effect?
choices: Greenhouse gases absorb much of the infrared from the ground but let most visible sunlight through
Longer wavelengths carry more energy per photon
The difference means Earth absorbs no sunlight
Infrared cannot travel through a vacuum
questions.explanation: By Wien's law the 5800 K Sun peaks in visible light and the 288 K ground in the infrared. Air is largely transparent to the first, while water vapor and CO₂ absorb strongly in parts of the second, so incoming energy gets in more easily than outgoing energy gets out. Longer wavelengths carry less energy per photon, and infrared crosses a vacuum like any light.

questions.stem: A negatively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A charged rod at the left and a metal sphere at the right, with plus signs on the sphere's left side, minus signs on its right side, and an arrow below the sphere pointing toward the rod. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The rod's negative charge pushes the sphere's free electrons to the far side, leaving the near side positive. The sphere stays neutral overall, but its positive side is closer to the rod, so the attraction is stronger than the repulsion and the net force points toward the rod. No protons move; only electrons do.

questions.stem: Put the steps for charging a metal sphere positively by induction, using a negatively charged rod, in order.
choices: Bring the negative rod near the neutral sphere
Connect the sphere to ground while the rod is near
questions.explanation: With the rod near, the sphere's electrons are pushed away, and grounding lets them escape to Earth. The ground must be removed before the rod: if the rod went first, electrons would flow back up from Earth and the sphere would end up neutral. Only after both steps is the sphere left positive.

questions.stem: Two point charges exert a force $F$ on each other. One charge is tripled and the distance between them is doubled. The new force is ___ times $F$. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $F \propto \dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$: tripling one charge multiplies $F$ by 3 and doubling $r$ divides it by $2^2 = 4$, so the factor is $3/4 = 0.75$.

questions.stem: Which statements about electric charge are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Rubbing a glass rod with silk creates new positive charge in the glass
The total charge of an isolated system never changes
A neutral object can be attracted by a charged rod
Every free charge is a whole-number multiple of $e$
When objects are rubbed together, protons move from one to the other
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved and quantized ($q = ne$), and a neutral object is attracted by polarization. Rubbing doesn't create charge: it moves electrons from one object to the other (the glass loses electrons to the silk). Protons are bound in nuclei and don't move in ordinary charging.

questions.stem: Two point charges exert a force $F$ on each other. Match each change to the new force.
left: Double both charges and the distance
questions.explanation: $F \propto q_1q_2/r^2$. One charge doubled: $\times2$. Distance doubled: $\times\tfrac14$. Distance halved: $\times4$. Both charges and the distance doubled: $\dfrac{2\times2}{2^2} = 1$, unchanged. "Half as large" would need, for example, one charge halved.

questions.stem: An electron is fired between two charged plates and is deflected downward. Name the numbered parts. (The dashed arrows show the direction of the field.)

image.alt: An electron gun at the left fires a beam between two horizontal plates; dashed arrows between the plates point up; the beam curves downward and continues to a screen at the right. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The field points from the positive plate to the negative plate, so with the arrows pointing up, the bottom plate is positive and the top negative. That agrees with the beam: electrons are pushed opposite to the field, down toward the positive plate. The gun produces the beam and the screen shows where it lands.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the net electric field at a point P due to several point charges in order.
choices: Find the distance from each charge to P
Find each field's magnitude and direction at P
Split each field into x and y components
Add the x components and the y components separately
Combine the totals into the net field's magnitude and direction
questions.explanation: Each field's size $k|q|/r^2$ needs the distance first. Fields are vectors, so they're added by components, and only at the end are the component totals turned back into a magnitude and direction. Adding magnitudes directly is the classic mistake this order avoids.

questions.stem: What is the magnitude of the electric field 0.30 m from a $+6.0$ nC point charge? Give only the number, in N/C, to 2 significant figures. ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: $E = k\dfrac{|q|}{r^2} = (8.99\times10^9)\dfrac{6.0\times10^{-9}}{(0.30)^2} = 599$ N/C, or 600 N/C to 2 significant figures, pointing away from the charge. (Forgetting to square $r$ gives 180 N/C.)

questions.stem: A metal object is in electrostatic equilibrium. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Any excess charge sits on its outer surface
The field inside the metal equals the field just outside it
Just outside the surface, the field is perpendicular to the surface
Excess charge spreads evenly over the surface whatever its shape
The electric field inside the metal is zero
questions.explanation: If there were a field inside the metal, free charges would still be moving, so in equilibrium it's zero and excess charge ends up on the surface. A field component along the surface would also push charges, so the field just outside is perpendicular. The inside field (zero) is not the same as the outside field, and charge is not spread evenly: it concentrates where the surface curves most sharply.

questions.stem: A proton moves horizontally into the space between two horizontal plates, where the electric field points straight down. While it is between the plates, the proton
choices: moves straight, because the field is perpendicular to its velocity
slows down along its original direction
questions.explanation: A positive charge is pushed along the field, so the proton feels a constant downward force $eE$ and has constant downward acceleration while its horizontal velocity stays the same: a parabola curving down, like a projectile. An electron in the same field would curve upward. A force perpendicular to the velocity still changes the direction of motion, and nothing acts along the original direction to slow it.

questions.stem: Each charge distribution is shown with a dashed Gaussian surface. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Left: a small charged ball inside a larger dashed circle. Middle: a long charged line through a dashed cylinder. Right: a flat charged sheet pierced by a short dashed cylinder. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The Gaussian surface copies the symmetry of the charge: a concentric sphere around a spherical charge, a coaxial cylinder around a long line, and a short cylinder (pillbox) poking through a flat sheet. On each, the field is the same size everywhere it crosses the surface and perpendicular to it, so the flux is just $E$ times an area.

questions.stem: Match each location to how the electric field there depends on the distance $r$ (from the center, the line, or the sheet).
left: Inside a thin charged spherical shell
Near a long straight line of charge
Near a large flat charged sheet
Inside a uniformly charged solid ball
questions.explanation: Outside a sphere: $E = kQ/r^2$. Inside a thin shell a Gaussian sphere encloses no charge: $E = 0$. Line: $E = 2k\lambda/r$. Sheet: $E = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$, independent of distance. Inside a uniform ball the enclosed charge grows as $r^3$, giving $E = kQr/R^3$.

questions.stem: A closed surface encloses a $+5.0$ nC charge and a $-2.0$ nC charge, and a $+4.0$ nC charge sits outside it. What is the net electric flux through the surface? Give only the number, in N·m²/C, to 3 significant figures. ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
questions.explanation: Only enclosed charge counts: $Q_{\text{enc}} = 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0$ nC, so $\Phi_E = \dfrac{3.0\times10^{-9}}{8.85\times10^{-12}} = 339$ N·m²/C. The outside charge's field lines enter and leave, adding zero net flux. (Including it would give 791.)

questions.stem: Which statements about Gauss's law are true? Select all that apply.
choices: If the enclosed charge is zero, the field is zero everywhere on the surface
It holds for every closed surface, whatever its shape
The flux through a closed surface depends on how big the surface is
Charges outside the surface add no net flux through it
It gives the field directly only for highly symmetric charge distributions
questions.explanation: Gauss's law is always true, and outside charges contribute zero net flux. It finds $E$ easily only when symmetry makes $E$ constant on a well-chosen surface. Zero net flux doesn't mean zero field: an outside charge makes a field on the surface whose inward and outward flux cancel. For a fixed enclosed charge, the flux is the same for any surface size.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding a field with Gauss's law in order.
choices: Identify the symmetry of the charge distribution
Choose a Gaussian surface on which E is constant and perpendicular to the surface
Find the charge enclosed by that surface
Put the enclosed charge into E times the area = Qenc/ε0 and solve for E
questions.explanation: The symmetry decides the surface (sphere, cylinder or pillbox). The enclosed charge depends on which surface you chose, and only once it is known can you put it into $E\cdot A = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$ and solve for $E$.

questions.stem: The picture shows two charged parallel plates. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two vertical parallel plates with solid arrows running from the left plate to the right plate and three evenly spaced dashed vertical lines between them. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The field points from high potential to low, so the plate the arrows leave is at the higher potential. The dashed lines are equipotentials: they're perpendicular to the field lines, and evenly spaced because the field between the plates is uniform.

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its SI unit.
questions.explanation: Field is force per charge (N/C, which equals V/m). Potential is energy per charge (J/C = V). Potential energy is an energy (J). Charge is in coulombs. Farads measure capacitance.

questions.stem: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 250 V. Its kinetic energy is ___ eV. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The energy gained is $|q\Delta V| = e(250\text{ V}) = 250$ eV, which is $4.0\times10^{-17}$ J. That's the point of the electron volt: the answer in eV is the voltage, for a charge of $e$.

questions.stem: Points are at different distances from a single negative point charge. Put them in order from highest potential to lowest (zero at infinity).
questions.explanation: $V = kq/r$ with $q$ negative, so $V$ is negative and its size grows as $r$ shrinks. The farthest point has the potential closest to zero, which is the highest; the nearest point is the most negative. (For a positive charge the order would reverse.)

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Wherever the potential is zero, the electric field must also be zero
Electric field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles
The potentials due to several charges add as vectors
A positive charge released from rest moves toward lower potential
The field does no work on a charge moved along an equipotential
questions.explanation: Field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials, so moving along one involves no work, and positive charges go "downhill" to lower $V$. Zero potential doesn't mean zero field: at the midpoint of a dipole $V = 0$ but the field is strong. Potential is a scalar, so contributions add as plain numbers, not vectors.

questions.stem: The picture shows a parallel-plate capacitor filled with a dielectric. In each molecule, the negative end faces the positive plate. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two horizontal plates with a shaded slab between them containing oval molecules, each with a minus sign at its top end and a plus sign at its bottom end, and a double arrow at the right spanning the gap. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The molecules' negative ends point up, so the top plate is the positive one. The insulating slab is the dielectric; its molecules polarize, and their bound charges partly cancel the field inside, which raises $C$ by the factor $\kappa$. The double arrow marks the gap $d$ in $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$.

questions.stem: A 2.0 μF capacitor and an 8.0 μF capacitor are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is ___ μF. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1{C_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac1{2.0} + \dfrac1{8.0} = \dfrac{5}{8.0}$, so $C_{\text{eq}} = 1.6$ μF, smaller than the smaller capacitor. (Adding them, 10 μF, is the parallel rule.)

questions.stem: A charged air capacitor has a dielectric slid between its plates. Match each quantity to what happens to it.
questions.explanation: The dielectric raises $C$ by $\kappa$ either way. A connected battery holds $V$ fixed (so $Q = CV$ rises). A disconnected capacitor keeps its charge, so $V = Q/C$ falls by the factor $\kappa$.

questions.stem: Several capacitors are connected in series across a battery. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each capacitor has the battery's full voltage across it
Each capacitor carries the same charge
The equivalent capacitance is the sum of the capacitances
The capacitors' voltages add up to the battery's voltage
The equivalent capacitance is less than the smallest capacitance
questions.explanation: In series there's one path, so every capacitor carries the same $Q$, the voltages add to the battery's, and $1/C_{\text{eq}} = \sum 1/C_i$ makes $C_{\text{eq}}$ smaller than the smallest. Full battery voltage on each and adding capacitances are the parallel rules.

questions.stem: In the parallel circuit shown on the right, which capacitor stores more energy?

image.alt: Two circuits: on the left a 12 V battery with 3.0 μF and 6.0 μF capacitors in series; on the right the same battery with the two capacitors in parallel.

choices: The 3.0 μF capacitor, twice as much
The 6.0 μF capacitor, four times as much
The 6.0 μF capacitor, twice as much
questions.explanation: In parallel both have the full 12 V, so $U = \tfrac12CV^2$ is proportional to $C$: $\tfrac12(6.0\times10^{-6})(12)^2 = 432$ μJ versus 216 μJ, twice as much for the 6.0 μF capacitor. (In the series circuit it's the reverse: same charge, so $U = Q^2/(2C)$ is larger for the 3.0 μF one.) "Four times" would come from wrongly squaring the capacitance ratio.

questions.stem: The dipole moment $\vec p$ of a pair of charges $+q$ and $-q$ points
choices: from the negative charge to the positive charge
from the positive charge to the negative charge
perpendicular to the line joining the charges
along the external field, whatever the dipole's orientation
questions.explanation: By convention $\vec p = q\vec d$ with $\vec d$ from $-$ to $+$. It's tied to the dipole itself, not to any outside field; note it points opposite to the field between the two charges.

questions.stem: Charges of $\pm3.0$ nC sit 2.0 mm apart in a uniform field of $4.0\times10^4$ N/C, with the dipole moment at $60^\circ$ to the field. What is the magnitude of the torque on the dipole?
questions.explanation: $p = qd = (3.0\times10^{-9})(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 6.0\times10^{-12}$ C·m, and $\tau = pE\sin60^\circ = (6.0\times10^{-12})(4.0\times10^4)(0.866) = 2.1\times10^{-7}$ N·m. Using $\cos60^\circ$ gives $1.2\times10^{-7}$; leaving out the angle gives $pE = 2.4\times10^{-7}$; doubling for "two forces" counts the couple twice ($4.2\times10^{-7}$).

questions.stem: A dipole sits in a uniform electric field at some angle to it. The net force and the net torque on it are
choices: a nonzero force and zero torque
zero force and a nonzero torque
questions.explanation: The forces $+q\vec E$ and $-q\vec E$ are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero. They act at different points, though, forming a couple with torque $pE\sin\theta$ (zero only when $\vec p$ is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec E$). A net force appears only in a nonuniform field.

questions.stem: A dipole with $p = 5.0\times10^{-12}$ C·m is aligned with a uniform field of $2.0\times10^4$ N/C. How much work does it take to turn it to point exactly against the field?
questions.explanation: $U = -pE\cos\theta$ goes from $-pE$ at $0^\circ$ to $+pE$ at $180^\circ$, so $W = 2pE = 2(5.0\times10^{-12})(2.0\times10^4) = 2.0\times10^{-7}$ J. $pE$ alone is the work to turn it only to $90^\circ$. It's not zero: the field resists the turn the whole way.

questions.stem: Far from a dipole, you double your distance from it (staying on its axis). The field becomes
questions.explanation: Far away the two charges' fields nearly cancel, leaving $E \approx 2kp/r^3$. Doubling $r$ divides $E$ by $2^3 = 8$. One-quarter would be a single point charge's $1/r^2$ behavior.

questions.stem: Even in a field of $10^6$ N/C, water molecules at room temperature are only very slightly lined up with the field. Why?
choices: The field cannot exert a torque on a molecule with zero net charge
Their thermal energy is hundreds of times larger than the energy $2pE$ needed to flip them
Water molecules have no permanent dipole moment
The torque is exactly balanced by the net electric force
questions.explanation: For water, $2pE \approx 1.2\times10^{-23}$ J in that field, while $k_BT \approx 4.1\times10^{-21}$ J at 300 K. Collisions keep scrambling the orientations, and the field only slightly biases them. A neutral dipole does feel a torque, water is strongly polar ($p \approx 6.2\times10^{-30}$ C·m), and in a uniform field there's no net force at all.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide molecules (O=C=O) have polar bonds, but CO₂ has no permanent dipole moment. Why?
choices: Carbon and oxygen pull on electrons equally
The molecule carries a net charge that hides its dipole
The molecule is straight, so its two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel
Dipole moments only exist in liquids
questions.explanation: Each C=O bond is polar, but in a straight molecule the two bond dipoles are equal and opposite, adding to zero. Water is bent, so its two O–H contributions don't cancel. CO₂ is neutral, and dipole moments belong to molecules in any phase.

questions.stem: Why is a scrap of neutral paper attracted to a comb whether the comb is charged positively or negatively?
choices: The comb transfers charge of the opposite sign to the paper through the air
Paper always carries a small negative charge
Gravity between the comb and the paper becomes stronger
The comb's field induces a dipole lined up with it, and the near end, in the stronger field, is pulled harder
questions.explanation: The induced dipole always lines up with the comb's field, so its near end has the opposite sign to the comb. The field is stronger nearer the comb, so the near end's attraction beats the far end's repulsion, for either sign of comb. No charge needs to jump across.

questions.stem: Which statement about how a microwave oven heats food is accurate?
choices: Water molecules are pushed toward the stronger field and rub against the walls
The oscillating field keeps turning polar water molecules, and collisions turn that motion into heat
The microwaves ionize water molecules, releasing energy
It works only because 2.45 GHz is a sharp resonance frequency of water
questions.explanation: The field reverses billions of times a second; water dipoles keep trying to follow it, and collisions with neighbors convert the motion into heat. Water absorbs over a broad range of microwave frequencies, so 2.45 GHz is not a special resonance, and microwave photons have far too little energy to ionize anything.

questions.stem: Charges of $\pm4.0$ nC are 5.0 mm apart. Their dipole moment is ___ $\times10^{-11}$ C·m. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $p = qd = (4.0\times10^{-9})(5.0\times10^{-3}) = 2.0\times10^{-11}$ C·m. (Using 8.0 nC, the difference between the charges, would double it; $q$ is the size of one charge.)

questions.stem: A dipole is in a uniform field. Match each orientation of $\vec p$ to its description.
questions.explanation: $U = -pE\cos\theta$ is $-pE$ when aligned (stable minimum) and $+pE$ when anti-aligned (unstable maximum). $\tau = pE\sin\theta$ is largest at $90^\circ$. In a uniform field the net force is zero at every orientation.

questions.stem: A capacitor keeps the same charge on its plates while a dielectric is inserted. Put the chain of causes in order.
choices: The plates' field acts on the dielectric's molecules
The molecules' dipoles line up partly with the field
Bound charge appears at the two faces of the slab
The bound charge partly cancels the plates' field inside
The voltage drops, so the capacitance rises
questions.explanation: The plates' field polarizes the molecules (permanent dipoles turn, or dipoles are induced). Inside the slab the neighboring ends cancel, but thin layers of bound charge are left at the faces, opposite in sign to the nearby plates. That reduces the field to $E_0/\kappa$, so $V = Ed$ drops and $C = Q/V$ goes up.

questions.stem: Which statements about electric dipoles are true? Select all that apply.
choices: In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero
The torque on a dipole is greatest when $\vec p$ is parallel to $\vec E$
Far from a dipole, its field falls off as $1/r^3$
An aligned dipole in a nonuniform field is pulled toward the stronger field
An aligned dipole has potential energy $U = +pE$
questions.explanation: Uniform field: equal and opposite forces, zero net force. The far field goes as $1/r^3$. In a nonuniform field the end in the stronger field wins, pulling an aligned dipole toward stronger field. The torque $pE\sin\theta$ is zero when $\vec p \parallel \vec E$, and the aligned energy is $-pE$, the minimum.

questions.stem: A dipole is in a uniform field pointing to the right. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Horizontal field arrows pointing right at the top and bottom. A tilted rod has a plus charge at its upper right end and a minus charge at its lower left end; an arrow from the plus charge points right, an arrow from the minus charge points left, and a blue arrow along the rod points toward the plus charge. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The positive charge is pushed along the field (right) and the negative charge against it (left). The dipole moment points along the rod from $-$ to $+$. The two forces are equal and opposite, so there is no net force, only a torque turning $\vec p$ toward the field.

questions.stem: An oil drop of mass $4.9\times10^{-15}$ kg hangs motionless between horizontal plates 1.0 cm apart when the voltage is 1000 V. What is the size of its charge? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $q = \dfrac{mgd}{V} = \dfrac{(4.9\times10^{-15})(9.8)(0.010)}{1000} = 4.8\times10^{-19}$ C, three electron charges. Using $d = 1.0$ (cm not converted) gives $4.8\times10^{-17}$; leaving out $g$ gives $4.9\times10^{-20}$, less than $e$, which is impossible for a free charge.

questions.stem: To hold a negatively charged oil drop still between horizontal plates, the electric field must point
choices: upward, so the top plate is negative
downward, so the top plate is positive
upward, so the top plate is positive
questions.explanation: The electric force must be upward to balance gravity. A negative charge is pushed opposite to $\vec E$, so $\vec E$ must point down, which means the top plate is positive (fields point from $+$ to $-$). An upward field would push the drop down along with gravity.

questions.stem: Why does the experimenter time each drop falling with the field switched off?
choices: To measure the drop's charge directly
To let the drop lose its charge
To check that the plates are level
To find the drop's radius, and so its mass, from its terminal speed
questions.explanation: The drops are far too small to weigh. With the field off, drag balances weight at terminal speed: $6\pi\eta rv = \tfrac43\pi r^3\rho g$, which gives $r$ and then $m$. Only with $m$ known does the balance condition give $q$.

questions.stem: Drop B falls (field off) at 4 times the terminal speed of drop A, made of the same oil. By Stokes's law, drop B's radius is
questions.explanation: $r = \sqrt{9\eta v/(2\rho g)}$, so $r \propto \sqrt v$: four times the speed means twice the radius. (Its mass, $\propto r^3$, is 8 times larger.)

questions.stem: Four drops have charges of 4.8, 8.0, 11.2 and 14.4 (in units of $10^{-19}$ C). What is the best estimate of the elementary charge from these data?
questions.explanation: Differences are all 3.2, and every charge is a whole multiple of 1.6: 3, 5, 7 and 9 units. 3.2 doesn't divide 4.8 evenly, and 4.8 doesn't divide 8.0. A unit of 0.8 also fits but would make every count even (6, 10, 14, 18) with no odd values, an unlikely coincidence; the largest unit that fits all the data is the natural answer.

questions.stem: Millikan's 1913 value of $e$ was about 0.6% below the modern value. What was the main cause?
choices: He used a value for the viscosity of air that was slightly too low
His oil evaporated during each measurement
He forgot to convert from centimeters to meters
Electrons had a different charge in 1913
questions.explanation: The air viscosity $\eta$ enters through Stokes's law, and the value he used was a little low, which made $e$ come out low. Oil was chosen precisely because it hardly evaporates, and the charge of the electron hasn't changed.

questions.stem: Why did the experiment use oil drops rather than water drops?
choices: Oil hardly evaporates, so a drop's mass stays constant while it is watched
Oil is a conductor and spreads charge evenly
Water drops fall too slowly to time
questions.explanation: Earlier cloud methods suffered because water droplets evaporated, changing their mass during a measurement. An oil drop keeps its mass, so one drop can be timed for hours.

questions.stem: During a run, the charge on a single drop could be changed by
choices: raising the voltage until the drop split in two
ionizing the air with X-rays or a radioactive source, so the drop picked up an ion
switching the light source on and off
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation makes ions in the air between the plates; a drop occasionally captures one and its charge jumps. Those jumps, always multiples of the same unit, are the most direct evidence that charge is quantized.

questions.stem: Quarks have charges of $\pm\tfrac13e$ and $\pm\tfrac23e$. Why doesn't this contradict the rule that free charges are whole multiples of $e$?
choices: Quarks are always bound inside particles such as protons and neutrons, never found free
Quark charges are too small to measure
Quarks carry no charge when they are moving
The rule only applies to oil drops
questions.explanation: Quarks are confined: they occur only in combinations, such as a proton (two up quarks, one down: $\tfrac23 + \tfrac23 - \tfrac13 = 1$) whose total is a whole multiple of $e$. Every isolated charge ever measured is a whole multiple of $e$.

questions.stem: A balanced oil drop is found to carry a charge of $6.4\times10^{-19}$ C. It has ___ excess electrons. Give only the number.
A drop's fall time (field off) over a known distance and its balancing voltage have both been measured. Put the steps for calculating its charge in order.
choices: Divide the fall distance by the time to get the terminal speed
Use Stokes's law to find its radius
Use the radius and the oil's density to find its mass
Calculate its charge from q = mgd/V
questions.explanation: Each quantity depends on the one before: distance and time give $v$; $v$ gives $r$ through $6\pi\eta rv = \tfrac43\pi r^3\rho g$; $r$ gives $m$; and with $m$ known, the balancing voltage gives $q = mgd/V$. (The two measurements themselves can be made in either order, which is why they are not steps here.)

questions.stem: Match each person to their part in the story of measuring $e$.
choices: Measured the charge-to-mass ratio of cathode-ray particles
Graduate student who worked on the oil-drop experiment
Claimed to see charges smaller than e
questions.explanation: Thomson measured $e/m$ in 1897; Fletcher worked with Millikan on the oil drops (and later said the use of oil was his idea); Holton's 1978 study of the notebooks started the debate about data selection; Ehrenhaft's "subelectrons" were not confirmed.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the oil-drop apparatus.

image.alt: A bulb sprayer at the top left with small drops above a horizontal plate that has a gap in its center; a second plate below; a small drop between the plates; a lamp at the left with rays; a tube at the right; and a battery symbol with an arrow through it wired to both plates. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The atomizer sprays drops above the top plate; a few fall through its hole. The light makes a drop visible in the microscope, and the adjustable voltage across the plates sets the field $E = V/d$ used to balance or raise it.

questions.stem: Which statements about the oil-drop experiment are supported by the historical record described in the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: Free charges of $\tfrac13e$ have been isolated in later oil-drop experiments
Millikan's notebooks record drops that he did not include in his 1913 results
Since 2019, $e$ has an exact value fixed by the definition of the SI
Later analyses found the excluded drops shifted $e$ by about 10%
Millikan's published value was about 0.6% below the modern value
questions.explanation: The notebooks do record unused drops (Holton, 1978); $e = 1.602176634\times10^{-19}$ C exactly since 2019; and the 1913 value was about 0.6% low. Analyses such as Franklin's found that including the excluded drops would change $e$ little but enlarge its uncertainty, nothing like 10%. No free fractional charge has been found.

questions.stem: A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm is in air that breaks down at $3.0\times10^6$ V/m. What is the highest potential it can reach?
questions.explanation: The surface field is $V/R$, so $V_{\max} = E_{\max}R = (3.0\times10^6)(0.10) = 3.0\times10^5$ V = 300 kV. Using the 20 cm diameter gives 600 kV; dividing instead of multiplying gives $3.0\times10^7$ V; using 0.01 m gives 30 kV.

questions.stem: A large and a small conducting sphere, far apart, are joined by a wire and charged. Which statement is correct?
choices: The small sphere has more charge and a stronger surface field
The large sphere has more charge, but the small sphere has the stronger surface field
Both have the same charge and the same surface field
The large sphere has more charge and the stronger surface field
questions.explanation: Connected conductors share one potential: $kQ_1/R_1 = kQ_2/R_2$, so $Q \propto R$ and the large sphere holds more. The surface field is $E = V/R$, so the smaller sphere's field is larger, by the factor $R_1/R_2$.

questions.stem: Spheres of radius 12 cm and 3.0 cm, far apart, are joined by a wire. What is the ratio of the large sphere's charge to the small sphere's?
questions.explanation: Equal potentials give $Q_1/Q_2 = R_1/R_2 = 12/3.0 = 4$. A ratio of 16 would come from wrongly using surface areas ($R^2$), as if the charge densities were equal.

questions.stem: Why does a Van de Graaff generator have a large, smooth, rounded dome?
choices: A large radius and no sharp points keep the surface field below breakdown at higher voltages
A large dome has a smaller capacitance, so it charges faster
Smooth metal is a better conductor than rough metal
The belt needs the room inside to turn
questions.explanation: At the surface $E = V/R$, so a bigger radius allows a higher voltage before the air breaks down ($V_{\max} = E_{\max}R$). Bumps and points act like tiny spheres with strong local fields that leak charge by corona. A larger sphere has a larger capacitance ($4\pi\varepsilon_0R$).

questions.stem: What is corona discharge?
choices: A full spark that jumps between two conductors
Charge flowing through a lightning rod to the ground
A faint glow where the air ionizes only in a thin region of very strong field near a sharp point
Light given off by a charged insulator as it is rubbed
questions.explanation: Near a sharp point the field can exceed the breakdown value in a small region while the field farther out is too weak for a complete spark, so the air ionizes only locally, giving a glow and a hiss (St. Elmo's fire). It slowly bleeds charge away.

questions.stem: On a clear day the electric field just above flat ground is 150 V/m, pointing down. What is the surface charge density on the ground? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
questions.explanation: The ground is a conductor, so just outside it $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$: $|\sigma| = (8.85\times10^{-12})(150) = 1.3\times10^{-9}$ C/m². The field points into the ground, so the charge is negative. Using the isolated-sheet formula $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ gives twice as much; dividing $E$ by $\varepsilon_0$ gives the absurd $10^{13}$.

questions.stem: What starts dielectric breakdown in air?
choices: The field pulls protons out of the air's nuclei
The air becomes a solid conductor when the voltage is high enough
Air molecules line up as dipoles and touch end to end
Free electrons gain enough energy between collisions to ionize molecules, setting off an avalanche
questions.explanation: A few free electrons are always present. In a strong enough field, each gains enough energy between collisions to knock another electron loose; the number doubles again and again, and the air along a path becomes a conducting channel of ionized gas.

questions.stem: According to the modern view described in the lesson, what does a lightning rod mainly do?
choices: It gives a strike a safe, low-resistance path to ground that bypasses the building
It drains the cloud's charge quietly so that lightning never strikes nearby
It repels lightning away from the building
It stores the lightning's energy in the ground for later use
questions.explanation: Franklin hoped points would drain clouds and prevent strikes, but a rod can't stop lightning. What it does is intercept a strike and carry the current to ground through heavy conductors instead of through the building.

questions.stem: What is the open puzzle about how lightning starts?
choices: Measured fields in thunderclouds are well below the breakdown strength of air, even at altitude
Nobody knows why clouds carry charge at all
Thunder is heard before the flash
questions.explanation: Fields measured inside storms rarely exceed a few hundred kV/m, below air's breakdown strength. Proposed explanations include field enhancement near ice particles and avalanches seeded by cosmic-ray electrons. The leading charging mechanism (ice-graupel collisions) is also still being researched, but that clouds are charged is well established.

questions.stem: Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down at a field of about ___ $\times10^6$ V/m. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: About $3\times10^6$ V/m, or 3 kV per millimeter, for gaps of about a centimeter. It's a rule of thumb that varies with pressure, humidity and gap size.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a cloud-to-ground lightning flash in order.
choices: Charge separates in the cloud, leaving negative charge low down
A faint stepped leader works its way down from the cloud
Upward streamers rise from tall objects on the ground
A streamer meets the leader, completing the channel
A return stroke carries a huge current along the channel
questions.explanation: The leader must approach before streamers rise to meet it, and the return stroke can only flow once the channel is complete. Its current heats the air to about 30,000 K, producing the flash and thunder.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Glow from partial ionization near a sharp point
Faint ionized channel working down from a cloud in jumps
Huge current surging along a completed channel
Uses corona to charge smoke particles and collect them
Belt that carries charge up into a dome
questions.explanation: Corona is partial breakdown at a point; the stepped leader and return stroke are stages of a lightning flash; a precipitator uses corona to clean exhaust gases. The belt describes a Van de Graaff generator.

questions.stem: Which changes would let a charged conducting sphere reach a higher potential before the gas around it breaks down? Select all that apply.
choices: Polishing away bumps and points on its surface
Moving it from sea level to a high mountaintop, where the air is thinner
Using a sphere of larger radius
Attaching a thin metal spike to it
Surrounding it with a gas of higher dielectric strength
questions.explanation: $V_{\max} = E_{\max}R$: a larger radius or a gas that withstands a stronger field both help, and smooth surfaces avoid the strong local fields at bumps. A spike creates a tiny radius with a huge local field, and the thinner air on a mountaintop breaks down more easily.

questions.stem: A lightning flash moves about 5 C through a potential difference of about $2\times10^8$ V. Roughly how much energy is released?
questions.explanation: $E \approx Q\,\Delta V = (5)(2\times10^8) = 1\times10^9$ J, an order-of-magnitude estimate (the actual value is somewhat less, since the potential difference falls as charge flows). $2\times10^8$ J mistakes the voltage for the energy (it leaves out the charge); $4\times10^7$ J and $2.5\times10^{-8}$ J come from dividing one by the other instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A wire connects a higher-potential end (+) to a lower-potential end (−). Name the numbered parts of the picture.

image.alt: A cylindrical wire between a + end on the left and a − end on the right, with electrons drawn inside. Marker 1 is at the circular end face, marker 2 on a bracket under the whole wire, marker 3 on an arrow above the wire pointing from + to −, and marker 4 on an arrow below the wire pointing from − to +.

questions.explanation: Conventional current runs from the high-potential (+) end to the low-potential (−) end, the way positive charges would move. The electrons that actually carry the current in a metal are negative, so they drift the opposite way, from − to +. The end face is the cross-sectional area $A$ and the bracket marks the length $L$, the two dimensions in $R = \rho L/A$.

questions.stem: A steady current of 3.0 A flows in a wire for 2.0 minutes. The charge that passes any point in the wire is ___ C. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $\Delta Q = I\Delta t = (3.0\text{ A})(120\text{ s}) = 360$ C. Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds gives 6.0 C.

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its unit.
questions.explanation: Current is in amperes (C/s); resistance in ohms (V/A); resistivity in ohm-meters, since $\rho = RA/L$ has units Ω·m²/m; power in watts (J/s). Electric bills charge for energy in kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh = (1000 W)(3600 s) = 3.6 MJ. The coulomb is the unit of charge.

questions.stem: Which changes would increase the resistance of a copper wire? Select all that apply.
choices: Using a wire of larger diameter
Replacing it with a nichrome wire of the same length and diameter
questions.explanation: $R = \rho L/A$. A longer wire has larger $L$; a hotter metal has a larger resistivity, because the vibrating atoms scatter electrons more often; nichrome's resistivity is about 60 times copper's. A larger diameter increases $A$ and lowers the resistance.

questions.stem: As the voltage across a filament light bulb is raised, its I–V graph bends over toward the voltage axis: each extra volt adds less current than the one before. This shows that the bulb's resistance
choices: increases as the filament heats up
decreases as the filament heats up
stays constant, as Ohm's law requires
falls to zero at high voltage
questions.explanation: The resistance at any point is $R = V/I$. Along a curve that bends toward the voltage axis, $V$ grows faster than $I$, so $R$ grows. A hotter metal filament has a higher resistivity. Ohm's law with constant $R$ holds only for ohmic parts, and a filament bulb is non-ohmic.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this circuit. (The two meters are drawn as blank circles; tell them apart by how they are connected.)

image.alt: A circuit loop. Marker 1 is beside a two-plate symbol on the left side. Marker 2 is at a lever between two contacts on the top wire. Marker 3 is at a blank meter circle on the top wire, in line with everything else. Marker 4 is beside a zigzag symbol between the top and bottom wires. Marker 5 is beside a second blank meter circle connected across the two ends of the zigzag.

questions.explanation: The long-and-short plates are the battery, the lever is a closed switch, and the zigzag is the resistor. The meter on the top wire is in series, so all the current passes through it: that is the ammeter. The meter connected across the resistor's two ends is in parallel with it: that is the voltmeter.

questions.stem: A 12 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is ___ Ω. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Product over sum: $\dfrac{12 \times 6.0}{12 + 6.0} = \dfrac{72}{18} = 4.0$ Ω, less than the smaller resistor, as it must be. 18 Ω would be the series total.

questions.stem: A 2.0 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 3.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω, all across an ideal 8.0 V battery. Put the resistors in order of the power they dissipate, largest first.
questions.explanation: The pair is $3.0 \parallel 6.0 = 2.0$ Ω, so the total is 4.0 Ω and the battery current is 2.0 A. The 2.0 Ω resistor gets $I^2R = 8.0$ W. The pair has $2.0 \times 2.0 = 4.0$ V across it, so the 3.0 Ω gets $V^2/R = 5.3$ W and the 6.0 Ω gets 2.7 W. In parallel, the smaller resistor takes more current and more power.

questions.stem: A battery with emf $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ supplies current to a resistor. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The terminal voltage is less than the emf while current flows
With the resistor disconnected, the terminal voltage equals the emf
The terminal voltage rises when the battery delivers more current
Some power, $I^2r$, heats the battery itself
questions.explanation: $V_{\text{terminal}} = \mathcal{E} - Ir$: less than $\mathcal{E}$ whenever $I > 0$, equal to it when $I = 0$, and lower (not higher) when the current increases. The internal resistance dissipates $I^2r$ inside the battery, which is why batteries warm up under heavy loads.

questions.stem: Match each statement to what it is based on or what it means.
questions.explanation: Charge can't pile up at a junction (junction rule), and a charge that goes around a loop returns to the same potential, so the gains and drops add to zero (loop rule). Series parts share one path, hence one current; parallel parts connect across the same two points, hence one voltage.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, the three bulbs are identical and the battery is ideal. Bulb A burns out (its filament breaks). What happens to bulbs B and C?

image.alt: A battery on the left, bulb A on the top wire, and bulbs B and C side by side in parallel between the top and bottom wires.

choices: B and C stay the same
B and C both go out
B goes out and C stays lit
questions.explanation: All the battery current passes through A before splitting between B and C. A broken filament opens that single path, so no current reaches B or C and every bulb goes out. Contrast this with removing B or C, which only changes how the current divides.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this RC circuit.

image.alt: A circuit loop. Marker 1 is beside a symbol with one long and one short plate on the left side. Marker 2 is above a two-way lever on the top wire, whose second contact leads straight down to the bottom wire. Marker 3 is above a zigzag on the top wire. Marker 4 is beside a symbol with two equal parallel plates on the right side.

questions.explanation: A battery has one long ($+$) and one short plate; a capacitor has two equal plates. The zigzag is the resistor. The two-way switch either connects the battery (charging) or bypasses it so the capacitor discharges through the resistor.

questions.stem: A 20 kΩ resistor is in series with a 50 μF capacitor. The time constant is ___ s. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $\tau = RC = (20\times10^3\ \Omega)(50\times10^{-6}\text{ F}) = 1.0$ s. Kilohms times microfarads gives milliseconds: $20 \times 50 = 1000$ ms.

questions.stem: A turn-signal flasher uses an RC circuit. Starting with an empty capacitor, put the stages of one cycle in order.
choices: The capacitor charges through the resistor
The capacitor's voltage reaches the threshold
A switch is triggered and discharges the capacitor
The empty capacitor begins charging again
questions.explanation: The capacitor's voltage rises with time constant $RC$ until it crosses a set threshold; that triggers a switch (which also flashes the lamp) and discharges the capacitor, and the cycle starts over. Choosing $R$ and $C$ sets how long each cycle takes.

questions.stem: A 9.0 V battery, a switch and a 3.0 kΩ resistor $R_1$ are in series with a parallel pair: a 6.0 kΩ resistor $R_2$ and an uncharged capacitor. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Just after the switch closes, no current flows through $R_2$
Just after the switch closes, the battery current is 3.0 mA
Long after the switch closes, the capacitor's voltage is 9.0 V
Long after the switch closes, the battery current is 1.0 mA
questions.explanation: Just after: the uncharged capacitor acts as a wire across $R_2$, so $R_2$ carries no current and only $R_1$ limits the battery current, $9.0/3.0\text{ k}\Omega = 3.0$ mA. Long after: the capacitor is a break, so $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in series: $I = 9.0/9.0\text{ k}\Omega = 1.0$ mA. The capacitor shares $R_2$'s voltage, $(1.0\text{ mA})(6.0\text{ k}\Omega) = 6.0$ V, not the full 9.0 V.

questions.stem: A capacitor charges through a resistor from a battery. Match each quantity to how it behaves after the switch closes.
questions.explanation: The capacitor's charge and voltage follow $1 - e^{-t/RC}$, rising toward $C\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{E}$. The current, and with it the resistor's voltage $IR$, follow $e^{-t/RC}$ and decay to zero. The loop rule ties them together: $\mathcal{E} = IR + q/C$ at every instant, with the emf fixed.

questions.stem: In a Wheatstone bridge like the one in the lesson, $R_1 = 150$ Ω and $R_2 = 300$ Ω share one side, and the adjustable $R_3$ shares the other side with the unknown $R_x$. The galvanometer reads zero with $R_3 = 220$ Ω. What is $R_x$?
questions.explanation: Balance: $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_x$, so $R_x = R_2R_3/R_1 = 300 \times 220/150 = 440$ Ω. 110 Ω inverts the ratio ($R_1R_3/R_2$); 205 Ω pairs the resistors wrongly ($R_1R_2/R_3$); 220 Ω assumes $R_x$ simply equals $R_3$, which is true only when $R_1 = R_2$.

questions.stem: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced. The battery is replaced with one of twice the emf. Why does the bridge stay balanced?
choices: The galvanometer's resistance increases to compensate
The internal resistance of the new battery cancels the change
The potentials at P and Q both double, so they stay equal
The current through the unknown resistor stays the same
questions.explanation: Each side of the bridge is a voltage divider, so the potentials at P and Q are both proportional to the emf. If they were equal before, they are still equal after doubling, and no current flows through the galvanometer. The emf cancels out of the balance condition $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_x$. The currents in the resistors do double.

questions.stem: A 9.0 V battery drives a voltage divider: $R_1 = 2.0$ kΩ on top and $R_2 = 1.0$ kΩ below, with output terminals across $R_2$. The Thévenin voltage at the terminals is ___ V. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $V_{\text{th}}$ is the open-circuit voltage, the unloaded divider output: $9.0 \times \dfrac{1.0}{2.0 + 1.0} = 3.0$ V. Using $R_1$ in the numerator gives 6.0 V, the voltage across the top resistor.

questions.stem: For the same divider (9.0 V battery, $R_1 = 2.0$ kΩ, $R_2 = 1.0$ kΩ, terminals across $R_2$), the Thévenin resistance is ___ kΩ. (Give a fraction or 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Replace the ideal battery with a wire. From the terminals, $R_1$ and $R_2$ both connect the same two points, so they are in parallel: $\dfrac{2.0 \times 1.0}{2.0 + 1.0} = \tfrac23 \approx 0.67$ kΩ. Check: $I_{\text{sc}} = 9.0/2.0\text{ k}\Omega = 4.5$ mA and $V_{\text{oc}}/I_{\text{sc}} = 3.0/4.5 = 0.67$ kΩ. Adding them (3.0 kΩ) is the resistance the battery sees, not what the terminals see.

questions.stem: A network has Thévenin equivalent $V_{\text{th}} = 6.0$ V and $R_{\text{th}} = 3.0$ Ω. A 9.0 Ω load is connected to its terminals. What current flows through the load?
questions.explanation: The load is in series with $R_{\text{th}}$: $I = \dfrac{6.0}{3.0 + 9.0} = 0.50$ A (and the load voltage is 4.5 V). 2.0 A ignores the load; 0.67 A ignores $R_{\text{th}}$; 2.7 A treats the two resistances as parallel.

questions.stem: The divider in the picture (12 V battery, 6.0 kΩ and 3.0 kΩ) feeds a load connected across terminals a and b. Which load resistance receives the most power?

image.alt: A 12 V battery with a 6.0 kΩ resistor on the top wire and a 3.0 kΩ resistor across terminals a and b, shown to act like a 4.0 V source in series with 2.0 kΩ.

questions.explanation: Seen from a and b, the divider is a 4.0 V source with internal resistance $R_{\text{th}} = 2.0$ kΩ. Maximum power transfer happens when the load matches it: 2.0 kΩ, which gets 2.0 mW. (3.0 kΩ gets 1.9 mW, 6.0 kΩ gets 1.5 mW, 9.0 kΩ gets 1.2 mW.) Matching the 3.0 kΩ resistor ignores the 6.0 kΩ one, which also contributes to $R_{\text{th}}$.

questions.stem: Two 1.0 MΩ resistors in series form a divider across 10 V. A voltmeter whose resistance is 1.0 MΩ is connected across the lower resistor. What does it read?
questions.explanation: Seen from the lower resistor, $V_{\text{th}} = 5.0$ V and $R_{\text{th}} = 1.0 \parallel 1.0 = 0.50$ MΩ. The meter is the load: $V = 5.0 \times \dfrac{1.0}{1.0 + 0.50} = 3.3$ V. 5.0 V is the reading of an ideal meter; 4.8 V would be a 10 MΩ meter; 6.7 V is the voltage across the upper resistor while the meter is connected.

questions.stem: Thévenin's theorem lets you replace which of these, as seen from two terminals, by one emf in series with one resistance? Select all that apply.
choices: A network of several batteries and resistors
A single battery with internal resistance
A circuit containing a filament bulb whose resistance changes with current
A voltage divider made of two resistors
questions.explanation: The theorem holds for linear circuits: ideal batteries and ohmic resistors, which includes a real battery modeled as an emf with internal resistance, and any divider. A filament bulb is non-ohmic, so the terminal voltage doesn't fall in a straight line as more current is drawn and no single $V_{\text{th}}$ and $R_{\text{th}}$ describe it at every load.

questions.stem: A source has $V_{\text{th}} = 12$ V and $R_{\text{th}} = 4.0$ Ω. Put these loads in order of the power they receive, largest first.
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{V_{\text{th}}^2R}{(R + R_{\text{th}})^2} = \dfrac{144R}{(R + 4)^2}$: 4.0 Ω gets 9.0 W (the matched load), 8.0 Ω gets 8.0 W, 1.0 Ω gets 5.8 W and 32 Ω gets 3.6 W. Power falls off on both sides of the match, more slowly for larger loads.

questions.stem: Match each idea to its description.
choices: Compares an unknown resistance with known ones
One emf in series with one resistance
A meter changes the voltage it measures
Adds the currents from each source acting alone
Makes a battery's internal resistance zero
questions.explanation: A balanced bridge gives $R_x$ from three known resistors. Any linear two-terminal network has a Thévenin equivalent. A voltmeter of finite resistance is a load, so it pulls the voltage down. Superposition adds the currents (not powers) from each battery alone, with the others replaced by wires.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this Wheatstone bridge.

image.alt: A diamond of four resistors. Marker 1 is beside a long-and-short plate symbol in the wire joining the top and bottom corners. Marker 2 is at a blank circle connecting the left and right corners. Marker 3 is beside the upper right resistor, which has an arrow drawn through it.

questions.explanation: The battery drives both sides of the bridge. The galvanometer bridges the two midpoints and shows zero at balance. The resistor with an arrow through it is adjustable; it is varied until the galvanometer reads zero.

questions.stem: Three branches connect junctions A and B. Branch 1: a 10 V battery and a 5.0 Ω resistor. Branch 2: a 5.0 V battery and a 5.0 Ω resistor. Branch 3: a 10 Ω resistor. Both batteries have $+$ toward A. Using superposition, find the current through the 10 Ω resistor.
questions.explanation: 10 V alone: $5.0 \parallel 10 = 3.33$ Ω in series with 5.0 Ω gives 8.33 Ω and 1.2 A; the pair has 4.0 V across it, so the 10 Ω carries 0.40 A. 5.0 V alone: the same structure gives 0.60 A, 2.0 V across the pair, and 0.20 A in the 10 Ω. Both flow from A to B through the 10 Ω, so the total is 0.60 A. (Check: A is at 6.0 V above B, and $6.0/10 = 0.60$ A.) 0.40 A and 0.20 A are the single-source parts; 1.5 A adds the emfs and ignores the other resistors.

questions.stem: A bridge has four 100 Ω resistors and a 10 V battery. A strain gauge in the $R_x$ position rises to 102 Ω. About how large is the voltage between P and Q (measured with a meter that draws no current)?
questions.explanation: P stays at $10 \times 100/200 = 5.000$ V; Q moves to $10 \times 102/202 = 5.050$ V. The difference is about 0.050 V = 50 mV. 0 V assumes the bridge is still balanced; 2.0 V and 0.50 V overstate how much a 2% change moves a divider's output.

questions.stem: An ideal 3.0 V battery drives current through a 1.0 Ω resistor. An ammeter with 0.50 Ω resistance is inserted in series to measure the current. What does it read?
questions.explanation: The meter adds its resistance to the loop: $I = 3.0/(1.0 + 0.50) = 2.0$ A, a third less than the 3.0 A that flows without it. That is the ammeter's version of the loading effect, and why an ammeter needs a resistance much smaller than the rest of its branch. 3.0 A ignores the meter's resistance; 6.0 A uses the meter's resistance alone ($3.0/0.50$); 9.0 A treats the meter as in parallel with the resistor ($1.0 \parallel 0.50 = 0.33$ Ω).

questions.stem: This picture shows the Drude model of a metal carrying a current. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A box filled with a grid of circles marked +. An electron (a circle marked −) sits at the left end of a zigzag path that bounces between the circles. Marker 1 is next to one of the + circles, marker 2 next to the − circle, marker 3 on an arrow above the box pointing right, and marker 4 on an arrow below the box pointing left.

questions.explanation: The fixed lattice of positive ions fills the metal; the free electrons zigzag between collisions. An electron is negative, so the field pushes it opposite to $E$: its net drift (marker 4) is opposite to the field (marker 3), even though each individual path segment points in a random direction.

questions.stem: Aluminum has about $1.8\times10^{29}$ free electrons per m³ and resistivity $2.65\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m. Use the Drude model, $\rho = m/(ne^2\tau)$, to estimate the mean free time.
