questions.explanation: $\tau = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\rho} = \dfrac{9.11\times10^{-31}}{(1.8\times10^{29})(1.602\times10^{-19})^2(2.65\times10^{-8})} = 7.4\times10^{-15}$ s. $1.6\times10^{-14}$ s uses copper's $n$; $1.3\times10^{14}$ is $1/\tau$, from inverting the fraction; $2.5\times10^{-14}$ s is copper's own value.

questions.stem: Silicon doped with phosphorus, whose atoms have five outer electrons, is called ___-type silicon.
questions.explanation: Four of phosphorus's five outer electrons go into bonds with silicon neighbors; the fifth is nearly free, so the extra carriers are negative electrons: n-type. Boron (three outer electrons) makes p-type silicon, with holes.

questions.stem: The electron mobility in copper is about $4.3\times10^{-3}$ m²/(V·s). What is the drift speed in a copper wire with a field of 0.034 V/m inside it?
questions.explanation: Mobility is drift speed per unit field, so $v_d = \mu E = (4.3\times10^{-3})(0.034) = 1.5\times10^{-4}$ m/s, still a fraction of a millimeter per second. $7.3\times10^{-5}$ m/s is the lesson's value for half this field (0.017 V/m); $1.3\times10^{-1}$ divides $\mu$ by $E$ and 7.9 divides $E$ by $\mu$. Only $\mu E$ has units of speed: (m²/(V·s))(V/m) = m/s.

questions.stem: According to the free-electron picture, why does a metal's resistivity increase as it gets hotter?
choices: Heat removes free electrons from the metal
The vibrating ions scatter electrons more often, shortening the mean free time
The metal expands, so its electrons have farther to travel
Hot electrons move more slowly through the lattice
questions.explanation: $\rho = m/(ne^2\tau)$. In a metal, $n$ hardly changes with temperature, but stronger lattice vibrations scatter electrons more often, so $\tau$ shrinks and $\rho$ rises. Thermal expansion changes the wire's size only slightly and isn't the main cause.

questions.stem: Unlike a metal, a pure semiconductor's resistivity falls as its temperature rises. Why?
choices: Its ions stop vibrating when heated
Its mean free time grows with temperature
Its atoms lose their bonds and become a metal
Heat frees many more charge carriers, which outweighs the extra scattering
questions.explanation: In a semiconductor almost all electrons are tied up in bonds, and heat frees more of them (each leaving a hole). The carrier density $n$ rises steeply, which outweighs the shorter mean free time from extra scattering, so $\sigma = ne\mu$ rises and $\rho$ falls. Thermistors use this effect.

questions.stem: Which statements about superconductors are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Below the critical temperature, the resistivity is exactly zero
A current started in a superconducting loop keeps flowing with no battery
Every metal becomes a superconductor if cooled enough
Some superconductors work above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, 77 K
questions.explanation: Superconductivity means exactly zero resistance below a critical temperature, so a loop current persists (for years in experiments). Copper-oxide ceramics such as YBCO superconduct at about 90 K, above 77 K. But not every metal superconducts: copper, silver and gold have not been found to at ordinary pressure; their resistance just levels off at a small value.

questions.stem: Match each element added to silicon with the type of silicon it makes.
questions.explanation: An atom with five outer electrons has one left over after bonding, a free electron: n-type. An atom with three leaves a bond one electron short, a hole: p-type. Silicon itself has four.

questions.stem: Put these materials in order of resistivity at room temperature, lowest first.
questions.explanation: Silver about $1.6\times10^{-8}$, copper $1.7\times10^{-8}$, nichrome about $1\times10^{-6}$, pure silicon about $2\times10^{3}$, and glass $10^{10}$ to $10^{14}$ Ω·m. Silver is the best conductor of all metals at room temperature, just ahead of copper.

questions.stem: A platinum thermometer has $R_0 = 100.0$ Ω at 0 °C and $\alpha = 3.85\times10^{-3}$ per °C. It reads 119.25 Ω. What is the temperature?
questions.explanation: $T = \dfrac{R/R_0 - 1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{0.1925}{3.85\times10^{-3}} = 50$ °C. 19 °C reads the 19.25 Ω change as degrees; 5000 °C divides $\Delta R$ by $\alpha$ without dividing by $R_0$; 119 °C reads the resistance as a temperature.

questions.stem: Which describes the current–voltage behavior of a silicon diode?
choices: A straight line through the origin, like a resistor
Equal current for either polarity, rising steeply above about 0.6 V
Almost no current in reverse; little current forward until about 0.6–0.7 V, then a rapid rise
Large current in reverse, none forward
questions.explanation: A diode is a one-way valve. In reverse bias the carrier-free layer at the p–n junction widens and almost no current flows. Forward, the current stays small until roughly 0.6–0.7 V for silicon, then rises steeply. It is strongly non-ohmic.

questions.stem: A metal has resistivity $2.0\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m at 20 °C and temperature coefficient $4.0\times10^{-3}$ per °C. At 70 °C its resistivity is ___ $\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m. (Give only the number.)
A filament bulb's cold resistance is about one-twelfth of its resistance when lit. At the instant it is switched on, the current is about
questions.explanation: The voltage is the same, so $I = V/R$: one-twelfth the resistance gives twelve times the current, until the filament heats up (within a fraction of a second). 144 squares the ratio, as if the current went as $1/R^2$; at fixed voltage it goes as $1/R$. (The starting power, $V^2/R$, is also about twelve times the running power.)

questions.stem: Silicon is doped with $2.0\times10^{22}$ donor atoms per m³, each freeing one electron, and the electron mobility is 0.12 m²/(V·s). What is its resistivity?
questions.explanation: $\sigma = ne\mu = (2.0\times10^{22})(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.12) = 3.8\times10^{2}$ (Ω·m)⁻¹, so $\rho = 1/\sigma = 2.6\times10^{-3}$ Ω·m. $3.8\times10^{2}$ is the conductivity, not the resistivity; $3.1\times10^{-4}$ leaves out the mobility; $2.6\times10^{3}$ has the wrong sign on the exponent.

cards.back: In a small enough region, gravity can't be told apart from acceleration. It rests on inertial mass = gravitational mass (tested to about 1 part in $10^{15}$).

cards.front: Two consequences of the equivalence principle
cards.back: Light bends in a gravitational field, and clocks lower in a gravitational field run slow.
A clock higher by $h$ runs fast by the fraction $gh/c^2$ (about $1.1\times10^{-16}$ per meter). For large distances: $GM(1/r_{\text{low}} - 1/r_{\text{high}})/c^2$.
Gravity: satellite clock gains about 45.7 μs/day. Speed: loses about 7.2 μs/day. Net: about +38 μs/day, which would be kilometers of position error per day.
Mass and energy curve spacetime, and free objects (and light) follow the straightest paths through it. Tested by light bending (1.75″ at the Sun), Mercury's 43″ per century, clock rates and more.
$r_s = \dfrac{2GM}{c^2}$: about 2.95 km per solar mass (Earth: 9 mm).
The boundary of a black hole; inside it, nothing, not even light, can get out. Far away, a black hole's gravity is the same as any object of equal mass.
$h = \Delta L/L$, about $10^{-21}$ for detected events; a 4 km LIGO arm changes by about $4\times10^{-18}$ m.
14 September 2015, LIGO: black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merged into about 62; about 3 solar masses ($5\times10^{47}$ J) left as gravitational waves.
A laser, a beam splitter, two 4 km arms with end mirrors, and a photodetector. A wave stretches one arm and squeezes the other, changing how the returning beams interfere.
Up, charm, top: $+\tfrac23e$. Down, strange, bottom: $-\tfrac13e$. Antiquarks have the opposite signs.
Proton = uud (charge +1); neutron = udd (charge 0).
Both are hadrons. Baryons: three quarks (proton, neutron), baryon number +1. Mesons: quark + antiquark (pions), baryon number 0.
Electron, muon, tau and their three neutrinos. They don't feel the strong force.
Strong: gluons. Electromagnetic: photon. Weak: W and Z bosons. Gravity: not in the Standard Model (graviton hypothetical).

cards.front: Range of a force from its carrier's mass
cards.back: $R \approx \dfrac{\hbar c}{mc^2}$, with $\hbar c = 197$ MeV·fm. W boson (80.4 GeV): about $2.5\times10^{-18}$ m. Massless carrier: unlimited range.
Particle of the Higgs field, which gives the W, Z, quarks and charged leptons mass. Found at the LHC in 2012, about 125 GeV.

cards.front: Where the proton's mass comes from
cards.back: Mostly strong-interaction energy ($E = mc^2$). Its three quarks add up to only about 9 MeV of its 938 MeV.

cards.front: Making a particle–antiparticle pair in a collider
cards.back: Head-on with equal speeds, all the kinetic energy is available: each beam particle needs at least $mc^2$ to make a pair of mass $m$. A fixed target needs much more.
$p = qBr$, true at any speed with $p = \gamma mv$. For charge $e$: $p$ (GeV/$c$) $= 0.300\,B$ (T) $r$ (m).
Conserve charge, baryon number, lepton number, energy and momentum. A decay at rest also needs more rest energy before than after.
Baryon number: $+\tfrac13$ per quark (+1 per baryon). Lepton number: +1 per lepton, −1 per antilepton. Proton decay ($p \to e^+ + \gamma$) would break baryon number and has never been seen.
$d$ (pc) $= 1/p$ (arcsec). 1 pc = $3.086\times10^{16}$ m = 3.26 light-years.
Objects of known luminosity (Cepheids, type Ia supernovae). Measured intensity $I = L/(4\pi d^2)$ gives the distance.
$z = \dfrac{\lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_{\text{emit}}}{\lambda_{\text{emit}}}$; for $z \ll 1$, $v \approx cz$.
$v = H_0d$ with $H_0 \approx 70$ km/s/Mpc (about 67 or 73 depending on method: the Hubble tension).
$1/H_0 \approx 14$ billion years for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc. The measured age of the universe is 13.8 billion years.
Expansion (Hubble's law), the 2.725 K cosmic microwave background, and the light elements (about 25% helium by mass).
Released about 380 000 years after the start, at about 3000 K; stretched about 1100 times to a 2.725 K blackbody peaking near 1 mm.

cards.front: Galaxy mass from a rotation speed
cards.back: $M(r) = \dfrac{v^2r}{G}$. Flat rotation curves mean $M(r)$ keeps growing with $r$: dark matter.
$\rho_c = \dfrac{3H^2}{8\pi G} \approx 9\times10^{-27}$ kg/m³ today, about five or six hydrogen atoms per cubic meter.
About 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy (Planck, 2018).
$T_s = T_e\left(\dfrac{2}{2 - \varepsilon}\right)^{1/4}$; the layer is at $T_a = T_s/2^{1/4}$. $\varepsilon \approx 0.78$ gives Earth's 288 K.
Earth radiates to space from about 5 km up, where it is near $T_e = 255$ K; temperature falls about 6.5 K/km, so the surface is about 288 K.

cards.front: Why more CO₂ warms even with a saturated band
cards.back: It raises the emission height to colder air, so the planet radiates less until it warms; the band's edges also absorb more.
$\Delta F \approx 5.35\ln(C/C_0)$ W/m²: 3.7 W/m² per doubling; about 2.2 W/m² from 280 to 420 ppm.
$\Delta T_0 \approx \Delta F/(4\sigma T_e^3)$, that is $\Delta F$ divided by about 3.7 W/(m²·K): about 1 to 1.2 K per CO₂ doubling.
$\Delta T = \dfrac{\Delta T_0}{1 - f}$ for $0 \le f < 1$. $f \approx 0.6$ gives about 3 K per doubling; small changes in $f$ near 1 give large changes in $\Delta T$.
Water vapor and ice–albedo amplify; clouds are the largest uncertainty (probably slightly amplifying); lapse-rate changes and the extra infrared from a warmer planet reduce warming.
Eventual warming per CO₂ doubling: best estimate about 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C (IPCC, 2021). Arrhenius (1896) estimated 5 to 6 °C; Manabe and Wetherald (1967) about 2.3 °C.
Absolute: the ± value in the measurement's unit (0.2 g). Fractional: absolute ÷ value, no unit (0.2/52.4 = 0.38%).
Round the uncertainty to 1 significant figure (2 if it starts with 1), then round the value to the same decimal place: $9.80 \pm 0.06$.
Random: scatter in both directions; averaging reduces it. Systematic: every reading shifted the same way; averaging does nothing, so check instruments and use another method.
$s_{\bar x} = s/\sqrt n$, where $s$ is the sample standard deviation (divide by $n - 1$). Four times the readings halve it.

cards.front: Uncertainty of a sum or difference
cards.back: Combine absolute uncertainties: $\delta q = \sqrt{(\delta x)^2 + (\delta y)^2}$ for independent random errors (never subtract them).

cards.front: Uncertainty of a product or quotient
cards.back: Combine fractional uncertainties: $\dfrac{\delta q}{|q|} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\delta x}{x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\delta y}{y}\right)^2}$.
$\dfrac{\delta q}{|q|} = |n|\dfrac{\delta x}{|x|}$: squaring doubles the fractional uncertainty (add directly, not in quadrature).
Quadrature ($\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$) for independent random errors; direct addition ($a + b$) gives a worst-case upper bound.
Rule of thumb: yes if their difference is less than about $\sqrt{\delta_1^2 + \delta_2^2}$; more than 2–3 times that is a real discrepancy.
$\dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{accepted}|}{\text{accepted}} \times 100\%$ (divide by the accepted value).
$\hat A = \vec A/A$; its components are the direction cosines, and $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.

cards.front: Scalar and vector projection of $\vec B$ onto $\vec A$
cards.back: Scalar: $\vec A\cdot\vec B/A$. Vector: $(\vec A\cdot\vec B/A^2)\,\vec A$. The rest of $\vec B$ is perpendicular to $\vec A$.
$\vec A\times\vec B = (A_yB_z - A_zB_y)\hat\imath + (A_zB_x - A_xB_z)\hat\jmath + (A_xB_y - A_yB_x)\hat k$. Check: perpendicular to both.

Forward around $\hat\imath \to \hat\jmath \to \hat k \to \hat\imath$: $\hat\imath\times\hat\jmath = \hat k$, $\hat\jmath\times\hat k = \hat\imath$, $\hat k\times\hat\imath = \hat\jmath$. Backward gives a minus sign; any vector crossed with itself is 0.
The area of the parallelogram on $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ ($AB\sin\phi$); the triangle is half of it.
$|\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C)|$ = volume of the box on $\vec A$, $\vec B$, $\vec C$; zero means the three are coplanar. Cycling the order keeps its value; swapping two flips its sign.

cards.front: Components in rotated axes (rotated by α counterclockwise)
cards.back: $A_{x'} = A_x\cos\alpha + A_y\sin\alpha$, $A_{y'} = -A_x\sin\alpha + A_y\cos\alpha$. Magnitudes and dot products don't change.

cards.front: Two checks for a computed cross product $\vec C = \vec A\times\vec B$
cards.back: $\vec C\cdot\vec A = 0$ and $\vec C\cdot\vec B = 0$, and $|\vec C| = AB\sin\phi$.

cards.front: Work done by a force along a displacement, in projection terms
cards.back: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d = F_\parallel\,d$, where $F_\parallel = \vec F\cdot\vec d/d$ is the component of the force along the motion.

cards.front: Helical motion in a uniform field
cards.back: Split $\vec v$: $v_\parallel$ along $\vec B$ is unchanged; $v_\perp$ circles with $r = mv_\perp/(|q|B)$. Pitch $p = v_\parallel\cdot 2\pi m/(|q|B)$.

cards.front: Pitch of a helix: which velocity component?
cards.back: The component along the field, $v_\parallel = v\cos\theta$. The radius uses $v_\perp = v\sin\theta$.

cards.front: Why a cyclotron can use one fixed frequency
cards.back: The orbit period $2\pi m/(|q|B)$ does not depend on speed (until near light speed), so ions always return to the gap after half a period.
$K_{\max} = \dfrac{q^2B^2R^2}{2m}$: set $r = R$ (dee radius) in $r = mv/(|q|B)$. Independent of the gap voltage.
Relativity: near light speed the orbit period grows, so ions fall out of step. Synchrocyclotrons and synchrotrons adjust frequency or field.

cards.front: e/m from crossed fields then a circle
cards.back: Undeflected: $v = E/B$. Then with $E$ off, $r = mv/(eB)$, so $e/m = E/(B^2r)$.

Measured the charge-to-mass ratio of cathode-ray particles (electrons) with electric and magnetic deflections; far larger than any ion's, and with a charge about the same as a hydrogen ion's, the particles had to be far lighter than atoms.
Where field lines converge the field is stronger and pushes spiraling particles back; a field strong at both ends traps them (Van Allen belts).
$V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$, from balancing $qE_H = qv_dB$ with $I = nqv_d(wt)$. $t$ = thickness along $\vec B$.

cards.front: What the sign of the Hall voltage tells you
cards.back: The sign of the charge carriers: positive and negative carriers (moving opposite ways for the same current) are pushed to the same edge.
$V_H \propto 1/n$; semiconductors have millions of times fewer carriers than metals, so the Hall voltage is much larger (microvolts in copper).
Resistor: in phase. Inductor: current lags voltage by $90^\circ$. Capacitor: current leads by $90^\circ$ ("ELI the ICE man").
$V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = IZ$; $V_L$ and $V_C$ point opposite ways, so each can exceed the source voltage.
$\tan\varphi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$; positive (current lags) if inductive, negative (current leads) if capacitive, 0 at resonance.
$P_{\text{avg}} = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\varphi = I_{\text{rms}}^2R$; power factor $\cos\varphi = R/Z$. Ideal L and C use no average power.
Inductive loads (motors) make current lag; adding capacitors (leading current) raises the power factor, cutting the current and wiring losses for the same real power.
$P_{\text{loss}} = (P/V)^2R_{\text{line}}$: ten times the voltage gives one hundredth of the loss.
Transformers step AC voltage up for low-loss transmission and down for safe use; 1880s–90s DC could not be transformed.
Use $I^2R_{\text{line}}$ with the line current, not $V^2/R_{\text{line}}$ with the transmission voltage (that voltage is across the load, not the wire).
Three AC voltages $120^\circ$ apart; balanced currents sum to zero and total power is steady, so big motors run smoothly.
$\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$; reflected light is completely polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence (parallel to the surface)
The reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular: $\theta_B + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$

cards.front: Why p light doesn't reflect at Brewster's angle
cards.back: The electrons that would send it oscillate along the reflected direction, and an oscillating charge does not radiate along its own line of motion

cards.front: Brewster's angle vs critical angle (going to lower n)
cards.back: Brewster: $\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$; critical: $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$. Brewster's angle is always smaller.
Scattering by particles much smaller than $\lambda$; intensity $\propto 1/\lambda^4$ (blue sky, red sunsets)
Strongest about $90^\circ$ from the Sun (typically 70–80% at most)
Two indices ($n_o$, $n_e$) for two perpendicular polarizations; calcite: 1.658 and 1.486 at 589 nm
$t = \dfrac{\lambda}{4|n_e - n_o|}$; turns linear light at $45^\circ$ into circular light
Delays one component by $\lambda/2$; rotates linear polarization at $\alpha$ to the fast axis by $2\alpha$
Liquid crystal between crossed polarizers: twisted (no voltage) rotates polarization $90^\circ$, bright; voltage untwists it, dark
$2t = m\lambda$, with a dark line where the plates touch
$\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda L}{2D}$ ($D$ = spacer thickness at distance $L$)
A height step of $\lambda/2$ in the air gap
Gap $t \approx r^2/(2R)$; dark rings at $r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R}$, dark center, rings crowd together outward
$N = \dfrac{2\Delta d}{\lambda}$: one fringe per $\lambda/2$ of mirror motion
$N = \dfrac{2L(n - 1)}{\lambda}$ as the cell fills
$\ell_c \approx \lambda^2/\Delta\lambda$: about 1 μm for white light; fringes vanish for longer path differences
Expected about 0.4 fringe of shift from an ether wind; saw almost none. Explained by special relativity.
Michelson interferometers with 4 km arms; detected gravitational waves in 2015 from arm changes of a few times $10^{-18}$ m
$(\Delta s)^2 = (c\,\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x)^2$; the same in every inertial frame.
$(\Delta s)^2 > 0$: a clock can go between the events (fixed order). $= 0$: only light connects them. $< 0$: no signal connects them; order depends on the frame.
For a straight trip between timelike events, the traveler's clock reads $\Delta s/c = \sqrt{(\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x/c)^2}$.
Position across, time up; with years and light-years, light moves at 45°. Objects at rest: vertical worldlines; moving objects: steeper than 45°.
The 45° light lines through an event. Inside the upper half: possible future; lower half: possible past; outside: no causal connection.
$x' = \gamma(x - vt)$, $t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^2)$. Reduces to $x' = x - vt$, $t' = t$ at low speed.
Events simultaneous in S and $\Delta x$ apart are $\Delta t' = -\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^2$ apart in S′: the one farther along the direction of motion happens first.
The stay-at-home twin's worldline is straight (inertial); the traveler's bends. Between two events the straight worldline has the longest proper time.
Earth: 10 yr. Traveler: each leg $\sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3$ yr, total 6 yr.
Receding: $f = f_0\sqrt{(1 - \beta)/(1 + \beta)}$; approaching: $f = f_0\sqrt{(1 + \beta)/(1 - \beta)}$. At $\beta = 0.8$ the factors are 1/3 and 3.
$Q = (\sum m_{\text{before}} - \sum m_{\text{after}})c^2$ with atomic masses; 1 u = 931.5 MeV. $Q > 0$ releases energy.
$K_\alpha = Q\,(A - 4)/A$ for a parent of mass number $A$ at rest (momentum is shared equally, energy inversely to mass).
$Q = [M(\text{parent}) - M(\text{daughter}) - 2m_e]c^2$, with $2m_ec^2 = 1.022$ MeV. For alpha and beta-minus the electrons cancel.
Beta electrons have a continuous range of energies up to Q; a third, unseen particle (Pauli, 1930) carries off the rest. Detected 1956 (Cowan and Reines).
Electron + positron at rest → two 0.511 MeV photons in opposite directions (used in PET). A photon of at least 1.022 MeV can make an electron–positron pair near a nucleus.
$K_{\text{th}} = -Q(1 + m_{\text{projectile}}/m_{\text{target}})$ for $Q < 0$; more than $|Q|$ because the products must keep the momentum.
U-235 fission: about 200 MeV each, $8\times10^{13}$ J/kg. D–T fusion: 17.6 MeV (14.1 MeV to the neutron), about $3.4\times10^{14}$ J/kg. Gasoline: about $4.6\times10^{7}$ J/kg.
Average fissions caused by the neutrons of one fission. $k < 1$ dies out; $k = 1$ steady (critical); $k > 1$ grows. Moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb them.
Gray: absorbed dose, 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Sievert: equivalent dose $H = w_RD$ ($w_R$ = 1 gamma/beta, 2 protons, 20 alpha).
Average U.S. resident: about 6 mSv per year, roughly half natural. Chest X-ray: about 0.1 mSv or less. Several Sv at once: severe radiation sickness, often fatal untreated.
Protection rules assume risk proportional to dose with no safe level. A cautious assumption; its accuracy at a few mSv is debated.

cards.front: Setting up a chase or meeting problem
cards.back: One origin, one positive direction, one clock for both objects; they meet where $x_A(t) = x_B(t)$. Check each root against the assumptions.

cards.front: Chaser from rest (constant $a$) catching a constant-speed object that is beside it at the start
cards.back: It catches up when its speed is twice the other's: equal distances in equal times mean equal average velocities.

cards.front: When is the gap in a chase largest?
cards.back: When the two speeds are equal (where the lines cross on a $v$–$t$ graph).
Ride with the constant-velocity object: the other moves at the difference of the velocities, with the same acceleration.
Solve the one-phase model; if the speed at the catch exceeds the top speed, split at the moment top speed is reached and close the remaining gap at the speed difference.
$d = vt_r + \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$: reaction distance grows with $v$, braking distance with $v^2$.

cards.front: Minimum braking to avoid a slower vehicle ahead (gap $D$, reaction $t_r$)
cards.back: $a = \dfrac{(\Delta v)^2}{2(D - \Delta v\,t_r)}$, with $\Delta v$ the closing speed.
Where a driver can neither stop (the distance to the line is less than $vt_r + v^2/(2a)$) nor clear the intersection before red; gone if $vt_y - W \ge vt_r + v^2/(2a)$.

cards.front: Angle to hit a target $(x, y)$ at speed $v_0$
cards.back: $A\tan^2\theta - x\tan\theta + (y + A) = 0$, with $A = \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$; discriminant positive: two angles, zero: one, negative: none.
$y = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2g} - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$: the edge of what speed $v_0$ can reach.
$x = \dfrac{v_0}{g}\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$ at $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}}$ (below 45°).

cards.front: Best launch up a slope of angle $\alpha$
cards.back: $\theta = 45^\circ + \alpha/2$ from the horizontal; $d_{\max} = \dfrac{v_0^2}{g(1 + \sin\alpha)}$ along the slope.

cards.front: Aiming straight at a target released at the instant of firing
cards.back: It hits (if it arrives before the target lands): both fall $\tfrac12gt^2$ below their gravity-free paths.
From rest at constant $a$, successive equal intervals cover $1 : 3 : 5 : 7$, because $d_n = \tfrac12a\tau^2(2n - 1)$.
A gentle ramp lowers the acceleration but keeps it constant, so motion slow enough to time with a water clock follows the same law as free fall.
Plot $h$ against $t^2$: a straight line through the origin with slope $g/2$.
$t = \sqrt{2d/g}$; 18 cm gives about 0.19 s.
About 9.78 m/s² at the equator to 9.83 m/s² at the poles; standard gravity is defined as 9.80665 m/s².

cards.front: Evidence that heavy and light bodies fall together
cards.back: Galileo's tied-stones argument; Stevin and de Groot's lead balls (Delft, 1586); the Apollo 15 hammer and feather (1971).
Reported by Viviani long afterward; historians doubt it happened as told.
Use $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ in $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}$ to get a quadratic in $\tan\theta$.

cards.front: Low shot vs lob to the same target
cards.back: The lob (higher angle) has the smaller horizontal speed, so it stays up longer and lands more steeply.

cards.front: When do the two hitting angles add to 90°?
cards.back: Only when the target is at launch height (level ground): $\sin 2\theta$ takes equal values at $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$.

cards.front: Range up a slope at launch angle $\theta$ (slope $\alpha$)
cards.back: $x = \dfrac{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta(\tan\theta - \tan\alpha)}{g}$ horizontally; $d = x/\cos\alpha$ along the slope.

cards.front: Highest point reachable straight above the launcher
cards.back: $v_0^2/(2g)$, the top of the safety parabola (a straight-up throw).
If heavier fell faster, a light stone tied to a heavy one would both slow it and (as a heavier pair) speed it up: a contradiction.

cards.front: Acceleration of a ball rolling down a ramp
cards.back: Constant but less than $g\sin\theta$ (solid ball: $\tfrac57g\sin\theta$), so distance still grows as $t^2$.
Assume no slipping, find the friction needed for the shared acceleration, then check it is at most $\mu_s n$. If not, the surfaces slip: use $\mu_k n$ against the relative sliding.
Opposite to the relative sliding (or tendency to slide) of the two surfaces. It can point in the direction of motion, as on a block riding an accelerating cart.
Static friction exactly at its limit, $f_s = \mu_s n$: use it for "largest force" or "steepest angle" questions.

cards.front: Stacked blocks, push F on the bottom block, frictionless floor: largest F before slipping
cards.back: $F_{\max} = (m + M)\mu_s g$; the top block's largest acceleration is $\mu_s g$.
Top block: $a = \mu_k g$ (friction forward). Bottom block: $a = (F - \mu_k mg)/M$.

cards.front: Ramp block $m_1$ tied over a pulley to hanging $m_2$: range that stays at rest
cards.back: $m_1(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta) \le m_2 \le m_1(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta)$

cards.front: Banked curve with friction: fastest speed
cards.back: $v_{\max}^2 = rg\dfrac{\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}$ (friction points down the bank).

cards.front: Banked curve with friction: slowest speed
cards.back: $v_{\min}^2 = rg\dfrac{\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta}$; no minimum if $\mu_s \ge \tan\theta$.

cards.front: Maximum acceleration of an all-wheel-drive car on level ground
cards.back: About $\mu_s g$: static friction from the road on the tires is what pushes the car forward.

cards.front: Fictitious force in a frame accelerating at $\vec A$
cards.back: $-m\vec A$ on every object, opposite the frame's acceleration; no third-law partner.
$\vec g_{\text{eff}} = \vec g - \vec A$. Elevator accelerating up: $g + A$; free fall: 0.

cards.front: Pendulum in a car accelerating at A
cards.back: Hangs backward at $\tan\theta = A/g$, with $T = m\sqrt{g^2 + A^2}$.
Fictitious force $m\omega^2 r$ outward, felt only in a rotating frame; never on the same diagram as a centripetal acceleration.

cards.front: Artificial gravity in a station of radius r
cards.back: $\omega = \sqrt{g/r}$, period $2\pi\sqrt{r/g}$; "down" is outward.
Acts on objects moving in a rotating frame, perpendicular to the velocity, size $2m\omega v$ (motion perpendicular to the axis); deflects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Nearly. Its rotation gives a centrifugal term of only $\omega^2R_E \approx 0.034$ m/s² at the equator, and a Coriolis effect that matters only for large, long-lasting motions.

cards.front: Inertial frame vs accelerating frame in one problem
cards.back: Pick one. Inertial: real forces only, $\sum\vec F = m\vec a$. Accelerating: add $-m\vec A$ and use accelerations measured in that frame. Both give the same physical answer.
$T = uR$: exhaust speed (relative to the rocket) times mass flow rate.
Thrust must exceed weight, $T > mg$; then $a = T/m - g$, which grows as propellant is burned.
$\Delta v = u\ln(m_0/m_f)$ in free space; from adding $u\,\Delta m/m$ over many small steps.

cards.front: Mass ratio for a given delta-v
cards.back: $m_0/m_f = e^{\Delta v/u}$: each extra $u$ of delta-v multiplies the needed ratio by $e \approx 2.72$.

cards.front: What does a rocket's delta-v depend on (free space)?
cards.back: Only the exhaust speed and the mass ratio, not the thrust or how fast the propellant is burned.

cards.front: Can a rocket go faster than its exhaust speed?
cards.back: Yes: when $m_0/m_f > e$, $\Delta v > u$. The exhaust speed is measured relative to the rocket.
Dropping empty tanks and engines means later burns push less dead mass, so the same propellant gives more delta-v.

cards.front: Sand onto a conveyor belt at rate R, speed v
cards.back: Force $Rv$, power $Rv^2$; the sand gains only $\tfrac12Rv^2$ of kinetic energy per second, and the other half becomes heat.

cards.front: Rain falling into a coasting cart
cards.back: Horizontal momentum is conserved: $m_0v_0 = (m_0 + \Delta m)v$, so the cart slows down.

cards.front: Sand leaking straight down out of a moving cart
cards.back: The cart's speed does not change: the sand leaves with the cart's own velocity.
$v_{2f} - v_{1f} = e(v_{1i} - v_{2i})$; solve it together with momentum conservation.

cards.front: Kinetic energy lost in a collision with restitution e
cards.back: $K_{\text{lost}} = (1 - e^2)K_{\text{rel}}$, with $K_{\text{rel}} = \tfrac12\mu(v_{1i} - v_{2i})^2$.
Total momentum zero; each velocity reverses and is multiplied by $e$; every kinetic energy is multiplied by $e^2$.

cards.front: Measuring e with a bouncing ball
cards.back: $e = \sqrt{h_{\text{after}}/h_{\text{before}}}$; each bounce reaches $e^2$ times the previous height.

cards.front: Total distance of a bouncing ball
cards.back: $D = h_0\dfrac{1 + e^2}{1 - e^2}$; total time $t_0\dfrac{1 + e}{1 - e}$ with $t_0 = \sqrt{2h_0/g}$.

cards.front: Light ball off a heavy wall moving toward it at V
cards.back: $v_{\text{out}} = e(v + V) + V$; elastic: $v + 2V$.
Elastic in the planet's frame (same speed in and out); in the Sun's frame up to $2U$ is gained (head-on limit), paid for by the planet's kinetic energy.

cards.front: Does e = 0.5 mean half the kinetic energy is lost?
cards.back: No. Speeds in the CM frame are halved, so energies there drop to a quarter: 75% of $K_{\text{rel}}$ is lost.

cards.front: Static friction on an object rolling down a slope
cards.back: Points up the slope; $f = \dfrac{c}{1 + c}Mg\sin\theta$ with $I_{\text{cm}} = cMR^2$

cards.front: Condition to roll without slipping down a slope
cards.back: $\mu_s \ge \dfrac{c}{1 + c}\tan\theta$

cards.front: Sliding ball with no spin on a level floor
cards.back: Kinetic friction slows $v$ and raises $R\omega$ until $v = R\omega$; final speed $v_0/(1 + c)$ ($\tfrac57v_0$ for a solid sphere)

cards.front: Why angular momentum about a point on the floor is conserved for a skidding ball
cards.back: Friction acts along the floor (zero torque about it); gravity and the normal force cancel

cards.front: Energy lost while a solid sphere skids into rolling
cards.back: $\tfrac{c}{1 + c} = \tfrac27$ of its initial kinetic energy
$\tau\Delta t = \Delta L$

cards.front: Center of percussion of a uniform rod pivoted at one end
cards.back: $\tfrac23L$ from the pivot: a blow there gives no impulse at the pivot

cards.front: Angular momentum of a rolling body about a point on the ground
cards.back: $L = Mv_{\text{cm}}R + I_{\text{cm}}\omega$
$\Omega = \dfrac{\tau}{L} = \dfrac{Mgr}{I\omega}$ (fast spin); faster spin means slower precession
Force along the member: pure tension or compression
Supports first; then $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$ at a joint with at most 2 unknowns; assume tension, negative means compression

cards.front: A-frame rafter force (load P at peak)
cards.back: $F = \dfrac{P}{2\sin\theta}$ compression; tie tension $F\cos\theta$

cards.front: Chords of a bridge truss loaded in the middle
cards.back: Top chord in compression, bottom chord in tension
Stands if $\tan\theta \ge \dfrac{1}{2\mu_s}$; wall force $N_w = \dfrac{W}{2\tan\theta}$
Tips first if $w/h < \mu_s$ (tips at $\tan\theta = w/h$); slides first if $\mu_s < w/h$

cards.front: Box pushed horizontally at height H
cards.back: Slides at $\mu_smg$, tips at $\dfrac{mgw}{2H}$; tips first above $H = \dfrac{w}{2\mu_s}$

cards.front: Semimajor axis from periapsis and apoapsis
cards.back: $a = \tfrac12(r_p + r_a)$ (distances from the center of the central body)
$r_pv_p = r_av_a$ (angular momentum)
$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$, set by the semimajor axis alone
$v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac2r - \dfrac1a\right)$
Burn forward onto an ellipse with $a_t = \tfrac12(r_1 + r_2)$, coast half of it, burn forward again; trip time $\pi\sqrt{a_t^3/GM}$

cards.front: Speed after moving to a higher circular orbit
cards.back: Lower than before ($v = \sqrt{GM/r}$), though both burns sped the craft up
$M = \dfrac{4\pi^2a^3}{GT^2}$ (mass of the central body)
$M_1 + M_2 = a^3/T^2$ with $a$ in AU, $T$ in years, masses in solar masses
The higher she climbs, the more floor friction is needed (her weight's lever arm about the foot grows); the top rungs are the risky ones

cards.front: Velocity-proportional damping: amplitude and energy over time
cards.back: Amplitude $\propto e^{-bt/(2m)}$, energy $\propto e^{-bt/m}$: the same fraction is lost every cycle.
$\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - (b/2m)^2}$; light damping barely changes the frequency.
$b_c = 2\sqrt{mk} = 2m\omega_0$ (equivalently $Q = \tfrac12$)

cards.front: Underdamped vs critically damped vs overdamped
cards.back: Under: oscillates with shrinking amplitude. Critical: fastest return with no overshoot. Over: creeps back slowly, no overshoot.
$Q = m\omega_0/b = \sqrt{mk}/b$; large $Q$ means light damping.
Energy lost per cycle $\approx 2\pi/Q$ of the stored energy; amplitude falls to about 4% ($e^{-\pi}$) after $Q$ cycles.

cards.front: Time for a damped amplitude to halve
Steady-state amplitude of a driven oscillator
cards.back: $A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}$; it oscillates at the driving frequency $\omega$.

cards.front: Driven oscillator: slow, resonant, fast driving
cards.back: Slow: $A \approx F_0/k$. At $\omega_0$: $A = F_0/(b\omega_0) = QF_0/k$. Fast: $A \approx F_0/(m\omega^2)$, small.
$\Delta\omega \approx \omega_0/Q$: high-$Q$ oscillators respond to a narrow band of frequencies.

cards.front: Phase of a driven oscillator at resonance
cards.back: Displacement lags the force by $90^\circ$, so velocity is in step with the force and the force always does positive work.
A periodic wave of frequency $f_1$ is a sum of sine waves at $f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \ldots$ (harmonics).
Odd harmonics only, amplitudes $\propto 1/n$.
All harmonics, amplitudes $\propto 1/n$.
Mainly the spectrum (which harmonics, how strong), plus how the sound starts and decays.
A tone at 600, 800, 1000 Hz is heard at 200 Hz: pitch follows the repetition rate $f_1$, even with no energy at $f_1$.
Harmonics with a node at the pluck point are not excited; plucking the middle removes the even harmonics.
Octave 2:1, perfect fifth 3:2, perfect fourth 4:3, major third 5:4.
Ratio $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$; $f = 440\cdot2^{n/12}$ Hz for $n$ semitones from A4.
$1200\log_2(f_2/f_1)$; 100 cents per semitone, 1200 per octave.
Fifth: 700 vs 702.0 cents (2 cents narrow). Major third: 400 vs 386.3 cents (about 14 cents wide).
String: $Z = \mu v = \sqrt{F_T\mu}$. Sound: $Z = \rho v$ (acoustic impedance, rayl).

cards.front: Fraction of intensity reflected at a boundary (straight on)
cards.back: $R = \left(\dfrac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$, $T = 1 - R$; equal impedances give no reflection.

cards.front: String pulse reflected from a heavier string
cards.back: Inverted, with amplitude ratio $(Z_1 - Z_2)/(Z_1 + Z_2)$; fixed end is $-1$, free end $+1$.
Air–tissue impedance mismatch reflects about 99.9%; gel (near water's $Z$) lets the sound in.
Soft tissue boundaries: about 1% or less. Soft tissue–bone: about 40%. Tissue–air: nearly 100%.
$d = vt/2$ (round trip), with $v = 1540$ m/s assumed for soft tissue.
Higher $f$: shorter $\lambda$, finer detail, but more absorption (about 0.5 dB/cm/MHz), so less depth.
$\Delta f \approx \dfrac{2fu\cos\theta}{v}$; the factor 2 is because the moving reflector shifts the wave twice.
A layer $\lambda/4$ thick with $Z = \sqrt{Z_1Z_2}$ cancels reflection at one frequency.
$F = \eta Av/d$: area $A$, relative speed $v$, layer thickness $d$; viscosity $\eta$ in Pa·s
Water $1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s; air $1.8\times10^{-5}$ Pa·s. Liquids get thinner when warmed; gases get slightly thicker.
$Q = \dfrac{\pi R^4\Delta P}{8\eta L}$ (laminar flow only); halving $R$ cuts $Q$ to 1/16
$R_{\text{flow}} = \dfrac{8\eta L}{\pi R^4}$, with $\Delta P = QR_{\text{flow}}$; pipes in series add, like resistors
$\text{Re} = \rho vD/\eta$ ($D$ = diameter). Pipe flow: laminar below about 2000, turbulent above about 4000
$F_D = 6\pi\eta rv$ for small, slow spheres; $v_T = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{9\eta}$, so $v_T \propto r^2$
$\gamma$ = force per unit length along a surface (N/m) = energy per area (J/m²); water about 0.073 N/m

cards.front: Pressure inside a drop and a bubble
cards.back: Drop: $\Delta P = 2\gamma/r$. Soap bubble (two surfaces): $\Delta P = 4\gamma/r$
$h = \dfrac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{\rho gr}$; water on glass rises (concave meniscus), mercury is depressed (convex)
$e = W_{\text{net}}/Q_{\text{in}}$: divide by the heat taken in (positive $Q$ only), not the net heat
$E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32nRT = \tfrac32PV$, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32\Delta(PV)$; and 1 kPa·L = 1 J
$e = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}}$ with compression ratio $r = V_{\max}/V_{\min}$; $r = 10$, $\gamma = 1.4$ gives 60%
$T_2 = T_1r^{\gamma - 1}$ (kelvins); air at 300 K compressed 18:1 reaches about 950 K

cards.front: Four strokes of a gasoline engine
cards.back: Intake, compression, power, exhaust
Gasoline: spark ignition, $r$ about 9–14, limited by knock. Diesel: compresses air alone, compression ignition, $r$ about 15–22, more efficient overall

cards.front: Why real cycles fall short of Carnot
cards.back: Heat enters and leaves across large temperature differences (creating entropy), plus friction and heat leaks; a rectangular PV cycle reaches far less than Carnot between its extreme temperatures
Self-ignition of a gasoline engine's fuel-air mixture before the spark, from too much compression heating; it limits the compression ratio
Compressor (work in) → condenser (releases $Q_H$) → expansion valve (pressure drops) → evaporator (absorbs $Q_C$); $Q_H = Q_C + W$
$R = L/k$ per unit area (m²·K/W); layers in series add: $Q/t = A\Delta T/R_{\text{total}}$
1 ft²·°F·h/Btu = 0.176 m²·K/W (R-13 is about 2.3 m²·K/W)
$P_{\text{net}} = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_s^4)$, kelvins; not $(T - T_s)^4$
$S = L_{\text{Sun}}/(4\pi d^2) \approx 1361$ W/m² at Earth; falls as $1/d^2$
$T_e = \left[\dfrac{(1 - a)S}{4\sigma}\right]^{1/4}$; Earth: 255 K with albedo 0.30

cards.front: Why the 4 in the planet formula
cards.back: Sunlight is absorbed over the disk $\pi R^2$ but infrared leaves the whole sphere $4\pi R^2$
Atmosphere passes visible sunlight but absorbs surface infrared and sends some back down; Earth's surface (288 K) is 33 K above $T_e$
$T_s = 2^{1/4}T_e \approx 303$ K for Earth: a simplified teaching model that overestimates the real 288 K
$\vec p = q\vec d$, from $-$ to $+$; units C·m. Water: $p \approx 6.2\times10^{-30}$ C·m.

cards.front: Torque on a dipole in a uniform field
cards.back: $\tau = pE\sin\theta$; it turns $\vec p$ toward $\vec E$. Net force is zero.
$U = -pE\cos\theta$: $-pE$ aligned (stable), $+pE$ anti-aligned (unstable).

cards.front: Work to flip a dipole from aligned to anti-aligned
cards.back: $W = 2pE$

cards.front: Why polar molecules align only slightly
cards.back: Thermal energy $k_BT$ is far larger than $pE$ even in strong fields; the small bias still gives a large $\kappa$.

cards.front: How a dielectric reduces the field
cards.back: Lined-up dipoles leave bound charge at the slab faces, opposite to the nearby plates; field inside becomes $E_0/\kappa$.

cards.front: Oil drop balanced in a field
cards.back: $qV/d = mg$, so $q = mgd/V$. For a negative drop, the top plate is positive.

cards.front: Finding e from a set of drop charges

cards.front: Conductivity with one kind of carrier

cards.front: SI base units for length, mass, time, current

cards.front: Prefixes: G, M, k, c, m, μ, n

cards.back: Keep as many significant figures as the input with the fewest.

cards.front: Sig figs rule for adding and subtracting
cards.back: Keep as many decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places.
Zeros between nonzero digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point. Leading zeros never are.

cards.front: What can dimensional analysis catch, and what can't it?
cards.back: It catches wrong powers and missing quantities, but not wrong pure-number factors like 2 or π.

cards.front: Arguments of sin, exp, ln must be…
cards.back: Dimensionless.

cards.front: When does an object speed up?
cards.back: When $v$ and $a$ have the same sign. Opposite signs: it slows down.
Velocity.

cards.front: Slope of a v–t graph; area under a v–t graph
cards.back: Slope = acceleration; signed area = displacement.

cards.back: The slope of the tangent line at that instant (rise over run between two points on the tangent).
$v = v_0 + at$

cards.back: $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$
$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$

cards.front: Stopping distance from speed $v_0$ at deceleration $a$
cards.back: $d = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}$ (proportional to $v_0^2$).

Positive: converging lens, concave mirror. Negative: diverging lens, convex mirror.
$d_i > 0$ real, $< 0$ virtual; $m > 0$ upright, $< 0$ inverted.

cards.front: Converging lens with object inside f
cards.back: Virtual, upright, enlarged image (magnifying glass).
$P = 1/f$ in diopters; nearsighted eyes need negative power.
$d\sin\theta = m\lambda$; spacing $\Delta y = \lambda L/d$ (small angles)
$a\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $m = \pm1, \pm2, \ldots$
$d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ with $d$ = 1/(lines per meter); highest $m \le d/\lambda$
$\theta_{\min} = 1.22\lambda/D$

cards.front: Thin film in air (one phase flip): bright reflection
cards.back: $2nt = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$
Physics is the same in all inertial frames; light speed $c$ is the same for all observers.
$\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$
$\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0$ ($\Delta t_0$ = proper time)
$L = L_0/\gamma$ (along the motion only)
$u = \dfrac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2}$
$p = \gamma mv$, $E = \gamma mc^2$, $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$, $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$
$E = hf = hc/\lambda$; $hc = 1240$ eV·nm
$K_{\max} = hf - \phi$; threshold $f_0 = \phi/h$

cards.front: Brighter light in the photoelectric effect
cards.back: More electrons, same maximum energy.
$hf = 13.6\text{ eV}\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2} - \dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$
$\lambda = h/p = h/(mv)$
$\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/(4\pi)$
$Z$ protons, $A$ nucleons, $N = A - Z$ neutrons
$E_B = \Delta m\,c^2$; 1 u ↔ 931.5 MeV

cards.front: Why do fission and fusion both release energy?
cards.back: Both move toward the peak of binding energy per nucleon near iron-56.
$T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda = 0.693/\lambda$; activity $R = \lambda N$
$\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K: hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.
$\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$, $h/(m_ec) = 2.43$ pm; largest (4.86 pm) for $\theta = 180^\circ$.
Stress $= F/A$ (Pa); strain $= \Delta L/L_0$ (no units).
$\dfrac{F}{A} = Y\dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0}$, so $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL_0}{YA}$; steel $Y \approx 2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa.
$k = YA/L_0$
$\dfrac{F}{A} = S\dfrac{\Delta x}{L_0}$, with $A$ the face the force lies along; fluids have no shear modulus.
$\Delta P = -B\dfrac{\Delta V}{V_0}$; water $B \approx 2.2\times10^{9}$ Pa.
Elastic limit: largest stress with full spring-back. Ultimate strength: greatest stress before failure.

cards.front: Normal near point and far point
cards.back: Near point 25 cm (by convention); far point infinity.
Diverging lens with $f = -(\text{far point})$, so $P < 0$.
Converging lens that images an object at 25 cm at the eye's near point: $\dfrac1f = \dfrac1{25} - \dfrac1{\text{near point}}$ (cm).
$M = \theta/\theta_0$, with $\theta_0 = h/(25\text{ cm})$ the best unaided angle.
$M = 25\text{ cm}/f$ (image at infinity); $M = 1 + 25\text{ cm}/f$ (image at near point).
$M = m_{\text{obj}}M_{\text{eye}} = \left(-\dfrac{d_i}{d_o}\right)\dfrac{25\text{ cm}}{f_e}$
$M = -f_o/f_e$; lenses about $f_o + f_e$ apart.
More light gathered (area) and finer resolution ($\theta_{\min} \propto \lambda/D$), not more magnification.
$n = 1, 2, \ldots$; $l = 0$ to $n - 1$ (s, p, d, f); $m_l = -l$ to $l$; $m_s = \pm\tfrac12$.
No two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers; at most 2 electrons per orbital.

cards.front: Electrons per subshell and per shell
cards.back: Subshell $2(2l + 1)$: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14. Shell $2n^2$.
$\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{hc}{eV}$ (depends only on the tube voltage)
$E_{K\alpha} \approx 10.2\text{ eV}\,(Z - 1)^2$
A matching photon triggers emission of an identical photon (same energy, direction, phase).
Population inversion (via a metastable level and pumping) plus mirrors to build up stimulated emission.

glossary.definition: Einstein's 1915 theory of gravity: mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects with no other forces on them follow the straightest paths through it. For weak fields and slow speeds it reduces to Newton's law of gravity.
The principle that, in a small enough region, being in a gravitational field cannot be told apart from being in an accelerating frame. It rests on the equality of inertial and gravitational mass.
The drop in frequency (rise in wavelength) of light climbing out of a gravitational field: by about $gh/c^2$ over a height $h$ near Earth. First measured in the laboratory by Pound and Rebka in 1959.
The slowing of clocks lower in a gravitational field. Near Earth a clock higher by $h$ runs fast by the fraction $gh/c^2$; GPS satellite clocks gain about 45.7 μs per day from it.
The bending of light from a distant source by the mass of a galaxy or cluster in front of it, which can brighten, distort or multiply the image. Used to map mass that can't be seen.
A region where spacetime is curved so strongly that nothing, not even light, can escape. Its boundary is the event horizon.
The boundary of a black hole, the point of no return: inside it nothing can get out. For a non-rotating black hole it is a sphere with the Schwarzschild radius.
The radius of a non-rotating black hole's event horizon, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$: about 2.95 km per solar mass.

A ripple in spacetime, produced by accelerating masses, that travels at the speed of light and stretches and squeezes lengths across its direction of travel by a tiny fraction $h = \Delta L/L$. First detected by LIGO in 2015.
The theory of the known fundamental particles (six quarks, six leptons, the gauge bosons and the Higgs boson) and of the strong, electromagnetic and weak interactions. Gravity is not part of it.

A particle with the same mass as another but opposite charge (and opposite baryon and lepton numbers). The positron is the electron's antiparticle; antiparticles are written with a bar, such as $\bar\nu$.
The conversion of a particle and its antiparticle into other particles, often photons. An electron and positron at rest give two 0.511 MeV photons moving in opposite directions.

The creation of a particle and its antiparticle from energy, for example a photon becoming an electron and a positron near a nucleus. The photon needs at least $2mc^2$ (1.022 MeV for an electron pair).
Any particle made of quarks and held together by the strong force: baryons (three quarks) and mesons (quark and antiquark).

A fundamental matter particle that feels the strong force and has fractional charge: up ($+\tfrac23e$), down ($-\tfrac13e$), and the heavier charm, strange, top and bottom. Quarks are always confined in hadrons.
A hadron made of three quarks, such as the proton (uud) and the neutron (udd). Baryons have baryon number +1.
A hadron made of a quark and an antiquark, such as the pion $\pi^+$ (u and anti-d). Mesons have baryon number 0.
The fact that quarks are never found alone: pulling them apart creates new quark–antiquark pairs, so they always come out bound into hadrons.

One of the three families of matter particles in the Standard Model, each heavier than the last: (up, down, electron, electron neutrino), (charm, strange, muon, muon neutrino), (top, bottom, tau, tau neutrino).
A fundamental matter particle that does not feel the strong force: the electron, muon and tau, and their three neutrinos.
A particle, such as a quark, lepton, proton or neutron, that obeys the Pauli exclusion principle. The matter particles of the Standard Model are fermions.
A particle that does not obey the Pauli exclusion principle, such as the photon, gluon, W and Z, and Higgs boson.
A particle whose exchange produces a force: the gluon (strong), the photon (electromagnetic), and the W and Z bosons (weak).
The massless gauge boson that carries the strong force between quarks.
The heavy gauge bosons (rest energies about 80 GeV and 91 GeV) that carry the weak force; their large mass gives the weak force its short range, about $10^{-18}$ m.
The particle of the Higgs field, which gives the W and Z bosons, quarks and charged leptons their masses. Discovered at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012, with a rest energy of about 125 GeV.
A conserved count: $+\tfrac13$ per quark, so +1 per baryon, −1 per antibaryon, and 0 for mesons, leptons and photons.

A conserved count: +1 for each lepton, −1 for each antilepton, 0 for everything else. Electron-, muon- and tau-type lepton numbers are each conserved in reactions (only neutrino oscillations mix them).
The study of the universe as a whole: its size, structure, history and contents.
Half the yearly back-and-forth shift of a nearby star against distant ones: the angle the Earth–Sun distance makes as seen from the star. Distance in parsecs is $1/p$ with $p$ in arcseconds.
The distance at which a star's parallax angle is one arcsecond: $3.086\times10^{16}$ m, or 3.26 light-years. A megaparsec (Mpc) is a million parsecs.
The distance light travels in one year, $9.46\times10^{15}$ m. It is a distance, not a time.
An astronomical object of known luminosity, such as a Cepheid variable star or a type Ia supernova; comparing its known power with its measured brightness, $I = L/(4\pi d^2)$, gives its distance.
The fractional increase in wavelength of light from a distant source, $z = (\lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_{\text{emit}})/\lambda_{\text{emit}}$. For small $z$ the recession speed is $v \approx cz$.
The proportionality between a galaxy's recession speed and its distance, $v = H_0d$, found by Lemaître (1927) and Hubble (1929). It reflects the expansion of space.
The constant $H_0$ in Hubble's law, about 70 km/s per megaparsec. Different methods give about 67 and about 73, a disagreement called the Hubble tension.

The time $1/H_0$, about 14 billion years for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc: how long ago all galaxies would have been together if they had always moved at today's speeds. The measured age of the universe is 13.8 billion years.
The theory that the universe was once extremely hot and dense and has been expanding and cooling for about 13.8 billion years. It was not an explosion from a point: space itself expands everywhere.
Blackbody radiation at 2.725 K arriving from every direction, released about 380 000 years after the Big Bang when the universe became transparent, and stretched into microwaves by the expansion.
A graph of the orbital speed of stars and gas against distance from a galaxy's center. Observed curves stay roughly flat far beyond the visible stars, evidence for dark matter.

Matter that has gravity but emits and absorbs no light, inferred from rotation curves, cluster motions, gravitational lensing and the CMB. It makes up about 27% of the universe; what it is remains unknown.
The unknown cause of the accelerating expansion of the universe, discovered in 1998 with distant supernovae. It makes up about 68% of the universe's energy density.

The density $\rho_c = 3H^2/(8\pi G)$ at which the universe's geometry is flat, about $9\times10^{-27}$ kg/m³ (five or six hydrogen atoms per cubic meter) today. The measured total density is very close to it.
A change in the net energy flow into the climate system, in W/m², before temperatures respond. For CO₂, about $5.35\ln(C/C_0)$ W/m², or 3.7 W/m² per doubling.

A change caused by warming or cooling that alters the energy balance further. Amplifying (positive) feedbacks include water vapor and ice–albedo; the extra infrared a warmer planet radiates is stabilizing.
The eventual global warming caused by doubling the CO₂ concentration, once the climate has settled: best estimate about 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C (IPCC, 2021).
The rate at which air temperature falls with height in the lower atmosphere, about 6.5 K per kilometer on average.
The average height from which Earth's infrared escapes to space, about 5 km, where the temperature is near the equilibrium temperature of 255 K. Adding greenhouse gases raises it.
The ± part of a measurement, in the same unit as the value: in $52.4 \pm 0.2$ g it is 0.2 g. It gives the range in which the true value plausibly lies.
The absolute uncertainty divided by the value, $\delta x/|x|$; it has no unit. Products, quotients and powers combine fractional uncertainties.
The fractional uncertainty written as a percentage: $0.2/52.4 = 0.38\%$.
Error that pushes repeated readings up and down unpredictably (reaction time, jitter). It shows up as scatter and is reduced by averaging.

Error that shifts every reading the same way (a zero offset, a miscalibrated instrument, a consistent misreading). Averaging does not reduce it; checking against standards or another method reveals it.
A measure of the spread of readings: $s = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2/(n-1)}$, roughly the typical distance of one reading from the mean.
The uncertainty of an average of $n$ readings, $s/\sqrt n$. Four times as many readings halve it; it does not reduce systematic error.

Finding the uncertainty of a calculated result from the uncertainties of the measured inputs: absolute uncertainties combine for sums and differences, fractional ones for products, quotients and powers.
Combining independent random uncertainties as the square root of the sum of their squares, $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, like the sides of a right triangle. Adding them directly gives an upper bound instead.
$\dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{accepted}|}{\text{accepted}} \times 100\%$: how far a result is from a trusted reference value.
A line through a plotted point covering its best value ± uncertainty; a good fit passes through most error bars.
The cosines of the angles a vector makes with the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes: $A_x/A$, $A_y/A$, $A_z/A$. They are the components of the unit vector $\hat A$, and their squares add to 1.
The component of $\vec B$ along $\vec A$: $\vec A\cdot\vec B/A = B\cos\phi$. Negative when $\vec B$ leans against $\vec A$.
The part of $\vec B$ that lies along $\vec A$: $(\vec A\cdot\vec B/A^2)\,\vec A$. What remains of $\vec B$ is perpendicular to $\vec A$.
$\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C)$. Its absolute value is the volume of the box (parallelepiped) with edges $\vec A$, $\vec B$, $\vec C$; it is zero when the three vectors lie in one plane.
A magnetic field that is strong at the ends and weaker in between; charged particles spiraling along it are pushed back from the strong regions and can be trapped (as in Earth's Van Allen belts).

A particle accelerator in which ions circle in a uniform magnetic field inside two hollow dees and are pushed across the gap between them by a voltage alternating at the cyclotron frequency; exit energy $q^2B^2R^2/(2m)$.
One of the two hollow D-shaped electrodes of a cyclotron; inside it the ions feel only the magnetic field and move in a semicircle.
A particle's charge divided by its mass, which sets how sharply fields bend it; for the electron, $e/m = 1.76\times10^{11}$ C/kg, first measured by J. J. Thomson in 1897.
The sideways voltage that appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, because the field pushes the moving charge carriers to one edge.
The voltage across a current-carrying strip in a perpendicular magnetic field: $V_H = IB/(nqt)$, with $t$ the thickness along the field. Its sign shows the carriers' sign.
The number of mobile charges per cubic meter in a material, $n$ (about $8.5\times10^{28}$ m⁻³ for copper, far less in semiconductors).
An arrow representing a sinusoidal quantity: its length is the amplitude (or rms value) and its angle is the phase. Phasors of out-of-step voltages are added as vectors.
In an AC circuit, the angle $\varphi$ by which the current lags the source voltage, with $\tan\varphi = (X_L - X_C)/R$ for a series RLC circuit (negative when the current leads).
The factor $\cos\varphi = R/Z$ in $P_{\text{avg}} = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\varphi$; 1 for a pure resistance, 0 for a pure inductance or capacitance.
Power wasted as heat in transmission wires, $I^2R_{\text{line}} = (P/V)^2R_{\text{line}}$; raising the transmission voltage reduces it.
High-voltage direct current: DC transmission at hundreds of kilovolts, made possible by modern power electronics, used for some very long lines and undersea cables.
AC supplied as three voltages a third of a cycle ($120^\circ$) apart; for a balanced load the currents add to zero and the total power is steady.
The plane containing the incoming ray and the normal to the surface. Light polarized perpendicular to it is called s-polarized; light polarized in it, p-polarized.
The angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence: $\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$. The reflected and refracted rays are then perpendicular.
Scattering of light by particles much smaller than its wavelength, such as air molecules; its strength goes as $1/\lambda^4$, which makes the sky blue and sunsets red.
Having two indices of refraction for two perpendicular polarizations, as calcite and quartz do; a ray entering such a crystal can split into two.

A slice of birefringent material that delays one polarization by a quarter wavelength relative to the other, $t = \lambda/(4|n_e - n_o|)$; it turns linear light at $45^\circ$ to its axes into circular light.
A slice of birefringent material that delays one polarization by half a wavelength; it rotates linear polarization at angle $\alpha$ to its fast axis by $2\alpha$.
Polarization in which the electric field keeps a constant size but rotates, its tip tracing a circle, as the wave passes; made from two equal perpendicular components a quarter cycle out of step.
An instrument that splits light into two paths and recombines it, so that a change in path length shows up as moving fringes; one fringe per wavelength of path change.
A glass plate polished flat to a small fraction of a wavelength, laid on a surface to test it; the fringes in the air gap are contour lines $\lambda/2$ apart in height.
Circular interference fringes in the air gap between a curved lens and a flat plate; in reflection the dark rings are at $r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R}$, with a dark center.
A partly reflecting plate that reflects about half of a light beam and transmits the rest, splitting it into two beams (or recombining two beams).
The path difference over which light stays in step well enough to interfere; roughly $\lambda^2/\Delta\lambda$, about 1 μm for white light and centimeters or more for lasers.
Space and time combined into one four-dimensional setting for events. Observers in relative motion divide it into space and time differently but agree on the spacetime interval.
A graph with position across and time up (often in years and light-years, so light moves at 45°). Events are points; the histories of objects are lines.
Something that happens at one place at one instant, such as a flash or a clock tick: a single point on a spacetime diagram.
The path of an object through spacetime. An object at rest has a vertical worldline; a moving object's worldline tilts, always steeper than light's 45° line.
The light paths through an event. Events inside its upper half are the event's possible future, inside its lower half its possible past; events outside can't be connected to it by any signal.
$(\Delta s)^2 = (c\,\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x)^2$ between two events: the same value in every inertial frame, even though $\Delta t$ and $\Delta x$ differ.
Two events with $(\Delta s)^2 > 0$: a clock can travel from one to the other, reading proper time $\Delta s/c$, and every observer agrees on their order.
Two events with $(\Delta s)^2 = 0$: only a light signal can connect them.
Two events with $(\Delta s)^2 < 0$: too far apart for any signal to connect them. Some frame sees them as simultaneous, and observers can disagree about their order.
The puzzle that a twin who travels away and back ages less, although each twin sees the other moving. It is resolved because only the stay-at-home twin stays in one inertial frame.
The change in frequency of light from a moving source: $f = f_0\sqrt{(1 - \beta)/(1 + \beta)}$ when receding and the inverse when approaching, with $\beta = v/c$.
The rest energy a nuclear reaction or decay converts: $Q = (\sum m_{\text{before}} - \sum m_{\text{after}})c^2$. Positive Q releases energy; negative Q needs energy supplied.

A neutral, nearly massless particle emitted in beta decay (an antineutrino in beta-minus, a neutrino in beta-plus). Proposed by Pauli in 1930 to explain the continuous beta spectrum; detected in 1956.
The antiparticle of the electron: the same mass, charge $+e$. Emitted in beta-plus decay; it annihilates with an electron.
The least kinetic energy a projectile needs to cause a reaction with $Q < 0$: $K_{\text{th}} = -Q(1 + m_{\text{projectile}}/m_{\text{target}})$ at nonrelativistic speeds.
A self-sustaining series of fissions, in which neutrons released by each fission cause further fissions.
The average number of neutrons from one fission that cause another, $k$. $k < 1$: the reaction dies out; $k = 1$: steady (critical); $k > 1$: it grows.
Material in a reactor, such as water or graphite, whose light nuclei slow fast neutrons by collisions so that uranium-235 captures them more readily.
A rod of neutron-absorbing material (boron or cadmium) moved into or out of a reactor core to keep the multiplication factor at 1.
The electric repulsion two nuclei must overcome to get within range of the strong force, roughly 0.5 MeV for hydrogen isotopes; it is why fusion needs extreme temperatures (and quantum tunneling).
Radiation energy deposited per kilogram of tissue, $D = E/m$, measured in grays (1 Gy = 1 J/kg).
SI unit of absorbed dose: 1 Gy = 1 joule absorbed per kilogram.
Absorbed dose multiplied by the radiation weighting factor, $H = w_RD$, measured in sieverts; it accounts for how damaging each type of radiation is.
The factor $w_R$ converting grays to sieverts: 1 for gamma rays, X-rays and electrons, 2 for protons, 20 for alpha particles, 2.5 to 20 for neutrons (ICRP 2007).
SI unit of equivalent dose (and effective dose). A typical U.S. resident receives about 6 mSv a year.
The assumption, used to set radiation protection limits, that cancer risk is proportional to dose with no completely safe level. Whether it holds at very low doses is debated.
In a problem with two moving objects, a time at which their positions are equal, found by solving $x_A(t) = x_B(t)$ with one shared origin and clock.
The time between seeing a hazard and starting to act (for a driver, until the brakes begin to work). The vehicle keeps its speed during it.
The distance covered during the reaction time at constant speed, $v t_r$; proportional to speed.
The distance covered while braking to a stop at constant deceleration $a$: $v^2/(2a)$; proportional to the square of the speed.
Reaction distance plus braking distance: $d = v t_r + v^2/(2a)$.

A stretch of road before a traffic light where, when the light turns yellow, a driver can neither stop before the line nor clear the intersection before red. It disappears if the yellow is long enough.
The higher of the two launch angles that hit the same target at the same speed: a longer, steeper flight than the low direct shot.

The boundary of the points a projectile can reach at launch speed $v_0$: $y = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2g} - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$. Every trajectory touches it once; points below it can be hit at two angles, points above it not at all.
For constant acceleration from rest, the distances covered in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio $1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : \dots$ (Galileo).
A light beam and detector that record the instant an object blocks the beam; used to time motion precisely.
The defined value $g_n = 9.80665$ m/s² used for calculations and units; the measured free-fall acceleration varies from about 9.78 m/s² (equator) to 9.83 m/s² (poles).
The point at which surfaces are just about to slip, where static friction is at its limit, $f_s = \mu_s n$; used to find a largest force, steepest angle or fastest speed.
The speed at which a banked curve needs no friction: $v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.
A force added in an accelerating frame so that Newton's second law works there: $-m\vec A$ for a frame with acceleration $\vec A$. No object exerts it, so it has no third-law partner.
A reference frame that accelerates or rotates relative to an inertial frame; Newton's laws hold in it only if fictitious forces are added.
The apparent gravitational field in an accelerating frame, $\vec g_{\text{eff}} = \vec g - \vec A$; a hanging string lines up with it.
The fictitious force in a rotating frame, $m\omega^2 r = mv^2/r$, pointing directly away from the rotation axis. It does not exist in an inertial frame.

The fictitious force on an object moving relative to a rotating frame, perpendicular to its velocity (size $2m\omega v$ for motion perpendicular to the axis); on Earth it deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
A quick sketch with one bar for each form of energy (kinetic, potential, thermal) at a chosen moment; with only conservative forces working, the bars always add to the same total.
The forward force on a rocket from expelling gas: $T = uR$, the exhaust speed times the mass flow rate.
The mass of propellant an engine expels per second, $R = \Delta m/\Delta t$ (kg/s).
The speed $u$ of a rocket's exhaust gas measured relative to the rocket; for chemical rockets roughly 2.5 to 4.5 km/s.
In free space, the speed a rocket gains by burning propellant: $\Delta v = u\ln(m_0/m_f)$, where $u$ is the exhaust speed and $m_0/m_f$ the mass ratio.
A rocket's mass at the start of a burn divided by its mass at the end, $m_0/m_f$. Reaching a delta-v of $\Delta v$ needs $m_0/m_f = e^{\Delta v/u}$.
The total change in speed a rocket or spacecraft can produce (or a maneuver requires); mission planners add up a delta-v budget.
Building a rocket as a stack of stages and dropping each one when its propellant is used up, so later stages don't have to accelerate empty tanks and engines.
The reference frame moving with a system's center of mass, in which the total momentum is zero. In a collision each velocity in this frame reverses and is multiplied by $e$.

The kinetic energy of two objects measured in their center-of-mass frame, $K_{\text{rel}} = \tfrac12\mu(v_1 - v_2)^2$; the only part a collision can turn into other forms, losing $(1 - e^2)K_{\text{rel}}$.
For two objects, $\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$: smaller than either mass and close to the smaller one when the masses are very different.

A flyby that changes a spacecraft's speed in the Sun's frame by passing close to a moving planet; the encounter is elastic in the planet's frame, and the planet's motion supplies (or absorbs) the energy.
A torque times the time it acts, $\tau\Delta t$; it equals the change in angular momentum it produces, $\Delta L$.

The point on a pivoted object where a sharp blow causes no impulsive force at the pivot; for a uniform rod pivoted at one end it is $\tfrac23$ of the way from the pivot. Related to the "sweet spot" of a bat.
How fast a gyroscope's spin axis swings around: $\Omega = \tau/L = Mgr/(I\omega)$ for a fast-spinning gyroscope with a horizontal axle.
A framework of straight members joined at their ends by pins, loaded at the joints, as in roof frames and bridges; each member is in pure tension or compression.
A light member acted on by forces at only two points; in equilibrium the two forces are equal, opposite and along the line joining those points.
The state of a member that is being pushed on at both ends, so it pushes outward on what it is attached to; the opposite of tension.
The point of an orbit closest to the central body (called perigee for Earth orbits and perihelion for orbits around the Sun).
The point of an orbit farthest from the central body (apogee for Earth orbits, aphelion for orbits around the Sun).
Half the long axis of an elliptical orbit, $a = \tfrac12(r_p + r_a)$; it sets the orbit's energy and period.
The total mechanical energy of a body in orbit, $E = -GMm/(2a)$; it depends only on the semimajor axis.
The speed of an orbiting body at distance $r$: $v^2 = GM(2/r - 1/a)$, from energy conservation.
A two-burn move between two circular orbits in the same plane along half of an ellipse that touches both; usually the most fuel-efficient two-burn transfer.
An orbit used to travel from one orbit to another, such as the half ellipse of a Hohmann transfer.
The constant $b$ in a velocity-proportional damping force $F = -bv$; units kg/s (N·s/m).
Damped lightly enough ($b < 2\sqrt{mk}$, $Q > \tfrac12$) that the system still oscillates, with shrinking amplitude.
Damped with $b = 2\sqrt{mk}$ ($Q = \tfrac12$): the system returns to equilibrium as fast as possible without overshooting.
Damped so heavily ($b > 2\sqrt{mk}$) that the system creeps back to equilibrium without oscillating, more slowly than with critical damping.

A dimensionless measure of how lightly an oscillator is damped: $Q = m\omega_0/b$. About $2\pi/Q$ of the stored energy is lost per cycle, and a driven oscillator's resonance peak is about $Q$ times the static response, with width about $\omega_0/Q$.
The frequency of a periodic force applied to an oscillator, set by whatever is pushing; in steady state the oscillator moves at this frequency.
For a driven oscillator, the motion left after the natural oscillation has died away: oscillation at the driving frequency with constant amplitude.
A damped auxiliary mass on a spring or pendulum, tuned to a structure's natural frequency, that swings out of step with the structure and absorbs its vibration energy.
Any periodic wave of frequency $f_1$ can be written as a sum of sine waves with frequencies $f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \ldots$ (its harmonics).
Breaking a wave into its sine-wave (harmonic) components, or, as Fourier synthesis, building a wave by adding them.
The set of frequencies in a wave and their amplitudes, often drawn as a bar graph of amplitude against frequency.
The quality that distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness, set mainly by the spectrum of harmonics and also by how the sound starts and decays.
The pitch relationship between two notes, set by the ratio of their frequencies: octave 2:1, perfect fifth 3:2, perfect fourth 4:3, major third 5:4.
The tuning system that divides the octave into 12 equal frequency ratios of $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$; a note $n$ semitones from A4 has $f = 440\cdot2^{n/12}$ Hz.
One twelfth of an octave in equal temperament: a frequency ratio of $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$, or 100 cents.
A unit for small pitch differences: 1200 cents per octave, 100 per equal-tempered semitone; cents $= 1200\log_2(f_2/f_1)$.
How hard a medium is to set moving by a wave; for a string $Z = \mu v = \sqrt{F_T\mu}$. Waves reflect where the impedance changes.
For sound, $Z = \rho v$ (density times sound speed), in kg/(m²·s) or rayl. The fraction of intensity reflected straight on at a boundary is $R = \left(\frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$.
A device that converts one form of energy to another; an ultrasound transducer uses a piezoelectric crystal to turn electrical pulses into sound and returning echoes back into electrical signals.
A layer of intermediate impedance between two media (ideally a quarter-wavelength thick with $Z = \sqrt{Z_1Z_2}$) that reduces reflection at their boundary.
Smooth flow in which a fluid moves in layers that slide past each other without mixing; in a pipe the speed profile is a parabola.
Irregular flow full of swirling eddies that mix the fluid; it needs a larger pressure difference than laminar flow for the same flow rate.
The dimensionless number $\text{Re} = \rho vD/\eta$, comparing a flow's inertia with its viscous friction; pipe flow is usually laminar below about 2000 and turbulent above about 4000.
Flow rate of a viscous fluid in laminar flow through a pipe: $Q = \pi R^4\Delta P/(8\eta L)$.
The force per unit length (equivalently, energy per unit area) of a liquid's surface, symbol $\gamma$; about 0.073 N/m for water at 20°C.
The rise (or fall) of a liquid in a narrow tube caused by surface tension: $h = 2\gamma\cos\theta/(\rho gr)$.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube: concave for a liquid that wets the wall (water on glass), convex for one that does not (mercury).
The angle at which a liquid surface meets a solid wall; below 90° the liquid wets the wall and rises in a narrow tube, above 90° it is pushed down.
An engine whose pistons repeat intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes.
The idealized gasoline-engine cycle of two adiabats and two constant-volume steps; its efficiency is $1 - 1/r^{\gamma - 1}$.
The ratio $r = V_{\max}/V_{\min}$ of an engine cylinder's largest volume to its smallest.
Uncontrolled self-ignition of the fuel-air mixture in a gasoline engine before the spark, caused by too much compression heating; it limits the compression ratio.

The idealized diesel-engine cycle: adiabatic compression of air alone, heat added at roughly constant pressure as fuel is injected and ignites, adiabatic expansion, and heat rejected at constant volume.
The refrigeration cycle used in most refrigerators and heat pumps: compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator, using the latent heat of the refrigerant.
The working fluid of a refrigerator or heat pump, chosen to boil at a low temperature so it can absorb heat by evaporating and release it by condensing.
For a layer, $R = L/k$ (m²·K/W per unit area); resistances of layers that heat crosses one after another add, and $Q/t = A\Delta T/R_{\text{total}}$.
A number $e$ from 0 to 1 giving how well a surface radiates (and absorbs) thermal radiation compared with a perfect blackbody, as in $P = e\sigma AT^4$.
The intensity of sunlight at Earth's average distance from the Sun, on a surface facing the Sun above the atmosphere: about 1361 W/m².
The fraction of incoming sunlight a planet or surface reflects; about 0.30 for Earth as a whole.
The temperature at which a planet radiates energy as fast as it absorbs sunlight: $T_e = [(1 - a)S/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}$, about 255 K for Earth.
A gas, such as water vapor or carbon dioxide, that lets most sunlight through but absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation.
The warming of a planet's surface above its equilibrium temperature because the atmosphere absorbs the surface's infrared radiation and sends part of it back down.
For charges $+q$ and $-q$ a distance $d$ apart, the vector $\vec p = q\vec d$, pointing from the negative to the positive charge; units C·m.
A molecule with a permanent electric dipole moment because its positive and negative charge centers do not coincide, such as water.
A dipole created when an external field pushes an object's positive and negative charges slightly apart; for modest fields its moment is proportional to the field.
Charge that appears at the surfaces of a polarized dielectric because the ends of its lined-up dipoles are not cancelled there; it partly cancels the applied field inside.
The drag on a small sphere of radius $r$ moving slowly at speed $v$ through a fluid of viscosity $\eta$: $F = 6\pi\eta rv$.
A runaway multiplication of free electrons in a gas: each electron, accelerated by a strong field, ionizes molecules and frees more electrons.
The sudden failure of an insulator in a strong field, when it becomes conducting (in a gas, by an electron avalanche) and a spark or arc passes.
The largest electric field a material can withstand before breakdown; about $3\times10^6$ V/m for dry air at sea level.
A machine that uses a moving belt to carry charge continuously into a large hollow metal dome, building up a high voltage.
A faint glowing discharge where the field near a sharp or thin conductor is strong enough to ionize the air in a thin layer, but not to make a full spark.
A pollution-control device that charges smoke or dust particles with a corona discharge and collects them on charged plates.
The faint channel of ionized air that works its way down from a thundercloud in jumps of tens of meters before a lightning strike.
The bright main surge of current (typically tens of kiloamperes) along a lightning channel once the leader has connected with the ground.
A pointed metal rod on a structure, connected to ground by heavy conductors, that gives a lightning strike a safe path to ground.
A circuit made only of ideal sources and ohmic resistors, so that currents and voltages are proportional to the emfs. Thévenin's theorem and superposition apply to linear circuits.
Two resistors in series across a source; the voltage across $R_2$ is $\mathcal{E}R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$ when nothing else is connected to it.

Two voltage dividers across the same battery with a galvanometer between their midpoints. When the galvanometer reads zero, $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_x$, which gives an unknown resistance from three known ones.
A very sensitive current meter. In a bridge it is used as a null detector, showing when no current flows.
